Cambodia's trade with ASEAN, EU posts double-digit growth during Jan.-Sept.

2026-10-12
14:43:58 CST
15:43:58 KST

PHNOM PENH, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia's trade volume with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the European Union (EU) rose steadily in the first nine months of 2026, driven by stronger supply chain linkages and regional trade pacts, according to a Ministry of Commerce report on Monday.
Total trade with the two blocs reached 19.29 billion U.S. dollars between January and September, up from 16.68 billion dollars during the same period last year.
The report highlighted that the kingdom's trade with fellow ASEAN member states grew 16 percent to 14.26 billion dollars. Meanwhile, its trade exchange with the EU rose 14 percent, reaching 5.03 billion dollars.
During the nine-month period, Cambodia's total global trade volume reached 58.48 billion dollars. Within this framework, the ASEAN market accounted for 24 percent of the total trade, while the EU market represented 8.6 percent.
Penn Sovicheat, a secretary of state and spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce, said that Cambodia's primary exports to both regions included garments, textiles, footwear, travel goods, bags, bicycles, car tires, electronic components, vehicle parts, and agricultural produce.
On the import side, the kingdom primarily brought in garment raw materials, construction supplies, vehicles, oil and gas, electronic goods, fertilizers, cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, supplements, fruits, and food items.
Thong Mengdavid, deputy director of the China-ASEAN Studies Center at the Cambodia University of Technology and Science, said the double-digit growth reflected Cambodia's deepening regional economic integration and successful trade diversification.
"This upward trajectory is driven by deepening supply chain integration, expanding cross-border commerce, and the trade advantages yielded by regional frameworks like the ASEAN Economic Community (AEC) and the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP)," he told Xinhua. ■

Sri Lanka financial system remains stable despite global risks: central bank
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:43:45 CST
15:43:45 KST

COLOMBO, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Sri Lanka's financial system remains stable despite heightened global risks, while banking sector credit grew 23.6 percent year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, up from 11.4 percent a year earlier amid strong private sector demand, the Central Bank of Sri Lanka said on Monday.
In its Financial Stability Review 2026, the central bank said the financial system remained stable during the first half of the year, supported by continued economic recovery, improved fiscal performance and adequate capital and liquidity buffers across banks and finance companies.
However, the bank warned that rapid credit growth, particularly household lending including vehicle financing and gold-backed lending, was creating potential systemic vulnerabilities. Rising household indebtedness, higher real estate prices and volatility in collateral values were also identified as emerging risks.
Household credit grew 25.4 percent year-on-year in the second quarter, compared with 14.8 percent a year earlier. Banks remained the main source of household financing, accounting for 62.5 percent of such credit.
Credit extended by finance companies expanded 45 percent year-on-year in the second quarter, driven largely by vehicle and gold-backed lending, compared with growth of 35.1 percent in the same period of 2025.
The central bank said geopolitical tensions, elevated energy and commodity prices, tighter global financial conditions and climate-related risks could spill over into the domestic economy through trade, tourism, remittances, capital flows and exchange rate movements.
The outlook for financial stability remains broadly positive, provided the economic recovery continues, fiscal consolidation progresses and prudent policies are maintained, the central bank said. ■

====================================================================================================

Letter from Mideast: Still waiting for peace near Gaza
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:43:44 CST
15:43:44 KST

by Xinhua writer Wang Zhuolun
JERUSALEM, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- From a hill on the outskirts of Sderot, the Israeli city closest to the Gaza Strip, the devastation across the border is clearly visible. Shattered buildings form a jagged skyline just a few kilometers away, yet they seem worlds apart.
Three years ago, on Oct. 7, 2023, a Hamas-led attack on southern Israel triggered a new round of bloody conflict in Gaza. Militants entered Sderot and stormed the local police station, where fighting raged through the night. Israeli forces eventually demolished the building as they retook it.
I still remember crouching amid the ruins as I covered the war's early days: fighter jets roared overhead, fear emptied the streets, and acrid smoke hung in the air. Not far away, each Israeli strike on Gaza sent another plume into the sky.
Back then, no one knew how long the war would last, much less how its repercussions would spread across borders and engulf much of the Middle East.
Three years on, I returned. The ruins are gone. A memorial square now stands where the police station once stood, with newly planted greenery and paved walkways. Visitors stop to look around. Sderot is gradually reclaiming a sense of normalcy.
It took less than three years to turn ruins into a square. But how long will it take to turn war into peace?
In the West Bank city of Bethlehem, Ali Mansour told me he had been out of work since the war began. Before the conflict, he traveled daily to work in Israeli-controlled areas. Afterward, Israel sharply restricted work permits for Palestinian workers, leaving him without a job.
What he has been waiting for, Mansour said, is not just a job, but the chance to regain the dignity of an ordinary working life.
In Jerusalem's Old City, Palestinian souvenir seller Rami Hamdan has felt the war's toll in another way. In once-bustling shops, merchants now sit idle, waiting for customers who rarely come.
"I stopped watching the news long ago. I don't even want to know what's happening anymore," he said. "I just want to shut myself off from this world of endless war."
Perhaps this is war's most enduring consequence. An explosion has a time, a place, and a casualty count. It becomes a headline, then a photograph. But long after the smoke clears, war persists in less visible ways: in families mourning loved ones, workers waiting for jobs that never return, children growing up under air raid sirens, and ordinary people facing each day with uncertainty.
Over the past three years, the fighting has widened into a regional conflict.
It spread from Gaza to the Israel-Lebanon border and the Red Sea before escalating into large-scale direct military confrontations involving Israel, the United States, and Iran. Rockets, missiles, and drones repeatedly crossed Middle Eastern skies.
Over these three years, I have written "escalation" and "ceasefire takes effect" more times than I can remember. Again and again, just as a war seemed to be nearing its end, another round of fighting began.
The expanding battle fronts kept testing what I thought I understood about war. As a frontline correspondent, I have learned that the worst never stays the worst for long, and what looks like an ending can turn out to be the prelude to something worse.
Before leaving Sderot, I met Shalom Levi, a local resident. Now 60, he has lived his whole life near the Gaza border.
In Hebrew, "shalom" is both a greeting and the word for "peace." Levi told me his parents chose the name to express their hope for peace.
Behind him stood the memorial square built on the ruins of the police station. Beyond it lay Gaza, still scarred by war.
New monuments have risen from rubble. New grass has taken root in scorched earth.
But a man named "Peace" is still waiting for his name to become more than a promise. ■

Roundup: Trump's "energy ceasefire" claim, diesel deal with Russia raise tensions with Ukraine
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:43:29 CST
15:43:29 KST

WASHINGTON, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- U.S. President Donald Trump announced an immediate "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine on Sunday, drawing surprise from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who said it was "news" to him.
"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform, adding that "both parties have agreed."
The declaration came just two days after Trump unveiled a diesel supply deal with Russia.
However, Zelensky told U.S. news outlet Axios that Trump's announcement "was news for me."
"But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire, Ukraine will agree," Zelensky said.
On Saturday, Trump said Russia was willing to reach a deal to end the conflict in Ukraine, but accused Zelensky of resisting a negotiated settlement. He also called for Ukraine to hold an election and choose a new leader who could make a deal with Moscow.
Zelensky responded that he would call a vote if Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to a 60-day ceasefire, and that it was "up to Ukrainians" to choose their leader. Presidential elections, originally due in 2024, have been postponed under martial law.
"Please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections," Zelensky told ABC News.
The Kremlin said Friday that Ukrainian drone attacks during Russia's parliamentary elections had effectively derailed prospects for an immediate resumption of peace talks.
The dispute over the ceasefire comes as rising energy prices have become a growing political concern for Trump ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
On Friday, Trump announced a deal with Putin under which Russia would supply diesel fuel to the United States and global markets. Trump described it as a necessary step to bring down soaring diesel prices, which he attributed largely to Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
Zelensky rejected the suggestion that he was responsible for rising energy prices, saying that "everybody in the world" knew that the war in the Middle East was a bigger factor.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Sunday that the diesel deal "is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe."
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Sunday backed Trump's call "for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now," describing it as "the best route to get energy and fuel back into world markets."
French President Emmanuel Macron said Sunday that France supports a "real energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine.
"Currently, Russia continues to refuse that, by lately intensifying further its strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure," Macron said. "France will continue to stay by the side of Ukraine and President Zelensky."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen fully supported Zelensky's call for a ceasefire protecting global food supplies and energy infrastructure, according to her post on X on Sunday.
The EU will discuss Ukraine's funding needs at its next meeting, including providing further funding for drones and missiles to strengthen Ukraine's defenses, she said. ■

15:43:14 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- The number of assaults on police officers in the Australian state of South Australia has surged by 25 percent, despite declines in several other categories of crime, according to official statistics released on Monday.
The latest figures released by South Australia Police showed that assaults on officers while on duty increased from 635 to 793 in the rolling 12-month period ending in August 2026, marking the 12th consecutive increase in such offences.
Meanwhile, the number of robberies fell by 13 percent, from 501 to 438, following a 16 percent decline in the previous reporting period.
Homicide and related offences dropped by 21 percent, from 53 to 42, while thefts from retail premises decreased by 3 percent to 21,757 incidents.
However, residential break-ins rose from 5,584 to 5,947, while non-residential break-ins increased from 3,391 to 3,513. Sexual offences also edged up from 2,704 to 2,718.
South Australia Police Assistant Commissioner David O'Donovan attributed the continued decline in robberies to police efforts targeting repeat offenders, including securing their detention or imposing strict bail conditions.
He said police remained aware of the trauma experienced by robbery victims and would continue working to reduce such offences. ■

====================================================================================================

World grain prices to continue growing in case of escalation in Black Sea — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:39:16 UTC
15:39:16 KST

ASTANA, October 12. /TASS/. Global grain prices will rise if the escalation in the Black Sea region continues as exports from countries in this area account for about 40% of the global wheat trade, Evgeny Karabanov, head of the analytics committee of the Grain Union of Kazakhstan, told TASS.
"Based on wheat production, consumption, and stock volumes, a positive balance shaped up in the market for the 2026-2027 marketing year. However, the escalation evolving in the Black Sea destabilized the global market in terms of available wheat supply. Against this backdrop, and due to droughts in Europe and the US, global wheat prices have surged by 20-30% (depending on the markets) over the past three months, reaching their highest level since August 2023," Karabanov said.
The situation in the Black Sea region will directly impact the global grain market as this sea is just as important for the global wheat market as the Strait of Hormuz is for the oil market, the expert noted. "Exports from Black Sea countries make up around 40% of the global wheat trade, while oil exports through Hormuz account for about 20% of global trade. In the event of a further long-term escalation in the Black Sea region, global grain prices will continue to grow and poor countries that rely on wheat imports will find themselves in a difficult economic situation," he added.
According to estimates by the Grain Union, at the end of the previous marketing year (September 2025 - August 2026), Kazakhstan exported 14.7 million tons of wheat and processed products in grain equivalent, which was the best result in the country's history. Deliveries were mainly directed to the markets of Central Asian countries, Afghanistan, Iran, and China.
"Due to worsening logistics issues linked to the actual blocking of exports through the Russian ports of the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea, alternative routes for supplying Kazakh grain to the global market through the port of Poti (Georgia) and Baltic ports will be significantly more expensive -- the price will not be competitive," Karabanov added.

Trump turns the screws on Kyiv as EU budget talks hit a wall

Good morning. It’s Monday. I’m Mared Gwyn. Today: Europe braces as Trump turns up the heat on Zelenskyy, and Ireland’s EU budget compromise falls dead on arrival.
Kyiv under pressure: For Ukraine, the past few days have brought back the distinct taste of the Oval Office showdown: public pressure on President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, accusations that Ukraine is obstructing peace and a growing fear (again) that the aim is not compromise, let alone a just peace, but to force Ukraine to surrender, our correspondent Sasha Vakulina writes this morning.
Blindsided: US President Donald Trump made a surprise announcement on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate ceasefire on attacks against energy infrastructure. There was just one rather significant problem: at least one of those parties appeared unaware of the agreement.
“If President Trump negotiated it with Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins,” Zelenskyy said in response. Ukraine, he added, was ready.
It was not entirely clear Moscow got the memo either, Sasha explains.After Trump’s announcement, Russia struck a thermal power plant in Kharkiv, before targeting several other power plants overnight. And that was only Sunday.
Diesel deal rattles Europeans: On Friday, Trump had also announced a deal with Vladimir Putin to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports, without informing Ukrainian or European negotiators who were in Miami for talks. It’s seen as an effort to bring down soaring diesel and gasoline prices, a major issue for American voters, ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
Zelenskyy did not mince his words, branding the deal “weak” and warning it would hand Putin “billions” more to wage war. Trump told him he “better damn well stop” striking Russian refineries, before taking it further and saying Ukraine needed a “new leader”. Putin’s leadership, notably, did not come up for discussion.
Rallying around Zelenskyy: There is another irony for Trump: publicly berating Zelenskyy has hardly proven an effective way of weakening him at home - quite the opposite. EU leaders have also been rallying behind the Ukrainian leader – and Zelenskyy is now expected to join leaders when they gather for a summit in Brussels this Thursday and Friday, sources have told Euronews.
Hard reckoning: News of the Trump-Putin diesel deal and the subsequent energy ceasefire is also set to dominate the conversation today in Brussels and Luxembourg, where foreign ministers are gathering, Jorge Liboreiro writes.
Once again, the EU finds itself scrambling to close ranks behind Zelenskyy and push back, with calculated criticism, against Trump’s Russian-friendly diplomacy.
The US Treasury’s sanctions waiver to enable the diesel sales, set to last until April 2027, has particularly enraged Europeans, who see their own sanctions regime undermined by Trump’s out-of-the-blue decisions. It must be noted that the majority of vessels that Russia uses to trade its refined oil products are subject to the G7 price cap ($100 per barrel).
Foreign ministers will today make clear their pressure campaign on Moscow will continue unabated by formally blacklisting more than 1,600 people and companies accused of enabling the war, a record number in one go.
“We are of course continuing our path,” Kallas said on sanctions upon arriving in Luxembourg this morning. “Our message is clear. If we want to end this war, the only way we can do this is putting more pressure on Russia, and we would call on the US to put the sanctions in place so we can finish this war,” she added.
More is needed: Russia’s all-out escalation has forced EU officials and diplomats to admit that their multibillion-euro support for Ukraine will fall short next year. But there are no easy solutions, Jorge writes in his in-depth analysis.
Warsaw watches: The mounting tensions have also raised the stakes of the Warsaw Security Conference kicking off this morning, with President Zelenskyy expected to address delegates from Kyiv in around an hour.
Our chief EU editor Maria Tadeo, on the ground in the Polish capital, reports that security is tight and the mood tense after Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Sunday that a man had been arrested on suspicion of plotting to assassinate him and his defence minister. More from our Warsaw colleagues.
Dead on arrival: Meanwhile, a new pitch to trim down the EU’s next long-term budget – known as the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) – tabled by Ireland over the weekend has been met with immediate pushback from the so-called frugal countries, which are demanding a much smaller spending pot.
“The size of the new proposal is not a basis for agreement. The EU budget must be affordable for those who bear the brunt of financing it,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in a statement on Saturday.
Dutch directness: Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen was even more blunt. “The Netherlands cannot accept this proposal. At this rate, there will be no deal by the end of the year,” he said in a statement. Sweden also rejected the proposal, insisting that the “overall volume” needs to come down.
Ireland, which currently holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, on Saturday pitched €141 billion in cuts to the previous proposal in an attempt to appease the frugals. The country’s EU affairs minister, Thomas Byrne, described the proposal as a “compromise designed to act as a catalyst” for wrapping up negotiations by the end of this year – a prospect that now looks increasingly remote.
Crunch time: EU leaders are set to tackle the budget issue when they gather for talks in Brussels on Thursday and Friday – and European Council President António Costa is pushing for a swift compromise. There has been a political push to wrap up the budget negotiations before the end of 2026 to prevent talks from being torpedoed by elections in major EU economies including France, Italy and Poland next year. My colleague Luca Bertuzzi has more.

Most stock markets rose early Monday as oil prices tumbled after US President Donald Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, which offset a fresh wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, my colleague Angela Barnes reports.
Both main crude contracts sank more than 1% following the announcement, reversing an initial spike that came in response to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia at the weekend.

The Iran-backed group on Sunday claimed multiple attacks over the past 24 hours and threatened to keep targeting the kingdom's transit hubs, calling them "a theatre of operations for our forces".
"The market is no longer paying full geopolitical premium on every headline, and that is probably the most useful signal in the morning price action," wrote SPI Asset Management's Stephen Innes.
He added: "The physical market remains tight enough to keep Brent above $100, but futures are refusing to treat every new escalation as the start of another straight-line inflation shock."

The Sudanese army said Monday that its air defenses had shot down a “hostile” strategic drone near the Wad al-Mahi area in southeastern Blue Nile state after crossing the border from Ethiopia.
In a statement, the army’s General Command said the drone was intercepted Sunday evening after being tracked from the moment it entered Sudanese airspace.
The military did not identify the drone’s operator or provide further details about its type, origin or intended target.
The development comes amid escalating fighting in Blue Nile state between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N).
On Oct. 9, the Sudan Doctors Network, a local medical group, said an RSF drone strike on a displacement camp in the Abu Shandi area of Wad al-Mahi killed 31 civilians, including four children, and injured 19 others.
On Oct. 3, Sudanese authorities accused the RSF of launching drone strikes targeting the governor’s residence and civilian sites in Damazin, the state capital.
The latest escalation has also triggered displacement, with the International Organization for Migration reporting that approximately 2,800 people fled 10 villages in Wad al-Mahi locality on Oct. 3 amid deteriorating security conditions.
Sudan has been engulfed in war between the army and the RSF since April 2023, leaving tens of thousands dead and around 13 million displaced, according to UN and international estimates.

Lai says Taiwan Bridges Project strengthens global academic ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:30:05 UTC
15:30:05 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) attended the closing ceremony of the Taiwan Bridges Project at National Taiwan University on Monday, praising the initiative for strengthening international academic cooperation and helping Taiwan develop future scientific talent, per RTI.
The project brought 31 Nobel laureates to Taiwan for lectures and academic exchanges in 2025 and 2026, connecting international researchers with Taiwanese universities and research institutions.
Lai said the initiative had built three bridges: a bridge of knowledge that brings world-class expertise to Taiwan and helps Taiwanese researchers engage internationally; a bridge between generations, through lectures and exchanges that inspire younger scientists; and a bridge of peace that promotes dialogue and encourages scholars to use their expertise to advance peace and prosperity, per CNA.
He said the project supports Taiwan’s ambition to cultivate three Nobel laureates in the sciences within 30 years. “I also firmly believe that a free academic environment encourages questioning, and a democratic society encourages dialogue,” Lai said.
He added that Taiwan would draw on its strengths in science, education, and democracy to work with international partners toward peace, prosperity, and a better future for humanity.
Academia Sinica President Chen Chien-jen (陳建仁) said the project’s most important achievement was using exchanges and dialogue to build bridges between research fields. These connections not only linked Taiwan with the world but also increased the international visibility of Taiwanese research, he said.
Chen said he hoped the project’s experience would lead to more cooperation across institutions, disciplines, and countries. He also expressed hope that the friendships and exchanges established through the initiative would continue to deepen and bring greater international attention to Taiwan’s scientific research.
The closing ceremony included a review of the project’s achievements and discussions about future cooperation. Participating institutions shared their experiences and presented digital records of the initiative’s activities.
Organizers said the project would provide a foundation for further international academic cooperation and exchanges across disciplinary boundaries.
The Taiwan Bridges Project was jointly organized by NTU, Academia Sinica, and partner academic and research institutions in collaboration with the International Peace Foundation. Nobel chemistry laureate Lee Yuan-tseh (李遠哲) helped initiate the program, which was supported by Lite-On Group founder Raymond Soong (宋恭源). Lai served as honorary chair.
The initiative reflects Taiwan’s effort to deepen international research connections and encourage young scientists to pursue ambitious research. Academia Sinica has emphasized that direct engagement with leading scholars can help researchers develop new ideas, strengthen long-term collaborations, and raise public support for basic science.

UK’s Burnham says Russia interfered in Brexit vote

The prime minister said Germany’s Friedrich Merz had told him the far-right AfD was linked to Russia, as he faces questions at home over Labour’s ties to the UAE.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Russia interfered in Britain’s 2016 referendum on leaving the European Union, in what is believed to be the first time a British leader has publicly acknowledged such meddling.
Burnham told The Rest is Politics podcast that on taking office in July he asked advisers whether Russia had interfered in the Brexit vote.
"I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was," he said. "These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia."
Moscow has long denied meddling in other countries’ elections or referendums.
Burnham’s remarks come as UK intelligence agencies warn of a growing threat of Russian interference in Britain’s democratic institutions. In 2020, a parliamentary committee found the government had failed to fully assess the possible impact of Russian state media and "troll" accounts on the referendum.
Burnham also said he had discussed possible links between Russia and Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party with Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin last week.
"You know he was saying to me that the AfD are clearly linked to Russia, funded I believe," Burnham said. "There is certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics."
Labour’s links to the UAE
At home, Burnham is under pressure over his ties to Manchester City, the Gulf state-backed Premier League club that was found guilty last month of widespread breaches of financial rules.
The former mayor of Greater Manchester was criticised for saying he would be "really concerned" to lose the club’s wealthy arab owners. Labour MPs have accepted around €325,500 in hospitality and foreign trips from the United Arab Emirates, far more than any other party, according to official records analysed by the British newspaper The Sun.
On the podcast, Burnham agreed to an opposition request to publish details of his meetings with the club’s owners, saying he had held only one significant meeting, in 2021.
This will not include information of Manchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak's private meeting with Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds in Downing Street on 14 September, 11 days before the club was found guilty.
The timing of the talks is suspicious although reports claim talks were held in his separate role as chief executive of Abu Dhabi’s sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala and focused on defence, security intelligence and trade.
Burnham has said the football issues were serious and subject to an independent process, but should be kept separate from questions of investment.

====================================================================================================

Herzog: ‘I'll do everything I can to prevent repeat elections’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:26:19 UTC
15:26:19 KST

President Isaac Herzog vowed to do everything in his power to prevent Israel from heading into another round of elections if the upcoming vote fails to produce a clear political outcome. "I'm doing everything I can to ensure Israel has a stable government," he said in an interview recorded ahead of Monday's People of the Nation conference, hosted by ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth. "But I'll go further than that: I will do absolutely everything I can to prevent repeat elections."
Herzog warned that Israel faces enormous national challenges and cannot afford repeated election cycles. "We need to wait for the results rather than pass judgment in advance, but we must do everything possible to avoid going through this again and again and again," he said.
In the wide-ranging interview, recorded several days before the conference and just over two weeks before Israel's elections, Herzog also renewed his call for a plea agreement to end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's criminal trial, warned that Israel's police force is overwhelmed and condemned violence by Jewish extremists against Palestinians in the West Bank as "an enormous moral stain" on the country.
During the judicial overhaul, you called for compromise. Three and a half years later, Israel is just as polarized, perhaps even more so. Do you think we've reached a point of no return?
"First of all, the danger is always there, and it remains very real. All it takes is one madman, and the danger becomes extremely serious. We're in an election period, and naturally, such a period is dangerous because it can lead to radicalization that could tear even deeper divisions into our society."
Are you concerned that one side might refuse to accept the election results?
"I believe everyone will accept the election results. I think Israeli citizens will go out and vote. I constantly urge Israelis to vote, and I remind everyone that elections are not a civil war. Elections are the way to resolve issues, make decisions and understand that the day after, we still go on together. Those who lose and those who win must all understand that they belong to the same people. Those who are elected must also look after those who were not."
If the election ends in deadlock, will you try to promote a unity government?
"I don't want to get into that right now. There are different opinions about the composition of the government and different political outlooks. Everyone understands which school of thought I come from, but it would not be right for me to say, two weeks before the election, what kind of government should be formed."
Do you think a pardon could help ease tensions in Israel and perhaps make it possible to form a government if there is a deadlock?
"The president has the full authority to task a member of Knesset with forming a government. That has nothing to do with pardons. After I hear from all the parties, in a process that the public will already be discussing because the results will come in about a week after the election, the consultations begin.
"As for the pardon issue, you're referring to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's trial. I've already said, and I keep saying, that this case needs to end, and it should end with a plea agreement. It needs to be resolved through a settlement.
"That's why I proposed mediation at the President's Residence a few months ago. Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara hesitated but agreed to come into the room. I said it would take place under the auspices of the President's Residence. The prime minister has not responded to this day, and I repeat: I'm leaving the door open, all the time."
Are you calling on the prime minister to accept your proposal?
"I'm not issuing calls. I'm waiting for a response, but that's not the issue right now. We're in the middle of an election, and it's clear to me that this isn't relevant during the election process."
Are you worried about the integrity of the elections and attempts to disrupt them?
"I'm working closely with the Central Elections Committee. Just last week, I brought the heads of the major technology companies here, together with the committee's chairman, Justice Noam Sohlberg, and his excellent team. We assessed different situations, considered extreme scenarios and heard how each company is responding.
"Even so, we must always consider the possibility that someone will try to sabotage the elections, whether from within Israel or from abroad. That's exactly what they're constantly working on, and they're doing so in a very impressive way."
We're living through a period of apparent anarchy and a breakdown of law and order in so many areas: in the south, in crime within Arab society and in the Haredi community. Just in recent weeks, hundreds of Haredi activists came to free a military draft dodger and rioted in Modiin in the middle of the night, while about 100 Jewish extremists descended on a Palestinian home and set it on fire. They also try to attack IDF soldiers, who seem unable to stop them.
"It's a miracle nobody was killed and there was no bloodshed. First of all, our police force is doing its best, but this country is a bit too much for it. We need a stronger police force and a much larger one because there are so many challenges here.
"Crime in Arab society is a disaster. We're talking about more than 1.3 million citizens living under terror, morning and night.
"The violence we saw in Modiin is intolerable. And what worries me most, what keeps me awake at night, is the violence we're seeing in the West Bank. It is an enormous stain on the face of the country, a moral stain.
"I hear about it from everywhere in the world. People say to me, 'What's happened to you? Don't you know how to restrain groups of rioters?' These are groups of rioters. They don't represent the settlement movement itself or its values in any way. Yet, on the other hand, they're receiving tacit legitimacy.
"I know the state institutions are taking action. But I personally went to the IDF's West Bank Division two weeks ago and sat down with the division commander and the brigade commanders."
And what did you hear from them?
"Deep frustration. They're facing extremely complicated situations. As one particularly impressive commander told me, 'I don't know whether someone speeding toward me in a car at night is a Palestinian coming to carry out a terrorist attack or a Jew coming to stage a provocation.'
"The incident in Jalud was extraordinarily dangerous, and it wasn't an isolated incident. We're talking about rocks being thrown at commanders.
"Innocent Palestinians must not be attacked, and actions of this kind cannot be allowed. The main thing that must be stated clearly is that the IDF and the security forces have achieved remarkable successes in fighting terrorism.
"Their job there is to fight terrorism, yet they find themselves confronting an utterly intolerable reality. That requires all the relevant authorities to sit down together, develop a serious plan and bring the full power of the state to bear, including clear directives from the political leadership."
Do you think administrative detention should be reinstated?
"I think that possibility needs to be examined. There are certainly cases in which we need to know how to use that tool. If there's no alternative, there's no alternative.
"We cannot continue allowing this phenomenon. It's eating away at the State of Israel and destroying everything good about its image around the world.
"Last week, we marked three years since October 7. Around the world, people spoke about October 7, about the terrible disaster, what we went through and the barbaric, criminal terrorism. And then, inevitably, someone brings up an incident like this in the West Bank. That is unacceptable because this is not Israel. It's a phenomenon we can and must confront."
Israel is facing an unprecedented international campaign against it. In some places, Israel has practically become a pariah. This isn't confined to a small minority, and it isn't just antisemitism. How are we supposed to confront this wave of hostility?
"There's enormous antisemitism, so many engines of incitement and so much poison. But we have to confront this phenomenon by doing more than simply identifying the problems. We need to ask what the solutions are.
"We must reach out to countries and companies, speak, make appearances, explain and show the beauty of Israel, its extraordinary achievements and its contribution to humanity. And, of course, we have to develop better public diplomacy tools.
"We're the Startup Nation. We can do a much better job in this regard."
What are you hearing from Jewish communities around the world?
"I invest an enormous amount of effort in this, in maintaining connections, offering support and strengthening communities.
"We need to understand that everything said and every action taken here, in the nation-state of the Jewish people, directly affects our brothers and sisters in the Diaspora, Jewish communities, their security, their standing and their ability to make their voices heard.
"They are threatened and challenged. This is a very complicated period for the Jewish people. At the same time, the Jewish people are demonstrating strength and resilience and fighting back.
"I encourage everyone: Stand up, fight, make your voices heard. Don't be afraid."
Within a few years, the Haredi education system is expected to become the largest in Israel. Does that worry you? And do you have deep relationships of trust with the Haredi community?
"I cannot say that something relating to the composition of Israeli society worries me. This is Israeli society. It's a challenge we have the strength to address.
"Take the issue of Haredi military enlistment, for example. On the eve of Tisha B'Av, I had the privilege of visiting the IDF's Hasmonean Brigade for the reading of Lamentations. I was moved because I saw Haredi soldiers, and I saw them in large numbers.
"An interview with me was recently published in the brigade's newspaper, which was distributed to thousands of households. It's simply wrong to assume that the entire Haredi community thinks or acts the same way. But we have to talk.
"There are trends we're identifying. There's a demographic trend, and we need to address it. We need to understand that things must change. I believe that future generations of Haredim won't be exactly the same as those today, just as citizens in other groups will also change.
"We have no choice but to sit down together and build a shared future for our children and grandchildren. This is an amazing country, an amazing people, with extraordinary strength. I want to see everyone included, and that creates challenges.
"For example, we need as much service by women in the IDF as possible, alongside the challenge of Haredi military service. We'll need to find the right balance and hold a respectful, serious discussion.
"I think the people of Israel have had enough of the division and hatred within our society because it gets us nowhere. God forbid, it can lead to disasters.
"That's why we must do everything possible. I'm doing everything I can and putting my entire heart and soul into it. People from every part of Israeli society are constantly coming to these rooms at the President's Residence. Sometimes they begin by shouting and almost coming to blows, and the meetings end with tears and embraces."
There's a feeling in Israel that the very concept of taking responsibility has disappeared. That applies to the October 7 massacre and even to the attempted attack involving a flydubai aircraft.
"I said this in my speech at Mount Herzl, about the need to investigate thoroughly, without fear or hesitation, and provide all the answers."
Through a state commission of inquiry?
"That issue is now the subject of a debate on the eve of the elections, about the composition of the commission and what kind of commission it should be.
"It's no secret that more than a year ago, I proposed a compromise under which Chief Justice Yitzhak Amit and his deputy, Justice Noam Sohlberg, would appoint a state commission of inquiry.
"But now, during the election campaign, I'm not taking a definitive position on the matter because ultimately it will be part of the election process and the voters' decision.
"I want to say one final thing. Since this conference is about the people of Israel, we have a wonderful, extraordinary people. Don't lose hope. Hold on to hope and think about the day after the war, which must also come.
"That means a day when we have strong, secure arrangements along our borders, and when we also begin an in-depth discussion about the future of Israeli society."

German Social Democrats' leader and Labor Minister Bärbel Bas resigns, amid coalition friction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:20:00 UTC
15:20:00 KST

Germany: Bas quits as SPD co-chair amid coalition friction
October 12, 2026
Bärbel Bas, a longstanding top official with Social Democrats (SPD), resigned her post on Monday citing the death of her stepdaughter and "open attacks" within Germany's ruling coalition of the SPD and Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrat (CDU) bloc.
"I am currently unable to muster the strength to fully carry out my government and party duties on short notice, I have decided to step down from both offices,” the 58-year-old said.
Who is Bärbel Bas?
A member of the parliament since 2009, Bas' star began to rise when she became president of the Bundestag in 2021 under the SPD-led coalition of former Chancellor Olaf Scholz.
Within her center-left party, Bas has been among its more progressive members.
Following the collapse of Scholz's government, the SPD became the junior coalition partners to Merz's conservative bloc.
She served as president of the Bundestag until 2025, when she became Merz's labor minister as well as co-leader of her party alongisde Lars Klingbeil.
Why is she resigning now?
After being widowed in 2020, Bas' stepdaughter recently passed away. The outgoing education minister said she needed time to process her grief, and that her party deserved strong leadership.
She added that recent infighting between the SPD and CDU over various policy matters hastened her decision.
The CDU has accused Bas of delayed or blocking several reforms the conservatives are keen to pass, including changes to Germany's struggling pension system and employment laws.
Bas said that she informed both Chancellor Merz and Lars Klingbeil before issuing her public statement.

All 73 passengers, crew rescued from stranded Solomon Islands ferry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:16:58 UTC
15:16:58 KST

Faisal Mahmud
12 October 2026•Update: 12 October 2026
All 73 passengers and crew aboard a Solomon Islands inter-island ferry stranded at sea since Friday have been safely rescued, provincial authorities announced Monday.
The Temotu Provincial Government said that everyone aboard MV Awka was transferred to rescue vessel MV Helper 1 and brought ashore at Vanikoro following a coordinated international operation.
The ferry suffered mechanical problems while travelling between Tikopia and Vanikoro, leaving it drifting in rough seas.
MV Helper 1 reached the stranded ferry Sunday night, followed by Royal Solomon Islands Police Force Patrol Boat Gizo.
The patrol boat began towing the ferry around midnight, while the transfer of passengers and crew was subsequently completed.
The provincial government thanked France, Australia, China and Vanuatu for assisting the operation.
Australia deployed an aircraft, while Chinese cargo vessel Sunnine 3 diverted from its route to deliver food, water and other supplies.
Earlier, local newspaper Solomon Star reported that the ferry had suffered an engine shutdown Friday, leaving only its electricity generator operational.

Addictive behaviour is falling among Portuguese teens but most vulnerable are still exposed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:16:48 UTC
15:16:48 KST

Portuguese teenagers are drinking and using drugs less and facing fewer problems, but risks are increasingly concentrated among those with multiple vulnerabilities, according to a new ICAD study on addictive behaviours.
There are fewer problems and lower levels of consumption among Portuguese teenagers, but the highest-risk behaviours are increasingly concentrated among young people who accumulate several vulnerability factors. This is the main conclusion of a new study by the Institute for Addictive Behaviours and Dependencies (ICAD).
The Study on Alcohol, Tobacco, Drugs and other Addictive Behaviours (ECATD-CAD 2024) examines the problematic dimension of addictive behaviours among pupils in Portuguese state schools aged between 13 and 18.
The findings point to an overall favourable trend compared with the picture observed in the previous edition of the study, carried out in 2019. According to ICAD, there has been "a consistent reduction in the experience of all the problematic situations analysed, including violent conduct, accidents, hospitalisations, risky sexual behaviours and other episodes with potential negative consequences".
This trend is unfolding in a context in which pupils report better academic performance, greater parental supervision and going out at night less often, factors which, according to the report, "appear to contribute to an environment that is generally more protective against risk behaviours".
Despite this positive development, ICAD warns that "in several indicators there is a growing concentration of the highest-risk behaviours in a relatively small group of adolescents, characterised by profiles of greater individual and social vulnerability, which makes it clear that the reduction in the overall number of consumers does not remove the need for intervention targeting specific groups".
Recent consumption of alcohol and, above all, illicit drugs remains one of the main factors associated with involvement in problematic situations. The report notes that, compared with 2019, this trend has become more pronounced.
"The group of pupils who use psychoactive substances show significantly higher prevalence of risky sexual behaviours, problems with the police, interpersonal violence, accidents and other potentially serious situations", ICAD states, while stressing, however, that most problematic situations do not occur immediately following an episode of consumption.
The report also distinguishes between drinking alcohol only and polyconsumption, identifying them as important factors in the likelihood of experiencing problematic situations.
Thus, adolescents who combine recent consumption of alcohol and illicit drugs "display substantially higher levels of involvement in accidents, problems with the police, cyberbullying and risky sexual behaviours when compared with those who consume only alcoholic drinks".
The analysis of the problematic dimension of the different addictive behaviours also shows that, in alcohol consumption, motivations linked to pleasure, fun and sociability remain predominant.
However, ICAD underlines that there is a significant proportion of young people who say they drink alcohol to forget their problems. According to the institute, this is an "indicator frequently associated with the development of harmful patterns of use and dependence".
The report also highlights that, in the case of cannabis, although most users do not present indicators of risk of dependency, "there is an increase in the proportion of users classified as high risk, alongside growth in the group without any identified risk".
Social media is a major concern among non-substance-related addictive behaviours
Among non-substance-related addictive behaviours, social media continue to emerge as the main concern, with a significant proportion of young people acknowledging that they spend too much time on these platforms.
In electronic gaming, including video games played exclusively online, indicators of problematic use remain broadly stable compared with the previous edition of the study. Gambling for money, meanwhile, although still involving only a minority of adolescents, shows an increase in prevalence, albeit accompanied by a slight decrease in indicators linked to the problematic dimension, such as the need to increase the amounts wagered.
There are also important differences between boys and girls. Male pupils continue to show greater involvement in problems with the police and in risky electronic gaming and gambling for money. By contrast, girls stand out for their higher prevalence of problematic use of social media and for resorting to alcohol consumption as a strategy for coping with emotional difficulties.
Social and family factors also have an impact. The profile most associated with problematic behaviours includes low academic achievement, weaker parental supervision, frequent nights out, and lower physical and emotional wellbeing. Conversely, good school performance, parental supervision and greater wellbeing act as protective factors.
Regional analysis also reveals changes compared with the previous study. Alentejo now appears as the region with the highest concentration of unfavourable indicators, followed by the Autonomous Region of the Azores, while Lisbon no longer occupies the position of greatest vulnerability observed in 2019.

3 men allege torture at BJP MLA’s house in UP (File photo: PTI image)
NEW DELHI: Police in Uttar Pradesh’s Moradabad are investigating allegations that three men were illegally confined and tortured at the residence of BJP MLA Sushant Singh over a missing gold bracelet belonging to the legislator’s son, PTI reported citing officials.The complainants have sought the registration of an FIR against six named persons, including the MLA’s aides, and nine unidentified individuals. However, no case had been registered so far, Moradabad SP (Rural) Kunwar Akash Singh said, adding that action would be taken after an investigation.
According to the victims’ family, Atul and Lavesh, who worked as domestic help at the legislator’s house, and their friend Ramu were held captive and tortured over the suspected theft of the gold bracelet.Ramu’s mother, Omwati, alleged that an aide of the MLA took her son from their home on October 7, while Atul and Lavesh were already being held at the residence.She claimed that the three men were hung upside down, beaten with belts, subjected to electric shocks and had salt rubbed into their wounds.All three were admitted to a hospital in Kashipur. Officials said Ramu’s condition was critical.Sushant Singh dismissed the allegations as baseless, maintaining that the domestic workers had only been questioned about the missing bracelet and had not been assaulted.Moradabad MP and Samajwadi Party leader Ruchi Veera demanded immediate justice for the victims and strict action against those responsible.Police said further action would follow the investigation.(With inputs from PTI)

designboom paris art week guide: what to see in and out of design miami and art basel 2026

2026-10-12

designboom paris art week guide: what to see in and out of design miami and art basel 2026
designboom maps the art, design, and cultural encounters worth seeking out across paris this october.
What to see across Paris during Art Basel Paris 2026
Paris enters its busiest art and design week with a program that looks as much to what has already existed as to what comes next. Across museums, galleries, historic buildings, and temporary spaces, the 2026 season brings together fashion archives, modernist furniture, contemporary sculpture, photography, craft, and experimental forms of hospitality, with many projects reconsidering how objects and images acquire meaning over time.
At the center of the week, Art Basel Paris returns to the Grand Palais while Design Miami.Paris takes over the Hôtel de Maisons. Beyond the fairs, museums and cultural spaces across Paris present projects that span art, fashion, architecture, and design: Ibrahim Mahama brings a network of artists and Ghanaian cultural histories to Fondation Cartier; Prune Nourry revisits the overlooked legacy of women sculptors at the Petit Palais; Jenny Holzer activates the Musée d’Orsay with texts and images; and the Musée des Arts Décoratifs marks 40 years of its fashion collections through four decades of exhibitions and 40 significant silhouettes.
Galleries turn to material memory and transformation, from Jean Prouvé’s architecture and Japanese ceramics to Wendy Andreu’s reworked furniture and Ais’s layered paintings. Temporary projects also blur the boundaries between disciplines, including WE ARE ONA’s collaboration with Rirkrit Tiravanija and chef Dalad Kambhu, where a shared meal becomes part of the artwork itself. From major institutional exhibitions to intimate gallery presentations, collectible design, food, and temporary interventions, this is designboom’s guide to what to see across Paris during Art Basel Paris and Design Miami.Paris 2026.
design miami paris / art basel paris 2026
Art Basel Paris 2026
Art Basel Paris returns to the Grand Palais from October 23rd to 25th, 2026, with its fifth edition that brings together 211 galleries from 41 countries and regions, while expanding beyond the fair through an extensive public program across Paris. Under new director Karim Crippa, the edition foregrounds the galleries, museums, institutions, and public spaces of the city as part of the fair’s wider cultural context.
The fair is organized across three sectors: Galeries, with 183 exhibitors; Emergence, with 16 solo presentations; and Premise, with 12 historically focused projects. This year, Premise moves into the larger Salon Seine, while Conversations relocates to the Grand Palais Auditorium for the first time. A record 12 joint booths will also bring together 24 galleries.
Outside the Grand Palais, the Public Program spreads across nine Parisian venues, including the Petit Palais, Palais d’Iéna, Cité de l’architecture et du patrimoine, Beaux-Arts de Paris, and several public squares and gardens. Highlights include Alice Diop’s Geste de Consolation at Palais d’Iéna, Tracey Emin’s sculptures at the Parvis des Droits-de-l’Homme, Kutluğ Ataman’s Küba at Beaux-Arts de Paris, and Robert Indiana’s LOVE Wall at Place Clemenceau.
 what: Art Basel Paris 2026
when: October 23rd–25th, 2026
where: Grand Palais, 3 Avenue du Général Eisenhower, 75008 Paris
Alice Diop – Geste de Consolation presented by miu miu
For her first exhibition project, French filmmaker Alice Diop transforms the Palais d’Iéna into a multimedia journey for Miu Miu’s 2026 Art Basel Paris Public Program commission. Geste de Consolation brings together film, photography, sculpture, poetry, dance, music, and live performance, centering acts of consolation conceived by Black women artists.
The project takes over four interconnected spaces. It begins with work by South African artist Zanele Muholi and a two-screen video installation by Diop, bringing together archival images and film excerpts that have shaped her own way of looking. This leads into Chambre à soi, a living room and library featuring carpets with a motif by Mary Lee Bendolph and books drawn from Diop’s intellectual influences. The central library opens onto a performance space where texts by writers including Penda Diouf, Zora Neale Hurston, June Jordan, Audre Lorde, Marie Ndiaye, and Zadie Smith are performed live. Choreography by Nadia Beugré and music by Angel Bat Dawid and her ensemble further extend the project beyond the conventions of a static exhibition. The journey ends with Simone Leigh’s monumental bronze Sentinel (Mami Wata), whose nearly five-meter-tall female figure references the West African water spirit whose image has travelled across Africa and its diasporas.
what: Alice Diop – Geste de Consolation
when: October 21st–25th, 2026
where: Palais d’Iéna, Paris
Tracey Emin brings three bronze figures to Paris
Presented by White Cube, Tracey Emin’s I Lay Here For You, I Followed You to the End, and I Will Not Be Alone occupy the Parvis des Droits de l’Homme outside the Cité de l’architecture et du patrimoine. The three bronze figures explore intimacy, vulnerability, and resilience through different poses of the female body. The works move from an elongated figure lying on the ground to a kneeling body and, finally, an upright seated figure, tracing, together, a shift from exposure and surrender toward strength and endurance.
 what: I Lay Here For You, I Followed You to the End, I Will Not Be Alone
when: October 14th – November 1st, 2026
where: Parvis des Droits de l’Homme, Cité de l’architecture et du patrimoine, Paris
Artworks take over Avenue Winston Churchill
Avenue Winston Churchill becomes an outdoor setting for works by Marcello Maloberti, Yinka Shonibare, Simone Fattal, Niki de Saint Phalle, Manfred Pernice, Alicja Kwade, Carmen Herrera, and Keita Miyazaki. The free-access program places sculpture and installation directly within the public realm, from monumental stone forms and concrete benches to neon, bronze, and recycled materials.
Marcello Maloberti’s CIEL suspends the French word for ‘sky’ 20 meters above the avenue, written upside down as if addressed to the sky rather than viewers below. Nearby, Yinka Shonibare’s Abstract Bronze VIII transforms a twisted bronze form with hand-painted Dutch wax patterns, while Simone Fattal’s Door takes the form of a weathered architectural fragment held together by long metal nails.
The selection also includes Niki de Saint Phalle’s colorful Cat Head Totem, Manfred Pernice’s four concrete benches in bank-group, and Alicja Kwade’s L’Élévation des Mondes, a precarious tower of ten polished stone spheres sourced from different parts of the world. Carmen Herrera’s geometric Angulo Amarillo and Keita Miyazaki’s A Symbiotic Form, made from salvaged car parts and pleated Japanese paper, extend the presentation into abstraction, material transformation, and ideas of fragility.
 what: Outdoor art program on Avenue Winston Churchill
when: October 20th – 25th, 2026
where: Avenue Winston Churchill, Paris
Kutluğ Ataman brings Küba to the Chapelle des Petits-Augustins
Kutluğ Ataman’s Küba transforms the Chapelle des Petits-Augustins at the Beaux-Arts de Paris into a multi-screen portrait of a community shaped by migration, poverty, and survival. First created in 2004, the 40-screen video installation gives each television to a different resident of Küba, a former settlement on the outskirts of Istanbul founded in the late 1960s by people fleeing political persecution.
Set among mismatched armchairs and salvaged furniture, the screens show residents speaking directly to the camera about their memories, fears, beliefs, and dreams. Their stories overlap without one voice taking precedence, allowing visitors to gradually piece together a collective portrait while moving through the installation. Ataman uses individual testimony to consider how identity is formed through storytelling, giving the community’s own voices control over its representation.
 what: Küba, 2004
when: October 20th – 25th, 2026, 10am–7pm
where: Chapelle des Petits-Augustins, Beaux-Arts de Paris
Design Miami.Paris 2026 returns for its fourth edition
Design Miami.Paris returns for its fourth edition to Hôtel de Maisons in the Faubourg Saint-Germain from October 20th to 25th, 2026, bringing together more than 20 international galleries alongside a Design at Large program. The fair focuses on collectible design across historical and contemporary practices, with presentations spanning French decorative arts, Scandinavian design, Italian design, artist-made jewelry, and large-scale works.
Highlights include historical pieces by Le Corbusier, Pierre Jeanneret, Charlotte Perriand, Robert Mallet-Stevens, Eileen Gray, and Pierre Chareau, alongside contemporary work by designers including Studio Lugo, Adélie Ducasse, and Vincent Dubourg. A Nordic thread runs through presentations by Modernity, Hostler Burrows, Galerie Maria Wettergren, and Galerie Eric Philippe. Design at Large extends the fair into the courtyard, interiors, and gardens of Hôtel de Maisons with larger-scale works. Galerie Patrick Seguin presents Jean Prouvé’s 6×6 Demountable House (1944), while Maison Parisienne shows a sculptural bench by Pierre Renart and Galerie Gastou features Irene Cattaneo’s monumental bronze swings Effi Briest. The program also includes the second edition of Design Miami x Apple: Designers of Tomorrow, focused in 2026 on Design for Presence, with four emerging designers selected to develop projects incorporating Apple technology.
what: Design Miami.Paris 2026
when: October 20th–25th, 2026; public opening October 21, 11am–7pm 
where: Hôtel de Maisons, 51 Rue de l’Université, 75007 Paris
Maison Parisienne
Pierre Renart and Maison Parisienne present a monumental wooden bench whose backrest unfolds into a curved ribbon, extending into a chaise longue. Made from a single flowing line of wood, the piece creates two facing seating areas designed for sitting and conversation.
Craftica Gallery
Craftica Gallery presents Korallion (2026), a birch plywood bench by Cyryl Zakrzewski that sits between sculpture and architecture. Designed for an outdoor setting, its fluid form responds to light, weather, and the passage of time while adding a sculptural element within the landscape.
Galerie Gastou
Galerie Gastou presents Irene Cattaneo’s Effi Briest, a group of monumental bronze swings inspired by the childhood swing in Theodor Fontane’s 1895 novel. Their weight and permanence contrast with the fleeting movement associated with swings, connecting the installation to the tension between childhood freedom and the social structures that shape adulthood.
Nilufar
Nilufar features a curated selection of vintage design alongside contemporary works, including Von Pelt Atelier’s Table Lamp Spring Fountain 2 (2025). Made in Spain, the lamp reinterprets the silver-plated decorative objects found in Spanish homes during the mid-to-late 20th century.
Galerie Patrick Seguin
 Galerie Patrick Seguin showcases furniture by Jean Prouvé, Charlotte Perriand, and Pierre Jeanneret alongside a 6×6 demountable house by Prouvé at Design Miami.Paris. The presentation brings together furniture and architecture to examine the shared ideas connecting the three designers’ practices.
The booth features Perriand’s Forme Libre low table from 1956, a Jeanneret sofa set from around 1955, and a Prouvé sideboard and Antony chair from around 1950. In the Hôtel de Maisons garden, Prouvé’s 1944 6×6 house is presented with a redesigned interior inspired by the chashitsu, the traditional Japanese tea pavilion.
Using natural materials including wood, the installation creates a dialogue between Prouvé’s architecture and Japanese approaches to living. It also draws on the designer’s connections with Japan, emphasizing affinities around simplicity, lightness, and material restraint.
Designers of Tomorrow – Design Miami.Paris x Apple
For its second year, Design Miami x Apple: Designers of Tomorrow focuses on ‘Design for Presence,’ exploring how design can encourage people to slow down, pay attention, and connect with their surroundings. Led by curator Rodman Primack, a jury of international design figures will select four emerging designers whose work incorporates Apple technology into their creative processes.
exhibitions, events and galleries AROUND PARIS
Fondation Cartier pour l’art contemporain – Ibrahim Mahama
Ghanaian artist Ibrahim Mahama transforms the Fondation Cartier pour l’art contemporain into a collective space for art, research, and exchange with The Harvest Season. For his first major exhibition in Paris, Mahama occupies the institution alongside nine artists and collectives connected through long-term collaborations, research, and exchanges, bringing together site-specific works and new versions of existing installations. The exhibition takes inspiration from the three art centers Mahama has established in Tamale, northern Ghana, since 2019. These spaces combine artistic production, education, and transmission, providing a model for thinking about how cultural institutions can emerge from local networks rather than operate separately from them. At the Fondation Cartier, this approach extends into a program of exhibitions, performances, music, talks, workshops, and masterclasses.
Among the central works is Parliament of Ghosts, a circular parliamentary chamber made from traditional Asante wooden stools. The installation refers to Ghana’s 1966 coup and the dissolution of its government, while also functioning as a stage for performances and discussions throughout the exhibition. Mahama also presents Things Fall Apart, a monumental reconstruction of a former Ghanaian glass bottle factory, using original materials to connect industrial heritage with questions of education, infrastructure, and possible futures. The exhibition expands through works by Dorothy Akpene Amenuke, Gideon Appah, James Barnor, CATPC, Courage Dzidula Kpodo, Zohra Opoku, Postbox Ghana, Tjaša Rener, and Feda Wardak. Their practices bring together textiles, photography, painting, architecture, archives, agricultural materials, and inherited infrastructure, extending Mahama’s interest in how histories and forms of knowledge can be carried forward and transformed.
 what: Ibrahim Mahama: The Harvest Season
when: October 22nd, 2026 – February 28th, 2027
where: Fondation Cartier pour l’art contemporain, Paris
Ginori 1735 – L’Art de la Convivialité
Ginori 1735 turns its Paris boutique on Rue du Faubourg Saint-Honoré into a showcase for bespoke tableware and hospitality design during October’s Art Basel Paris and Design Miami.Paris. L’Art de la Convivialité brings together custom creations, limited editions, and artisanal techniques developed for hotels, restaurants, cafés, chefs, architects, and designers.
A fully dressed table presents selected pieces created for special hospitality projects, showing how the Italian porcelain maker adapts its decorative language, forms, and colors to individual settings. The presentation focuses on the production process behind these commissions, from shaping and glazing the porcelain to firing and hand decoration.
 what: L’Art de la Convivialité
when: October 2026
where: Ginori 1735 Paris Flagship Store, 69 Rue du Faubourg Saint-Honoré, 75008 Paris
Thomas Houseago and Théo Mercier
For the 2026 Reiffers Initiatives Mentorship, sculptors Thomas Houseago and Théo Mercier transform the foundation’s Paris space into an exhibition and working environment, bringing together two generations and distinct approaches to sculpture. Houseago will work under the foundation’s glass roof for several weeks, creating a new group of works on site, while Mercier will fill the ground floor with sculptures, found objects, antiques, and works in progress from his Paris studio.
The exhibition keeps traces of the artists’ working processes visible. Houseago’s temporary atelier remains intact for the exhibition, alongside recent sculptures including a monumental bronze owl and one of his masks. Mercier’s installation reconstructs his studio not as a literal replica, but as a representation of the relationships between objects and forms within his practice.
 what: Reiffers Initiatives Mentorship 2026, Thomas Houseago and Théo Mercier
when: October 23rd – December 12th, 2026
where: Reiffers Initiatives, 30 Rue des Acacias, 75017 Paris
WE ARE ONA presents Dalad’s with Rirkrit Tiravanija
WE ARE ONA brings together artist Rirkrit Tiravanija and chef Dalad Kambhu for Dalad’s, a temporary restaurant during Art Basel Paris 2026. For seven days, the project activates a secret location in the 17th arrondissement into a setting where Thai cuisine, contemporary art, and hospitality meet around a shared table.
Tiravanija creates the restaurant’s central installation from two stainless-steel boats inspired by traditional Thai fishing boats. Reimagined as communal tables, the boats incorporate steam pots for cooking, turning the installation itself into part of the dining experience.
Kambhu serves a four-course lunch and seven-course dinner, bringing her interpretation of Thai cuisine to the project. The collaboration extends Tiravanija’s longstanding interest in cooking, eating, and social interaction as artistic forms, while connecting the boats’ cultural references with Kambhu’s approach to Thai food and memory.
 what: Dalad’s
when: October 19th–25th, 2026
where: secret location, Quartier de l’Étoile, 75017 Paris
Guerlain – L’Heure des Possibles
For L’Heure des Possibles, Guerlain brings together more than 30 international artists at La Maison Guerlain on the Champs-Élysées, using l’heure bleue, the fleeting interval between day and night, as the exhibition’s starting point. Curated by Hervé Mikaeloff and Benoît Baume, the exhibition spans photography, sculpture, installation, and other media around ideas of perception, transition, and possibility. The exhibition is divided into three chapters: to contemplate, to experience, and to take the plunge. The sequence moves from works concerned with light and perception toward more intimate encounters with transformation and, finally, the uncertainty and possibilities that emerge from change.
Artists including James Turrell, Ann Veronica Janssens, Todd Hido, Rineke Dijkstra, Christian Boltanski, Annette Messager, Laure Prouvost, Ugo Rondinone, Rinko Kawauchi, Friedrich Kunath, Yoann Bourgeois, Barthélémy Toguo, Xie Lei, and Zao Wou-Ki are among those featured. The visual works are accompanied by an olfactory component developed by Guerlain Perfume Director Delphine Jelk. Working with selected artists, Jelk has created bespoke scents to accompany their works, while also presenting a new interpretation of Guerlain’s L’Heure Bleue, the fragrance originally created in 1912.
 what: L’Heure des Possibles
when: October 21st – November 15th, 2026; opening reception October 20 at 7pm
where: La Maison Guerlain, 68 Avenue des Champs-Élysées, 75008 Paris
Jordan Casteel – Winter Sun
Jordan Casteel presents Winter Sun, a new series of paintings at Thaddaeus Ropac Paris Marais, marking the American artist’s first exhibition in France and her most significant presentation in Europe to date. Created during the first half of 2026, the paintings use a cool, earthy palette to consider dormancy and renewal, hope and grief, and the changing relationship between the artist, her community, and the environments she inhabits.
Casteel continues to work from photographs, meeting her subjects within their own environments. The approach extends her interest in portraying people of color and mapping the social landscapes of the communities around her, while recent works also introduce a more autobiographical dimension following the birth of her son.
 what: Winter Sun
when: October 19th–December 23rd, 2026;
where:Thaddaeus Ropac Paris Marais, 7 Rue Debelleyme, 75003 Paris
Jenny Holzer – J’ai vu
Jenny Holzer transforms the Musée d’Orsay inside and out with J’ai vu, a museum-wide activation. Drawing on texts from the museum’s archives and the historical period represented in its collection, Holzer brings fragments of letters, literature, and political commentary to the museum’s façade, galleries, and public spaces. The project begins with light projections across the former railway station’s facade along the Seine, while inside, a site-specific LED installation streams colorful text through the museum.
Holzer’s metallic redaction paintings and newly created stone benches extend the project into the galleries, engaging with works from the museum’s collections and the architecture of Gae Aulenti. Outdoor projections will take place on several evenings around the October opening, with dates to be announced.
 what: J’ai vu by Jenny Holzer
when: October 20th, 2026 – February 21st, 2027; outdoor projections on selected evenings around the opening
where: Musée d’Orsay, Paris
Monet – Painting time
The Musée de l’Orangerie marks the centenary of Claude Monet’s death with Monet: Painting Time, an exhibition examining how the artist’s work evolved from capturing fleeting impressions to exploring the experience of duration. Nearly 40 paintings trace this progression, from his Impressionist works of the 1870s through the Haystacks, Poplars, and Rouen Cathedral series to the Water Lilies that occupied him until his death in 1926.
The exhibition brings together works from the Musée d’Orsay and Musée Marmottan Monet, alongside loans from French and international collections. Its final section focuses on the Nymphéas, connecting the series to the Musée de l’Orangerie’s permanent panoramic installation, which Monet conceived as an immersive environment.
 what: Monet: Painting Time
when: September 30th, 2026 – January 25th, 2027
where: Musée de l’Orangerie, Paris
Simone Fattal and Kerry James Marshall at Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris
The Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris hosts two major solo exhibitions this fall, bringing together more than five decades of work by Simone Fattal and over four decades of painting by Kerry James Marshall. The exhibitions offer two distinct approaches to history, memory, identity, and representation, spanning painting, sculpture, ceramics, collage, drawing, and installation.
Simone Fattal: Des villes au fond d’un lac brings together around 100 works from across the Lebanese-American artist’s career, from her early landscape paintings to her ceramics and collages. Τhe exhibition groups works around recurring ideas and forms, including Fattal’s engagement with literature, archaeology, mythology, and the Mediterranean. Her ceramic figures draw on ancient Mesopotamian and Greek epics, while later paintings and collages return to landscape, nature, memory, and personal experience.
Kerry James Marshall: The Histories is the artist’s first exhibition in France and brings together 70 works, including eight new paintings made specifically for the exhibition. Organized across eleven chronological and thematic groups, the presentation traces Marshall’s ongoing engagement with the representation of Black life, from early paintings of the 1980s and works addressing the Middle Passage to scenes of everyday life, portraits of historical figures, and later paintings that revisit the traditions of Western art history.
what: Simone Fattal: Des villes au fond d’un lac and Kerry James Marshall: The Histories

Bourse de Commerce – Pinault Collection – ‘Remember Me’
For Remember Me, the Pinault Collection brings around 700 photographs by more than 70 artists to the Bourse de Commerce, drawing from its holdings of more than 8,000 photographic prints. Marking the bicentenary of photography, the exhibition traces the history of the medium through works ranging from Gustave Le Gray and Dorothea Lange to Cindy Sherman and Wolfgang Tillmans. Curator Matthieu Humery organizes the exhibition as an open-ended sequence of correspondences around themes including seriality, composition, portraiture, and photography’s own disappearance. Memory provides a connecting thread, with historical images placed alongside contemporary works that reinterpret, echo, or disrupt them.

Fondation Louis Vuitton – Gustave Fayet
Fondation Louis Vuitton features Gustave Fayet: Collector – Designer, bringing together more than 255 works from Fayet’s dispersed collection alongside 375 of his own creations. Spanning painting, ceramics, textiles, furniture, rugs, wallpaper, and books, the exhibition examines how collecting and making were closely connected in the work of the French collector, artist, and designer.
The exhibition includes works by Vincent van Gogh, Paul Gauguin, Odilon Redon, Edgar Degas, Paul Cézanne, Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Berthe Morisot, Pierre Bonnard, Edouard Vuillard, and Henri Matisse. A second section focuses on Fayet’s own decorative practice, including ceramics, watercolors, pattern designs, rugs, and restored textiles and garments.
Among the highlights are Van Gogh’s Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear, three major paintings by Gauguin, and Odilon Redon’s monumental decorative panels Day, Night, and Silence, originally created for Fayet’s Abbaye de Fontfroide. Designed by Robert Carsen, the exhibition occupies all spaces of the Fondation Louis Vuitton and unfolds across 28 sections, presenting Fayet not only as a collector but also as a designer, patron, entrepreneur, and advocate for modern art.

Grand Palais – Cezanne et nous
The Grand Palais presents Cezanne et nous, an exhibition tracing Paul Cézanne’s influence from the late 19th century to the present through nearly 180 works. Bringing together artists including Paul Gauguin, Henri Matisse, Pablo Picasso, Piet Mondrian, Joan Mitchell, Bridget Riley, and Peter Doig, the exhibition examines how successive generations have interpreted, appropriated, and challenged Cézanne’s approach to painting.
The exhibition follows Cézanne’s growing influence from the artists and collectors who discovered his work in Paris in the late 1880s through the avant-garde movements of the 20th century. His interest in the relationship between painting and reality became a point of reference for both lyrical and geometric abstraction, as artists repeatedly revisited his formal language and ideas.
