Trump ‘really mad’ at Zelensky – media
US President Donald Trump is furious with Vladimir Zelensky over Kiev’s continued attacks on Russian oil refineries, with Washington reportedly threatening to cut off weapons supplies and intelligence sharing unless Ukraine stops the strikes, according to Axios and the Financial Times.
The confrontation comes after Trump struck a diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease a global fuel shortage that has sent American energy prices soaring.
Kiev has continued to target Russian refining facilities despite repeated warnings, with Trump accusing Zelensky of deliberately hurting American consumers and farmers while refusing opportunities to end the conflict.
“Trump is really mad. He feels Zelensky is taking the US for granted,” a White House official told Axios on Sunday. The source argued that Kiev’s attacks on Russian refineries are doing more damage to its relationship with Washington than to Russia.
US officials contacted Kiev and several European capitals over the weekend, threatening to suspend intelligence sharing and the NATO-backed Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) mechanism, through which European countries purchase American weapons for Ukraine, according to the Financial Times, which cited officials familiar with the discussions.
Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner also reportedly warned Ukrainian representatives during talks in Miami on Friday that Washington could stop sharing intelligence if Kiev continues to ignore the president’s demands, according to a Ukrainian official cited by Axios.
A US official, however, denied making direct threats, saying the negotiators instead reminded Kiev of Washington’s extensive military and intelligence support and urged it to stop taking actions that hurt American consumers.
The confrontation has threatened to derail broader negotiations aimed at ending the Ukraine conflict. Witkoff and Kushner have reportedly put their planned trip to Moscow on hold until Kiev and its leading European backers clarify whether they are prepared to support a unified peace proposal.
Trump reached a diesel deal with Putin on Friday after Zelensky ignored at least half a dozen requests to stop striking Russian refineries, according to earlier Axios reporting. The US Treasury subsequently eased sanctions on Russian diesel exports until April 2027, while Moscow pledged substantial fuel deliveries to help alleviate global shortages.
Zelensky called the move a “weak decision,” arguing that the agreement will provide Russia with additional revenue. Trump hit back, accusing the Ukrainian leader of creating problems for the world and suggesting that it is time for Ukraine to elect a new leader capable of reaching a deal.
On Sunday, Trump unexpectedly announced that Moscow and Kiev agreed to an immediate ceasefire covering attacks on energy infrastructure. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social.
The announcement caught Kiev by surprise, with Zelensky saying it “was news for me.” Moscow has also yet to confirm the agreement.
A White House official described the proposed agreement as a “refinery for refinery” arrangement, under which both sides would stop attacking oil refineries, but not necessarily other energy infrastructure, according to Axios. Kiev has said the deal would disproportionately benefit Russia, since Ukraine has only one largely nonfunctional refinery and fully relies on imported fuel.

Officials said the redeveloped Huanggang port’s opening went smoothly on Monday morning, with Chief Secretary Eric Chan expecting a relatively quiet first day so staff can prepare to handle more travellers in future.
Speaking to reporters, Chan said he doesn't expect the port to be too busy on the day of its opening, which will give staff time to familiarise themselves with operations at the facility.
"There’s a reason we chose today to open. The National Day holiday has just ended. Today, we believe there will be fewer visitors, so everyone has time to get familiar with the operations. We hope that by the time the next peak arrives, our colleagues will be fully used to it. That’s the best approach," he said.
Chan added that if the new "collaborative inspection and joint clearance" model works well, the government will consider extending it to other border checkpoints.
Secretary for Security Chris Tang said more than 5,000 people used the redeveloped Huanggang port in the first two hours after it opened at 6.30am –  a 60 percent increase compared with before its renovation. 
Nearly 1,000 vehicles also passed through, up 30 percent. 
He said all the self-service "collaborative inspection" channels are working normally, and passengers can go straight through without waiting. 
As for vehicles using the joint one-stop lane, waiting times are under five minutes, he added. 
Tang said a joint command centre set up with Shenzhen authorities will help keep operations running smoothly on both sides of the border.
"For the joint operation room between Shenzhen and Hong Kong authorities, we will operate as long as it’s necessary, in particular during high peak season, for example on weekends or during the Apec conference. We’ll ensure that we’ll have sufficient manpower... We are ready to take the challenge," he said.
Transport chief Mable Chan said public transport carried more than 3,000 people to and from Huanggang port in the first two hours of operations.
The secretary for transport and logistics said contingency plans are in place ahead of the travel rush expected over the upcoming Chung Yeung Festival long weekend.
"We will not underestimate the challenge to be brought about in the coming long weekend. So, we have already agreed with the police to arrange a public transport cover area, which is very near to this new Huanggang boundary control point," she said.
"We can arrange some emergency and contingency arrangements and stacking of franchised buses, minibuses and even taxis in the buffer area. We can accommodate around 200 vehicles there."

El Nino sets temperature record in key Pacific zone: EU monitor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
02:40:00 UTC
11:40:00 KST

El Nino sets temperature record in key Pacific zone: EU monitor
PARIS – An intensifying El Nino broke a temperature record in a key zone of the Pacific in September, the EU’s climate monitor said on Oct 12, in another sign the weather pattern is gaining exceptional strength.
Global forecasters have been warning for months that the El Nino in 2026 will likely become the strongest ever observed and the latest record has tumbled even before the episode’s expected peak later in 2026.
The warming phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino raises sea temperatures in the tropical Pacific, triggering changes in weather that can increase the risk of drought and flooding, and exacerbate man-made global warming.
The Copernicus Climate Change Service said sea surface temperatures in a tell-tale El Nino monitoring region of the Pacific, known as Nino3.4, had reached an “all-time high” of 29.70 deg C in September.
This exceeded the peak temperatures of previously strong El Nino events of 1982/1983, 1997/1998 and 2015/2016, “underscoring the exceptional intensity of the current El Nino”, the EU monitor said.
But in a statement to AFP, Copernicus said it “cannot yet say that the current El Nino is the strongest ever recorded”.
As climate change raises ocean temperatures, it can make recent El Nino events appear stronger than past ones, complicating historical comparisons.
Copernicus said it had adopted a new index, which accounts for the warming of tropical oceans, that suggested the current event is not yet stronger than past ones.
But the values observed in September “point to an already exceptionally strong El Nino, especially given that the event has not yet reached its peak”, Copernicus told AFP.
Not all forecasters use the same scale to interpret El Nino.
On Oct 9, Japan’s weather agency said that El Nino conditions had reached their “strongest intensity on record”, with temperatures in the phenomenon’s monitoring area 4 deg C above normal.
Record ocean temperatures
As El Nino gathers strength, global average sea surface temperatures hit a record 21.05 deg C for September, topping the previous high of 20.92 deg C for the same month in 2023, according to Copernicus.
Overall, the world experienced its second-hottest September on record, with surface air temperatures averaging 16.27 deg C, the EU service said.
September was 1.63 deg C hotter than the pre-industrial average, a period defined as 1850-1900.
Nations agreed at the 2015 UN climate talks in Paris to keep global warming “well below” 2 deg C above pre-industrial levels, while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 deg C, in order to limit the effects of climate change.
But the United Nations declared in September that the long-term 1.5 deg C target would be missed in a matter of years.
“We are in a new run of months above 1.5 deg C, and with a strong El Nino still intensifying it is likely to last into 2027,” Copernicus director Carlo Buontempo said in a statement.
“Crossing the Paris Agreement’s long-term limit is only a matter of time. How far we overshoot, and for how long, is still up to us,” he said.
Scientists say it is crucial to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels to limit the period of “overshoot” above 1.5 deg C and bring temperatures back down as quickly as possible.
Experts have warned that this El Nino would likely push global temperatures to a new record in 2027.
El Nino warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.
It typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months. AFP

North Korea fires missiles towards sea, escalating tensions on Korean Peninsula (Reuters image)
North Korea fired multiple ballistic missiles towards its eastern waters on Monday, South Korea’s military said, as Pyongyang continued its weapons testing amid heightened tensions and a prolonged freeze in diplomatic engagement.South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said the missiles were launched from an area near the North Korean capital, Pyongyang. Japan’s Defence Ministry detected at least two missiles and assessed that they had landed in waters outside the country’s exclusive economic zone.South Korea’s presidential office condemned the repeated launches, saying they violated United Nations Security Council resolutions and urging Pyongyang to stop such activities immediately.The latest launches came days after South Korea flight-tested its first domestically developed hypersonic weapon on Friday. Designed to travel at least five times the speed of sound and evade missile defence systems, the weapon was described by President Lee Jae Myung as an important step towards strengthening the country’s conventional defence capabilities.North Korea has intensified its weapons development as leader Kim Jong Un seeks to expand the country’s arsenal of nuclear-capable systems.
On October 3, Pyongyang conducted a test of what it described as a hypersonic intermediate-range missile designed to penetrate missile defence systems in South Korea and Japan.The country has also carried out missile tests and live-fire drills and commissioned a new warship, underscoring Kim’s push to strengthen its military capabilities despite repeated US and South Korean offers to resume diplomatic engagement.Tensions on the Korean Peninsula have also been aggravated by a series of land mine explosions near the heavily militarised inter-Korean border last month that injured three South Korean soldiers. South Korea’s military and the US-led United Nations Command concluded that the blasts were caused by mines planted by North Korea. Pyongyang has denied responsibility and dismissed Seoul’s demands for an apology.
Kim has halted diplomatic engagement and cooperation with South Korea in recent years, describing the neighbouring country as a permanent enemy. Nuclear negotiations with Washington have also remained stalled since 2019, when talks broke down during US President Donald Trump’s first term.Kim has so far rejected Trump’s overtures to revive dialogue. Pyongyang has demanded that Washington abandon what it calls its “hostile” policy and drop denuclearisation demands as a precondition for negotiations.The impasse has complicated Lee’s efforts to pursue engagement with North Korea. While advocating dialogue and adopting a more conciliatory tone, the South Korean president has also called for stronger conventional defence capabilities and reduced reliance on the United States.Washington unilaterally scaled back a major military exercise with South Korea in August, with Trump citing his “very good relationship” with Kim.

SYDNEY, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Authorities on Monday declared an extreme fire risk across Sydney due to forecast high temperatures and dry lightning storms.
The Rural Fire Service in the state of New South Wales (NSW) on Monday implemented a total fire ban for Greater Sydney and the neighboring Greater Hunter region, urging residents to take immediate action to protect their lives and property.
The Bureau of Meteorology forecast that the maximum temperature would reach 35 degrees Celsius in central Sydney on Monday afternoon, with temperatures of up to 37 degrees Celsius forecast for the city's western suburbs.
"Gusty winds from the Outback will blow across Sydney today, bringing dry desert air, and pushing temperatures into the mid or even upper 30s," the weather bureau said.
"If any fires start in the conditions, they can spread quickly and be very hard to contain."
Rural Fire Service Commissioner Trent Curtin told Australian Broadcasting Corporation radio that the conditions would be exacerbated by possible severe thunderstorms forecast to hit large parts of the state.
He said that the storms were not expected to bring much rainfall and that fires ignited by dry lightning could be a problem for authorities. ■

Feature: Zheng Qinwen rediscovers inner fire with historic China Open triumph
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:31:22 CST
11:31:22 KST

by sportswriters Li Chunyu, Wang Chunyan and Hu Jiali
BEIJING, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Sealing victory with an ace, home favorite Zheng Qinwen claimed her maiden WTA 1000 title at the China Open on Sunday, becoming the first Chinese player to win the tournament's women's singles crown amid roaring cheers on Diamond Court.
Known as "Queen Wen," Zheng defeated Russia's 19-year-old Mirra Andreeva 7-5, 6-4 to complete a remarkable comeback from injury.
Dressed in a red gown at her post-match press conference, the Olympic champion summed up her triumph in a few words: "I found my inner fire back."
As her winning ace landed, Zheng sank to the court in celebration, recalling the moment she captured Olympic gold on the red clay of Roland Garros at Paris 2024.
But the journey between those two moments of glory had been anything but smooth.
"I know how much I can inspire people after winning the Olympic gold. I keep trying to reach the best version of myself, but the injury changed my momentum," said Zheng, who reached the semifinals of the 2024 China Open.
The former world No. 4 underwent elbow surgery in July 2025 after a first-round exit at Wimbledon, beginning a frustrating period of recovery marked by setbacks and uncertainty.
"Sooner or later, I would have to go through this kind of surgery. But because of a lack of understanding of recovery, not enough visits to doctors or receiving advice from different doctors, I was making some wrong choices," she said.
Just over two months after surgery, Zheng returned to competition at the 2025 China Open, only to withdraw in the third round.
"I was really rushed. I wanted to play the matches, and my doctors told me I was able to play in those matches. But after these tournaments, the condition worsened, which took me longer to recover. This is a good lesson for me," Zheng reflected.
The prolonged absence brought pressure and doubts over whether she could regain the form that had made her one of China's brightest sporting stars.
Yet Zheng refused to let outside voices distract her, gradually discovering that the difficult period had also offered an opportunity for personal growth.
"The biggest takeaway is that lows are not necessarily bad. I rediscovered myself to see my shortcomings in skills and weaknesses of personality. Being positive every day is difficult. When I was in tough moments, I had an extra energy to make a breakthrough. The lows actually helped me improve," she said.
After falling outside the world's top 100 earlier this year, Zheng began her resurgence at the US Open, where she reached the quarterfinals as a qualifier.
Returning to Beijing, she strung together seven consecutive victories to make history on home soil.
"To play in China is like playing the fifth Grand Slam for me. They are the same important. I want to perform super well in front of the home crowd. This brings me extra pressure, but also helps me to put the efforts on court," she said.
The tournament also brought moments of personal celebration.
On October 1, China's National Day, Zheng wore red as she defeated compatriot Shi Han, explaining afterward that "red brings energy and power."
On Thursday, she celebrated her 24th birthday in Beijing wearing a blue-purple gown reminiscent of a wedding dress. Three days later, the China Open trophy arrived as a belated birthday gift.
"Now, at 24, I've become more mature. I am mentally more stable than I used to be. When I am making choices on and off the court, I am more clear-minded," she said.
"I want to be a more aggressive player. It has always been my dream and ambition."
Despite her latest achievement, Zheng says there is still more to come.
"If not for the surgery, I could keep going higher. The surgery stopped my progress somehow. I have to start from zero again. I really want to see what I can do in the future," she said.
Having endured months of uncertainty, Zheng said the setbacks had given her a deeper appreciation of every victory.
"There have been many chapters going through this journey. I just didn't expect that the lows this time continued that long. That is why I treasure the opportunities now. I know how much effort I have made behind each win."
For the newly crowned China Open champion, the journey is far from over.
"Honestly, I'm eager to know what's going to come next in my career," she said. "Tennis is a beautiful sport. I don't want to have a regret the day that I retire from tennis."
And as "Queen Wen" looked ahead to the next chapter, she had one reminder for herself:
"Be humble, keep my head up. Don't let the crown drop." ■

Long March Origin choir carries forward Red Army spirit
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:31:19 CST
11:31:19 KST

Zou Weimin (1st L), the director of the Long March Origin choir, conducts a performance at a middle school in Yudu County, east China's Jiangxi Province, Sept. 3, 2026. This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March. As one of its important starting points, Yudu County in east China's Jiangxi Province, a place best known as the starting point of the Long March by the Central Red Army, the historic military maneuver in modern Chinese history, has become more than a place of remembrance.
It was from Yudu that more than 80,000 Red Army soldiers crossed the Yudu River and began the Long March in 1934, the roughly 12,500-kilometer trek later described by American journalist Harrison Salisbury as "a great human epic."
On the stone tablet in front of the memorial museum of the Central Red Army's departure for the Long March here in Yudu, three Chinese characters meaning "Long March Origin" are engraved. The "Long March Origin" not only indicates that this place was the starting point of the important strategic transfer of the Red Army at that time, but also carries the profound understanding of the Long March spirit by the people of Yudu to this day.
You can see the words "Long March Origin" frequently in Yudu, and the Long March Origin choir is a prominent presence.
In this red revolutionary land of Yudu, almost everyone can share family stories connected to the Red Army's Long March. The Long March Origin choir, established in 2010, is composed of over 100 descendants of Red Army soldiers from all walks of life in the county. Over these years, they have not only performed the "Suite of Songs on the Long March" in Yudu and across Jiangxi in their spare time, but also carried forward the spirit of the Long March along the Long March route with their songs.
The choir's first performance was staged on June 30, 2011, which was dedicated to the 90th anniversary of the founding of the Communist Party of China. So far the choir has performed over 730 charity performances. "We hope that the choir will complete 1,000 performances by the 100th anniversary of the victory of the Long March," said Zou Weimin, the director of the choir. (Xinhua/Wang Jingqiang)

Brazil's Lula seeks to rally nonvoters ahead of presidential runoff
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
10:31:15 CST
11:31:15 KST

SAO PAULO, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on Sunday urged his supporters to reach out to voters who abstained from the Oct. 4 first-round election as he seeks reelection in the presidential runoff scheduled for Oct. 25.
"We have an obligation to talk to people who think they no longer have the right to vote," Lula told a rally in Sao Paulo, calling on supporters to encourage those who sat out the first round to cast their ballots in the runoff.
In the first round, Flavio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party won 47.03 percent of the valid votes, ahead of Lula of the Workers' Party, who garnered 45.16 percent. The abstention rate reached 21.08 percent, the highest since 1998, with about 33.4 million eligible voters staying away from the polls.
According to the organizers, the rally brought together political leaders, government officials and representatives of organizations involved in education, science and technology.
In his speech, Lula outlined priorities for a possible new term, including professional training in artificial intelligence, development of the digital industry, the energy transition and public security reform to combat organized crime.
Meanwhile, Flavio Bolsonaro also campaigned in Sao Paulo on Sunday, meeting with mayors and reelected Sao Paulo Governor Tarcisio de Freitas to consolidate political support ahead of the runoff.
A Datafolha poll released Thursday put Bolsonaro at 49 percent and Lula at 45 percent, a result within the survey's two-percentage-point margin of error. Another 5 percent of respondents said they intended to cast blank or invalid ballots, while 1 percent remained undecided.
Since Brazil resumed direct presidential elections in 1989, no candidate who finished second in the first round has gone on to win the runoff. The 1.87-percentage-point gap between Bolsonaro and Lula in this year's first round was the narrowest recorded during that period. ■

Hurricane Simon weakens to Category 3 as rains flood Mexico's Pacific coast
MANZANILLO, Mexico Oct 11 - Hurricane Simon weakened to a Category 3 storm on Sunday as it moved parallel to Mexico's Pacific coast, bringing strong winds and heavy rain that flooded homes.
The storm, packing maximum sustained winds of 125 mph (205 kph), was located about 110 miles (175 km) west-northwest of the port city of Manzanillo at 6 p.m. (0000 GMT Monday), the U.S. National Hurricane Center (NHC) said.
"Additional weakening is forecast but Simon is still expected to be a strong hurricane as it passes near the coast of west-central Mexico tonight," the forecaster's advisory said.
Simon was moving northwest at 5 mph (7 kph) and was expected to move farther offshore on Monday before turning back toward Mexico's coast on Wednesday, it added.
In Manzanillo, residents waded through flooded streets on Sunday morning as soldiers helped families remove water from their homes after the storm brought heavy rain overnight.
"The beds, the refrigerators, the stoves, all the furniture got wet. The whole house flooded," Cecilia Palomar told Reuters outside her home.
"My mother doesn't want to leave. We took her to my brother's, to higher ground. She's an elderly woman, but she doesn't want to leave. She doesn't want to be away from her home."
Hurricane conditions were likely already occurring within the hurricane warning area and were expected to spread northward overnight, the NHC said.
Simon was forecast to bring an additional 2 to 4 inches (50 to 100 mm) of rain to parts of Colima, Jalisco, Nayarit and Sinaloa through early Thursday, with isolated areas receiving up to 8 inches more.
Total rainfall from the storm could reach 30 inches in parts of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco, raising the risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides, particularly in mountainous areas, the NHC said. Dangerous storm surge and destructive waves were also expected along parts of the coast.
Mexican authorities placed 28 municipalities across Jalisco and Colima under the highest cyclone alert level, while another 93 municipalities were under high alert, according to civil protection bulletins.
Puerto Vallarta International Airport temporarily closed, while authorities suspended non-essential activities and opened emergency shelters in threatened coastal communities.
Earlier on Sunday, President Claudia Sheinbaum urged residents of coastal communities in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to remain indoors as the storm, then a Category 4 hurricane, approached the coast.
On Saturday, residents in Manzanillo had appeared largely calm despite the approaching storm, with some businesses boarding up storefronts and civil protection personnel closing beaches and urging people to stay away from the shore.
The storm comes days after Hurricane Polo struck Mexico's Baja California Peninsula as a Category 2 hurricane, knocking down trees and power poles and flooding streets. REUTERS

New York’s notorious Rikers jail awaits elusive closure

New York’s notorious Rikers jail awaits elusive closure
NEW YORK – New York’s notorious Rikers Island jail, long criticised for unsanitary and violent conditions, will miss a deadline for the vast complex to close down, prompting disappointment from activists.
The jail, which opened in 1932 and has counted John Lennon’s killer Mark David Chapman, rapper Tupac Shakur, and Sex Pistols musician Sid Vicious among its residents, was due to shutter by 2027.
That was a pledge by former mayor Bill de Blasio, responding to persistent issues ranging from staff shortages, broad drug use and broken cell doors and windows.
He promised to replace Rikers with smaller facilities, but their construction is lagging behind schedule.
Lauren Stossel, a former psychiatrist at the jail who now sits on New York City’s independent Board of Correction, has raised several concerns about the jail.
“Conditions generally, I think, are very poor,” she told AFP, adding that violence is “rampant”.
Rikers, which sits on the East River between the Bronx and Queens boroughs, primarily holds people who are awaiting trial in New York, as was the case for disgraced producer Harvey Weinstein.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who took office in 2026, has strongly supported closing Rikers, but has acknowledged the city will not meet the 2027 deadline.
‘Hopeful’
“We are very focused on advancing the closure of Rikers Island on the fastest timeline possible,” said Dana Kaplan, who is overseeing the Mayor’s efforts to shutter the jail.
“This can’t just be a project that’s about replacing one set of buildings with the other. It really is about a transformational vision of our city’s pretrial justice system.”
“We see the closure of Rikers Island as part of shutting the door on what has been a stained history in our city of a correctional system that does nothing to serve the people in its custody or the staff that work there every day,” Kaplan said.
The first calls to close Rikers date back to the 1960s, driven by dangers for both inmates and correction officers – three of whom were injured by an inmate in early September.
Politicians and public opinion rallied to the cause in the 2010s, partly due to fierce campaigning by families and former inmates.
Darren Mack, who was once held at Rikers and co-founded the Freedom Agenda criminal justice non-profit, pointed to the “human cost and the financial cost” of the jail.
The Vera Institute of Justice non-profit, which wants to see Rikers closed, has attributed 48 deaths in New York City jails from 2022 to 2025, while Rikers has an annual operating budget of nearly US$3 billion (S$3.84 billion).
Insha Rahman, president of Vera, said both the Covid-19 pandemic and the previous administration of mayor Eric Adams produced delays in shutting down Rikers.
But, she added, “I feel more hopeful today about the progress and the opportunity in front of us than I have at any other moment”.
Until the jail can be closed, activists and city officials are calling for basic repairs such as to hundreds of cell doors that are broken.
They also want better social and educational programmes, as well as a reduction in the inmate population from over 6,500 to 4,000 – driven by quicker court proceedings and transferring people to other units. AFP

Lin, ranked No. 6 in the world, lost 7-11, 9-11, 11-7, 11-8, 11-5, 7-11, 9-11 to Matsushima, who had recently reached the top of the world rankings. The result gave Matsushima his second men's singles title at a WTT Grand Smash event.

Matsushima took the opening game after recovering from Lin’s fightback to level the score at 7-7. He then won a closely contested second game to establish a 2-0 lead.
Lin responded by changing the pace and direction of his shots while using his trademark backhand flicks to disrupt Matsushima’s attacks. He won the next three games.
Matsushima fought back in the sixth game, stringing together four consecutive points after the score reached 6-6 to force a deciding game.
In the seventh, Matsushima surged to a 6-0 lead. Lin mounted a late comeback but couldn't close the gap, and Matsushima won 11-9 to clinch the title.
Before the tournament, Lin had won six of his seven previous meetings with Matsushima. However, Matsushima defeated him in their most recent encounter at the ITTF World Cup earlier this year, per CNA.
The result marks Lin's second runner-up finish in a WTT Grand Smash men's singles event this year, reaching the final of the Singapore Smash in March, where he lost in straight games to China's Wang Chuqin.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked four Chinese military aircraft, six naval vessels, and three official ships around Taiwan between 6 a.m. on Sunday and 6 a.m. on Monday.
The four People’s Liberation Army aircraft entered the country’s northern, central, and southwestern air defense identification zone, according to the MND.
In response, Taiwan deployed aircraft, naval ships, and coastal-based missile systems to monitor PLA activity.
So far this month, Taiwan has tracked Chinese aircraft 67 times and ships 125 times. Since September 2020, China has increased its use of gray zone tactics by incrementally increasing the number of military aircraft and naval vessels operating around the country.
Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

Saudi Arabia says 1 dead, 11 injured in latest attack on Riyadh airport
Sunday’s strike on King Khalid International airport kills a Pakistani national.
A projectile has struck Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International airport, killing one person and injuring 11, according to the country’s civil aviation authority.
The General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) identified the deceased in Sunday’s attack as a Pakistani resident and said the injured were transferred to several hospitals for medical care.
The strike on terminals 3 and 4, which serve domestic flights, occurred a day after a Houthi missile hit the airport, killing 12 people and wounding more than 300, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.
India’s embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday due to injuries sustained in Saturday’s attack, bringing the death toll to 13.
Following Sunday’s attack, GACA said damage assessments and safety inspections of the airport were under way.
A witness on board a taxiing aircraft at the airport told the Reuters news agency that a projectile struck the tarmac next to several parked planes at about 8:30pm (17:30 GMT) on Sunday, causing a fire.
The witness said the aircraft returned to the gate, where the passengers disembarked and were told to leave.
The Riyadh airport has been struck four times in the past five days. Houthi attacks on King Khalid airport on Thursday killed at least three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, according to GACA.
The airport has been closed since Saturday’s attack, which was the deadliest in the country since the US-Israel war on Iran began in late February.
The Houthis claimed responsibility for the strikes before Sunday’s.
The airport attacks have escalated the war in Yemen and threaten to draw in the US military. US President Donald Trump says he is weighing whether to join the fight against the Houthis.
The escalation puts further pressure on global oil supplies and prices, as well as on commercial shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb strait off the Yemeni coast, a crucial alternative waterway to the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump had said he intends to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who is seeking help against the Houthis, but there were no signs on Sunday that the US president had followed up on his claim.
There are fears that US intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through Bab al-Mandeb, further restricting the flow of oil out of the Gulf.
The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month. The Saudi-led coalition, backing forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government, has been trying to seize them back.

Start-ups are betting on AI to predict the future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
02:10:00 UTC
11:10:00 KST

Start-ups are betting on AI to predict the future
- Startups are using AI to make future forecasts on markets, politics and culture, and some models now match or beat top human “superforecasters”.
- AI prediction tools have won competitions and helped users make big gains, while firms say they are already affecting trading and may soon dominate prediction markets.
- The technology is spreading into government, business, science and insurance, but experts warn that wider access could raise risks if countries like Russia or China build better systems.
AI generated
NEW YORK – Several start-ups are betting that they can leverage artificial intelligence to make better forecasts than even the most specialised experts when it comes to topics as varied as stock market movements, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz or how a Shakira song will perform on music charts.
By 2030, “we’re going to feel that what we were doing for our decision-making was complete Stone Age thinking”, Dan Schwarz, co-founder of the forecasting company FutureSearch, said.
AI forecasting models are already on a par with the best “superforecasters” – gifted individuals whose estimates are markedly superior to those of ordinary people – thanks to troves of data acquired from both public and private sources.
In early September, two AI models made history when they took the top spots in the Metaculus Cup, a competition among prediction champions, both human and non-human.
FutureSearch’s in-house human wizard, superforecaster Tom Liptay, is aware that “he’s not secure in his job” in the medium term, Schwarz said.
“He knows that these things are going to surpass him.”
Theo Summer, who co-founded Preseen with Veniamin Veselovsky, used AI tools to turn US$35 (S$44.80) into US$1.9 million in just seven months on the American prediction-making site Kalshi.
The idea is not to guarantee a result but to define a probability of occurrence, with the ability to cross-check assumptions related to several interconnected events – for example, changes in the price of oil and the war in the Middle East.
“Right now, the quickest buyers are normally the hedge funds, just because if they think they can make money off something, they can move pretty fast,” Veselovsky said.
Algorithms have shaped Wall Street for more than a decade, but the rise of AI forecasting is likely to further increase the automation of financial markets.
“It’s probably already having a small impact because we already have customers who use it when making trading decisions,” said Toby Shevlane, the co-founder of another forecasting start-up called Mantic.
Now-famous prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket, which are used by millions of Americans, are also becoming inundated by AI use.
It might soon be too late for retail investors, who do not have access to expensive AI tools, to profit on those types of consumer-oriented trading sites because “they will soon just be dominated by AI forecasting systems”, Veselovsky said.
Risk management
The most advanced models no longer just predict events, either.
They can also formulate their own questions about the future and then assign probabilities based on the different possible outcomes, Shevlane said.
Their sphere of influence is beginning to extend beyond finance, as well, with potential applications in government policy, corporate decision-making, scientific research, and insurance risk assessments.
Mantic provides a large American company with likely scenarios of regulatory developments in its sector and has also worked for the British government.
Companies “are interested in risks and how to monitor them”, Shevlane said.
Meanwhile, other customers might be more interested in medical research, particularly to help make decisions around which types of treatments would be best to fund, Schwarz said.
Widespread access to these types of tools can come with costs, though.
“I think that good can be derived from this,” Veselovsky said, but “I’m also a little bit scared because, you know, maybe Russia or China has better systems.” AFP

World leaders urged to ‘course correct’ as UN nature goals fall short
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
02:09:00 UTC
11:09:00 KST

World leaders urged to ‘course correct’ as UN nature goals fall short
- World leaders are being urged to “course correct” before COP17 in Yerevan, as the UN says nations are off-track on 2030 biodiversity goals.
- The 2022 nature pact set 23 targets, including cutting pollution and protecting 30% of land and oceans, but current pledges would reach only 27% of land and 12% of oceans.
- Money and subsidy reform are major problems, with countries far short of the US$200 billion yearly finance goal and the new Cali Fund raising only US$6,000 so far.
AI generated
PARIS – Nations are steeling themselves for a disappointing report card at October’s UN biodiversity summit, with governments falling short on their commitments to protect the plants, animals and ecosystems that sustain life on earth.
The so-called COP17 summit in Armenian capital Yerevan will be a reckoning for the nearly 200 nations that joined the landmark “Paris Agreement for Nature” in 2022 but have been slow to act on its objectives.
It set 23 targets for halting and reversing nature loss by 2030, including reducing pollution, protecting threatened species and conserving 30% of the world’s land and oceans.
But the world is off-track to meet these goals, according to a draft review by the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), which oversees the biennial international negotiations on protecting the natural world.
“COP17 comes at a critical moment,” An Lambrechts from Greenpeace International told AFP.
“The most important outcome from Yerevan must therefore be a clear course correction. Governments need to move beyond restating promises and agree on concrete actions.”
Astrid Schomaker, executive director of the UN biodiversity convention, told AFP that progress was being made and the 2030 goals were “still reachable – but only with significant change being made”.
This includes reducing incentives for politically sensitive industries like agriculture and fossil fuel production, areas where governments have made very little headway to date.
“Do I think we’re moving in the right direction? Yes, but way too slowly,” Schomaker said.
Around 10 heads of state are expected in Yerevan for a leaders’ summit on Oct 16 to start proceedings “and tell the negotiators to be ambitious and constructive” when talks formally begin on Oct 19, she said.
Money tensions
The nature summit comes weeks before the annual international climate negotiations, or COP31, in neighbouring Turkey, and is the first time nations have taken stock of progress since the biodiversity pact was adopted.
Drawing on national reports and other inputs, a “global review” of collective improvements and pitfalls is being finalised.
A draft scorecard published in July painted a mixed picture of progress.
Some countries have taken strides towards the “30x30“ conservation goal (protecting 30% of the earth’s land and waters by 2030), said Campaign for Nature in a September analysis.
But, taken together, government pledges would cover only 27% of land and inland waters by the end of this decade if enacted in full. For oceans, the figure would be just 12%.
Money is a major barrier to the success of the biodiversity goals and an expected source of tension at COP17.
Nations are lagging behind a pledge to raise US$200 billion (S$256 billion) a year for biodiversity by 2030 from public and private sources, including US$30 billion a year in international finance for developing countries.
Wealthy countries are under pressure to fill the ga,p but face their own budget challenges, making the issue politically fraught.
The United States, which is not a party to the biodiversity convention, is not involved in the talks.
“The more time you spend talking about funding, the less you talk about objectives,” said a French government official.
‘Unite and fight’
Attention at the Yerevan summit is expected to focus on how the private sector can make up the shortfall.
Under scrutiny will be the lacklustre performance of the Cali Fund, a milestone UN initiative launched in February 2025.
The fund aimed to raise US$1 billion a year from corporations for conservation in developing countries but so far has attracted just US$6,000.
“Everyone was hoping... this would be a game changer. And we continue to believe that it absolutely has the potential”, although corporate engagement had been “slower” than anticipated, said Schomaker.
Subsidy reform has also proved to be a roadblock, with barely any movement towards the 2030 goal of reducing nature-harmful incentives by US$500 billion a year.
For every dollar invested in protecting or restoring nature, about US$30 still goes into activities that degrade it, according to UN figures.
In October, more than 130 businesses and financial institutions – including Nestle and H&M Group – called on governments to reform incentives, citing US$2.6 trillion in annual public spending “that rewards practices depleting the soils, water and ecosystems”.
Guido Broekhoven from nature conservation organisation World Wildlife Fund International told AFP that repurposing subsidies must be “a matter of priority” at COP17.
Greenpeace’s Lambrechts said: “At a time when geopolitical tensions are putting multilateral cooperation under pressure, it’s even more important to show the world that our decision-makers can still be united in the fight for the survival of life on earth.” AFP

A new trend in nuclear energy: Squeezing more power out of old plants

WASHINGTON – Building a nuclear power plant is a long, hard slog. So lately, many companies are eyeing a faster, cheaper solution: Squeezing even more power out of old reactors that were built decades ago.
This process, known as a “power uprate”, involves upgrading key components inside nuclear plants such as controls, turbines or pumps so that they can generate more electricity.

The energy careers of senior Communist Party cadres have given them technical expertise, foresight and management skills
With the rising strategic significance of energy, especially due to the need to support China’s artificial intelligence (AI) development, members of the Communist Party’s 20th Central Committee with energy backgrounds – the country’s “movers and shakers” in this strategic sector – merit closer attention.
Among them are former or current power-company executives, petroleum managers, nuclear-safety officials and specialists in water administration. Many built their expertise over decades, establishing themselves as energy technocrats before taking on responsibilities beyond their original industries. Their biographies reveal a recurring route into political leadership – deep specialisation first and diversification of political experience later, highlighting the growing presence and power of this leadership cohort.
More experience, greater representation
Our data set identifies 34 energy sector members, including 21 full members and 13 alternates. They account for 10.2 per cent of the 205 full members, 7.6 per cent of the 171 alternates and 9 per cent of the combined membership. Three of them were elected to the Politburo in October 2022, representing 12.5 per cent of its 24 members. As of this year, their median ages are 64 among full members and 60 among alternates.
By October 2022, 29 of the 34 had at least 10 years of energy experience. This included 16 of the 21 full members. Nineteen had careers spanning 20 years or more.

No room for Jewish grief at Oct. 7 protests in New York City - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
01:57:29 UTC
10:57:29 KST

Over the last three years, Jews have wrestled with many questions about the Palestine solidarity movement that emerged with great force after Oct. 7, 2023. Is it simply a movement deeply critical of the State of Israel? Is its anti-Zionism intrinsically antisemitic? Can meaningful coalitions be built between the movement and peace-seeking Jews who remain connected to Israel?
On Wednesday night, the third anniversary of Hamas’ attacks on southern Israel and the war that followed, I came face to face with what I believe are the movement’s most extreme elements. What I saw was a form of political expression that had become indistinguishable from hatred. Progressives ignore this extremism at our peril.
I wasn’t planning to go to a protest. In fact, I chose to go to the Israelis for Peace vigil specifically because the poster said that no flags or signs would be allowed. I wanted a space to grieve the day without having to argue about it.
My first thought when I arrived at Union Square in Manhattan was: I’m in the wrong place. I saw a massive crowd rallying with Palestinian flags, bullhorns, and drums. I passed a minyan of anti-Zionist Neturei Karta members in kaffiyehs davening Ma’ariv, the evening prayer.
The protesters had shown up to protest the vigil. It’s worth pausing on that: They were there to protest the vigil. Masked people carrying signs decrying Israel, with Hamas and Hezbollah paraphernalia, were sitting in the neatly lined chairs prepared for mourners.
Protesters were there to rage
The vigil still went forward. But to get in, I needed an NYPD escort.
It was almost impossible to hear the speakers over the chanting crowd. The few words I heard from the mourners were desperate cries of grief and pleas for coexistence.
The speakers recited testimonies of victims murdered and brutalized at the Nova music festival and at kibbutzim in Israel’s Gaza envelope. Organizers read letters from survivors and their families: “If we want any path forward, how dare we not talk about the pain of both peoples at this moment?”
Yonatan Zeigen, son of the legendary Israeli peace activist Vivian Silver, who was murdered by Hamas at Kibbutz Be’eri, spoke about upholding his mother’s peace-building legacy, a legacy Hamas itself sought to desecrate.
Others shared testimony from Gazans about the devastation of the war on their family and community. Many speakers at the vigil used the word “genocide” to describe the war and registered their total opposition to it.
None of it mattered. The protesters weren’t there to listen. They were there to rage.
While the slogans have been reported elsewhere, they bear repeating.
“Brad Lander, you can’t hide, we charge you with genocide!” they shouted at the Democratic congressional candidate. To Mayor Zohran Mamdani, they yelled, “Zohran, you can’t hide, we charge you with genocide!”
The protesters called the mayor a “bootlicker,” asking, “Zohran, how many kids have you killed today?” and “How dare you call yourself a Muslim?” When an imam spoke at the vigil, I couldn’t hear what he said; the crowd erupted in chants of “Traitor! Traitor! Traitor!”
The mayor said nothing, holding his candle and looking at the protesters. I wondered what was going through his head. How did he feel hearing the chant he had once defended, “Globalize the intifada,” directed at him, and at the kinds of progressive American Jews and Israeli Jews he had made kosher with his presence at their vigil? What did the phrase even mean in this context?
Of course people shout at politicians. Social movements have used ugly rhetoric before, and they’ve always had their fringes. In the late 1980s, members of the AIDS activist group ACT UP interrupted Mass at St. Patrick’s Cathedral to protest the Catholic Church’s opposition to contraceptives and LGBT rights. During the Iraq War, people accused politicians of personal complicity in war crimes.
Space for all suffering from last three years, Jewish and Palestinian alike
But on Wednesday night, hundreds of people physically surrounded a group of speakers representing some of the most progressive voices in the Jewish community: leading rabbis and activists, American and Israeli. They were there to provide a space for all the suffering of the last three years, Jewish and Palestinian alike. The mob was there to quite literally scream at them. At that gathering, they seemed to be saying that only one kind of death was worthy of grief, and it wasn’t Jewish.
The ensuing silence about these protesters from many in this movement, including, prominently, Mamdani, contrasts with the willingness of many in the Jewish community who regularly and openly issue tokhachah (rebuke) to Jews in the Diaspora and in Israel whose words and actions we believe violate our moral commitments.
The implicit argument seems to be that acts undertaken in the name of Palestinian resistance are both necessary and beyond reproach when they come from the powerless, or those claiming to represent them.
Powerlessness does not absolve anyone
This is profoundly twisted moral logic. A group pursuing what it believes to be a righteous cause is not thereby exempt from the moral standards that apply to everyone else.
Powerlessness does not absolve anyone of the obligation to recognize the intrinsic dignity of other human beings. If it did, one would assume that anything stateless Jews did in the years after the Holocaust would be justified, a conclusion that the Palestine solidarity movement quite clearly rejects.
Anti-Zionists and Jews who maintain a connection to Israel often hold fundamentally different views about the conflict. Yet Mamdani, one of the world’s most prominent anti-Zionists, chose to attend a vigil mourning all those who have lost their lives on and since Oct. 7.
The protests that greeted the mayor revealed something more troubling than a failure to bridge political divides: an unwillingness to make room for Jewish grief.
Leaders in the Palestine solidarity movement should reckon with that failure. Those who seek a just and peaceful future for all the people living in the land between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea must be willing to challenge dehumanization within their own political movements.
Much of the media coverage from that night focused on what happened at the protest. There’s been less attention paid to how the vigil ended. I’m not sure if it was originally on the program, but Rabbi Amichai Lau-Lavie led the group in a recitation of Kaddish Yatom, the mourner’s prayer.
The Kaddish is commonly understood as a prayer for the dead. But the liturgy doesn’t explicitly mention mortality or comfort in grief. Instead, as Rabbi Elie Kaunfer argues, it gives voice to the experience of God’s absence. When we grieve, God can feel distant, and God’s presence in the world diminished. The liturgy responds with a collective prayer for the return of a God of compassion and justice.
Mourners typically recite the Kaddish in hushed tones. At the vigil, we chanted what was, by necessity, the loudest Kaddish Yatom I have ever heard. For a moment, holding those ancient Aramaic and Hebrew words, it felt possible to filter out the shrill screams and bullhorn sirens coming from behind us.
Protected by police barricades, we huddled together and prayed. It was a powerful Jewish counterprotest: No amount of suffering gives anyone permission to abandon humanity because we are, all of us, made in the image of the divine. In that moment, the God of compassion felt both very close and incredibly far away.
The author is a rabbinical student at the Jewish Theological Seminary.

We expect a person’s actions to follow from choices they have made. We do not always expect these…
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
01:42:33 UTC
10:42:33 KST

We expect a person’s actions to follow from choices they have made. We do not always expect these choices to be rational or good, but we do expect the person to understand that they have wilfully decided to pursue a particular course of action.
But sometimes the ability to choose is completely impaired by the physical circumstances of the body. In such a situation, a human being cannot choose to do anything and their actions are no different from those of a wild animal. There is no act of will here, as these actions are outside the realm of control and possibly even outside the realm of consciousness. If these actions are also harmful to the person or others, we might consider them a kind of natural disaster. Here the conditions of nature work to produce a particular outcome over which there is no possible control or decision.

One person was killed, and nearly a dozen were hurt in a new attack on Riyadh's international airport on Sunday, Saudi authorities reported, a day after a strike claimed by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
Saudi-led coalition forces in Yemen said an unidentified projectile had targeted Riyadh's international airport Terminal 4 on Sunday, causing a fire. Eleven people were wounded in addition to the fatality, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.
Coalition forces also said Saudi air defenses had intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of King Khalid International Airport. They later added that a drone had been intercepted and destroyed in the country's Eastern Province, and a ballistic missile launched towards Khamis Mushait had been intercepted. Emergency alerts were also issued in Abha, in the south, early on Monday, but the danger had since passed, the Saudi Civil Defense said.
The strikes have exposed vulnerabilities in Saudi defense capabilities as the kingdom wages an air campaign against the Houthis, who are fighting a ground war in Yemen against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.
Footage released by Saudi state television of the Saturday attack on the Riyadh airport showed scores of religious pilgrims lined up at a gate as they prepared to travel to Islam's two holiest sites. A bright orange flash sent people running in panic, while parts of the roof appeared to cave in. The airport was closed after the attack, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.
Houthis claim responsibility for attacks
In a televised speech on Sunday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed responsibility for Saturday's attack and said the group had also struck the airport in Dammam in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province and two facilities of Saudi oil giant Saudi Aramco.
The Saudi government's media office and Aramco did not respond to requests for comment.
The Saudi civil aviation authority confirmed the strike on Dammam's King Fahd International Airport late on Sunday, adding that "damage assessments and safety inspections of airport facilities are under way."
An eyewitness aboard a taxiing aircraft at Dammam told Reuters that around 8:30 p.m. (1730 GMT) on Sunday, they saw a projectile strike the tarmac beside several parked aircraft, causing a fire. The witness said the aircraft returned to the gate. Passengers disembarked and were told to leave.
Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 showed several delays and cancellations on Sunday for arrivals and departures at Dammam airport, the kingdom's third-largest.
The Houthis earlier on Sunday had renewed their warning against using Saudi airports. "We urge everyone to take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions," the group said.
Britain's embassy in Saudi Arabia, in a post on X, advised British citizens against all but essential travel to Jeddah, Dammam and all airports in the kingdom except the airport in Medina.
US aviation authorities issued a notice to US airlines to use caution while flying to or over the kingdom.
'Worst is yet to come,' Houthis warn
Saudi Arabia has recently stepped up its military involvement in Yemen, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a government counteroffensive after the Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.
The Houthis said on Sunday that Saudi Arabia carried out 124 air strikes in Yemen in the past 24 hours. "Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," Yemen's Houthi-run foreign ministry said in statements carried by Al Masirah television.
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war with Iran that the US and Israel launched in February.
In a Telegram post, Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said he told his Saudi counterpart that Tehran was ready to help facilitate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
Energy conference going ahead
A five-day conference of the international energy organization WPC Energy opened as planned on Sunday at a convention center about 10 km (6 miles) from the Riyadh airport, the Saudi energy ministry said.
A ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum also went ahead, according to a media advisory from the ministry. It was not clear which ministers attended.
Italy's energy minister, Gilberto Pichetto Fratin, whose country was co-hosting, had said on Friday he would participate remotely via video link.
German officials were trying to organize a return flight for economy minister Katherina Reiche. She was supposed to return to Berlin from Riyadh on Monday, but the ministry said her flight was likely unable to take off.
Separately, Saudi authorities announced that schools in Riyadh would shift in-person classes to remote learning from Sunday until Thursday.
Sunday's attack brought the death toll in attacks on Riyadh's airport to 18 for the week. In Saturday's attack, the dead included four Saudis while the remainder were foreign nationals, Saudi authorities said.

The hostage deal that never was: Netanyahu's political calculations and the price paid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
01:37:09 UTC
10:37:09 KST

July 2024 was a pivotal month in the war in Gaza. A deal agreed upon by all sides was on the table. 
Netanyahu had given his consent; Sinwar, under pressure from Qatar in Doha and from the IDF on the ground, had given his consent; control of the Philadelphi Corridor, which Netanyahu had presented as an existential issue, had been resolved through a creative arrangement involving sensors and an Egyptian commitment; the IDF was desperate for a respite; the Israeli negotiating team had thrown its weight behind the effort; and the Hostages and Missing Families Forum had mobilized to help. By July 27, it had all fallen apart.
Not all the details of the deal were made public. On its margins were several personal elements of public interest. To make it easier for Netanyahu to agree to the deal, the Hostages and Missing Families Forum approached Karim Khan, the prosecutor of the International Criminal Court in The Hague. Khan's role was to seek the cancellation of the request to the court to issue arrest warrants against Netanyahu and then-Defense Minister Yoav Gallant.
Such a possibility exists if a person suspected of war crimes is found to be working toward peace. Alongside the Israelis, a request has been made to the court to issue arrest warrants against Sinwar, Mohammed Deif and Ismail Haniyeh. For the sake of balance, the deal was supposed to cancel their warrants as well.
Why did Khan agree to remove the cloud hanging over Netanyahu and Gallant? An Israeli involved in the process points out that a different kind of cloud was hanging over Khan himself: A female employee of the court had accused him of sexual harassment. Khan assumed that an Israeli hand, perhaps the Mossad, was behind the complaint. If he freed Netanyahu and Gallant from their arrest warrants, the complaint would disappear in an instant.
Khan, who visited the communities near the Gaza border in early December 2023, agreed to hear more and more testimonies from survivors of the massacre. The Hostages and Missing Families Forum arranged to fly them to The Hague.
But the negotiations failed. They could not have succeeded because they contained an inherent flaw: Mossad head David Barnea, IDF hostage affairs chief Nitzan Alon and and Shin Bet head Ronen Bar, who led the Israeli negotiating team, saw every problem as an obstacle that needed to be overcome; Netanyahu saw every problem as a blessing, a gift that would spare him the need to reach an agreement.
In principle, Netanyahu and Hamas were playing the same game. He and they behaved like the groom in the old Jewish joke who demanded on his wedding night that the bride be stripped of all her clothes. Once she was undressed, he declared: "I don't like her nose."
The hostages paid the price, some with their lives, others with another year of terrible suffering in the tunnels.
Why does this matter now? Because it sheds light on the decision-making process of the outgoing government. At every stage of the negotiations, someone from Netanyahu's office made sure to secretly update Smotrich. He would burst into a meeting to which he had not been invited or call a news conference and threaten to bring down the government if an agreement was signed. Ben-Gvir would immediately follow with a similar threat.
Netanyahu would explain to the Americans that they had to understand: He did not have a majority in the Knesset to approve the agreement, and he could not allow his government to collapse.
As more details emerge from the three-year saga, it becomes increasingly clear that the recurring coalition crisis was a bluff, a performance staged for Israel's security chiefs and the Biden administration.
Smotrich would not have left the government in the middle of realizing his messianic vision in the West Bank. Ben-Gvir would not have left for the same reason a cat does not walk away from a bowl of cream, not while there is still something left to eat.
Netanyahu was not obeying them. He was using them.
If Smotrich and Ben-Gvir were not the reason the deal collapsed, what was? I can only speculate.
First, the timing. The proposed deal came too late for the hostages and their families, but too early for Netanyahu. He found it difficult to agree to a deal that would be interpreted as ending the war just nine months after the massacre. Israelis, including his own supporters, would have asked what had happened to total victory.
Second, the deal was too convenient for him. He would have struggled to explain how he had arranged a pardon for himself in The Hague alongside the murderers of October 7 and prosecutor Khan.
Third, the skies were clearing in America that July. Biden had been forced to abandon his bid for a second term, and Trump had agreed to reconcile with Netanyahu after two and a half years of estrangement.
Netanyahu was not about to put his name to a hostage deal that would strengthen Biden and Harris. By October 2025, with Trump in the White House, Netanyahu had no leverage left in America and no allies remaining. He was forced to say yes.
He can tell himself that waiting was worthwhile. In the intervening period, Sinwar, Deif and Haniyeh, his fellow subjects of arrest warrants in The Hague, were killed. Trump was elected president and agreed to strike Iran, and perhaps he will strike again in the future.
True, none of the war's objectives was achieved. True, Israel's standing in the world deteriorated dramatically. But why be petty?
"We will not surrender" is Likud's election slogan, accompanied by an AI-generated image of the leader looking to his right and slightly downward, toward Israelis stuck in traffic on the Ayalon Highway.
Netanyahu has traveled a long and bitter road from the promise of "total victory" in 2024 to the promise of "we will not surrender" in 2026. He promised a knockout and settled for a draw. And he dragged the country down with him every step of the way.

Integrating Solar Protection as an Envelope Strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
01:30:00 UTC
10:30:00 KST

Heat waves are becoming more and more frequent worldwide, prompting architects to reconsider how building envelopes are conceived and designed. The focus is no longer solely on limiting heat loss during the colder months, but also on controlling how much heat enters buildings during periods of intense solar radiation. By understanding solar shading as a design decision rather than a decorative or interior-conditioning element, it becomes part of passive energy-efficiency strategies that can contribute to thermal and visual comfort while reducing cooling demand.
Many decisions related to the thermal performance of buildings focused on retaining heat during the winter. However, the increasing frequency of extreme temperatures is shifting attention toward preventing overheating without compromising daylight, views, or connections to the outdoors. Buildings with large glazed surfaces, for example, require strategies to control solar radiation and prevent excessive heat gains. An office building with a glazed west-facing facade may experience its highest cooling demand between 3:00 and 7:00 p.m., when direct sunlight strikes the glass. With an integrated solar-shading strategy, this heat gain can be reduced before the HVAC system has to compensate for it.
Solar Shading as a Design Decision
Considering solar shading from the earliest stages of a project means moving beyond the idea of treating it as a complementary element added once the facade has been resolved. By coordinating orientation, the proportion of glazed surfaces, glass and facade types, fabric selection, and system installation, each design decision influences the building's energy performance by changing how it receives, filters, reflects, or transmits solar radiation.
This perspective also reframes one of the questions that can guide the design process. Instead of asking how to remove heat once it enters a building, the more fundamental question is how to keep it out in the first place. Exterior shading systems intercept solar radiation before it reaches the glass, thereby reducing the thermal load that the HVAC system would otherwise have to compensate for. This is illustrated by an energy simulation conducted by Bandalux using ESBO software for a 9-square-meter room with a south-facing orientation in Madrid. With 3.6 square meters of glazing, Type C glass, Screen 351 Ebony technical fabric, and an exterior shading system, the simulation achieved up to a 70% reduction in energy consumption associated with HVAC.
Beyond Temperature: Designing for Comfort
But solar shading is not solely a matter of thermal performance. Its impact extends to visual comfort, glare control, the use of natural light, visual connections to the outdoors, and the overall quality of interior spaces. Designing a solar-shading strategy means finding a balance and recognizing that, beyond exterior solutions, interior systems can also provide benefits. According to Bandalux analyses, a white interior fabric can reduce air-conditioning energy consumption by up to 30%, while the air-cell structure of Cellular shades can improve insulation in both summer and winter.
A fabric with a lower openness factor can limit solar radiation and glare while increasing privacy and thermal comfort. Conversely, a higher openness factor allows more natural light to enter while maintaining a more direct visual connection with the surrounding landscape. The choice cannot be separated from the building's orientation, climate, program, and the specific conditions of each facade. Color and reflectance also influence this performance. In exterior systems, dark fabrics can absorb a greater portion of solar radiation before it reaches the glazing, while light-colored fabrics used indoors have a greater capacity to reflect incoming radiation. In turn, high reflectance can help reduce the amount of energy absorbed and the resulting heat buildup within the shading system itself.
Among these variables, the position of the solar-shading system relative to the glass largely determines its effectiveness. An exterior system acts as a first barrier against the sun by intercepting radiation before it passes through the glazing. An interior system, by contrast, comes into play after some of that energy has already entered the building, making it less effective at reducing heat gain, although it can provide other benefits related to comfort and insulation.
Solar Protection as a Building Envelope Strategy
The effectiveness of a shading system depends on more than the fabric itself. The technology used, movement control, and reduction of lateral light gaps can all influence its performance. Solutions based on ZIP systems, constant fabric tension, and greater wind stability make it possible to work with larger surfaces and respond to the specific conditions of each facade.
In this regard, exterior solutions with ZIP guides, such as Z-Box, Z-Box Secret, and Z-Box Solar, can reduce thermal transmission and HVAC-related energy consumption by up to 70% by intercepting solar radiation before it reaches the glass. These systems can be conceived as components of the building envelope that improve energy performance, enhance comfort, reduce cooling demand, and contribute to buildings better prepared for increasingly demanding climate conditions.
Automation expands the possibilities of this strategy. Through sensors and control systems, shades and blinds can adjust their position according to variables such as solar radiation, outdoor temperature, wind, or occupancy schedules. In this way, solar shading no longer depends solely on manual user intervention and can adapt to changing conditions throughout the day. Solar sensors can activate the systems as radiation levels increase; temperature sensors can respond to overheating conditions; wind sensors can automatically retract exterior systems when certain thresholds are exceeded; and time-based schedules can account for orientation, time of day, or season.
Integration with other building systems takes this approach a step further. In offices, hotels, hospitals, or educational buildings, motorized shades can be coordinated with HVAC, lighting, and building management systems. A west-facing facade, for example, can automatically deploy its shading during periods of peak solar exposure while artificial lighting adjusts according to the amount of available daylight. Bandalux offers Lynx, an application that manages and automates its motorized solar-shading solutions. By creating customized scenarios based on the needs of each project, it can help optimize the energy performance of homes, offices, and other buildings, reducing manual intervention and supporting more efficient energy use.
Against demanding climate conditions, solar shading raises a broader question that goes beyond the selection of a particular product or system: when should a building's thermal performance begin to be designed? The answer may lie among the earliest decisions about the building envelope.
Orientation, glazing, window-to-wall ratio, fabrics, reflectance, openness, positioning, and automation are all part of a chain of decisions that determines how a building receives and manages solar energy. Integrating these factors from the outset makes it possible to address thermal and visual comfort in coordination, rather than attempting to correct overheating after the architecture has already been defined. Designing for heat means recognizing solar radiation as a design condition and transforming the building envelope into a mediating interface between the building and its surroundings. Automation can enable this interface to respond dynamically; passive strategies can reduce the energy required to condition interior spaces; and architecture can reclaim an active role in environmental regulation.

UK PM Andy Burnham says it is ‘clear’ Russia interfered in 2016 Brexit vote

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said it is “clear” that Russia interfered in the country’s 2016 Brexit vote, warning French and German voters of the same threat.
“I asked the question coming to Downing Street: Was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? And I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was,” Burnham said in an interview with The Rest Is Politics podcast released on Sunday.
Burnham’s comments mark the first time a UK prime minister has publicly acknowledged that Russia interfered in the UK’s vote to leave the European Union. Burnham did not provide evidence for or details on the claim.
He said that “these things are important now to put clearly on the record, and, I believe, help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia.”
Burnham said he spoke with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz about possible links between Russia and the far-right Alternative for Germany party when the two leaders met last week in Berlin.
In his address to the United Nations General Assembly in September, Burnham also condemned Russia’s attempt to interfere in the UK’s 2019 general election.
According to a 2020 report by Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee, the UK government had failed to ask for a deep assessment of Russia’s interference in the 2016 referendum. The report did confirm that Russia had meddled in the 2014 Scottish independence referendum, however.
Russia has repeatedly denied meddling in Western democracies or interfering in another country’s elections or referendums, casting the UK as being gripped by “anti-Russian hysteria”.
UK reconsiders Brexit
Last month, Burnham argued that the UK should reconsider options for a future relationship with the EU, including rejoining the bloc, reigniting the decisive debate more than a decade after the historic vote.
He said that the UK’s departure from the bloc had failed to fulfil Brexit supporters’ pledge of “taking back control”, and instead has made the UK weaker economically and on immigration.

Hurricane Isaias leaves trail of destruction across the US Gulf Coast

As of midafternoon Sunday, roughly 356,000 customers remain without power in southern Alabama and the northwestern region of Florida, according to data from PowerOutage.com, an independent tracking website.
At its peak, the storm knocked out power to nearly 800,000 homes and businesses across the Gulf Coast.
Sarah Gatewood, a spokesperson for the utility company Florida Power and Light (FPL), announced that workers from across Florida and more than two dozen other states had mobilised to restore power.
At least four deaths have been linked to Isais after it made landfall as a Category 2 storm on the five-tier Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale.
The tempest churned northward into Alabama on Saturday with fierce tropical-storm-force winds before weakening into a post-tropical cyclone and tracking further north towards the Appalachians.
Though its power is waning, the storm continues to endanger the mid-Atlantic region with the potential for flash flooding.
According to the National Weather Service (NWS), surface observations indicate that Isaias now has maximum sustained winds of 160 km/h (100 mph) and an estimated minimum central pressure of 28.88 inches, or 978 millibars.
Across Florida and Alabama, residents have reported damage from the storm’s high-velocity winds.
A Rest and Relax Inn in the resort city of Pensacola, Florida, saw its roof sheared off during the hurricane, and a boathouse was flattened in Destin.
The immediate struggle for basic necessities was most stark in Pensacola, the westernmost part of the Florida Panhandle, where the storm downed power grids and caused widespread structural damage.
Hundreds of cars lined the block around a United Cajun Navy distribution site, a volunteer disaster relief organisation, on Saturday morning.
Pensacola’s Mayor DC Reeves warned of critical drinking water shortages following the storm, which affected drinking wells and water infrastructure. Residents, he said, remain under an advisory to boil tap water before use.
“We are winding down day three of storm response and recovery operations, and we remain focused on public safety, clearing debris, and restoring critical infrastructure and services,” Reeves said on social media.
Isaias also forced the indefinite closure of Pensacola International airport, Florida’s 10th-largest airfield, due to severe damage.
Fallen trees and power lines continue to make travel hazardous in Houston County, Alabama, which remains under an emergency flash flood warning, according to state emergency officials.
“Due to the impacts of Hurricane Isaias, all Houston County roads are closed until further notice,” the agency posted on X.
