Zelenskyy imposes sanctions on Russian ballistic missile makers and two other groups
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has enacted a National Security and Defence Council decision to impose sanctions on Russian entities involved in the production of ballistic missiles, those helping Russia evade financial sanctions and individuals acting in Russia's interests in the temporarily occupied territories.
Source: Office of the President of Ukraine
Details: The first sanctions list includes 70 Russians involved in the production of Iskander-M and Zircon ballistic missiles, which Russia uses to launch large-scale attacks on Ukraine.
Ukraine is imposing sanctions on key employees of Russian defence industry and chemical sector businesses involved in maintaining an uninterrupted industrial production cycle for ballistic missiles.
They include: employees of the Votkinsk Plant; the V. V. Bakhirev Institute of Mechanical Engineering; Radar MMS; Granit-Electron; Anozit; Aviatek; Metafrax Chemicals; Altai; Nevinnomyssk Azot; Azot; the Salyut, Strela, VNIIR-Progress, Mashinostroitel, Avangard, Sverdlov and Morozov plants; the Voskresensky Aggregation Factory; and the Polyus and Submicron research institutes.
The statement noted that all these facilities are already subject to sanctions imposed by Ukraine and, to some extent, by the US, the EU, the UK, Switzerland, Australia, Japan, Canada and New Zealand. Ukraine will now work with its partners not only to fully align sanctions against these Russian defence industry and chemical sector entities but also to target their key employees.
The sanctions package targeting those helping Russia evade financial sanctions covers 28 individuals and 27 legal entities. These include companies operating cryptocurrency exchanges, cryptocurrency exchange services and their executives and owners. Restrictions have also been imposed on the executives and owners of companies belonging to the A7 shadow banking network, which publicly offers tools to circumvent financial sanctions. The US had previously imposed sanctions on the A7 network.
Under a separate decision, sanctions have been imposed on 10 individuals, 21 legal entities and two maritime vessels that support Russia and act in its interests in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.
"They finance Russia's unprovoked and aggressive war against Ukraine and the Ukrainian people, plunder our natural resources, and spread Russian propaganda. These include collaborators who serve the aggressor, work for it, and assist the Russian occupiers. They also include enterprises that provide internet and television services, conduct geological exploration, and manufacture electronics and metal products in Ukraine's temporarily occupied territories," the Office of the President of Ukraine said.

The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28. Tehran responded with missile and drone attacks across the region and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, while Washington later imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports.

War and high debt to dominate IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok

War and high debt to dominate IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok
The US-Israel war on Iran and its inflationary impact will dominate the agenda.
Finance officials from around the world will gather in Bangkok this week under the shadow of a widening war in the Middle East, the biggest-ever energy supply shock and rising interest rates that together pose daunting risks to already-sluggish global economic growth.
The US-Israel war on Iran, now in its eighth month, and its inflationary impact are slated to dominate the agenda and sideline conversations during the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank, held outside Washington for the first time in three years.
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva told Reuters News Agency that 18,000 people were registered to attend the meetings, 4,000 more than the last off-site meetings held in Morocco in October 2023.
Notably absent will be United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who dispatched two senior officials in his stead while he handles some “domestic engagements”, a US official said. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Warsh will attend and is slated to participate in a public event with Georgieva on October 16.
Several other finance ministers were also staying home due to domestic budget and election duties, but most central bankers would attend, Georgieva said.
Bessent’s decision to skip the high-profile gathering and a meeting of the Group of 20 (G20) major economies, which the US leads this year, may frustrate counterparts amid rising tensions over the Iran war, Ukraine’s battle against Russia’s invasion, and the US move to impose sanctions on the International Criminal Court.
Fossil energy reserve release
The Group of Seven (G7) countries have agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves under pressure from US President Donald Trump, who is keen to see lower petrol prices before November elections that could see his Republican Party lose control of Congress.
Trump on Friday announced a deal with Russia that would provide even more diesel to global markets and a temporary waiver of US sanctions designed to deprive Moscow of revenues for its war on Ukraine. The move drew swift criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
More than one billion barrels of oil have been released, mainly from onshore commercial inventories, since the start of the war on February 28. But industry executives say the amount of oil in storage that is accessible to the global market is running low, making the market more fragile and fuelling pressure on prices.
The IMF has signalled little change in its forecast for three percent global growth in 2026, and may edge its forecast for next year slightly higher. But some countries will see downgrades, including Ukraine, now in its fifth year of war against Russia’s invasion, and Gulf countries hit by Iranian strikes and sharply reduced energy exports.
IMF research released on Tuesday showed that sharp spikes in food and energy prices are an increasingly common source of crises that drive inflation expectations higher for longer, worsen poverty and threaten economic stability.
One headache for policymakers is the growing public debt burden that is sapping growth and adding inflationary pressures. The IMF says public debt is at the highest level since World War II and will exceed 100 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) before 2030.
Advanced economies, led by the US, have the highest debt-to-GDP ratios, but emerging markets and low-income countries are particularly vulnerable, given a perfect storm of challenges: capital outflows in search of higher US rates, weather extremes triggered by the El Nino climate phenomenon, and a lack of investment in artificial intelligence (AI), which has mitigated negative supply shocks in the US and other rich countries.
Developing countries are particularly vulnerable given high public debt levels that will have to be renegotiated at higher interest rates. Together, they face $400bn in debt payments to external creditors in 2026, and interest payments already exceed 10 percent of revenue on average.
Many lower-income countries are worried about new IMF recommendations for loan programmes that call for fewer but deeper reforms as a condition for approving lending, a change that many fear will lead to painful austerity measures.

The president who can’t say his name
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
18:45:36 UTC
03:45:36 KST

Three weeks before Michigan decides whether to send the first Muslim senator to Washington, the president still cannot or will not say the man’s name.
“Mike Rogers, the great American Patriot and Republican Candidate for the U.S. Senate from Michigan, completely obliterated Mohammed El-Sayed in the big debate tonight,” Trump wrote on Truth Social after Thursday’s debate.
Rogers had skipped it.
“Mohammed is a Jihadist lunatic who hates our Country, the Black People of Detroit, and wants to see the U.S. fail.”
The candidate’s name is Abdul El-Sayed. Mohamed is his middle name, inherited from his Egyptian immigrant father. He rarely uses it. Yet the president repeats it so relentlessly that it reads less like a mistake than a strategy distilled into a single word.
El-Sayed has stopped pretending to be surprised.
“He knows my name is Abdul,” he said. “He says it every day.”
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called the attacks “bigoted bulls—,” adding that El-Sayed “is on the road to being the next Senator from Michigan no matter how much bigoted bulls— a weak and desperate Donald Trump throws at him.”
Dawud Walid, of the Michigan chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, recognized the tactic for what it was.
“He is intentionally saying his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, to say, ‘Look, this guy is outside what we would consider to be a normative America.’ It’s a political tactic, and we’ve seen it before.
READ: American Senate candidate accuses Netanyahu of pushing US into Iran war
The cruelty is not what is remarkable here. The timing is.
A sitting president does not usually spend the final weeks of a campaign fixated on a single state’s Senate race unless he believes something larger rides on it.
Something does.
Michigan’s open Senate seat, vacated by retiring Democrat Gary Peters, sits inside a chamber Republicans currently control 53 to 47. Democrats need a net gain of four seats on Nov. 3 to take it back, and Michigan would not count among those gains. It is a seat they already hold, and one of the two Democratic-held seats Republicans most want to flip.
A Rogers victory would enlarge the Republican majority and make an already narrow Democratic path elsewhere even tighter. An El-Sayed victory would leave the arithmetic exactly where it stands.
The real stakes, then, are not whether Michigan can flip the Senate in a single stroke. The question is whether Republicans can afford to miss even one opportunity to widen their majority, particularly in a state the president carried twice.
The polling suggests they may not be able to.
El-Sayed led by just over three points in the RealClearPolitics average through Oct. 6, 48.1 to 44.9. Marist put him up seven points in late September. So did Suffolk. Even Fox News, hardly a sympathetic outlet, found him ahead by one point among likely voters in its most recent poll. That marked a reversal from August, when Rogers led by four.
Bettors on Polymarket now give El-Sayed a 69 percent chance of winning.
Money has followed the nerves.
Through Oct. 10, Republican-aligned spending in the race had reached $78 million, compared with $63 million from Democrats. Nearly all of it has been funneled into advertisements branding El-Sayed, a Rhodes Scholar and physician, as “dangerously radical” and “too extreme.”
The ads tie him to Hasan Piker, a streamer who once said America “deserved 9/11,” in the hope that the association will stick where attacks on his policies have not.
Trump himself has yet to set foot in Michigan to campaign for Rogers. El-Sayed has turned the president’s absence into a taunt of his own.
Standing before a crowd in Port Huron this month, dressed in a black V-neck shirt and gripping a handheld microphone, he issued a challenge.
“Donald, if you’re watching, don’t wuss out, man.”
He has called Rogers a coward. He has called the president afraid.
The nerves extend far beyond Michigan.
READ: Former military secretary accuses Netanyahu’s office of falsifying Oct. 7 records
Democrats lead the generic congressional ballot by roughly nine points in Nate Silver’s running average, their widest margin of the cycle. For the first time, they have broken 50 percent support. Trump’s approval rating sits in the high 30s across most tracking polls.
Forecasters now give Democrats an 82 percent chance of retaking the House and better-than-even odds of capturing the Senate.
Should both chambers fall, the final two years of this presidency would unfold before a Congress armed with subpoena power and with nothing left to trade.
That is the arithmetic from which a lame duck is made. It is why one Senate race in one Midwestern state has drawn the kind of presidential attention usually reserved for an election with Trump’s own name on the ballot.
El-Sayed is not without self-inflicted wounds.
Leaked audio captured him declining to take a clear position on the death of Iran’s former supreme leader, out of deference to grieving constituents in Dearborn. The recording gave Republicans an opening they have refused to relinquish.
Some Michigan Democrats, including strategist Adrian Hemond, have worried aloud that El-Sayed’s reluctance to court skeptical factions within his own party could cost Democrats a seat they should hold comfortably.
Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who remained neutral during the primary, has since worked to unify the party behind him. The alternative, she warned, is a senator “beholden to President Trump.”
Even El-Sayed’s allies acknowledge that his candidacy is built on remaking the electorate, not courting its center.
None of this guarantees him a seat in the Senate.
Three weeks is a long time. Leads within a poll’s margin of error can vanish overnight. Michigan Republicans have not won a Senate race since 1994, for reasons that reach far beyond any single candidate.
Rogers knows that history better than most. He lost to Slotkin by less than a point in 2024—close enough to keep him running, but not close enough to make Republicans comfortable about running him again.
Yet a president reduced to repeatedly misnaming his opponent on a platform built for far graver pronouncements is offering an answer of his own.
Strength does not usually sound like that.
Fear sometimes does.

Saudi Arabia needs allies against the Houthis, but will it turn to Israel? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
18:30:52 UTC
03:30:52 KST

US President Donald Trump lives in a transactional foreign policy universe. You give, you get. You don’t give, don’t expect much.
Israel has given a lot and, in return, gotten a lot. It has fought wing to wing with the US in Iran, provided valuable intelligence and demonstrated the military capabilities Washington wants to see in an ally.
In April, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said, “To our Israeli allies, thanks for being a brave, capable and willing ally on this battlefield. The rest of the world and the rest of our so-called allies saw what real capabilities look like. They should take some notes.”
America’s “legacy” allies – from NATO countries to South Korea – have not stepped up to anywhere near the same degree. They have consequently been on the receiving end of more than just harsh words.
Trump ordered joint military exercises with South Korea scaled back, citing Seoul’s refusal to help with the Iran campaign, and threatened to cut off trade with Spain after Madrid denied Washington the use of its bases for strikes on Iran.
And then there is Saudi Arabia.
Many have been puzzled by Washington’s reluctance to intervene directly in the Saudis’ battle with the Houthis. This battle took a particularly deadly turn on Saturday when the King Khalid Airport in Riyadh was struck by a missile, killing 12 people and injuring more than 300, the most serious attack in Saudi Arabia in a decade.
This came as tensions between the Saudis and the Houthis steadily escalated – Saturday’s attack was the third such attack in a week, since the Saudis launched a counter-offensive against the Houthis to push them back from the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Despite all that, Trump has wavered. Washington has provided intelligence and targeting assistance, but the president has so far stopped short of direct military intervention. On Saturday, he said he was considering joining the Saudi strikes.
Why the hesitation?
The explanations offered range from reluctance to become engaged in another major military campaign less than a month before the midterm elections to concern about weapons stocks depleted by the war in Iran.
Saudi Arabia's refusal to join the Abraham Accords
Another possible explanation is Trump’s frustration with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s steadfast refusal to join the Abraham Accords. Saudi normalization with Israel would have given Trump an important diplomatic prize before the elections.
If this is indeed the case, then it fits into a pattern. In July, the US and Saudi Arabia signed a nuclear cooperation agreement, opening the door to a major commercial role for American companies. Trump then said he would not proceed unless the Saudis joined the Abraham Accords.
You give, you get.
Saudi normalization with Israel has long been the Middle East’s diplomatic holy grail.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s former military secretary, Avi Gil, said in a long, revealing interview with Israel Hayom on Thursday that the desire to bring Saudi Arabia into the Abraham Accords helped explain Israel’s restraint toward Hamas and Hezbollah in the run-up to October 7.
Israel wanted to avoid an escalation that could derail the normalization process. He said the two countries were “closer than people realize” to a deal.
But Israeli action didn’t scuttle the process. Hamas did that all on its own.
Since then, the Saudis have made clear – even as the Iranian threat loomed larger and normalization with Israel made good strategic sense in trying to create a new security architecture for the region – that without a pathway to a Palestinian state, they were not going to normalize.
That leaves a familiar gap between strategic logic and political feasibility, since – with October 7 so fresh and raw – it is highly unlikely that any Israeli government in the foreseeable future would agree to a Palestinian state.
Israel and Saudi Arabia face threats from Iran and its allies. Both have an interest in preventing the Houthis from threatening shipping, airports, and regional stability. Those shared interests provide a strong argument for cooperation. They have not, however, proven enough to overcome the political obstacles to establishing an open relationship.
Further evidence of where Riyadh was looking for its regional security architecture came in August, when it signed a joint defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey. Rather than bringing its relationship with Israel into the open, Saudi Arabia was strengthening an alternative framework with two Muslim powers.
The pact’s promise was sweeping: an attack on one would be considered an attack on all. So far, the response to the Houthi campaign has not matched that rhetoric. Turkey has reportedly begun providing defensive and technical assistance, but that is a long way from joining Saudi Arabia in striking the enemy attacking it.
Signing this pact showed that Saudi Arabia – while interested in maintaining intelligence cooperation with Israel and keeping it discreet – was seeking far-reaching security arrangements elsewhere.
Then an Omani pilot planned to crash a flydubai plane full of Israeli passengers into Ben-Gurion Airport, only to be thwarted by some brave and resourceful passengers and crew members, and Jerusalem got an unvarnished view of where it stands with the Saudis.
Yes, the Saudis allowed a distressed plane full of Israeli passengers to land at a civilian-military airfield in Tabuk. And, yes, Saudi medical personnel cared for Israeli passengers. Both were consequential acts of assistance in a moment of acute danger.
But Riyadh adamantly refused Israel’s request to send its own aircraft to collect the passengers. A replacement flydubai plane brought them home.
Cooperation, but to a point
This exposed the boundary between practical cooperation and public acceptance. Allowing an Israeli plane to pick up the passengers would be one gesture too far on the road to normalization: one which would have been staunchly opposed by much of the Saudi public and undoubtedly weaponized against the Saudis by the Iranians.
Whatever the precise calculations behind that refusal, the political message was clear: cooperation could proceed, but only so far.
Ten days later, Saudi Arabia’s own airport was targeted, and all of a sudden it is looking for allies in its fight with the Houthis.
That attack inevitably led to speculation that this might bring Israeli-Saudi security cooperation into the open and lead to closer ties to combat a common threat. Weakening the Houthis, after all, would serve Israeli interests as well as Saudi ones. The group’s hostility toward Israel is not exactly a secret.
But shared enemies don’t necessarily lead to joint military operations. Public Israeli involvement could carry political costs for Riyadh and provide ammunition for those seeking to portray the Saudi campaign as serving Israel.
The Saudi leadership would have to weigh those costs against the benefits of the assistance. Israel, in turn, would have to decide what risks it should take on the Saudis’ behalf and what it could expect in return.
While the airport attack does not guarantee a breakthrough between Israel and Saudi Arabia, it does force Riyadh to face this question: does it make sense to keep one of its potentially strongest regional partners at arm’s length?
And for Israel, the question is a variation on Trump’s transactional theme: How much should it give when the Saudis are still unwilling to publicly be seen taking?

Nude Trump sculpture sparks political controversy at European Parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
18:26:08 UTC
03:26:08 KST

Nude Trump sculpture sparks political controversy at European Parliament
TEHRAN- A gold-covered sculpture depicting US President Donald Trump naked and sitting on the back of a frail man has sparked a political controversy at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, drawing criticism from several European lawmakers and a call by Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico for its removal, while others have defended the artwork as a form of political satire and freedom of expression.
Created by Danish artist Jens Galschiøt, the 2.6-meter sculpture, titled “The Orange Plague” and also known as “The King of Injustice,” was unveiled on October 7 as part of a three-day exhibition hosted by Danish Member of the European Parliament Per Clausen. The installation was removed on October 8, according to Italian broadcaster Sky TG24, which reported that the exhibition had been scheduled to run for three days.
The work portrays Trump as a naked, overweight figure covered in 23-karat gold leaf, holding a golf club in one hand and scales of justice in the other. He sits on the shoulders of a smaller, frail man, whose posture suggests that he is struggling under the weight, while a globe resembling a golf ball lies near the man's feet.
An inscription at the base of the sculpture offers a pointed commentary on the relationship between power and responsibility.
“I am sitting on the back of a man. He is sinking under my burden. I will do anything to help him. Except stepping down from his back,” the inscription reads.
The text presents an ironic image of a powerful figure who claims to help those beneath him while refusing to abandon the position that causes their suffering.
According to Euronews and The Art Newspaper, Galschiøt conceived the work as a protest against Trump's climate and foreign policies, which he believes undermine international cooperation and efforts to address the climate crisis.
Slovak prime minister calls for removal
The exhibition drew criticism from Robert Fico, who called on European Parliament President Roberta Metsola to have the sculpture removed.
According to Slovakia's news agency TASR, Fico objected to the installation despite acknowledging his disagreements with some of Trump's policies. He argued that political differences should not justify what he regarded as an insult to a partner country on the premises of a European institution.
Fico also questioned whether those supporting the display would accept similar depictions of French President Emmanuel Macron or German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. His remarks brought diplomatic sensitivities into a debate over the limits of political satire.
Other lawmakers also criticized the artwork. Belgian MEP Barbara Bonte described the installation as a disgrace, while Hungarian lawmaker Ernő Schaller-Baross questioned what he considered a double standard in the treatment of political leaders. Irish MEP Barry Cowen also called the sculpture “silly and objectionable” and said he had written to the parliament to express his opposition.
The objections highlighted divisions within the European Parliament over whether the sculpture represented legitimate political expression or an inappropriate use of the institution's premises.
Danish lawmaker defends the display
The sculpture was brought to Strasbourg at the invitation of Danish MEP Per Clausen, who defended the decision to exhibit it.
Clausen, who invited Galschiøt to exhibit the sculpture, dismissed concerns about a possible negative reaction from Trump.
“If someone is so thin-skinned that they cannot tolerate this sculpture being exhibited in the European Parliament, then they have no place on the world stage,” Clausen said, according to Euronews.
The exhibition was approved by the European Parliament's quaestors, a cross-party group responsible for certain administrative matters. The approval allowed the work to be shown in designated exhibition space but did not make it an official artwork commissioned or endorsed by the institution.
Galschiøt has described the sculpture as a personal attack on Trump, an approach he said differed from his usual focus on political systems.
“Normally I attack systems, but in this case, I will attack Trump personally,” the artist told The Art Newspaper.
 
Galschiøt said the work was intended to draw attention to the reluctance of governments and organizations to challenge the US president openly because of potential economic and political consequences.
“Nations as well as NGOs are afraid to openly raise the subject [of] how to deal with Trump and his policies, fearing tariffs, fund-cuts, deportations or the like,” the artist wrote on his website, in a statement quoted by The Art Newspaper.
The sculpture's gold finish also carries a satirical message. Galschiøt told the publication that Trump's extensive use of gold in his properties, including the Oval Office, inspired the decision to cover the figure in the precious metal.
The artist also drew inspiration from Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale “The Emperor's New Clothes”, in which a vain ruler parades naked while those around him pretend that he is wearing magnificent garments. The story's central theme — the reluctance to challenge authority even when its failings are obvious — reinforces the sculpture's political message.
Miniature replicas extend the protest
The Strasbourg exhibition was accompanied by an effort to circulate the artwork beyond the parliament building. Galschiøt produced approximately 20,000 miniature, 3D-printed versions of the sculpture, distributing them to visitors and parliament staff. He also made the digital design files freely available online for people wishing to print their own copies.
The idea was inspired by Hong Kong's democracy movement, whose supporters produced miniature reproductions of Galschiøt's "Pillar of Shame". The original sculpture, created in 1997 to commemorate human rights violations including the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown, was dismantled in Hong Kong in 2021.
“The Orange Plague” had previously appeared at demonstrations in Copenhagen opposing US pressure over Greenland and at the COP30 United Nations climate conference in Belém, Brazil, in 2025.
Following its Strasbourg appearance, Galschiøt planned to display the sculpture again at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, in November 2026.
In a report published on October 9, Euronews also placed the installation within a broader tradition of satirical art targeting Trump, noting how artists have used exaggerated and often gilded depictions of the president to challenge his public image and political influence.
The controversy surrounding the sculpture illustrates how political art can become a point of contention over freedom of expression, diplomatic sensitivities and the role of public institutions.

Syria between potential intervention in Yemen and domestic crises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
18:25:07 UTC
03:25:07 KST

Syria between potential intervention in Yemen and domestic crises
TEHRAN – The costs and risks of Syrian intervention in Yemen could begin to mount from the moment a decision is made.
Following Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa’s visit to Riyadh a few days earlier, reports on October 7, citing U.S. officials, said Saudi Arabia and Syria were discussing the possibility of deploying Syrian forces to Yemen to participate in military operations against the Sanaa government.
According to reports, between 10,000 and 20,000 soldiers could be sent, with the 90th and 84th Divisions among the formations under consideration. Al-Sharaa was reportedly seriously weighing the proposal but has not yet made a final decision.
Meanwhile, Ahmad Mowaffaq Zaidan, an adviser to the Syrian presidency, denied that Riyadh had asked Damascus to send troops to Yemen. Syria’s official position has emphasized that rebuilding the country remains the priority and that any military cooperation must proceed through official channels and within existing bilateral frameworks.
The official denial, however, does not negate the existence of multiple reports suggesting that various options are under consideration. Nor do the leaks amount to a finalized agreement. To date, there has been no official announcement of a Syrian decision to intervene, no confirmed Saudi request, and no publicly disclosed agreement on the matter.
The significance of these reports, however, extends beyond the question of whether Syrian forces will ultimately be deployed to Yemen. The very fact that such a possibility is being discussed raises broader questions about the regional role Syria’s new leadership might assume, the limits of its commitments to its allies, and the criteria it will apply when deciding whether to intervene militarily beyond its borders.
Lebanon and Yemen: Why the different calculations?
The debate takes on greater significance when viewed alongside President al-Sharaa’s position on the possibility of intervening in Lebanon against Hezbollah, despite an explicit appeal from U.S. President Donald Trump himself. Al-Sharaa ruled out Syrian military intervention in Lebanon, arguing that such a move would require a request from the Lebanese government and that neither the Syrian army nor the country’s internal situation was ready for such a step.
These considerations are even more consequential in the case of Yemen. Geographically, Yemen is much farther away, and its conflict is exceptionally complex. Military intervention could expose Syria to security and political risks extending well beyond the battlefield.
If the Syrian army’s lack of readiness was sufficient reason to rule out intervention in Lebanon, what has changed to make sending thousands of troops to Yemen a viable option? Have Syria’s military capabilities improved sufficiently within a matter of months to support a large-scale overseas deployment? Or does Damascus’s relationship with Riyadh lead it to assess the risks differently?
What could Damascus gain and lose?
Reports suggesting that Syrian forces could be sent to Yemen are closely linked to the central role Saudi Arabia has played in supporting the new leadership in Damascus.
Riyadh has been one of al-Sharaa’s most prominent political backers and has helped advance Arab and international efforts to restore engagement with Syria. It has also played a role in efforts to lift sanctions and create conditions for the country’s reintegration into the region. For Damascus, relations with Riyadh extend beyond economic interests to encompass the pursuit of political and security support at an exceptionally sensitive stage of the country’s transition.
Damascus may view closer military cooperation with Riyadh as an opportunity to build political trust, secure economic and security assistance, and expand its room for regional maneuver. Through such cooperation, it could also seek to demonstrate that Syria is a capable partner able to contribute to a broader framework of Arab security, rather than simply a country seeking external assistance.
These potential benefits, however, are not enough on their own to justify sending thousands of troops into a foreign conflict. Military intervention abroad inevitably carries serious consequences. In addition to exposing Syrian forces to retaliatory attacks, it could expand the circle of Syria’s enemies and draw the country into a conflict whose outcome and terms of settlement it cannot determine independently.
The risks become even more pronounced if the proposed mission remains poorly defined.
Would Syria’s role be confined to protecting Saudi facilities and strategic sites, with its forces assigned clearly defined defensive responsibilities? Or would Syrian troops participate in offensive operations inside Yemen?
The distinction between these scenarios is fundamental. It would determine the legal, military, and political risks involved, as well as whether the mission would remain limited and time-bound or evolve into a prolonged military entanglement.
Domestic crises cannot be overlooked
These discussions are unfolding as Syria continues to face serious and deeply complex domestic challenges.
The integration of the “Syrian Democratic Forces” into state institutions has yet to produce a final settlement. Arrangements governing control, administration, and security in northeastern Syria remain contested, while ongoing protests and political mobilization in Hasakah Governorate underscore the depth and gravity of the unresolved issue.
The situation is even more precarious in the south, where much of Suwayda Governorate remains outside the Syrian state’s control. The far-reaching demands advanced by the community’s spiritual leader, Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri, reflect the depth of the divisions confronting the government.
At the same time, Israel’s invasions and aggression continue across southern Syria. This is occurring alongside the resumption of excavation and fortification work aimed at completing the occupying regime’s so-called “Sufa 53” line inside Syrian territory, consolidating new realities on the ground at the expense of Syrian sovereignty.
Under these circumstances, the challenge is not simply to restore control over the territory facing aggression but to prevent the fragmentation of central authority in parts of Syria, at a time when the capital itself remains within the reach of the Zionist regime’s military aggression.
How, then, can a state facing a direct threat near its capital and struggling to preserve its territorial integrity in the south seriously consider sending thousands of troops to Yemen, thousands of kilometers away? What strategic imperative could justify diverting troops and resources to a foreign theater while the struggle to consolidate sovereignty within the country’s own borders remains unresolved?
Between a leak and a decision
Potential military involvement could offer Damascus an opportunity to strengthen its relationship with Riyadh and open the door to economic and political benefits. Yet these gains remain speculative unless they translate into tangible results, while the costs and risks of intervention could begin to mount from the moment a decision is made.
A state that has yet to complete the reconstruction of its army, economy, and institutions cannot afford to treat overseas military interventions as bargaining chips in a broader contest for regional influence.

Yemen breaking the blockade and beginning a new phase

Yemen breaking the blockade and beginning a new phase
LONDON – How Ansarallah succeeded in breaking the Saudi-imposed air blockade on Yemen is worthy of attention. The process began with an Ansarallah delegation’s trip to Tehran to attend the funeral of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, who was assassinated in a joint U.S.-Israeli air raid on his office on February 28.
The delegation flew from Sanaa International Airport to Tehran but was forced to land at Hodeidah Airport on its return after Saudi jets bombed Sanaa airport.
The delegation’s journey to Tehran and its return marked the beginning of a new phase in line with broader regional developments. The message was clear: the emerging balance of power no longer allowed the Saudi-imposed air blockade on Yemen to continue.
Amid the war between the United States and Iran, the message was that any settlement must be comprehensive and include the entire Axis of Resistance, allowing it to exercise its rights without being denied recognition. The new equation became one in which a blockade would be met with a blockade, and the continuation of the blockade on Yemen would lead to countermeasures affecting the other side.
Developments then progressed to the point where the balance of power on the ground began to shift in favor of Ansarallah, representing the extension of the Axis of Resistance towards control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Ansarallah began advancing and taking control of the western coast of the Red Sea, reaching beyond Mokha. This advance extended to a point in the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the island opposite it.
This development was not coincidental. Rather, it formed part of a broader process aimed at changing the balance of power in the region. Ultimately, the situation developed to the point where the Axis of Resistance came to control the Strait of Hormuz, while the Bab al-Mandab Strait also came under the its control.
The combination of control and influence over the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab means that approximately 40% of global energy supplies have come under the influence of the Axis of Resistance. Having this degree of influence over the world's most important energy corridors makes the bloc a far more influential force globally. This shift in the balance of power is ushering all resistance fronts into a new phase.
We are facing a new situation unlike any previous one in terms of the scale of its influence and its capacity to alter existing equations. No previous situation has reached this level of influence. It could bring the Axis of Resistance to a level of influence equal to, or perhaps greater than, that of the U.S.-Israeli alliance, despite the latter’s military and intelligence superiority.
This American-Israeli superiority, which has severely struck the resistance fronts in Gaza, Lebanon, and the West Bank, has now been met by a corresponding counterweight. Control over the Bab al-Mandab is overturning the balance of power, with consequences for the Israeli occupation entity as a whole. The importance of these developments is that they do not concern military confrontation alone; they also affect strategic and economic interests connected to energy and global trade.
This is occurring alongside a transformation in the image of the Israeli occupation entity in global public opinion, where it has become increasingly rejected in the conscience of the world. One indication is that a British minister has declared that Gaza represents a reproach to the global conscience.
Similarly, the actions of settlers in the West Bank, including acts of destruction and violations, have come under condemnation, to the point that some Western officials have described them as terrorists. These developments are new, and they would not have emerged in the same form were it not for the changes that have taken place in the balance of power and influence in the region.
Control over and the ability to influence global energy supplies do not affect the military dimension alone; it also extends to the global economy. Influence over energy supplies affects energy prices and consequently the prices of consumer goods, including food items and metals. It may also have repercussions for global stock exchanges and financial markets. Therefore, control over the corridors that affect the supply of energy, metals, fertilizers, and food gives the Axis of Resistance greater capacity to influence the global economy and financial markets.
Taken together, these developments could constitute a turning point in the course of the world and in the nature of the balance of power that exists within it. We may be facing the possibility of building a new world in which the balance of power differs from that which prevailed during previous periods. In this new world, the resistance bloc could play an influential role. Accordingly, what began as steps to break the blockade on Yemen could extend beyond the borders of Yemen and the region, becoming part of a broader shift in the global balance of power.
The United States does not want to enter this war because direct American involvement would mean preventing US ships from passing through the Red Sea. Washington also does not want to become involved in two wars simultaneously.
The United States is therefore compelled to pursue a piecemeal settlement, one that does not encompass all fronts, including the Yemeni front. There may be a settlement to the U.S.-Iran conflict, but the Yemeni issue itself must ultimately be resolved through a Saudi-Yemeni dialogue.
However, acknowledging the Yemeni situation and the effective control that Ansarallah exercises over parts of Yemen entail an American recognition of the new reality. It would also form part of a broader recognition of Iran and the larger resistance bloc.
The strikes against Saudi Arabia’s oil and energy infrastructure are part of the Yemeni pressure campaign against the Saudi Kingdom. On the one hand, Saudi Arabia is being placed under pressure from the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. On the other hand, pressure on global energy supplies creates additional pressure on Saudi Arabia to accept the situation in Yemen, including the role of Ansarallah.
Yemen is following a principle of responding to siege with siege. When the Yemeni capital is attacked, Yemen also strikes Riyadh’s energy infrastructure.
The persistence of the Yemeni position, combined with Saudi Arabia’s inability to overcome Yemen and the failure of other parties to enter the fighting alongside the kingdom, will ultimately give the Yemenis the upper hand. This could lead to a settlement that recognizes the existence and role of Ansarallah in Yemen. This, in turn, will serve the broader regional context: a U.S.-Iranian agreement that will acknowledges the new balance of power and recognize the right of the Axis of Resistance to exist and maintain its position in the region.

Shargh: Iran must avoid its opponents’ traps
Shargh devoted its commentary to the challenges and schemes facing a powerful Iran. International politics is not based on ideal concepts of fairness, and genuine “win-win” outcomes rarely exist. In every negotiation, one party typically gains more than the other, making power and influence the principal factors shaping diplomatic results. Iran’s rivals are attempting to create situations that could draw the country into costly and internationally justifiable conflicts. Such efforts are designed to weaken Iran and provide advantages to its foes. For that reason, Shargh stressed the importance of strategic patience and careful decision-making. Diplomacy without power is ineffective in today’s world, and identified the Iranian people as the country’s most valuable source of strength. It concluded that foreign governments increasingly recognize the significance of public support in Iran and therefore seek opportunities to exploit vulnerabilities or create political and social pressure.
Sobh-e-No: military action not in Trump’s interest
Sobh-e-No examined the reasons why the United States is unlikely to launch a military strike against Iran before the November elections. Iran possesses significant capabilities and cannot be easily pressured into accepting Washington’s demands. Any major strategic error by Trump could generate two separate challenges at once: a security crisis abroad and political repercussions inside the United States. The article also noted that Trump has historically preferred avoiding lengthy military engagements and instead favors using military power as leverage to achieve political objectives. According to the paper, launching an attack before an election would eliminate that leverage while exposing Washington to unnecessary risks. As a result, Trump has chosen to postpone any serious military option until after voters cast their ballots. It further argued that years of maximum economic and military pressure have not compelled Iran to surrender. The trip was more than a routine diplomatic gathering, presenting an opportunity to combine regional diplomacy with environmental cooperation. However, Sazandegi argued that the ultimate success of such efforts will depend on whether discussions and agreements reached during the summit can be transformed into practical policies. In its view, only concrete measures aimed at reducing tensions and addressing ecological challenges will ensure meaningful results for the region.
Arman-e-Emrooz: Looking beyond the West-East divide

The newspaper argued that the rise of China, India, Indonesia, and other emerging powers demonstrates that Asia is no longer merely an arena for Western competition. Instead, it has become one of the world’s most significant centers of economic growth, political influence, and strategic power. The article suggested that these changes provide Iran with an opportunity to rethink its place in the international system. It argued that Iranian foreign policy should move beyond the traditional choice between the West and the East. Expanding strategic options, the newspaper said, requires a broader and more flexible approach rather than simply replacing one geopolitical orientation with another. Within this framework, Arman-e-Emrooz highlighted the concept of the “Global South” as a useful basis for foreign policy. It argued that the idea allows Iran to connect issues of national identity, geopolitical interests, and economic priorities. By emphasizing shared experiences of independence and development, benefiting from shifts in global power distribution, and expanding cooperation in trade, investment, energy, technology, transportation, and security, Iran could strengthen both its regional and international position.

Hive dwellers vs. screen players: The anatomy of two societies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
18:11:48 UTC
03:11:48 KST

Hive dwellers vs. screen players: The anatomy of two societies
TEHRAN - This question has puzzled many astute observers in the West — and echoed through the stunned minds of Trump and Netanyahu alike: Why, following the assassination of the leadership, did the Iranian government not collapse like governments in other countries?
In the first week, a thoughtful friend in the West posed this question to me by email. To answer it thoroughly by invoking Shia history and Imam Hussein might well prove incomprehensible to a Western mind. I therefore tried to frame my answer using concepts drawn from Western literature itself. I wrote to my friend about a book by Maurice Maeterlinck, titled *The Life of the Bee*, which a kind neighbor had gifted me in my youth, before the revolution.
The point I am about to share may make the question easier for a Western reader to grasp. Maeterlinck notes that before a real-world experiment, all researchers assumed that the sovereign ruler of the hive was the queen, and that everything existed to serve her and her desires. They therefore designed an experiment: they placed a ring at the entrance of a beehive through which worker and soldier bees could pass easily, but which the queen, owing to her larger body, could not pass through.
They then staged a mock attack on the hive. Following their natural instinct, the bees mobilized to save the queen first. Since the only exit from the besieged hive was through that ring, the queen became stuck in it while trying to escape. After some time, her protective guards assumed she was refusing to leave. They stung her to death, selected another larva capable of becoming a queen to replace her, and established a new hive with a young queen elsewhere.
The scientist's conclusion is profound and fascinating. From then on, he stripped the title of "God of the Hive" from the queen, redefining that supreme force as the "invisible spirit of the hive."
This is precisely what happened in Iran, with one difference: the executioners this time were real aggressors, yet once again their violent methods failed to conquer the invisible spirit of the hive.
I will elaborate on the difference between a nation whose god is the invisible spirit of the hive and the peoples of other countries, with more precise explanations. I have a filmmaker friend named Seyyed Reza Mirkarimi, the director of several monumental works of Iranian cinema, whose name and films you can look up. He offers a striking interpretation of those countries surrounding Iran that have been independent for only a few decades. He compares them to cinematic backlots during the production of grand Hollywood epics.
To better understand his analogy, imagine a film about the era of Alexander the Great being shot on a set at Cinecitta in Rome — thousands of extras, towering props, and magnificent scenery.
Viewed from the camera angle, on the big screen, or even in IMAX, we marvel at its grandeur. Even the actors, deeply immersed in their roles through rehearsal, believe in their characters for a time. Yet once the false glamour of the screening subsides, or filming concludes, they realize they merely stepped out of their true selves for a brief spell to live in someone else's skin.
Once shooting wraps, all those grand sets are dismantled and replaced by another set of deceptive facades. That is the sum total of a magnificent, dazzling life lived on a cinematic backlot devoid of true identity. Perhaps the very next day after filming ends, even the lead actor is not permitted to enter, wander around, or reminisce about the past.
The disparity between many newly established Arab states — filled with heterogeneous populations such as Pakistanis, Indians, and others — and the original indigenous Arab inhabitants precisely mirrors the role of these film extras. Their sole reason for being present is to collect a paycheck and grab a slice of that fleeting fame and profit for tomorrow, without leaving any lasting impact on the future of that cinematic backlot.
Yet the Iranian nation — and even the leadership that was assassinated — believes in the spirit of the hive. That is why, for two hundred and twenty days, men and women, young and old, have stood steadfastly in the public squares and streets.
In closing, I recommend that you, the reader of this essay, seek out and read the legendary Persian tale The Conference of the Birds by the Iranian poet Attar of Nishapur. The plot is briefly as follows: a flock of birds from across the world gathers to find a mythical bird named the Simurgh atop Mount Qaf and make him their leader. On the final day of the journey, atop Mount Qaf, only thirty diverse birds remain; the rest have fallen behind along the way, offering various excuses. They do not behold a mythical Simurgh; instead, they realize that the legendary Simurgh is, in fact, their own collective gathering. They no longer need to wait for a miraculous bird to lead them.

Global anti-Israel protests coordinated in advance by international alliance, documents show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
18:10:59 UTC
03:10:59 KST

Pro-Palestinian protests across the world last week were coordinated in advance by an international alliance that prepared campaign slogans, media messaging and protest tactics, including calls to shut down city squares, encircle government buildings and blockade corporate hubs, The Jerusalem Post's review of campaign documents found.
This was first reported on by Fox News Digital, which found that "long before the first demonstrators gathered, the messages for the protest's 'communications framing' and transnational action plan had already been written, the banners designed, the tactics circulated and the media strategy laid out."
Behind the protest preparation and framing is a London-based coalition called Global Alliance for Palestine (GAFP), an international alliance of around 200 organizations that are focused on Palestine advocacy.
Ahead of the week of October 7, which marked the third anniversary of the Hamas attacks, GAFP released press statements and media toolkits encouraging pro-Palestine movements, student groups, trade unions, and civil society organizations worldwide to unite under the banner ‘End the Genocide, Defend the Land’.
GAFP was behind the Global Day of Action on October 10, as well as a direct legislative pressure campaign asking parliamentarians to demand immediate arms embargoes, emergency debates, suspended trade agreements, and binding human rights sanctions against Israel.
In the toolkit for October 10 protests, viewed by the Post, GAFP called for protesters to "shut down city squares, encircle government buildings, and blockade complicit corporate hubs."
Rather than a symbolic march, GAFP said the purpose of the global day of action was to interrupt business-as-usual.
Among the other suggested protest actions were walk-outs, sit-ins, and blockades.
Groups encouraged to use language 'impossible to ignore'
In a GAFP concept paper for the Global Alliance for Palestine, organizers share guidelines for 'Communications Framing' and 'Core Messages' about Israel. The document encourages groups to use language that is "disciplined, credible, urgent and impossible to ignore."
GAFP also published a list of slogans such as "From Every Street, One Demand: End Genocide, End Occupation" and "Israel Kills. The Media Justifies."
The Post identified 181 organizations in the coalition, with the organizations being spread out across the world.
Among the most high-profile participating organizations are CodePink, the Freedom Flotilla, and regional BDS chapters.
Israel's Foreign Ministry called out the "prewritten accusations, coordinated slogans," and "orchestrated disruptions."
"A calculated effort to hijack headlines, dominate the narrative and demonize Israel. The hatred is loud. The coordination is documented," it said.
While many of the hundreds of protests across the world may have appeared to be independent and unconnected, the understanding of GAFP's campaign indicates that this may not have been the case.

“The massive fire is the fate of any non-compliant oil tanker that seeks to disregard the security and laws of the Strait of Hormuz,” the IRGC Navy warned.

People who worry more tend to have more negative dreams, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
18:00:53 UTC
03:00:53 KST

Among 389 Italian adults, stress emerged as the most central element in a web of connections linking worry, anxiety and depression, according to a study published in BMC Psychology. People who reported more worry and more depressive symptoms also tended to report more negative dreams, a pattern consistent with the idea that waking concerns carry over into sleep.
Dreams have long been associated with people’s emotional lives. The continuity hypothesis of dreaming proposes that concerns and feelings from waking life can continue into sleep and influence dream experiences. For example, people under pressure may dream about threatening or emotionally intense events.
However, it is difficult to determine how different dream experiences relate to different forms of distress. A person may remember dreams frequently without finding them upsetting, while another person may rarely recall dreams but feel strongly affected by the dreams they do remember. Research on dreams and research on worry, which has been linked to poorer sleep, have also largely been conducted separately.
Vittorio Lenzo of the University of Catania in Italy led a team investigating these relationships. The researchers surveyed 389 Italian-speaking adults recruited through university mailing lists, social media and online blogs. Participants were 18 to 64 years old, with an average age of about 24, and the sample included 330 women, 50 men and nine non-binary participants.
Participants completed an online survey containing three questionnaires. The Mannheim Dream Questionnaire asked how often people recalled their dreams, how emotionally intense their dreams were, how positive or negative their dreams usually felt, how often dreams affected their daytime mood and how often they told other people about their dreams. Each of these features was measured with a single question.
The Penn State Worry Questionnaire measured pathological worry, meaning persistent and difficult-to-control thoughts about possible future problems. Participants also completed the Depression Anxiety Stress Scale, which measures symptoms related to depression, anxiety and stress.
Lenzo and colleagues then used network analysis. In this type of analysis, each psychological feature is treated as a point in a network, and the connections between points represent how strongly two features are related after accounting for all the others. This approach can show which variables are most strongly linked to the rest of the network.
On average, participants reported high levels of worry, enough to be considered clinically elevated compared with normative data. Depression, anxiety and stress formed a closely connected cluster, with the strongest connection between anxiety and stress. Worry was most strongly associated with stress and only weakly with anxiety and depression, which the authors suggest may reflect worry’s role in sustaining prolonged tension.
Within the dream measures, people who recalled their dreams more often were also more likely to tell others about them, the strongest connection in the entire network. Frequent dream recall was moderately associated with more emotionally intense dreams, which were in turn linked with the feeling that dreams affected daytime mood.
The links between dreams and distress were weaker. People whose dreams tended to be more negative in tone reported more depressive symptoms and more worry, and people who felt their dreams affected their daytime mood reported more anxiety. The authors note that this pattern fits the continuity hypothesis, since people who worry a great deal may carry that vigilance into sleep.
Stress was the most central variable in the overall network, meaning it had the strongest total connections to the other variables, while depression, dream recall and dream intensity were among the least central. Dream emotional tone had what researchers call a negative expected influence, meaning its connections to the rest of the network ran mostly in the opposite direction from those of distress.
The authors concluded that “dream experiences are integrated components of a dynamic system of emotional functioning.” They suggest that more positive dream experiences might help dampen distress, while stress may amplify it. They also propose that worry and depression could lead to more negative dreams, which might in turn feed next-day anxiety, though both ideas require testing in studies that follow people over time.
There are a few things to keep in mind. Because the data were collected at a single point in time, the study cannot show whether dreams influence distress, whether distress shapes dreams, or both. The participants were a convenience sample of mostly young women recruited online, which limits how far the findings can be generalized.
All information was self-reported, and dream experiences depend on people’s memories, which may introduce bias. Each dream feature was measured with a single question, the connections between dreams and distress were small, and while the network was generally stable when tested using repeated statistical resampling, some individual connections were less certain.
The study, “Dream experiences and psychological distress: a network analysis of pathological worry, depression, anxiety, and stress,” was authored by Vittorio Lenzo, Chiara Fioretti, Alessandro Musetti, Raffaele De Luca Picione, Christian Franceschini, Patrizia Strano, Maria C. Quattropani and Alberto Sardella.

Iran to pursue legal case over US strike on Minab school in foreign courts: Gharibabadi
MINAB – Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister for Legal and International Affairs says Tehran is pursuing legal action over the American strike on the Shajareh Tayyebeh school in Minab, with documentation completed and a special committee formed to file lawsuits in foreign courts.
Kazem Gharibabadi made the remarks on Sunday during a visit to the school site and in meetings with the families of the victims, stressing that legal follow-up is underway at both the domestic and international levels.
"The martyrdom of 168 people — mostly schoolchildren, along with a number of parents and teachers — is a great tragedy for the families, the people of Minab and all of Iran, and we share in the grief and suffering of these families," Gharibabadi said.
He said schools, academic and educational centers and hospitals are protected under international humanitarian law during armed conflicts, adding that attacks on such sites constitute a serious violation of those rules.
Gharibabadi said the documentation of the incident has been collected inside the country and that the judicial case will be heard after completing the necessary procedures. He added that relevant bodies are preparing dossiers for filing claims abroad.
"A special committee with the participation of relevant agencies has been formed in Tehran to follow up on this crime, and the documentation received from the judicial system will form the basis for legal action to file lawsuits in several countries," he said.
He noted that the Foreign Ministry, the Legal Vice Presidency and other responsible bodies are deploying their capacities for the legal, political and diplomatic pursuit of the case, adding that the President has emphasized the need to follow up on the crimes committed.
"The families of the martyrs of the Shajareh Tayyebeh school must witness justice being served," Gharibabadi said. "The follow-up of this case will not be limited to inside the country, and we will use international legal capacities to hold the perpetrators accountable."
Referring to other cases related to attacks carried out during the war, including the strike on the Lamerd stadium, Gharibabadi said their legal pursuit is also on the agenda and efforts are underway to pursue the responsibility of the perpetrators in competent authorities.
He also praised the role of the people of Hormozgan in defending the country and stressed support for the martyrs' families and continued pursuit of their legal demands, saying the Foreign Ministry will use its full capacity to help ensure accountability and justice.
On the Strait of Hormuz, Gharibabadi said the waterway has become a symbol of Iranian identity and that Iran will use its capacities to confront enemies. Stressing that Iran was not the initiator of the war, he said the country is defending itself against aggression, has not started a war in the past two centuries, but has stood against aggressors.
He also warned that Iran's response in what he described as the 40-day war differed from that in the 12-day war, cautioning that in the event of renewed military action by the enemy, the Islamic Republic's reaction will be different from the past, and expressed hope that the other sides will act rationally to avoid a repeat of the confrontation.
In the early hours of Feb. 28, 2026 — the first hours of what Tehran describes as the joint US-Israeli aggression against Iran — the Shajareh Tayyebeh school in Minab was hit three times at intervals by missiles. In the incident, 168 people, including schoolgirls and schoolboys, as well as teachers, school staff and parents, were killed.
In a separate incident, five people, including a child, were killed and 68 others, mostly women and children, were injured in a US airstrike late on Sept. 1, 2026, on a residential house in the port of Kuhestak in Sirik County, where people were attending a wedding ceremony. Kuhestak is located in Sirik County in southeastern Hormozgan Province.
Minab, the second most populous county in Hormozgan Province with a population of over 300,000, is located 90 kilometers east of Bandar Abbas.

Araghchi calls for international accountability for environmental destruction in wars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:54:24 UTC
02:54:24 KST

Araghchi calls for international accountability for environmental destruction in wars
TEHRAN — Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has called for stronger international mechanisms to prevent and address environmental destruction during armed conflicts, stressing that the international community must move beyond expressions of concern and ensure effective accountability for those responsible.
Addressing the international conference “Ecocide: The Silent War Crime” in Tehran on Sunday, Araghchi said large-scale environmental destruction during warfare was not merely an ecological concern but an issue directly linked to the right to life, public health, food security, international peace and security, and the rights of future generations.
“Environmental protection must move beyond declarations of commitment and enter the realm of accountability, responsibility and effective international action,” he said, warning that the consequences of environmental damage could persist for years or even decades after hostilities end.
Araghchi emphasized that warfare threatens not only human lives, cities and economic infrastructure but also water resources, soil, air quality, forests, agricultural land, energy infrastructure, natural habitats and biodiversity. The release of hazardous substances, contamination of vital resources and destruction of ecosystems can impose lasting costs on civilian populations long after the fighting has stopped.
Gaza, Lebanon and Iran face lasting environmental damage
Citing Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, Araghchi highlighted the far-reaching environmental consequences of military attacks across the region.
In Gaza, he pointed to the collapse of water and wastewater networks, damage to waste-management systems, contamination of water and soil, coastal pollution, and the accumulation of vast quantities of rubble and potentially hazardous materials.
He noted that the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) has reported unprecedented environmental damage in the Palestinian territory, warning that the destruction of essential infrastructure and contamination of natural resources could affect public health and living conditions for decades.
In Lebanon, Araghchi highlighted damage to forests and agricultural land caused by military attacks and resulting fires. He referred to reports submitted to the United Nations documenting the burning of millions of square meters of land and damage to tens of thousands of olive trees. He also recalled the extensive coastal pollution following attacks on oil-storage facilities, illustrating how damage to industrial infrastructure can generate environmental consequences far beyond the immediate site of an attack.
Turning to Iran, the foreign minister addressed the environmental risks associated with US and Israeli attacks on Iranian oil, refinery and energy facilities in March 2026.
He cited a UNEP assessment from that month concerning attacks on oil facilities in and around urban areas, including Tehran, where fires released hazardous compounds into the environment.
Such pollutants, Araghchi warned, can spread from the atmosphere into soil and water resources and ultimately affect the food chain, creating risks that extend well beyond immediate economic losses.
The consequences are particularly serious for civilians, children and future generations, who may continue to suffer the health and environmental effects of wartime contamination long after the conflict has ended.
International law must ensure accountability
Araghchi stressed that international law must not remain indifferent to environmental destruction and violations of fundamental human rights during armed conflicts.
He called for the effective implementation of international humanitarian law, particularly the principles of distinction and proportionality, alongside a thorough assessment of the direct, indirect and long-term environmental consequences of military operations.
The principle of distinction requires parties to distinguish between military objectives and civilian objects. The principle of proportionality prohibits attacks expected to cause incidental civilian harm excessively in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. International humanitarian law also provides specific protection for the natural environment against certain forms of damage during armed conflicts.
Araghchi argued that no state or actor should consider itself above international responsibility. Extensive ecosystem destruction, severe contamination of water and soil, and lasting damage to natural resources must be addressed through effective mechanisms for prevention, independent documentation, damage assessment, compensation and accountability.
He said Iran supports legal and expert discussions aimed at strengthening international environmental protection, including consideration of recognizing ecocide as a distinct international crime.
The concept of ecocide broadly concerns exceptionally severe environmental destruction. Proposals to establish it as a separate international crime have gained attention in international legal discussions, although its precise definition, scope, and legal status remain subjects of debate.
For Iran, Araghchi indicated, strengthening international protection requires moving beyond general declarations and developing practical mechanisms capable of establishing responsibility and addressing the consequences of environmental destruction.
Iran warns against double standards in environmental protection
The foreign minister also warned against double standards and the politicization of environmental issues, insisting that environmental obligations must be applied fairly, transparently and without discrimination.
Environmental protection, he said, must not become a privilege for some countries and an obligation on others.
Araghchi further called for serious examination of the legal, humanitarian and environmental consequences of unilateral coercive measures that restrict countries' access to financing, clean technologies and essential equipment needed to protect the environment, manage ecological emergencies and address climate change.
He argued that environmental justice requires developing countries to have access to financial resources, scientific expertise and clean technologies necessary to respond to environmental challenges without unnecessary or discriminatory barriers.
He also stressed that independent documentation of environmental damage, scientific assessment of its long-term effects, and arrangements for compensation and rehabilitation should form an integral part of the international response to armed conflicts.
Three priorities for international cooperation
Araghchi proposed three priorities for strengthening international cooperation to prevent environmental destruction and address its consequences.
First, he called for stronger international legal frameworks and clear criteria for identifying, assessing, and responding to cases of extensive and severe environmental damage.
Second, he proposed the establishment of impartial, science-based mechanisms to document environmental damage caused by armed conflicts, assess its long-term consequences, determine applicable legal responsibilities and facilitate compensation.
Third, he urged expanded regional and international cooperation to prevent environmental destruction, restore damaged ecosystems and support countries and communities that lack adequate financial resources or technical capacity.
COP31 offers an opportunity to address the environmental costs of war
Araghchi also identified the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) as an opportunity to draw greater international attention to the environmental and climate consequences of military attacks.
He said Iran was prepared to contribute its scientific, legal and diplomatic capabilities to collective efforts aimed at preventing large-scale environmental destruction, strengthening regional cooperation and promoting international accountability.
The foreign minister emphasized that environmental damage caused by armed conflict cannot be treated as a secondary consequence of war. Its effects on public health, food security, natural resources and the livelihoods of affected communities make it an issue of international concern.
Concluding his remarks, Araghchi called on the international community to ensure that those responsible for environmental destruction do not escape accountability.
“Nature has no voice at the negotiating table or on the battlefield,” he said, stressing that collective action is necessary to prevent environmental devastation from coming at the expense of humanity's future.

Powers greater than US tried to conquer Iran but ended up in ‘dustbin of history,’ Rezaei says

Powers greater than US tried to conquer Iran but ended up in ‘dustbin of history,’ Rezaei says
TEHRAN — Iran’s top security official says Tehran will determine the outcome of its confrontation with Washington, rules out a return to previous diplomatic norms and warns of potential retaliation against US assets in the event of renewed aggression.
Major General Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC), has warned that the United States will face the same fate as previous powers that attempted to subjugate Iran, saying even stronger empires ultimately disappeared into the “dustbin of history.”
In an exclusive interview with Press TV on Saturday, Rezaei said Washington had suffered repeated defeats in its confrontation with Iran and had increasingly resorted to economic warfare, which he characterized as a response to its failure to achieve its objectives through military pressure.
He stressed that Iran, rather than the United States, would determine when the confrontation ends, adding that Tehran would continue to resist until its demands were met.
Addressing the US military presence in West Asia, Rezaei pointed to the withdrawal of American forces from Iraq as evidence, in his assessment, of Washington’s failure to impose its military agenda on the region. He described the development as vindication of Iran’s longstanding opposition to the deployment of US forces in the region.
Rezaei also said more than 30 million Iranians had registered for the Janfada (Sacrifice for Iran) campaign, which was intended to mobilize volunteers prepared to take up arms in the event of US aggression.
On diplomacy, the SNSC secretary said Iran would not return to its previous diplomatic norms, while emphasizing that Tehran was not abandoning diplomacy altogether.
His remarks signaled that, although diplomatic engagement remained an option, Iran’s approach would be shaped by its assessment of the confrontation with Washington and the need to secure its demands.
Rezaei also warned that renewed US aggression could expose American assets to retaliation, including key data systems and artificial intelligence sensors.
Rezaei invokes ancient Rome to counter ‘civilizational war’ narrative
In a separate part of his remarks, Rezaei invoked the defeat of Roman forces by the Sasanian Empire under King Shapur I to challenge the framing of the confrontation with Iran as a civilizational war by US officials.
The reference draws on a significant episode in Iranian history. In 260 AD, Shapur I defeated the Roman emperor Valerian at the Battle of Edessa and captured him, marking a major setback for Rome in its eastern campaigns.
By invoking that episode, Rezaei placed the current confrontation within a broader historical narrative of Iran’s resistance to foreign powers and attempts at domination.
Hormuz tensions and the dispute with Washington
Rezaei also identified Washington and its regional allies as central to the tensions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most strategically important maritime corridors for oil and gas shipments.
Iran’s restrictions on passage through the strait followed the latest round of US-Israeli military aggression. The disruption affected a critical route for international energy trade and contributed to heightened concerns over global oil and energy supplies. The resulting market pressures also prompted the United States and the International Energy Agency (IEA) to draw on strategic reserves on multiple occasions.
Following the signing of an Iran-US memorandum of understanding in Islamabad in June, Tehran reopened the waterway. Iran subsequently said Washington had breached the understanding by imposing a blockade on Iranian ports, prompting the country’s armed forces to close the maritime corridor again.
The dispute over the strait has become a major point of contention between Tehran and Washington, linking military developments and diplomatic commitments to the security of international shipping and global energy markets.
Rezaei’s remarks underscored Tehran’s position that any resolution to the confrontation must take account of Iran’s security demands and its role in the region. His comments also made clear that Iran does not regard a return to the previous diplomatic framework as inevitable, even as it continues to leave the door open to diplomacy.
