Bombs that pushed Iran across the rubicon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:44:29 UTC
02:44:29 KST

Bombs that pushed Iran across the rubicon
Two wars launched by the US and Israel under the false pretext of stopping Iran's nuclear weapon may have made it more likely
TEHRAN – Donald Trump says he went to war to ensure Iran never gets the bomb — dozens of times and counting. Yet the war fought in the name of non-proliferation has acted like a boomerang: far from closing Iran's path to the bomb, it may have pushed Tehran closer to it.
The US and Israel say they attacked Iran twice to prevent it from acquiring a nuclear weapon. Yet at the time of both attacks, both US intelligence and the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) assessed that Tehran was not building one.
 
No evidence has emerged that Iran is currently racing to build a bomb. But a growing number of Western analysts argue the wars themselves have strengthened Tehran's incentive to do so — while inside Iran, calls to revise the nuclear doctrine and reconsider membership in the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) have moved from the margins to the mainstream.
 
The result is the central paradox of the current confrontation: a preventive war that may have produced the very outcome it claimed to prevent.
 
The justification vs. the assessment
Washington's stated rationale has been consistent: Iran must not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon.
But two key institutions directly contradicted the claim that Iran was actively pursuing one.
US intelligence: Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard testified to Congress in March 2025 that Iran was not building a nuclear weapon and that Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei had not reauthorized the weapons program suspended in 2003. A leaked US intelligence assessment reported by News24 on March 18, 2026, after the US operation known as Midnight Hammer, again found "no effort to rebuild enrichment" and concluded that Tehran had not moved to weaponize.
The IAEA: Director General Rafael Grossi said on June 19, 2025, amid the first war: "We found no indication of an active, systematic plan to build a weapon in Iran." He added that military strikes would only "delay the indispensable diplomatic work" needed for long-term assurance that
Iran does not acquire a weapon.
In other words, both attacks were launched not against an ongoing weaponization program documented by inspectors or spies, but against capabilities and intentions that Washington and Tel Aviv insisted could turn into one.
The second war removed a barrier: the fatwa
For two decades, Iran's principal political-religious barrier to a bomb was explicit: a fatwa by Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei declaring the production, stockpiling and use of nuclear weapons haram (forbidden).
Iranian officials repeatedly cited the fatwa as the reason Iran had the technical capacity but not the intent. Former Foreign Minister and former Atomic Energy chief Ali Akbar Salehi said in February 2024 that Iran possessed "all the pieces" needed for a weapon but had not assembled them — a restraint Tehran attributed to the Leader's ruling.
Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei was martyred in the joint US-Israel airstrike on the morning of February 28, 2026, in his office in central Tehran.
His successor, Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, has made no clear public statement on the nuclear fatwa. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi acknowledged the uncertainty in an interview with Reuters on March 18, 2026, saying Iran's position against weapons would not undergo "significant change," but adding that fatwas depend on the issuing jurist and that he could not yet judge the new Leader's jurisprudential view. Any change, he said, would depend on the new Leader.
But that key religious prohibition that underpinned this doctrine for 20 years no longer exists — removed by those who coveted Iran's collapse and US domination over Iran.
In Washington and Tel Aviv, a quiet consensus: the bombing is making the bomb more likely
The most striking warning came, paradoxically, from inside Israel's own intelligence establishment. Danny Citrinowicz, who until recently ran the Iran branch of Israeli military intelligence, told The Times of Israel last summer that kinetic action would push Tehran "to cross the Rubicon on the nuclear file." The war, he said, would not prevent an Iranian bomb. It would accelerate it.
Citrinowicz was not alone, and what followed over the next year was something rare in the normally fractious world of arms control: agreement. From different capitals, disciplines and politics, analysts began describing the same mechanism — a state under existential bombardment, watching its declared, inspected sites destroyed, rationally concluding that only an undeclared deterrent could prevent the next round.
At Carnegie, James Acton argued that the premise of "obliteration" was an illusion. Iran, he noted, had almost certainly dispersed fissile material and key equipment before the strikes, and with what it retained it could, if it ever chose weaponization, move "in less than a year, even significantly less than a year." Eric Brewer, a former US intelligence analyst now at the Nuclear Threat Initiative, put it more bluntly to Reuters in May: as far as anyone knows, Iran still has all of its nuclear material, much of it in places American munitions cannot reach.
The institutional voices followed. Daryl Kimball of the Arms Control Association observed that the campaign had exposed the ceiling of force: bombing could neither erase knowledge nor permanently eliminate capability. Ellie Geranmayeh of the European Council on Foreign Relations noted that capability was "largely still in place," and that without inspectors — themselves now sidelined by war — existing stocks could be enriched to weapons grade with alarming speed. Even the press that had initially cheered restraint turned sombre. Time warned that destroyed centrifuges can be rebuilt but a changed strategic calculus cannot be undone; The Guardian editorialised that prevention by bombardment, absent any diplomatic endgame, historically hardens proliferation incentives rather than softening them.
The most systematic verdict arrived in August 2026 from Defense Priorities in Washington. In an explainer titled "A Security Dilemma Made Worse," it concluded that by waging a war that threatened the very survival of the Iranian state, the US and Israel had strengthened Tehran's motive to acquire the one weapon that might deter a third war. Proliferation was not inevitable, it wrote — merely more likely than before the strikes. Trita Parsi at the Quincy Institute and Ali Vaez at the International Crisis Group, neither of them hawks, reached the same destination by a shorter road: Tehran's determination to obtain a deterrent, they wrote, had been "dramatically increased," and rebuilding from under the rubble with an explicit weapons goal was now thinkable in a way it had not been before.
In short, deterrence theory was working — but in reverse. A country that finds conventional deterrence insufficient, and international verification incapable of protecting it, does what threatened states do: it reconsiders.
In Tehran, the unsayable is now said aloud
For years, even raising the question of a bomb in public in Iran was taboo. The fatwa of Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei stood like a wall around the debate: possession itself was forbidden, and that was the end of it. The wall is gone now, and the debate that has rushed into its place would have been unimaginable two years ago.
It began as a whisper. In October 2024, Kamal Kharrazi — the urbane head of the Strategic Council on Foreign Relations — said calmly that if an existential threat emerged, Iran would revise its doctrine. On April 1, 2026, during the US-Israel war against Iran, his house in Tehran was struck by US-Israeli aircraft. His wife was martyred in the attack and he was severely wounded, succumbing to his wounds eight days later. The capability, he noted, existed. Only the Leader's ruling stood in the way. That same month, 39 members of parliament wrote privately to the Supreme National Security Council asking for precisely such a revision.
Then came the first war, and the whispers grew louder. Ali Shamkhani, the veteran security official martyred on the first day of the second war, on February 28 of this year, appeared on state television in October 2025 and said, with the bluntness of a man who felt history had vindicated his doubts, that had he known then what he knows now, he would have supported building the bomb in the 1990s. By September 2025, the private letters had become a public petition: more than seventy MPs wrote to the president and the Council declaring an arsenal "necessary for nuclear deterrence" and openly asking for the fatwa to be reinterpreted — production for deterrence, they argued, was not the same as use.
What is remarkable is not merely the content but the setting. The argument is now made on camera, in parliament, and from the Friday pulpit. When Hojjatoleslam Haj Ali Akbari told worshippers in Tehran on October 9 that the nuclear program "belongs to the Iranian nation" and that there is a domestic demand to revise membership in the NPT, no one in the establishment criticized him. A month earlier, Nezamoddin Mousavi, a former MP close to the Revolutionary Guards, had told Ensaf News what many in the system now say privately: ambiguity did not prevent war.
It was time, he said, to review the doctrine, the worth of the NPT, and the meaning of deterrence after the strikes on Iran's own facilities.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi still holds the official line — no significant change, he told Reuters in March — but even his reassurance contained the seed of doubt. Fatwas, he acknowledged, belong to the jurist who issues them, and the new Leader, Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, has not yet spoken. In Tehran today, that silence is itself the story.
A 47-year-old dream turned nightmare
Seen from Tehran, the two campaigns were never really about centrifuges. The US and Israel knew better than anyone that Iran was not pursuing a nuclear weapon — their own intelligence services and the IAEA had told them so. What they pursued was a 47-year-old dream: regime change in Iran.
The calculation was that a heavy air campaign, combined with inciting street unrest, would finally realize that old fantasy. But aggression still needs a pretext. And what better pretext than the nuclear file — an issue they had spent more than two decades turning into a lever for global anti-Iran propaganda and for imposing wave after wave of sanctions?
Iran stood firm. The dream did not come true. Instead, it has curdled into a nightmare — one whose ultimate cost for Iran's enemies is still unknown, and still growing. The wars meant to foreclose Iran's nuclear options have instead opened the most serious national debate in its history about whether those options should be reconsidered, and have left Washington and Tel Aviv facing an Iran more convinced than ever that only its own strength can guarantee its survival.

Iran has described the US response to its seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz as “insufficient”, saying Washington must clarify its position on unresolved issues.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said on Sunday that the US had accepted some conditions but remained unclear on others, according to state media.
“We presented seven conditions to the Americans and clearly stated that the Strait of Hormuz would not be opened to them, and no negotiations would take place until these conditions are met,” he said.
Iran presented the proposal during the UN General Assembly, offering to reopen the strategic waterway and restore normal maritime passage within seven days if its conditions were met. Washington later responded through Qatari intermediaries.
Rezaei said Iran was “no longer in the process of responding to the Americans” and that Washington needed to clarify the issues still unclear to Tehran.
"In their response, they have accepted some of our conditions, while others remain unclear," he said.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Tehran said in late September that it had received a US response to its latest proposal to revive the collapsed ceasefire in the Gulf, days after US President Donald Trump said he had rejected it.
Qatar and other mediators have exchanged messages between Washington and Tehran in efforts to end the conflict and reopen the strait.
Before the war began in late February with US and Israeli attacks on Iran, the waterway carried a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas.

Spanish police dismantle Ceuta’s last migrant camp ahead of royal visit
Spanish authorities dismantled the last remaining migrant encampment in Ceuta on Sunday morning, two days before a planned visit by King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia to the Spanish enclave bordering Morocco.
Spain’s National Police said in a social media statement that more than 350 officers were deployed alongside the Civil Guard, local police and the army, with armoured vehicles and police vans supporting the operation.
Officers cleared the Guano settlement on El Trampolin beach, close to the Moroccan border. The makeshift camp was estimated to house around 500 migrants who had not been identified by Spanish authorities following an influx in late July.
Thousands of people crossed from Morocco into Spanish territory by sea and land during that period, with at least 100 people reported to have died attempting the journey.
According to Spanish newspaper El País, adults from the camp were taken to a temporary detention facility in warehouses at Tarajal, near the border, for identification ahead of their expected transfer to other facilities.
Children were also among those sleeping in makeshift tents and on mattresses on the beach. Some held signs reading: "I am a minor".
Spanish authorities said the children would be taken to the National Police headquarters before being moved to available reception centres.
Spain’s ombudsman, Ángel Gabilondo, urged the country’s autonomous communities to show "solidarity" by taking in migrant children who had been in Ceuta since July. He said he hoped the crisis "will not leave a wound" in a city experiencing "much pain and suffering".
The National Police said Sunday’s operation was necessary to maintain public order and security. It was the fifth major police operation to clear public spaces since 29 September.
Ángel Víctor Torres Pérez, Spain’s minister for territorial policy and democratic memory, said 12,000 people had returned to Morocco between 10 August and Sunday.
He described the returns as "voluntary", saying many had realised their cases would end in expulsion because they did not meet the requirements for asylum.
According to Spain’s Interior Ministry, nearly 25,000 migrants have arrived irregularly in the country so far this year. On Saturday night, a Maritime Rescue vessel rescued 96 people, including nine women and two children, from a small boat off Lanzarote.
The leader of the opposition People’s Party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, pledged to make Ceuta a priority if he became prime minister following the snap election scheduled for 29 November. Incumbent Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called the election on Monday.
Felipe and Letizia are expected to begin their visit to Ceuta on Tuesday and attend a ceremony commemorating migrants who died.
The visit comes amid tensions between Madrid and Rabat. Speaking at the opening of Morocco’s parliamentary session earlier this week, King Mohammed VI said cooperation with Spain would not be subject to "pressure, threat, or blackmail".
He added that Rabat would not allow certain politicians to "instrumentalise" the situation.

As it stands, most polls conducted show that neither the bloc under Benjamin Netanyahu nor the opposition bloc under Gadi Eisenkot will gain enough seats in the election, which could mean a hung parliament and another vote months later.
This would mean that, in order to oust Netanyahu's government, an Eisenkot bloc would have to negotiate support from Israel's Palestinian parties, which are polling to have enough seats to potentially bring the bloc over the line.
"It is a reflection of the fact that Palestinian citizens and the Arab parties have a significant amount of clout because of the fracture of the current Israeli electoral landscape," Amjad Iraqi, Senior Analyst for Israel and Palestine at the International Crisis Group, said of Jabareen's announcement.
"Whether it's the joint-list or Ra'am [the second Palestinian bloc], everyone can see that the seats that the Arab parties will take will kind of decide whether a coalition can come about," he told The New Arab.

Iraqi added that the Joint-List should be mindful of Ra'am, the other main Arab Palestinian party running in the election, which has been more willing to put aside Palestinian statehood in order to join coalitions.
In an environment where Jewish-Israeli politicians in the Eisenkot Bloc have ruled out working with Israel's Palestinian parties, Iraqi said that there's also a question about whether Eisenkot would bring himself to seek the support of the parties, despite what polling shows.
"It's too difficult for Eisenkot to bring himself to ally with the parties or to ensure his other Jewish-Israeli coalition partners will also sit or be allowed to be propped up by the two Arab parties," Iraqi said, adding that they could be "quite resentful that they are beholden to the bargaining of these Arab parties, whether its because of racism or because they think it's a political handicap."
In September, Israel's Central Elections Committee banned the participation of the Joint List and Ra'am, as well as candidates for the Joint List Hadash MK Offer Cassif and Balad head Sami Abou Shehadeh, with widespread consensus among Jewish-Israeli political parties. The bans were later overturnned by the Supreme Court, while Abou Shehadeh withdrew his candidacy.
Among the plethora of different options, including a hung parliament resulting in fresh elections, or a deal between Netanyahu's Likud and Eisenkot, Iraqi said that "Israeli elections have a proclivity towards surprises, so I wouldn't write off anything".

IAI to unveil new tactical radar that seeks out low-flying drones at US's AUSA military expo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:15:46 UTC
02:15:46 KST

Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) announced on Sunday that it will unveil a new radar solution that can detect low-flying drones from its position suspended high above the ground.
The system, known as POINT@AIR, brings long-range radar detection and persistent surveillance to a compact, highly mobile aerostat platform. The unveiling was made at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting & Exposition in Washington, taking place this week.
The radar’s elevated position extends its line of sight beyond terrain and other ground-level obstructions, supporting earlier detection of low-altitude threats, while enabling forces to adapt surveillance coverage as mission requirements evolve.
In that sense, a heavy focus will be on anti-drone defense, an area where Hezbollah exposed IDF weaknesses during the 2026 conflict, leading to significant IDF losses.
The system will not replace MMR radar technology and other radars which are primarily focused on long-range detection, but will supplement them in certain specific areas where the threats, such as drones, are evolving.
Persistent operation, rapid relocation capabilities
Designed for persistent operation and rapid relocation, the system can operate without reliance on permanent infrastructure and can detect and track multiple aerial, maritime, and ground targets.
This is one of the new major issues, given that enemy threats have become more unpredictable regarding where and how they will attack from.
It supports multiple missions simultaneously, prioritizes targets according to operational requirements, and interfaces with command-and-control systems to contribute to an integrated operational picture, signaling the continued move toward greater integration of AI and the full network of sensors.
IAI's CEO Guy Bar Lev: 'Seeing the battlespace is the starting point for every effective defense'
Guy Bar Lev, president and CEO of IAI, said, “Seeing the battlespace is the starting point for every effective defense. The more persistent and comprehensive that view becomes, the better equipped forces are to understand what is unfolding, anticipate threats and act with confidence. IAI is increasingly developing next-generation capabilities that expand the boundaries of situational awareness and provide our customers with greater visibility, flexibility and time to respond.”
Dror Bar, CEO of ELTA Systems and EVP at IAI: “POINT@AIR reflects a fundamental shift in how persistent surveillance can be delivered - bringing sophisticated radar capabilities to an elevated platform that is smaller, more mobile and adaptable to the mission. Our goal was not simply to reduce the size of an existing solution, but to rethink what an aerostat-based radar could achieve. By combining advanced AESA technology, long-range detection and 360-degree coverage in a compact configuration, POINT@AIR gives operators the ability to establish persistent awareness where fixed infrastructure may not be practical.”
Based on the proven ELM-2083 radar family, POINT@AIR incorporates advanced Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) technology, with electronic scanning in both azimuth and elevation combined with mechanical rotation to provide 360-degree coverage.

Israel’s next leader should be chosen by Israelis, not Washington - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:15:36 UTC
02:15:36 KST

Israel owes an enormous debt of gratitude to the United States – to Democratic and Republican administrations, to president Joe Biden for standing beside us after the horror of October 7, to President Donald Trump for confronting Iran and advancing the Abraham Accords, to Evangelical Christians who have defended the Jewish state when others abandoned it, and above all to the American people.
Yet gratitude must never become submission, because Israel’s prime minister must be chosen by Israelis in Jerusalem, not by a president, donors, or political strategists gathered at Mar-a-Lago.
Trump has said that staying out of Israel’s October 27 election would be appropriate. He has also suggested that he might endorse someone. More recently, he shared an article highlighting a poll favorable to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc.
That may not constitute a formal endorsement, but in a close election, it is political intervention by suggestion. Our country is not a client state, an Evangelical political project, or a Trump-branded Middle Eastern property. Gaza is not an empty beachfront awaiting luxury towers, and Israel is not a corporation whose controlling shares belong to foreign patrons.
We are a sovereign democracy whose citizens bury the dead, send children to war, and live with the consequences.
Trump understands the power of uncertainty. By saying that he may endorse a candidate without naming one, he encourages every Israeli contender to seek his approval. Netanyahu can present himself as Trump’s natural partner. His challengers must assure Washington that they will protect the alliance.
Trump gains leverage before casting a single political coin. This is not merely affection for Netanyahu. Trump values loyalty, public credit, and the image of being the decisive dealmaker. He sees diplomacy through transactions, leverage, and visible victories.
That approach can produce breakthroughs, as the Abraham Accords demonstrated. But nations are communities of memory and responsibility, not properties to be acquired, redesigned, and branded.
Netanyahu understands this theater. For years, he has used photographs, speeches, and meetings with American presidents to reinforce the argument that only he can manage Israel’s most important alliance. His message is familiar: Without me, Israel will be isolated. Without me, Washington will turn away. Without me, the country is unsafe.
That is not democratic confidence. It is manufactured dependency. Israel’s future also cannot be managed by a narrow diplomatic circle embodied by Netanyahu’s longtime confidant Ron Dermer, despite his experience.
Dermer helped cultivate American and Gulf relationships. But diplomacy conducted mainly through leaders, billionaires, investment channels, and palace intermediaries leaves ordinary citizens outside the room. Israel needs institutions, public accountability and many voices, not one prime minister, one emissary, and one foreign patron.
Gadi Eisenkot's political rise
The rise of Gadi Eisenkot exposes the weakness of that argument. Israelis themselves have presented another credible leader: a former military chief with decades of security experience, personal sacrifice, and a reputation for sobriety. Recent polling has placed Eisenkot’s Yashar Party near or ahead of Likud, and one survey showed him leading Netanyahu as the public’s preferred prime minister.
Americans do not have to support Eisenkot. Trump does not have to like him. Evangelical donors do not have to agree with every decision he may make. But they must respect the possibility that Israeli citizens, after October 7, want a different kind of leadership less theatrical, less divisive and more accountable.
Trump should promise not to endorse a candidate. American political organizations and major donors should show the same restraint. They may support Israel and advocate for their beliefs, but money, access, and presidential prestige should not select its government.
Israeli candidates must also stop campaigning as applicants for American approval. They should tell voters what they will do about security, diplomacy, living costs, national service, social inclusion, and the failures of October 7. Their mandate must come from Israelis.
The next government should protect the American alliance as a relationship between democratic nations, not political personalities. Israel worked with Biden despite disagreements. It can work with Trump without surrendering its independence. Institutional alliances endure; personality arrangements collapse.
Eisenkot should make this principle central to his campaign. He can thank Trump for his contributions, honor Evangelical friendship, and recognize Biden’s support during Israel’s crisis while stating clearly that no outside leader will receive a veto over Israeli democracy. That position is not anti-American. It is the foundation of an alliance between equals.
I write as an Ethiopian-born Israeli-American who loves both countries. America taught me the importance of constitutional government and peaceful transfers of power. Israel taught me that Jewish sovereignty carries responsibility.
Those lessons lead to the same conclusion: Friends may advise, assist, and disagree, but citizens must decide. Israel’s election belongs to the nurse in Jerusalem, the reservist returning from Gaza, the struggling family in Beersheba, the Arab teacher in Nazareth, and the Ethiopian-Israeli mother whose children serve a country that still too rarely allows her community to represent it.
My teacher, Rabbi Jonathan Sacks, z”l, expressed this principle clearly: “Whoever governs in Israel does so only under the authority delegated by God on the one hand, the people on the other.” That covenantal principle applies equally to domestic politicians and foreign benefactors. Israel’s democratic authority comes from its people, not from Mar-a-Lago, royal palaces, billionaires, or political donors.
President Trump may be Israel’s friend. Evangelical Christians may be among Israel’s most loyal supporters. President Biden and millions of Americans deserve our gratitude.
But none of them is Israel’s kingmaker. Let the citizens of Israel choose. If they choose Gadi Eisenkot, Washington should respect that decision.
Israel’s future must be decided in Jerusalem, not at Mar-a-Lago.
The writer is a former New York City Supreme Court detective, an investigator and educator in conflict resolution and restorative peace, and a moral diplomacy expert. His upcoming book, Moral Diplomacy for a Broken World, is inspired by the late Rabbi Jonathan Sacks.

====================================================================================================

The world’s goodwill toward Israel was the exception, not the rule - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:15:22 UTC
02:15:22 KST

When I was 19, my father and I took my rabbi, Sinai Adler, to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum in Washington because the rabbi was a survivor, and he refused to believe that the American government kept a permanent exhibition in which it admitted it could have interrupted the machinery of Auschwitz and chose not to.
He needed to see the admission with his own eyes. The gallery held a US War Department letter explaining the decision not to bomb the rail lines and a reconnaissance photograph of the camp taken from an American bomber. That photograph was made 17 days after Rabbi Adler had been brought through the gate.
As we walked out, my father tried to lift him. The halls were thick with school groups, and most of the children were not Jewish, which my father offered as proof that the world had learned something and that the next generation would not repeat the crime. Rabbi Adler answered that they were only coming to study their mistakes and to learn how to do it better the next time.
Years later, in a study hall in Israel, a student told him that German visitors were standing at the back of the room. They had come, they said, to see the miracle of the Jewish state. Students argued that these Germans had not been alive during the war and that six decades had passed. Rabbi Adler had them removed from the campus.
Those two scenes can be filed under trauma if you want an easy label. Rabbi Adler was a careful reader and a disciplined mind, and the conclusions he drew did not begin in shock.
He returned again and again to the Talmudic teaching that Esau hates Jacob. He treated that line as an operating instruction. Gentiles will persecute Jews, and a Jew who forgets that fact is unprepared for what history holds.
I hear the same complaint about Israel that I have heard for years. If only the country explained itself more clearly, if only the press operation were sharper, the world would grant the benefit of the doubt and perhaps even real support, especially after the massacre of October 7.
The evidence offered for that hope is the long stretch of Western backing that Israel enjoyed through most of its first seven decades. There were breaks in that pattern.
The West changes how it treats Israel
US President Dwight D. Eisenhower threatened Israel over the Sinai campaign of 1956. France embargoed arms on the eve of the Six Day War. Boycott campaigns gathered in universities and unions. Still, until about three years ago, the West as a bloc treated Israel as a partner more often than as a defendant.
The hope that better public relations will restore that climate misreads the record. Rabbi Adler and the sages were right about the ground under our feet. Antisemitism is the baseline we can count on. Support is the exception.
A common theory holds that the goodwill of those first decades was an aftershock of the Holocaust, a period in which even polished antisemites understood that Europe had gone too far and that open annihilation had become embarrassing.
That aftershock never erased the double standard. Friends still applied rules to Jerusalem that they would not apply to themselves. The pockets of hostility were the older pattern showing through the courtesy. The courtesy has worn off. The Holocaust survivor bump has ended. Baseline antisemitism has returned. We can argue about the date it faded.
But its end is no longer in dispute.
Support from Evangelical Christians is the large exception that still holds, and it grows out of their theology rather than out of a sudden affection for Jewish power.
Other help arrived from sources that were moral and strategic at once. US president John F. Kennedy approved weapons sales. US politician Henry M. Jackson tied aid for the Soviet Union to the release of Jews who wanted to leave. American president Richard Nixon ordered the airlift that kept Israel standing in the Yom Kippur War.
Those acts matter, and we should remember them with gratitude. They do not rewrite the longer pattern. Not all the gentiles hate us all of the time, but most gentiles will hate us most of the time. History is stubborn on this point for anyone who finds the sentence extreme.
Zionism began because that pattern would not dissolve. For two thousand years millions of Jews absorbed hatred and exile as a condition of life and waited for gentile mercy to improve.
Early Zionists first trusted emancipation and the Enlightenment to repair the Jewish situation from outside. When the repair failed, they concluded that the Jewish people needed a state of their own, a place that could shield them from persecution, let them work at full capacity, and for many restore a life of sanctity in their own land.
At eye level from Rabbi Adler’s seat in his study sat a set of Mishna books that he liked to take down for guests. The volumes had been printed in Berlin in 1936, three years after Hitler took office and three years before the first mass killings.
The publisher added an introduction that explained away the Mishna warnings about trusting gentiles. Those laws, the introduction said, belonged to an ancient world in which pagans hated Jews. The German gentile of the present was the most refined man civilization had produced. Jews could rely on him and did not need to apply the old suspicion. The books were still on the shelf when the refined men began the work the introduction had declared impossible.
The belief that Jews can talk the nations into permanent friendship treats 20 centuries of evidence as a public-relations problem. “Never again” was not coined to fund a better press office.
It was coined to remind Jews what happens when they rest their survival on the goodwill of people who have already shown them the limit of that goodwill.
The museum photograph, the German visitors at the back of the hall, and the Berlin Mishna of 1936 belong to one argument. Learn the baseline. Build as if the exception will not last. Keep the state strong enough that the next improvement in gentile technique never gets its laboratory.
The writer is a Zionist educator at institutions around the world and recently published a new book, Zionism Today.

====================================================================================================

Iran at the threshold, Israel outside the room - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:15:11 UTC
02:15:11 KST

One justification for war with Iran was that time was running out. Tehran, Israelis were told, was “racing” toward nuclear weapons, “a step away” from a bomb.
Yet Iran has been near the nuclear threshold for years. Its distance from a weapon has never depended solely on centrifuges, enriched uranium, or the time needed to produce fissile material. US intelligence assessed that Tehran had acquired capabilities bringing it close to the threshold but had not decided to cross it. A crucial barrier was political.
Six months into the war, it is difficult to say that barrier has strengthened. Nuclear facilities have been damaged, but subsequent US intelligence assessments do not indicate a significant increase in the time Iran would need to produce a weapon.
Questions remain about its enriched uranium stockpile, while discussion in Iran about crossing the threshold has become more open. The war has also opened a front in the Strait of Hormuz and increased Israel’s diplomatic costs, particularly in the United States. Whether it has made Israel safer from nuclear threats remains unclear.
The only effort in the past decade that successfully imposed agreed, monitored, verifiable limits on Iran’s nuclear program was diplomatic. The 2015 agreement dramatically reduced its enriched uranium stockpile, restricted enrichment and centrifuges, and introduced extensive monitoring.
The International Atomic Energy Agency and Western intelligence assessments found Iran compliant with its core nuclear commitments. Missiles, proxies, and other security issues could – and still can – be addressed separately.
When the Trump administration withdrew unilaterally in May 2018 and reimposed sanctions, the IAEA was still verifying compliance. Iran began exceeding the limits afterward. Israel’s push for US withdrawal, followed by the shift from diplomacy to war, demands a sober assessment of this strategy’s costs.
A low-risk diplomatic option remains largely unknown to Israelis. Since 2019, regional states have gathered annually at UN headquarters in New York for the Conference on the Establishment of a Middle East Zone Free of Nuclear Weapons and Other Weapons of Mass Destruction. Its seventh session takes place this November. Iran and the Arab states participate. Israel is invited but stays away.
Israel has long argued that disarmament cannot be separated from regional security; that arrangements must be developed by regional states with their consent; and that states cannot relinquish capabilities considered essential while remaining in conflict with their neighbors.
It has rightly opposed focusing exclusively on its nuclear capabilities while ignoring missiles, chemical and biological weapons, and other threats. These concerns remain relevant.
They do not, however, require postponing disarmament discussions until peace, recognition, normalization, and extensive confidence-building measures have been achieved. Arab states see this approach as an endless series of prerequisites before weapons of mass destruction reach the table.
Peace, confidence-building, arms control, and disarmament can advance in parallel. War only increases the need for communication, escalation prevention, monitoring, and agreements.
Changing the regional landscape
Participation in November would not require Israel to relinquish weapons attributed to it, join the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), abandon nuclear ambiguity, or accept a future treaty in advance. The conference operates by consensus: regional states participate, and decisions cannot be imposed on Israel.
Several longstanding Israeli demands are therefore already met. If Israel wants missiles, delivery systems, escalation prevention, regional security, and confidence-building on the agenda, it should make those demands inside the room.
Participation could itself build mutual confidence. Israel would discuss weapons of mass destruction directly with its neighbors without committing to an outcome. Arab states and Iran would have to accept Israel as a full, equal negotiating partner.
This would not constitute normalization: states conditioning full relations on ending the occupation and reaching an Israeli-Palestinian settlement could retain their positions. But accepting Israel as a legitimate participant would matter to a country that has long insisted recognition and regional relations are essential to disarmament.
The United States also stays away. Alongside its own reservations, Washington has linked its absence to incomplete regional participation and Israel’s opposition to the format.
An Israeli shift could enable an American one. The government formed after October’s elections could invite Washington to join it in November. After months of confrontation with Iran, this would be a significant diplomatic gesture without advance commitments to disarmament, NPT accession, or an unwritten treaty.
There are precedents. Israel participated in Arms Control and Regional Security talks with Arab states in the 1990s and consultations on a weapons of mass destruction conference in 2013–2014; Iran attended one meeting.
Beginning in 1980, Israel joined the UN General Assembly consensus supporting a nuclear-weapon-free Middle East for over two decades, while retaining reservations about how to achieve it. Attending November’s conference would revive a tradition of raising objections and demanding conditions while continuing to talk.
Meanwhile, the regional landscape is changing. Saudi Arabia is expanding its civilian nuclear program and security alliances, including the Mecca Agreement with Turkey and nuclear-armed Pakistan. Iran is reconsidering its nuclear future, and another confrontation remains possible.
Burying one’s nuclear head in the sand does not preserve freedom of action. It leaves others free to shape the reality Israel must confront.
The next government should arrive in New York with Israel’s security interests, reservations, demands, and proposals – and ask Washington to join it. It need not commit to disarmament. Entering the room does not endanger Israel’s security. In today’s regional reality, remaining outside requires an explanation.
The writer is a guest writer at the Mitvim Institute and an advocate for eliminating nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction from the Middle East. She is the founder and executive director of the Middle East Treaty Organization (METO).

Bennett vows to shift 30 billion shekels from draft dodgers; Winter proposes 25% Haredi exemption
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:13:55 UTC
02:13:55 KST

Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett unveiled what he called a "service revolution" on Sunday, promising extensive financial benefits for soldiers and reservists while cutting state support for those who evade military service. At the same time, Ofer Winter, leader of the Amcha Yisrael party, presented a competing conscription plan that would recognize up to 25% of each ultra-Orthodox draft-age cohort as full-time Torah scholars, effectively allowing them to avoid military service.
With just over two weeks remaining before Israel's October 27 election, the rival proposals place the contentious issue of ultra-Orthodox military enlistment at the center of the campaign.
Speaking at an election event, Bennett, chairman of the Beyachad party, outlined a package that includes free daycare for reservists, 50% discounts on certain payments and a housing subsidy of 1 million shekels for eligible service members.
"A vote for Netanyahu and Deri, who promise another four years of state-funded draft evasion, is a vote that guarantees the next disaster," Bennett said, referring to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Shas leader Aryeh Deri.
"For 17 years, Netanyahu has funded draft evasion in exchange for staying in power. Netanyahu is dismantling the IDF, and he knows it. The chief of staff has raised 10 red flags. Hamas is building up its strength along the borders, and the IDF is crying out for reinforcements. It is short 20,000 soldiers."
Bennett argued that the government could no longer continue providing financial support to those who avoid service while the military faces severe personnel shortages.
"As long as Netanyahu, Deri, Smotrich and Goldknopf keep paying people not to enlist, who exactly is going to provide our soldiers with the reinforcements they need?" he asked.
"We will take 30 billion shekels from the draft dodgers and transfer that money to those who serve. That is the service revolution: Anyone who does not serve the country will not receive a single shekel from the state."
Winter's plan: Higher military pay, but exemptions for up to 25% of Haredim
Winter's Amcha Yisrael party also released the main points of its proposed military service reform on Sunday, pledging to make combat soldiers and reservists a national priority.
According to the party, the plan rests on three elements: legislation and financial benefits, establishing military service frameworks adapted to different populations, and Defense Ministry supervision and enforcement of recognized religious study institutions.
The party said implementation would be anchored in a future coalition agreement and the state budget, including the necessary legislation, regulations and enforcement mechanisms.
Among its proposals is a substantial increase in salaries for soldiers performing mandatory service, with combat soldiers receiving double their regular pay toward the end of their service.
However, the proposal also creates a formal exemption mechanism for some Haredi men.
Under the plan, the number of yeshiva students eligible for recognition as full-time Torah scholars would depend on the IDF's operational requirements and its ability to absorb new recruits, with an upper limit of 25% of each Haredi draft-age cohort.
That would leave a significant share of eligible ultra-Orthodox men outside military service, despite Winter's repeated declarations that he intends to end widespread draft evasion.
The party said its model would establish a clear legal framework governing each citizen's obligations to the state and the benefits available according to their contribution.
"The guiding principle is clear: Those who give will receive. Those who do not give will not receive," the party said.
Every citizen reaching service age would be required to report to the authorities and establish their status through one of three tracks: military service in the IDF, national or civilian service, or enrollment in a recognized and supervised religious study program.
The party said the arrangement would ensure that every citizen has a defined legal status, an established service track and a corresponding set of rights and obligations.
It also pledged to pass the necessary legislation before the next government is sworn in, rather than settling for a general commitment to address conscription at a later stage.
Under the proposal, the defense minister and Defense Ministry would oversee the implementation of the different tracks, including eligibility criteria, enforcement and supervision.
The ministry would be required to submit a report every six months to the Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee detailing oversight of yeshivas.
According to the party, the framework would also help protect young ultra-Orthodox men who choose to enlist and their families.
Winter has previously declared that Amcha Yisrael will not join a government unless legislation integrating Haredi men into military service is passed before the coalition is formed.
"We intend to integrate the Haredi public into the IDF without compromises and without delays," Winter said previously. "No more of the same. What was will not be again. Those who have failed to integrate Haredim into the IDF until now will not succeed in doing so in the future. If Amcha Yisrael is strong in the next government, these things will happen."
Likud launches campaign against Winter despite his support for Netanyahu
While Winter has repeatedly stated that he would recommend only Netanyahu for prime minister, Likud is conducting an aggressive, paid social media campaign aimed at preventing Amcha Yisrael from crossing the electoral threshold required to enter the Knesset.
"He did say he would go with Netanyahu, but we're not sure that's true," a senior Likud official said.
The campaign uses targeted advertising aimed at specific voter groups, featuring dozens of videos and past statements by candidates on Winter's electoral list, including comments made several years ago.
Likud's goal is to drive voters away from Amcha Yisrael and keep it below the electoral threshold.
The campaign has focused particularly on Winter's second-ranking candidate, Arab Israeli activist Yoseph Haddad.
One widely circulated video features an interview Haddad gave approximately five years ago in which he expressed support for a two-state solution and the establishment of a Palestinian state.
Social media users pointed out that the interview took place roughly two months after Operation Guardian of the Walls, Israel's military operation against Hamas in May 2021, even though Haddad has said that his views changed following that conflict.
The dispute follows earlier attempts by Netanyahu's office to break up Winter's party before the deadline for submitting electoral lists.
According to sources familiar with discussions involving Netanyahu's aides and Haddad's associates, much of the effort focused on persuading Haddad to leave Amcha Yisrael in exchange for a reserved position on Likud's Knesset list.
The approaches reportedly continued until shortly before Amcha Yisrael formally presented its candidates.
Haddad rejected the offers, leaving Winter's party intact as it heads into the election while facing pressure from the very party whose leader Winter has promised to support.

At least 139 migrants dead after boat to Yemen capsizes

Breadcrumb
At least 139 migrants dead, including some children, after boat from Djibouti to Yemen capsizes
At least 139 migrants, including at least 15 children, have died and around 84 are missing after a boat carrying more than 300 people capsized while sailing from Djibouti to Yemen, the United Nations International Organisation for Migration said on Sunday.
The boat, carrying 305 people, capsized near Guhere, north of Obock, a port town in Djibouti, during the night of 8-9 October, the IOM said, citing survivor accounts.
Around 82 people survived the shipwreck, the statement said. An Ethiopian government spokesperson did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Photographs shared by the UN agency showed worn-out sandals and sneakers washed up on the shore.
"Our teams are on the ground alongside local authorities to provide emergency assistance," said Alexandre Coissac, IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti.
"This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities," Coissac said.
Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations, the IOM statement said, adding that local authorities are also providing medical care to survivors and arranging burials for the deceased.
The Djibouti government could not be immediately reached for comment.
The migrants were heading to Yemen, with the hope of eventually making it to wealthier Gulf nations, even as Yemeni nationals themselves flee their country, which is experiencing the most serious escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia-backed government forces and the Iran-backed Houthis since a UN-brokered truce in 2022. 
"Despite the violence in Yemen, migrants are still making the perilous journeys hoping to make it to the Gulf countries," the IOM statement said.
Fighting in Ethiopia
Fighting has also broken out in Ethiopia since last month in the biggest escalation of violence since the 2020-2022 Tigray war.
An IOM official told Reuters that the UN agency had documented heavy migrant traffic along the so-called Eastern Route through Djibouti for several years.
"People continue to use the route amid changing conditions in Ethiopia and Yemen, although the volume and direction of movement can shift over time," the official said.
Ethiopian migrants interviewed for the agency's most recent situation report on Djibouti from 20 September to 30 September said they left their country because of difficult living conditions, including the impact of drought.
"Some migrants also reported that they were fleeing conflict and forced recruitment by armed forces," the report said.
Multiple residents of Tigray, where fighting erupted on 23 September, have told Reuters that they had seen Tigrayan rebels forcibly recruit young men into the defence forces. The rebels have denied conducting forced recruitment.
The conflict has sparked fears of a return to all-out war, with Ethiopia and Eritrea severing relations over alleged Eritrean support for the rebel alliance seeking to overthrow Ethiopia's government. Eritrea has denied backing the alliance.
Severe risks
The so-called Eastern Route presents many dangers, including accidents at sea, trafficking and arbitrary arrests once on land. In 2025, more than 900 migrants died or went missing along the route, according to IOM's Missing Migrants Project, as the number of people undertaking the journey increased by 18 percent.
IOM has described the crisis sparked by the fighting in Yemen as alarming, with displacement figures surging to 200,000 from 76,000 in mid-September, according to data released by the agency last week.
More than 3,700 people have fled Yemen by sea to Djibouti as of last week, it said.

Two remembrance days in memory of October 7 - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

One peculiarity of the State of Israel is the large number of formally celebrated remembrance days.
Remembrance days around the world frequently commemorate events connected to wars, joyous events (such as victories), or tragic events (such as the Holocaust).
One could argue that the multiplicity of remembrance days in Israel reflects the multiplicity of wars and tragic events that befell the Jewish people in general, and the Jewish state in particular, since biblical times and more specifically during the last 85 years.
The most recently added remembrance day – that commemorating the atrocities of October 7, 2023, and their aftermath – is unusual, in that despite the general agreement in Israel that the day should be marked, there are politically based disagreements as to how the commemoration should take place.
The differences, between those who support the government and those who support the opposition, are over who is directly responsible on the Israeli side for October 7, and whether more could have been done by the government to save at least some of the 41 hostages captured alive and returned dead.
Opposition spokesmen and some of the families who received their dear ones in plastic bags blame Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for this tragedy and for allegedly caring more about his political survival than the fate of the hostages.
Netanyahu and his supporters argue that this criticism is unfair and libelous and fails to take into account broader national security interests.
As a result, for the past three years there have been two separate commemoration ceremonies.
Two October 7 commemorations
The first one is organized by the state on 24 Tishrei, two days after Simchat Torah, which in 2023 occurred on October 7. This ceremony is called the Remembrance Day for the Fallen of the Swords of Iron War.
This year it occurred on Monday, October 5. The ceremony, which was held on Mount Herzl in Jerusalem and was attended by President Isaac Herzog, Netanyahu, Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, Supreme Court President Isaac Amit, and IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir, was divided into two parts.
The first part was a state memorial for the casualties of the IDF and other security forces on October 7, and the three-year war that followed. The second part was a state memorial for the civilians who were massacred in the Gaza border communities on October 7, and civilian hostages killed after that in the Gaza Strip.
The second ceremony, held on October 7 in Tel Aviv’s Yarkon Park – the National Memorial Ceremony of October 7 Families – was organized this year by the Kumu movement.
Kumu is a nonpartisan organization of bereaved families, founded in 2024 by Yonatan Shamriz, whose brother Alon was one of three Israeli hostages who managed to escape their captivity in December 2023 but were accidentally shot by IDF forces in Gaza who failed to identify them.
Though Kumu is nonpartisan, it does not conceal the fact that it holds the government responsible for what happened on October 7. It is also critical of the fact that Netanyahu has so far failed to take personal responsibility and has avoided setting up any sort of inquiry committee to investigate who is responsible for Israel having been caught by surprise, and for some of the failures that followed.
The ceremony drew an audience of about 50,000, with no government representatives. Though the leaders of the five main Jewish opposition parties – Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid, Avigdor Liberman, and Yair Golan – were present, none of them participated officially.
The two hosts of the ceremony were actress Shani Cohen and former hostage Eli Sharabi, whose wife and two daughters were murdered by Hamas terrorists on October 7, after Eli was abducted from his home in Kibbutz Be’eri to Gaza. His brother Yossi was abducted to Gaza on the same day, but was killed while in captivity, apparently during an IAF attack on the area where he was held.
At the ceremony, survivors and bereaved family members briefly told their stories, while Cohen and Sharabi added commentary. Well-known Israeli singers also participated. It was a highly emotional event, but Sharabi distinguished himself by managing to keep a straight face throughout and concealing his emotions.
It should be noted that the National Memorial Ceremony was broadcast in full and in real time on Channels 11, 12, 13, 15 and 99. Channel 14 was the only Hebrew news channel that did not broadcast the ceremony.
During the ceremony, Channel 14 broadcast its program The Patriots, as usual.
Every once in a while, in the course of the ceremony, I switched over to Channel 14 to see whether it would show a modicum of respect for the feelings of the bereaved families and avoid attacking those attending the ceremony.
But, alas, these were false expectations. The panel members were their usual nasty, insulting, mocking selves.
One of the regular panelists stated that the supporters of the bereaved families of those killed as hostages, who could allegedly have been saved had the government acted differently, are hypocrites who don’t give a damn about the hostages, and are only interested in bringing down Netanyahu.
I expected the program’s host, Yinon Magal, to call the panelist to order in honor of the day. But he said nothing, and his facial expression indicated that he was pleased by the remark.
Then I suddenly remembered that the previous morning, on his talk show together with Ben Caspit on Radio 103fm, Magal had mentioned the names of 13 of over 282 contributors to a Hebrew book published in 2024, with a picture of Netanyahu on its cover, titled “Mr. Depriver – the heritage of he who abandoned the hostages.”
Yinon said of the 13: “All the names I have mentioned shall be remembered eternally in disgrace, on a pillory. These are the most despicable persons living in the State of Israel, who falsely accused Benjamin Netanyahu of a blood libel.”
Eleven of the names mentioned were of returned hostages, or of relatives of hostages who had perished in Gaza. They included Shamriz.
Magal finally apologized for mentioning the hostages, but the damage was done.
What are the chances of the two ceremonies being united next year? Well, that depends on who wins the election in two weeks.
The writer has written journalistic and academic articles, as well as several books, on international relations, Zionism, Israeli politics, and parliamentarism. From 1994 to 2010, she worked at the Knesset Library and the Knesset Research and Information Center.

India's 'cockroach' leaders vow to keep up election protests
Leaders of India's youth-led "cockroach" movement on Sunday pledged to press on with protests against the country's election commissioner, hours after they were released from detention, as authorities sought to thwart major demonstrations in New Delhi.
The rallies in the capital come after weeks of opposition mobilisation following allegations of misconduct during a nationwide voter roll revision that critics say could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling party.
The Election Commission of India, which oversees the voting process in the world's most populous nation, has denied wrongdoing.
Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), and two other leaders were released Sunday, one day after they were detained when they landed in New Delhi to take part in a protest at the Jantar Mantar site in the heart of the city.
Thousands of protesters have been detained since Saturday, according to the group and media reports.
"We will not back down," Saurav Das, another top CJP leader, told reporters after his release.
"We urge people to come out and carry out peaceful protests," he added, vowing to continue until Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resigns.
Smaller rallies took place in Delhi on Sunday. Dozens of protesters were detained near Jantar Mantar, which remained blocked off, AFP journalists witnessed.
Police have not commented on the detentions.
Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said at least 16 journalists had also been detained, calling the police actions "unacceptable".
"Covering events of public interest is not a crime," RSF said in a statement. "It is their job."
In July, protests organised by the CJP over exam irregularities forced the resignation of the education minister, marking a rare climbdown by Modi's administration.
'Important to show up'
Ahead of Saturday's rally, authorities mounted a sweeping security operation across the capital, shutting down metro stations and more than 200 trains while imposing a ban on public gatherings in several areas.
Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel remained deployed on Sunday, but metro stations reopened and previously restricted mobile services were restored.
"I was detained for 10 hours yesterday," said Aarti, 37, who gave only one name. "I have come again today because it is important to show up."
The protest leaders were released on the condition that they would maintain "peace for one year", Ratna Singh, the CJP's head lawyer, said in a social media post.
The Supreme Court, hearing petitions challenging Saturday's detentions and other security measures, directed the authorities to ensure protesters gathering peacefully were not detained illegally.
"Detention shall only be after following a legal procedure," Justice Joymalya Bagchi said in oral remarks.
The court also ordered authorities to ensure there was no disruption to internet connectivity as seen on Saturday.
'An embarrassment to India'
The CJP has emerged as one of the most significant political challenges to Modi during his third term in power, winning millions of followers on social media since it was launched in May as a satirical party.
Soon after his release, the CJP's Dipke took aim at Modi, calling him "an embarrassment to India".
"Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully," he said in a social media post.
The revision of voter rolls resulted in more than 133 million names being removed from electoral lists, according to media reports.
Critics say the measure has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims, potentially benefiting Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.
Election authorities say the move was aimed at eliminating duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries.
The detention of protesters on Saturday triggered sharp criticism and accusations that Modi's government was stifling dissent.
The UN human rights office called for the immediate and unconditional release of all those "arbitrarily detained" in Delhi -- a comment the Indian government called "misplaced".
Rahul Gandhi, leader of the opposition Congress party, said he was planning to march to the Supreme Court on Monday with "every single person who believes in democracy".
"There is nothing to fear," he said on social media. "These cowards can do absolutely nothing to us."

Ethiopian official promises change in Tigray after troops retake regional capital
A former Tigray leader, now advising Ethiopia's prime minister, promised a "visible change" in the region on Sunday after government-allied units retook Mekelle city following renewed fighting with opposition forces.
Ethiopian Airlines resumed flights to the city of Mekelle on Sunday for the first time since rebels led by the Tigray People's Liberation Front seized the airport on 23 September. They withdrew on 3 October, when government-allied fighters entered the city.
Renewed fighting in Tigray has undermined the 2022 peace agreement that ended a two-year war, as mounting tensions between Ethiopia and neighbouring Eritrea have raised fears of a wider conflict.
"I would like to assure you on this occasion that we will bring visible change, a change beyond mere hope," Getachew Reda, an adviser to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, told supporters who greeted him and intelligence chief Redwan Hussein at Mekelle airport. He did not elaborate.
The 2020-2022 war in Tigray caused about 500,000 civilian deaths from violence, famine and the collapse of health services, according to researchers at Ghent University in Belgium.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front joined six other opposition groups last month in an alliance seeking to oust Abiy.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres urged all parties on Friday to cease hostilities and resume dialogue. He warned that fighting risked further destabilising the wider region.
Ethiopia told the UN Security Council on Friday that it was taking self-defence measures, accusing Eritrea of sending troops across the border and occupying parts of northern Ethiopia.
Ethiopian authorities previously have accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF, an allegation Eritrea has denied.
Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos did not specify the measures being taken. His letter to the council did not identify the occupied areas or provide evidence supporting the allegations. The Associated Press could not independently verify the claims.
Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh urged the council to condemn what he called Ethiopia's "unprovoked declaration of war". His response did not confirm or deny the alleged troop crossings.
The dispute deepens a rift between the two countries whose armies fought together against the TPLF during the 2020-2022 war.

In June, Egyptian security forces detained hundreds of people, including foreigners, on the border with Sudan, accusing them of illegal gold mining and smuggling.
More than 50% of gold mined in Sudan was smuggled out of the country, according to a U.N. Panel of Experts Report in 2024.

Saudis might step up strikes on Houthis even further after airport attack, experts tell 'Post'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:37:03 UTC
01:37:03 KST

Saudi Arabia is unlikely to back down in the face of the Houthis following an attack on Riyadh’s airport that killed 12 people and wounded 309, with the kingdom likely stepping up its military campaign against the Iran-backed terror group, regional experts told The Jerusalem Post.
The attack, which marked a significant escalation in the Houthis’ campaign against Saudi Arabia, has exposed the kingdom’s vulnerability to strikes against civilian infrastructure. Bernard Haykel, a senior fellow at the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies (FDD), said Saudi Arabia had long understood the Houthis’ ability to carry out such attacks, particularly with what he described as support from Iran and Iraqi Shiite militias.
“My sense is that they’re not going to buckle. They’re not going to just capitulate to the Houthis because of this,” he explained.
Haykel said Riyadh now faces a choice between reaching an accommodation with the Houthis or intensifying its military campaign against them, adding that he expects the Saudis will pursue the latter course and rely more heavily on Yemeni forces opposed to the group.
“I think that they’re going to ramp up against the Houthis,” he said.
The attack comes as Saudi Arabia faces the consequences of a broader regional conflict that Riyadh had sought to avoid. According to Haykel, Saudi leaders opposed the war against Iran and made considerable efforts to prevent it, but now recognize that they will have to bear some of its costs.
“They realize that they have to pay a price,” he said.
Former ambassador says attack shocked Saudis
Michael Ratney, former US Ambassador to Saudi Arabia and senior advisor at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said the scale and audacity of the attack had shocked the Saudis, even though they were familiar with the Houthis’ military capabilities.
Ratney noted that the Houthis had already carried out several strikes against airports, including in Riyadh, during the preceding week, while the latest was the most serious of those incidents. “I think they were shocked, but in a way understood that this is what the Houthis are all about,” Ratney explained.
He identified the targeting of civilian airports as a particularly significant escalation. In the past, the Houthis had generally focused on military installations and energy infrastructure, including Saudi military bases and energy facilities.
“For them to target civilian airports with the expectation of civilian casualties is really a new escalation for the Houthis,” Ratney said.
The attacks put Riyadh in a difficult position as it seeks to achieve its military objectives in Yemen without triggering a wider escalation that could expose additional Saudi infrastructure to retaliation.
Ratney said Saudi Arabia’s immediate military priority was to help the Yemeni army retake positions along the coast near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait that the Houthis had seized the previous month.
“They’re determined to get the Houthis off of the Bab el-Mandeb,” he said, adding that Riyadh would probably then look for a way to de-escalate the conflict.
Riyadh growing concerns over lack of American assistance
Both experts pointed to Riyadh's concerns about the limits of American military assistance, especially as Washington deploys forces and resources across the region.
Haykel said Saudi Arabia was disappointed that the United States was not better prepared to help defend the kingdom against attacks from the Houthis and Iran, particularly given the potential shortage of missile-defense systems.
“I think there’s disappointment that the Americans are not better prepared and better able to help in fighting the Houthis and the Iranians,” he said.
At the same time, Haykel said Saudi leaders understand that American military power has limits, particularly when US forces are already heavily committed across the Persian Gulf.
Ratney said the United States was providing some assistance behind the scenes, including intelligence sharing, targeting and operational planning. But he added that Riyadh would prefer more direct American involvement in airstrikes.
“Clearly what they would like is US support on airstrikes, and I think there is some frustration,” he said.
The attack could influence Washington’s willingness to provide more overt military support, Ratney said, although he cautioned that Trump’s response was difficult to predict.
Still, Ratney said neither Saudi Arabia nor the United States appeared eager to escalate the conflict further.
Saudis worried about further strikes on civilian infrastructure
The concern is that intensifying military operations against Iran or the Houthis could provoke disproportionate retaliation, with civilian infrastructure rather than military targets bearing the consequences.
“None of them really want to escalate at this point because they see the result,” Ratney said.
The attack also raises questions about whether Israel could play a greater role in helping Saudi Arabia counter the Houthi threat, given Israel’s experience confronting Iranian-backed groups and its advanced intelligence and air-defense capabilities.
“The political risk of that outweighs any kind of military benefits that they might derive,” Ratney said, explaining that Saudi leaders are reluctant to see Israeli politicians publicly highlight or take credit for cooperation between the two countries.
Haykel was more skeptical about Israel’s ability to deliver a decisive military blow against the Houthis, particularly through intelligence-led operations targeting the group’s leadership.
He said Israel had developed extensive intelligence capabilities against Hezbollah in Lebanon, allowing it to target the organization’s senior figures and commanders. He does not believe Israel currently possesses a comparable level of intelligence on the Houthis in Yemen.
“If the Israelis had the intelligence on the Houthis to, say, destroy the leadership of the Houthis and the second-, third-tier commanders, you know, what they did to Hezbollah, basically, if they could do that in Yemen, that would be an incredible service and help in this war,” Haykel said.
For Riyadh, the immediate challenge remains how to deter further Houthi attacks without becoming trapped in another prolonged and costly conflict in Yemen. Both experts agree that it will be hard.

Hundreds join 'I'm not Jewish, I'm a Zionist' trend, 'Post' analysis finds - exclusive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
16:37:00 UTC
01:37:00 KST

A social media trend in which non-Jewish users publicly declare themselves non-Jewish Zionists has spread rapidly across X, with a Jerusalem Post exclusive analysis identifying more than 600 matching posts from nearly 550 accounts over the course of just over a week.
The posts follow a recognizable formula: "I'm not Jewish. I'm [nationality, religion or identity]. And I am a Zionist."
The Post wrote a code to analyze X and ascertain where the trend started and who is amplifying it. This analysis uncovered 613 posts published between October 4 and October 11, with relatively little activity during the first several days before the trend accelerated sharply on October 9.
The dataset contained just three matching posts from October 4, followed by 13 on October 5, 10 on October 6, 22 on October 7, and 26 on October 8.
That number then jumped to 131 on October 9, roughly five times the number captured the previous day. Another 270 matching posts were published on October 10, followed by 138 captured on October 11 as of the time the data was collected.
In total, 539 of the 613 posts analyzed, or approximately 88%, were published from October 9 onward.
From scattered declarations to a viral formula
Declarations of support for Zionism by non-Jewish users predate the current trend, and the earliest posts located by the Post do not yet display the standardized format that has now become more widespread.
Among posts found on October 4 were broader declarations such as, "I'm not Jewish, but I am a Zionist."
By October 5, however, users had begun inserting their national identity into the declaration. One early example read, "I'm not Jewish. I am Irish, and I am a Zionist."
An October 6 post similarly stated, "I'm English, I'm not Jewish, but I am a Zionist."
By October 7, the three-part structure began appearing more frequently, including variations identifying the poster as American, Canadian or Iranian before declaring support for Zionism.
One example posted by Dutch writer Bart Schut on October 11 read, "I'm not Jewish. I'm a Dutch atheist. And I am a Zionist."
The Post's dataset included posts referencing a wide range of national identities, including Iranian, American, Canadian, German, Finnish, Irish, Italian, New Zealander, English, Polish, Australian, British, Dutch, Czech, Japanese, Portuguese and Nigerian, among others.
Some users went further, combining national and religious identities. References to Christians, Catholics, atheists, Muslims, Hindus and agnostics all appeared in the posts analyzed.
Hundreds of accounts join trend
The 613 posts collected by the Post came from 549 separate X accounts, indicating that the volume captured in the analysis was not primarily produced by a small number of accounts repeatedly posting the same phrase.
Most accounts appeared only once in the dataset.
The available data does not establish that the posts were centrally coordinated or part of an organized campaign. Rather, it demonstrates the rapid replication and adaptation of a common linguistic template across hundreds of accounts.
The timing suggests that the phenomenon changed significantly around October 9, just two days after the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks.
After the Post captured 74 matching posts in total between October 4 and October 8, another 539 appeared from October 9 onward.
The trend had also begun drawing attention from users on X itself by that point, with posts explicitly referring to the growing number of "I'm not Jewish, but I'm a Zionist" declarations as a trend.
For example, on October 9, user Oren Barsky wrote: "the 'I’m not Jewish, but I’m a Zionist' trend is one of the most moving things I’ve seen on this platform."
By October 11, Barsky said the trend is "basically [his] whole feed."
How the Post analyzed the trend
The Jerusalem Post collected public X search results using multiple variations of the phrases "I'm not Jewish" and "Zionist," covering posts published between October 4 and October 11.
Duplicate post URLs were removed, leaving 613 posts from 549 unique accounts for analysis.
The dataset is not an exhaustive record of every post participating in the trend. The figures instead provide a snapshot of the trend visible through public X search results and demonstrate its growth within the period analyzed.
Either way, amid the widespread hostility toward Israel and Zionism, the emergence of a trend centered on expressions of solidarity with Israel and the Jewish people's right to self-determination marks a notably positive shift in the social media discourse.
