21:00:00 KST

Djibouti shipwreck: Death toll rises to 139 as 84 remain missing
At least 139 migrants have died after their boat capsized off Djibouti, with a further 84 people still missing, the UN migration agency (IOM) said on Sunday.
The toll rose from 109 after the bodies of 30 more people were recovered. Search and rescue efforts are continuing.
The boat was carrying 305 people from Djibouti towards Yemen when it went down near Guehere, north of Obock, in the early hours of Friday. About 82 people survived.
IOM described it as one of the deadliest shipwrecks recorded on the Eastern Route, which runs from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula.
On the move, despite risks
The shipwreck comes as Djibouti deals with continued traffic in both directions.
Since 10 September, IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix has recorded more than 20,000 movements into the country from Ethiopia, as migrants keep heading for the Gulf despite the return to full-scale fighting in Yemen.
Over roughly the same period, more than 3,700 refugees have arrived from Yemen, while 539 Ethiopian migrants have come back from there.
Alexandre Coissac, IOM’s chief of mission in Djibouti, told journalists in Geneva on 6 October that the country was facing “overlapping emergencies”.
“Djibouti is therefore confronting movements in both directions,” Mr. Coissac said, adding that migrants were increasingly becoming stranded, with more than 3,000 seen along routes in Djibouti between 20 and 30 September, often without access to basic services.
“No one gets into a boat like that unless they believe there is no other safe way,” said IOM Director General Amy Pope.
Safe pathways ‘save lives’: Pope
“We cannot keep treating these deaths as normal. Safe and legal pathways save lives. I am asking governments and donors to act before the next boat goes down.”
Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and recovery operations as fears grow for those still unaccounted for.
IOM is providing emergency assistance to survivors at its Migrant Response Centre in Obock, including healthcare, psychosocial support, food, shelter and protection services.
‘Deeply saddened’
The UN Resident Coordinator in Djibouti, Jose Barahona, said he was deeply saddened by the loss of at least 139 lives, among them children.
“Our thoughts are with the victims, the survivors and the families waiting for news of their loved ones,” Mr. Barahona said on social media. “We express our solidarity and welcome the ongoing search and rescue efforts.”
Every life lost at sea is a tragedy, he added, recalling the Secretary-General’s recent warning that such deaths underline the urgency of protecting people on the move, expanding safe migration pathways and strengthening international cooperation.

Sustaining livelihoods amid crisis in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Sustaining livelihoods amid crisis in Gaza
Nidaa, Hanaa and Hanin have different stories, but share a common thread: the determination to build something of their own and keep it going despite extraordinary challenges facing them in war-ravaged Gaza.
Following the devastation of the past three years, productive capacity in Gaza has been severely damaged, markets disrupted and the cost of basic goods has risen sharply.
Their experiences reflect different parts of the same challenge: sustaining livelihoods that still exist, helping businesses restart and creating new opportunities where livelihoods have disappeared.
Running a business today means navigating uncertainty at every turn. Yet amid these challenges, women continue to find ways to work, adapting their businesses, learning new skills and somehow – supporting their families.
Nidaa: A livelihood built from childhood
Nidaa, 35, has her own business raising and selling chickens, ducks and rabbits in the southern city of Khan Younis.
“I was passionate about this business since I was a child,” she said. “My mother worked with animals, and she taught me everything she knew. During the war, I faced many challenges with continuing my business. However, I insisted on continuing.”
When her home was destroyed during the war and she was displaced, she managed to save some of her animals and move them to Khan Younis.
Trained as a teacher, Nidaa chose to follow her passion for raising animals, turning it into a business that helps support her family, including two brothers with disabilities. But there have been constant challenges.
‘During the time of famine, I lost many animals’
“Especially during the time of famine, I lost many animals,” she recalled. “Food became very expensive.”
Right now, challenges include shelter for the coming winter, access to safe water and limited ingredients for food for the birds and animals, she said.
“I don’t know how I will take care of them without a proper shelter,” she said.
Through the UN Development Programme (UNDP) partnership with the local Chamber of Commerce, she received a grant to purchase animals and equipment, alongside training to strengthen her production skills.
Now, Nidaa’s ambition goes beyond sustaining what she has today.
“I hope that my business will grow,” she said, “and I can inspire other women to work with animals.”
Hanaa: Starting again after loss
In Gaza City, Hanaa, 49, started a family dairy business with her husband in 2021.
During the war, she lost her husband, one of her sons and her business. She was left supporting her three remaining children while also caring for five children who lost both parents.
With encouragement from her eldest son, Fouad, Hanaa decided to restart the business despite limited resources and severe shortages of milk and other raw materials.
“Sometimes, the people who need us are the reason we find the strength to keep going,” Hanaa said, adding that she chooses to remain strong and resilient in the face of many challenges.
The destruction of Gaza’s electricity system has made dairy production particularly difficult. Power interruptions can cause products to spoil, resulting in losses at a time when resources are already scarce.
With grant support, Hanaa was able to resume producing cheese, milk, labneh and laban, with hopes of growing her business into a larger production facility and build a more stable source of income for her family.
Hanin: Learning a new trade
For other women, starting over begins with a new skill.
Hanin, 36, is learning carpentry. From southern Khan Younis, she travels to Deir al-Balah to complete 80 hours of vocational training, followed by entrepreneurship and business-planning training.
“This is something unique, especially for women,” Hanin said. “It’s needed now more than ever, because there are limited sources of wood for furniture, and many people lost their furniture during the war.”
More than 200 trainees will receive skills development in carpentry, textiles, recycling, compost production, data science, graphic design and digital marketing.
For Hanin, learning carpentry is not simply about completing a training course. It offers a pathway towards earning an income and potentially building a business of her own.
Foundations for the future
For women entrepreneurs, access to finance and skills is important, but their ability to sustain and grow their businesses also depends on the systems around them.
That means reliable energy and water, functioning markets and access to the equipment and materials they need.
Supporting women-led businesses is therefore about more than individual livelihoods, according to UNDP.
It also helps preserve local productive capacity, generate income and keep economic activity rooted in Palestinian communities, laying the foundation for locally driven recovery.
What’s UNDP doing in Gaza?
Nearly two million Palestinians have experienced repeated displacement since the war began. Here are some ongoing efforts to help them recover:
- Since October 2023, UNDP has supported 6,000 emergency employment opportunities
- Nidaa and Hanaa are among 30 women whose businesses are being supported as part of UNDP’s Gaza Neighbourhood Approach initiative, which brings together shelter, essential services and livelihood opportunities to help communities regain some of the basic conditions they need to function
- UNDP’s Programme of Assistance to the Palestinian People (PAPP) supports micro, small and medium enterprises with grants, equipment and skills development
- The REVIVE housing project has already helped build homes for displaced Palestinians

‘These attacks must cease immediately’: Guterres condemns deadly Houthi strike on Riyadh airport
UN Secretary-General António Guterres has condemned a Houthi missile attack on Riyadh’s main airport that Saudi authorities say killed 12 people and wounded more than 300.
In a short statement issued late on Saturday, he said attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure violate international law. “These attacks must cease immediately,” Mr. Guterres said.
Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said on Sunday that 309 people were wounded in the strike on King Khalid International Airport, some of them critically.
The dead include at least four Saudis, two Bangladeshis, a US citizen, plus others from Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan. Operations were suspended and flights diverted.
Late on Sunday, Saudi authorities reported that another projectile had hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh, causing further injuries and a fire.
Third strike
It was the third Houthi attack on the airport this week. Thursday’s strikes killed three Saudis, including a Saudia pilot, and earlier attacks on King Khalid and Abha airports reportedly killed three more and wounded 36.
Houthi media reported the airport in Yemen’s capital Sana’a – which the group has controlled for years – had been hit by an airstrike on Sunday, blaming Saudi Arabia for the attack.
According to news reports, the vice-president of Yemen’s internationally recognised government called on Sunday for decisive action by regional and international partners to end the Houthi aggression.
Long war
The Iran-backed Houthis have fought the Saudi-backed government since 2014. A 2022 ceasefire largely held until this summer. In September, the Houthis swept down Yemen’s Red Sea coast, capturing the port of Mokha and islands in the Bab al-Mandab strait.
Early this month, government forces launched a counteroffensive, backed by Saudi-led air strikes, aiming to retake all Houthi-held territory – including Sana’a. The Houthis have answered with missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Spillover from US-Iran conflict
The battle for Bab al-Mandab, the narrow gateway to the Red Sea, is a spillover from the US-Iran conflict which has destabilised global oil and gas supplies through the vital Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
With Iran continuing to disrupt the strait, the Red Sea has become vital for Saudi oil exports.
Saudi officials and the Yemeni government say they have now regained control of the Red Sea chokepoint – but the Houthis have denied the claim.
Security Council
The UN Security Council met Friday morning in New York on Yemen where Special Envoy Hans Grundberg said the country had slid back into full-scale war.
The conflict is intensifying, raising regional security and economic risks, he told amassadors.
UN Deputy Emergency Relief Coordinator Mohamed Yahya said over 200,000 people have been displaced since August, the highest new displacement since the now-shattered 2022 truce.

President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky attends a joint news conference with U.S. President Donald Trump’s Special Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner outside the Mariinskyi Palace following negotiations in Kyiv, Ukraine, on September 6, 2026. (Getty Images)

The exchange came as Kiev pressed its campaign against infrastructure deep inside Russia, with a drone attack on Oct. 11 shutting down a data center run by Russian technology giant Yandex, the third strike on the company’s facilities in four days.
“Ukraine will be ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure,” Zelensky wrote on X.
“It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but [Russian President Vladimir] Putin does not want to do so,” he said, adding that any de-escalation must be reciprocal and backed by real guarantees.

Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well,” Sybiha wrote.

“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does,” Trump said.
The U.S. president, who on Oct. 9 struck a deal with Putin to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, has been urging Zelensky for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
He has sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia’s war effort.
The Ukrainian drone attack on the Yandex data center in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, caused outages across the company’s services, leaving users in dozens of Russian cities and in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia unable to order taxis or access banking services, according to Russian independent news outlet Astra.
“As a result of the drone attack, the infrastructure of Yandex’s data center in Vladimir was damaged. Operations at the data center have been completely halted,” said the Yandex Cloud Telegram channel.
A Moscow resident, Eduard Malyavko, said the outages had “direct impact” and weren’t just about “convenience.”
“It’s also about work,” he said, adding that they also affected “healthcare and everything else.”
Yandex, often described as Russia’s Google, runs the country’s most popular search engine and a wide range of digital services, and is heavily involved in Russia’s artificial intelligence development.

The Vatican did not say whether the nodule is believed to be malignant.

The late Pope Francis, Leo's predecessor, died at age 88 and was increasingly frail in his later years.

Israel unearths 2,000-year-old section of Jerusalem aqueduct that brought water to Temple Mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:47:34 UTC
20:47:34 KST

A 300-meter-long section of Jerusalem’s Lower Aqueduct, originally constructed in the Hasmonean period, was recently unearthed south of Kibbutz Ramat Rachel, near the capital, the Israel Antiquities Authority (IAA) announced on Sunday.
The aqueduct was part of a sophisticated ancient water system that carried spring water from the Gush Etzion area to the Temple Mount in Jerusalem through Solomon’s Pools.
Hasmonean architects designed the aqueduct so water could flow by gravity alone, adapting the route to move smoothly across hills and bedrock. They installed cleanout points along the system, providing access to the channel for blockages or routine maintenance.
"The Lower Aqueduct was an impressive engineering project, probably built in the time of the Hasmonean kings to supply water to Jerusalem, explained IAA Excavation Directors Dr. Benyamin Storchan and Gil Freid. “The system was so well planned that it remained in intermittent use until about 100 years ago.”
“The aqueduct runs about 21 km from Solomon's Pools, south of Bethlehem, to Jerusalem. Along most of the route, the water flowed along a very gentle gradient, dropping just one meter in elevation per kilometer."
Section exposes ancient water system's history
The newly exposed section, located in an area slated by the Israel Land Authority for a new neighborhood, reveals several stages in the water system’s history.
Initially, the water flowed through a built and plastered channel. However, about 500 years ago, during the Ottoman period, they installed ceramic pipes within the original aqueduct.
At the same time, the outer wall was plastered, and small stones were pressed into it while the plaster was still wet, creating a distinctive surface that accompanied the aqueduct along its route.
These repairs reflect the aqueduct's importance and the ongoing effort to maintain Jerusalem's water supply.
"The aqueduct is an engineering marvel. Even today, with all our modern technology, building such a system would require extensive planning and effort,” said Dr. Amit Re'em, IAA Jerusalem district archaeologist. “The thought that about 2,000 years ago they managed to bring water to Jerusalem this way is astonishing, and we want the public to be able to appreciate this achievement up close.”
“The dream and vision of the Israel Antiquities Authority is to create a continuous park that will allow people to walk alongside the aqueduct from southern Jerusalem to the Old City, and we are already advancing this initiative together with the Jerusalem Municipality and other partners."
Aqueduct to be incorporated into new neighborhood
The ILA and the IAA are planning to preserve the aqueduct and incorporate it into the main entrance of the new neighborhood.
According to Yehuda Eliyahu, acting director of the ILA, "The spectacular discovery of the ancient aqueduct in the heart of the area planned for the new neighborhood in Jerusalem reminds us that we are continuing a glorious chain of generations of building and development.”
“The Israel Land Authority is pleased to lead extensive modern development while showing national responsibility and carefully safeguarding our historical heritage assets,” Eliyahu said. “Integrating the aqueduct into the entrance of the new neighborhood will give residents and visitors a direct connection to Jerusalem's rich history and to the deep bond of the people of Israel with its eternal capital."
Heritage Minister Amichai Eliyahu echoed the sentiment, adding that "The aqueduct, whose construction is attributed to the days of the Hasmonean kings, tells of a leadership that knew how to think ahead: to expand Jerusalem's capacity to absorb residents, pilgrims, and public life around the Temple.”
“Integrating the aqueduct into the new neighborhood today continues this story: the city is growing, and we are glad that its integration into the new neighborhood will allow future generations to get to know this heritage up close."
The research on Jerusalem's Lower Aqueduct will be presented at the 19th "New Studies in the Archaeology of Jerusalem and Its Region" conference, held in Jerusalem and Tel Aviv and initiated by the Israel Antiquities Authority, Tel Aviv University, the Hebrew University, and Tagliyot – Israel Institute of Archaeology.

The Ben-Gvir effect exposes the West’s discomfort with Jewish power - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:47:32 UTC
20:47:32 KST

National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has become a sort of political lightning rod, drawing high-voltage tension and intense global as well as domestic criticism.
While the obvious reasons for this widespread antipathy concern firstly his positions – death penalty for terrorists, voluntary emigration of Gazans, expansion of Jewish settlement, opposition to Palestinian statehood, to name but a few – they do not explain by themselves this peculiar phenomenon.
However “radical” one may consider them to be, these substantial positions, backed by a long-standing ideology, remain political stances that can be supported, opposed, or debated on their own terms.
Beyond his political program, it is also Ben-Gvir’s manner (or lack thereof) that is being targeted: the theatrical provocations, the confrontational language and the social media stunts. From suggesting a moat of crocodiles around a prison holding Hamas terrorists to publicly humiliating the Gaza flotilla terror supporters, Ben-Gvir understands the power of an image.
And he uses it as a method, a method whose impact is reaching far beyond Israel’s borders, making the debate around him more existential than political. All these, combined with his unapologetic Jewish pride and his rejection of political correctness, trigger a revealing reaction, the “Ben-Gvir effect.”
The recent statements by U2 band member Bono about the Israeli minister illustrate the reach of this effect.
The Irish singer not only compared Ben-Gvir’s remarks about Gazans to the rhetoric of Heinrich Himmler, the architect of the Nazi extermination machinery, but he also claimed that the leader of Otzma Yehudit had put Judaism “in the shade.”
Whatever one thinks of Ben-Gvir’s words, this shift from criticizing a politician or a specific policy to conflating them with Judaism itself deserves scrutiny, because it goes deeper than the standard debate over extremism.
Understanding the criticism directed at Itamar Ben-Gvir
Ben-Gvir may be a lightning rod, and a convenient one, but he did not create the storm that has been gathering above Israel and the Jews since October 7.
He was democratically elected to the Knesset, and his party, which recent polls put at around eight seats in the upcoming elections, is an important component of the current coalition. His critics on the Left see a threat to democracy and the rule of law, and the ones on the right view his provocations as a liability to quieter diplomacy.
He and his party, treated as pariahs for many years, are now part of the political mainstream, whether one likes it or not. In fact, their ideology is not far removed from the historic Right. The core difference lies in language and the Jewish part of the equation.
The new generation of the modern national-religious camp has left the European reference point and its anxieties behind.
Instead, they return to a native Jewish and religious character, rooted in the reality of being here, with no regard for convention or the sensibilities of Western audiences – whom Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is so familiar with.
The national security minister feels no need to moderate his tone when speaking about Jewish sovereignty or particularism.
The backlash against Ben-Gvir thus often shifts from moral objection to personal attack, at times even evoking historical, antisemitic caricatures of the Jew. Yet Ben-Gvir, who, to some extent, projects this image of himself, uses it as a tool of political deterrence. Focusing on the image, however, obscures what matters more.
Beyond aesthetics, the “Ben-Gvir effect” exposes an ancient anxiety: the Western world tolerates the Jew under subjection, but hates and fears the Jew who exerts sovereign power. While this hostility does not make all criticism antisemitic, it does seem to derived from it.
Abroad, Ben-Gvir is often collapsed with Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich into a single patronizing category, the “Ben-Gvirs and Smotriches,” Israel’s convenient symbol for a threatening extreme.
By reducing him to a caricature, one avoids having to engage with the real ideas he embodies, ideas that are an integral part of Israel’s democratic political landscape.
Ultimately, the disproportionate rage surrounding him exposes the global and domestic difficulty of accommodating a specific, unapologetic figure: the Jew on his own land, claiming spiritual attachment, possessing raw political power, and refusing to apologize for any of it.
BEHIND BEN-GVIR’S positions lies a strong national-religious conception of Israel that has acquired a larger audience since October 7, as many Israelis are asking questions about identity, sovereignty, and security with a renewed sense of urgency.
Thus, the visceral secular reaction to Ben-Gvir hides something even deeper than just an aversion to his bad manners and alleged racist positions. The problem lies with what he represents: a loud, proud, nationalist religious Jew.
And this Jew, for many in Israel and abroad, is difficult to come to terms with. He is the antithesis of the “court Jew,” the cosmopolitan and universalist Jew who has had to master the codes of the surrounding society to survive, a Jew not necessarily unproud but careful about particularism, and accommodating about his identity.
He is also quite different from the “New Hebrew,” the socialist and secular pioneer, symbol of the building of the country. But this evolution is not simply about style; it is a transformation of the Jewish character itself.
And this Jewish part of the equation is unsettling to secular culture. Beyond beliefs, it is the very existence of a visibly religious person that inevitably raises questions that modern European tradition has relegated to the private sphere: God, transcendence and meaning. And although these questions never disappeared, they were toned down within Israel’s secular-Zionist tradition.
This friction could help explain the discomfort surrounding Ben-Gvir. He is not simply promoting a national-religious agenda; he wears his Jewish identity and attachment to the land openly, refusing to translate them into a universalist vocabulary. He brings his faith out of the private sphere, thrusting it into questions of sovereignty, land, national identity and political power.
While the place of religion in the Jewish state has been a fault line in Israeli society since its creation, and has been dividing Israelis long before October 7, it has become a very raw existential battlefield as it occupies more space within the public debate.
Considering the Jewish particularity of Israel, this conversation needs to happen. But for it to happen, Israel and its citizens need to allow for an accepting, tolerant, and inclusive space, without knee-jerk reactions, without violence, and with a genuine will to understand the other. From his newly gained position, Ben-Gvir himself could actually be helping to bridge these differences.
The Ben-Gvir effect has brought front stage a long-muted Jewish nationalism, attracting intense animosity but also discreet curiosity from Western leaders seeking strategies against radical Islamism and terror.
To capitalize on this attention, Ben-Gvir must change his method from mere provocation to more mature communication, and adopt a syntax that speaks to the international community without compromise or accommodation.
This gives the national-religious camp an opportunity to assert their ideology into the mainstream as an impossible-to-ignore reality in Israel and abroad. Ultimately, the fierce reaction Ben-Gvir triggers reveals as much about those responding as it does about the man himself.
The author holds a PhD from Tel Aviv University and is a regular contributor on Zionism, Israeli society, and Jewish identity.

US Army urges adoption of Israeli battlefield medicine as IDF cuts casualty deaths by half - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:47:16 UTC
20:47:16 KST

The US Army is recommending that American military medical teams study and adopt Israeli battlefield medicine techniques after the IDF reduced the mortality rate among combat casualties by more than half, Fox News reported, citing IDF data and an official US Army report.
Advances in combat medicine developed by the IDF in recent years have helped significantly reduce deaths among soldiers wounded in battle. The US military is now urging a closer examination of these Israeli methods ahead of future conflicts.
According to data presented to Fox News, the mortality rate among combat casualties stood at approximately 15% during the Second Lebanon War in 2006, compared with 7.1% during the Swords of Iron War.
The US report cited nearly identical figures, showing a decline from 14.8% in 2006 to 7.1% in 2024, despite a significant increase in the proportion of wounded soldiers suffering severe injuries.
One of the most important changes has been a dramatic reduction in the time required to deliver advanced medical treatment to wounded soldiers.
According to a senior IDF combat medicine expert, during the Second Lebanon War, it took between 15 and 20 minutes for advanced medical care to reach a wounded soldier. Currently, such treatment can be administered immediately or within just four minutes.
Positioning medical personnel closer to combat troops, rapidly evacuating casualties by helicopter, and making medical decisions directly on the battlefield are considered key factors behind the improvement.
IDF expands use of blood units on battlefield
The IDF has also expanded the use of blood products on the battlefield, according to the Fox News report. Since 2013, greater emphasis has been placed on rapidly treating hemorrhages, including administering plasma at the point of injury.
Blood units are transported to forward positions in refrigerated containers carried by medical teams, allowing treatment to begin before wounded soldiers are evacuated to a hospital.
In its 78-page report, titled "Israeli Defense Force Medical Lessons Learned," the US Army warned that Israel had been forced to make painful adjustments during active combat, but that the American military now has an opportunity to learn from that experience in advance.
"The time to prepare is now," the report stated, emphasizing that clinical and tactical knowledge alone is insufficient.
The authors recommended studying Israel's medical evacuation systems, medical data collection, preventive medicine practices, and ability to continue providing advanced medical treatment under high-intensity combat conditions.

Could Egyptian military deployment in Somalia upset Horn of Africa balance of power? - analysis
Unknown

2026-10-11
11:47:05 UTC
20:47:05 KST

Egyptian technical military teams, including advisors, trainers, and officers, are reportedly preparing for the deployment of troops to Somalia, in the first such move since the signing of a joint military cooperation agreement between the two sides in 2024, The New Arab reported on Friday.
This potentially important development comes as Pakistan and Turkey may also be deploying forces to Saudi Arabia to support the Kingdom’s defenses against the Houthis.
The report at The New Arab says the deployment to Somalia could come “in light of bilateral security and military cooperation between the two countries and within the African Union Mission, widely known as AUSSOM.” It also comes as Turkey has forces in Somalia. However, despite the support, this has not stabilized Somalia enough.
The report added that “the Egyptian troops will reportedly be positioned in the Ceelcade region which used to house the Cisiley Airfield on the immediate northern outskirts of Mogadishu, within the Middle Shabelle region - in the low-lying semi-arid coastal hinterland just north of the Banaadir administrative boundary, around 400 kilometers from the nearest point to Ethiopia's shared border with Somalia.”
Any deployment could tip the balance of power in the Horn of Africa. In early October, Egypt reached out to leaders in Eritrea, Sudan, and Somalia. Egypt is concerned about the spiraling military conflicts that are taking place to the south of Egypt. It’s worth understanding this. Egypt’s military met Somali Defense Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi in September.
Houthis advance to Bab el-Mandeb strait, target Saudi airports
This all comes amid many developments. On one side of the Red Sea, the Houthis advanced in September to the Bab el-Mandeb strait. Then Saudi Arabia backed a Yemeni government offensive against the Houthis. Now the Houthis are targeting Saudi airports. Riyadh is a friend of Egypt.
Egypt and Somalia have four other major conflicts. Ethiopia's conflicts involve the federal government in Addis Ababa, led by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, and several regional movements. The most devastating recent conflict was the Tigray war, fought from 2020 to 2022 between federal forces and their allies, including Eritrean troops, and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). On September 21, seven rebel groups in Ethiopia formed a new alliance. Egypt has opposed the Ethiopian Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam.
In Sudan, Egypt backs the Sudanese army. The army is fighting a civil war. The US has tried to push for a ceasefire and banned Sudan from the UN General Assembly. Sudan's civil war began in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), commanded by General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, commonly known as Hemedti.
The SAF represents Sudan's established military institutions and is associated with the internationally recognized state authorities. The RSF emerged from paramilitary networks linked to the Darfur conflict and has developed its own military, economic, and territorial power. Support for both sides fuels Sudan's conflict. For instance, Sudan’s military accuses the UAE of backing the RSF. This conflict has likely destabilized Ethiopia.
Meanwhile, in Somalia, the government is fighting terrorist groups such as al-Shabaab. Somalia’s government also doesn’t control most of the country. Israel recognized Somaliland in December 2025. Puntland also operates as an autonomous state. Egypt sending forces could change things in Somalia and also potentially affect Ethiopia. It could also change Eritrea’s calculations.
Libya split between Turkey-backed GNU, Egypt-backed Haftar
Libya, a bit farther away in North Africa, borders Egypt and Sudan. As such, it also has a role to play.
In western Libya, the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity (GNU) is one part of the mosaic of the country. In eastern Libya, Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar commands the Libyan National Army (LNA), also known as the Libyan Arab Armed Forces. His coalition controls much of eastern and southern Libya and is aligned with the rival eastern-based political authorities.
In the past, Turkey backed the GNU while Egypt, the UAE and others backed Haftar. In September, The New Arab reported that Saddam Haftar, Khalifa's son, went to the UAE for meetings. Whether true or not, what these reports indicate is intense interest in the Horn of Africa by media in the Gulf.
These four conflicts - Sudan, Somalia, Libya, and Ethiopia - are increasingly interconnected. Ethiopia's renewed fighting and tensions with Eritrea threaten wider instability in the Horn of Africa. Sudan's war involves cross-border armed networks, while Somalia's security depends partly on neighboring countries' military commitments. Libya remains influenced by competing interests from the Mediterranean, the Gulf, and elsewhere. Any change in the balance could reverberate to the Red Sea, the Eastern Mediterranean, and the Indian Ocean.

Kuwait, Lebanon, Syria leading options for Abraham Accords expansion, CSA report assesses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:47:00 UTC
20:47:00 KST

The Council for a Secure America (CSA) has ranked Kuwait as the Middle Eastern country most likely to join the Abraham Accords, followed by Lebanon and Syria, as changing political and security conditions reshape prospects for normalization with Israel.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
CSA released its “Abraham Accords Expansion Opportunities: Middle East Analysis” report on October 8, assessing nine Muslim-majority countries without formal diplomatic relations with Israel: Kuwait, Lebanon, Syria, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Qatar, Iraq, Yemen, and Iran.
More than 80% of Israelis surveyed by CSA in June 2026 support the Abraham Accords, which established relations between Israel and the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Morocco, and Sudan in 2020.
CSA Executive Director Jennifer Sutton said recent events have “reinforced the need for America's continued engagement in the region.”
The rankings were based on expert analysis, primary and secondary sources, and CSA polling. Researchers examined domestic political power, government structures, public opinion, statements by political leaders, relations with Israel and the United States, regional alliances, economic and energy interests, and ongoing conflicts. CSA said the rankings measure both governments’ willingness and political ability to normalize relations and could change as regional conditions evolve.
Kuwait thought to be closest to normalization with Israel, CSA survey shows
Kuwait ranked first despite its longstanding opposition to normalization and laws barring trade with Israel. CSA pointed to
Mishal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah’s growing authority since suspending parliament in May 2024, closer ties with the UAE, and strong security ties with Washington. Kuwait also came under Iranian attack during the 2026 Iran War. Israel’s ambassador to the UAE, Yossi Shelley, said in September that Kuwait could join the accords within six months. 
Lebanon placed second following significant diplomatic activity with Israel. The countries signed a US-brokered “Trilateral Framework” in June under which Lebanon recognized Israeli sovereignty for the first time, followed by additional talks. CSA polling found 41% of Lebanese believed peace with Israel was likely, although only 32% supported normalization. Hezbollah’s continued presence and failure to fully disarm remain major obstacles.
Syria ranked third after talks with Israel accelerated following the fall of the Assad regime. President Ahmed al-Sharaa said in September that the countries had “almost reached agreements on 90%” of their outstanding issues, with a security agreement potentially preceding peace negotiations. CSA found 54% of Syrians believed peace was likely, 53% supported a security arrangement and 46% supported normalization. The dispute over the Golan Heights remains a key obstacle.
Saudi Arabia, previously seen as a leading candidate for normalization, has moved further away since October 7, 2023, and the 2026 Iran War. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman said in November 2025 that he was prepared to work toward joining the accords, but CSA said the Iran war and concerns over Israel’s regional alliances have made Riyadh increasingly wary.
Oman has also become less likely to normalize despite a history of contacts with Israel. Sultan Qaboos bin Said hosted several Israeli leaders, but under Sultan Haitham bin Tariq, Oman has repeatedly rejected normalization and strengthened its role as a mediator with Iran and other regional actors.
Full normalization with Qatar dependent on peace agreement with Palestinians
Qatar maintains working contacts with Israel and serves as a mediator between Israel and Hamas, but says full diplomatic relations depend on an Israeli-Palestinian peace agreement. CSA said Doha’s ties with Iran and support for the Muslim Brotherhood make accession to the accords unlikely in the near term.
Iraq remains an unlikely candidate because of Iranian influence and a 2022 law criminalizing normalization with Israel. CSA singled out Iraqi Kurdistan as an exception, citing its longstanding contacts with Israel and greater public openness toward diplomatic relations.
Yemen’s continuing civil war makes normalization highly unlikely. The Iran-backed Houthis are actively hostile to Israel, while other Yemeni factions have previously expressed openness to relations. CSA said a future postwar government could reconsider the issue, but little movement is possible while the country remains divided.
Iran ranked last. Relations with Israel ended after the 1979 Islamic Revolution, and decades of hostility have developed into direct warfare. CSA concluded that normalization is not possible under Iran’s current regime.

Zohran Mamdani and the limit New York’s Jews must set - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:46:42 UTC
20:46:42 KST

On the third anniversary of October 7, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani gave the victims of the worst massacre of Jews since the Holocaust one sentence of grief. He named Hamas and its war crimes. Then he turned.
“The suffering did not begin nor end that day,” he wrote, and the rest of his statement, more than twice as long, was an indictment of Israel: genocide, occupation, apartheid, American tax dollars, and arms shipments.
Jewish organizations responded with outrage, as they have many times before. It is not enough. Outrage is what a provocateur wants. Every condemnation confirms that he holds the power to wound, and he pays nothing for it.
Anyone who has worked with someone who tests limits knows you do not contain that person by shouting. You set a calm, consistent boundary and attach a consequence to it.
First, though, the pattern has to be seen clearly. As a psychoanalyst who has spent decades studying the minds of perpetrators and those who sympathize with them, I look at the structure of a statement rather than its slogans. The structure says more.
The grief was short. Mourning requires the capacity to stay with another person’s pain without needing to change the subject.
The mayor could not stay. When grief for Jews becomes intolerable to someone, it is usually because it threatens a story he needs to believe, in which Jews are never the victims.
The word “Jews” is missing, as the ADL’s Jonathan Greenblatt pointed out. To name the victims as Jews would be to admit why they were killed.
Hamas did not murder 1,200 people and drag 251 into Gaza because of a policy dispute. It did so because they were Jews.
Erasing the word erases the motive, and erasing the motive clears the way for a reversal: within a few lines, the victim becomes the perpetrator. This is projection in its plainest form.
The wish to annihilate is lifted off the actual killers and placed onto those who defended themselves. Once that move is made, the anniversary no longer belongs to the dead. It belongs to the accuser.
Jewish New Yorkers asked for one day. Not agreement with Israeli policy, not silence on Gaza; just one day on which their dead could be their dead. The mayor of the city with the largest Jewish population outside Israel could not give them that.
Since a mayor’s words set the city’s emotional temperature, this is about more than hurt feelings. Those who already hate hear that their hatred is righteous. The rise in attacks on Jews in New York did not happen in a vacuum.
So what must be done now?
The boundary should be this: Jewish institutions in New York, including the federations, synagogues, major agencies, and Jewish elected officials, should agree that the mayor will not be invited to Jewish community events, not be given photo opportunities, and will not speak from Jewish platforms.
This holds until he meets one public condition: he must name the victims of October 7 as Jews and acknowledge that they were murdered because they were Jews. The condition is stated once and is not negotiated.
Mamdani needs the image of Jewish acceptance in order to claim he is not hostile to Jews. The community can stop providing it.
Two further steps give the boundary weight. First, the community should hold its own civic October 7 memorial, with the Governor, Council members, and non-Jewish allies standing beside it, so that the city’s memory of that day no longer belongs to the mayor.
Second, every antisemitic incident in New York and the city’s response to it should be documented and sent each month to the City Council, Albany, and the Justice Department. Outrage fades. A record does not.
This asks something of Jewish leaders that outrage does not: discipline. A boundary that one federation honors and another breaks for a ribbon-cutting is worse than none, because it teaches the mayor that the community can be divided.
The limit works only if it is held together.
One sentence of grief followed by a long accusation is not mourning. It is the appropriation of mourning.
Jewish New Yorkers do not need to argue with it. They need to stop lending it their presence.
The writer is a Tel Aviv–based psychoanalyst and counterterrorism scholar. https://www.amazon.com/Nancy-Kobrin/e/B002RF9D5Y

Saudi Arabia extends Riyadh airport closure after strike kills 12
Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International Airport will remain closed until at least midnight local time on Sunday following a strike that killed 12 people and injured 309 others, the latest in a series of deadly attacks on the Riyadh transport hub.
The closure was extended until midnight local time on Sunday, according to a notice to air missions, or NOTAM, issued by Saudi aviation authorities. Flights have been cancelled or diverted while officials assess damage to the airport.
The Saudi-led coalition blamed Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis for Saturday’s attack. The dead included four Saudis, two Bangladeshis and one person each from the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt. Some of the injured remain in critical condition, according to the General Authority of Civil Aviation.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree renewed the group’s warning on Sunday against using Saudi airports. His statement, which exempted Mecca and Medina, described other airports as "potential targets and sites for operations by our forces" and urged airlines, airport workers and travellers to take the warning seriously.
The statement also said Saudi Arabia "bears responsibility for any failed interceptions".
Earlier attacks on the airport this week killed four people and damaged a Saudia aircraft on the ground, according to Saudi authorities. The repeated strikes have made the protection of passengers and airport staff an immediate concern alongside the disruption to flights.
Questions remain over whether those inside the airport received an actionable public warning before Saturday’s strike, and what procedures were in place after the earlier attacks.
Saudi Arabia already operates a National Early Warning Platform. The Saudi Civil Defence says it uses cell-broadcast technology to send emergency messages, accompanied by a distinctive tone, to phones connected to mobile networks in the affected area. Its purpose is to warn the public and explain what action people should take to protect themselves.
That public-alert function is distinct from intercepting an incoming missile -- the questions concern both whether a threat was detected and whether information reached people in time to act.
During Iranian attacks in March, at the onset of the war launched by the US and Israel, residents of Riyadh received Arabic- and English-language messages warning of a "hostile aerial threat" and instructing them to remain indoors or in a safe place away from windows and doors. Reporting on a 18 March incident, however, placed the alerts shortly after explosions were heard.
The Civil Defence also issued mobile warnings for Riyadh and nearby Al-Kharj on 19 September amid escalating Houthi attacks, followed by all-clear messages – showing how the platform has been used during the current escalation.
The attacks come as Riyadh hosts major international energy meetings. The WPC Energy Congress, running from Sunday to Thursday, is proceeding as scheduled, while organisers previously said the Future Investment Initiative would go ahead from October 26 to 29. The latter announcement preceded the latest deadly strike.
The US embassy has meanwhile urged American citizens to avoid King Khalid International Airport and its surrounding areas, and to exercise extreme caution when using other major Saudi airports.

Leaders of a popular Indian youth movement vowed to continue protests Sunday after their release from police custody, following a crackdown on demonstrations demanding the resignation of the country’s election chief over controversial voter list revisions.
The protests were triggered after authorities removed more than 130 million voters from the list since last year. Critics say the move is politically motivated. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party and the Election Commission deny manipulation allegations.
The Cockroach Janata Party's three leaders – Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka – were freed on condition that they commit "no breach of peace for one year,” Ratna Singh, the movement's legal director, said in a social media post. It was unclear what the condition meant or whether it would restrict their participation in protests.
Police boarded the leaders' flight from Mumbai after it landed in New Delhi Saturday and took them into custody as they prepared to lead a demonstration in New Delhi.
After his release, Dipke called Modi "an embarrassment to India.”
"Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully," he wrote on X.
Das, a spokesperson for the movement, urged supporters to take to the streets. "A situation has been created where the state is at war with its own citizens," he told reporters Sunday.
Following Saturday's protests, authorities launched a sweeping security crackdown in the capital, detaining more than 2,000 protesters, including several opposition lawmakers.
Train services to the capital were canceled, metro stations closed and mobile internet suspended in parts of the city.
Most of those detained were released late Saturday, police said.
Small groups of protesters returned to the Indian capital Sunday, staging marches across the city. The police quickly broke up most of the demonstrations, detaining some protesters again.
Protesters are demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the chief election commissioner. Modi’s party has said the voter revision is needed to eliminate duplicate and ineligible entries.
The Cockroach movement began as an online satirical campaign this summer after India’s chief justice compared unemployed young people to parasites. Many young Indians embraced the remark, adopting the cockroach as a symbol of resilience.
Protests led by the group forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister in July, a rare setback for the prime minister, who has been in power for more than 12 years.

At least 109 dead, over 100 missing as migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti

At least 139 dead, 84 missing as migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti
Search and rescue operations conducted after vessel carrying more than 300 people capsizes near Guhere.
At least 139 people, including 15 children, have died and 84 are missing after a boat capsized off the coast of Djibouti, according to the United Nations migration agency.
In a statement on Sunday, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) quoted survivors as saying that the incident happened near Guhere off Djibouti’s eastern coast in the Gulf of Aden near the Bab al-Mandeb strait from Thursday night to before dawn on Friday.
The boat was heading from Djibouti to Yemen with more than 300 people on board. More than 80 people – all Ethiopians – survived the shipwreck while Djiboutian search and rescue operations continued.
“Our teams are on the ground alongside local authorities to provide emergency assistance,” IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti Alexandre Coissac said, lamenting the “devastating loss of life”.
That number only includes those buried by authorities in Djibouti. Others have been buried by the migrants themselves but they won’t be added to the official count until authorities can verify the bodies, Alexandre Coissac, IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti, told the Associated Press.
“This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities,” Coissac added.
Undeterred by instability
Crossing Bab al-Mandeb, a waterway that measures just 20km (12.4 miles) at its narrowest points between Djibouti and Yemen, is a popular but dangerous route for thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa.
Many embark on this journey in search of employment and safety in Gulf countries, undeterred by the rising instability in the region due to the US-Israel war on Iran and the resumption of fighting in Yemen between government forces and Houthi fighters last month.
The IOM said it had recorded “more than 20,000 incoming movements to Djibouti from Ethiopia” since September 10. Last year, more than half a million people tried to move along this route into Yemen, and at least 900 people died or are missing, according to the agency.
Djibouti is not only a place where migrants depart from, but several thousand people are also fleeing to the country from Yemen due to the renewed conflict.

High-tech companies discuss ways to boost ties at 3rd Russia-Iran ICT Forum
TEHRAN – Leading Iranian and Russian companies have explored ways to expand bilateral cooperation in advanced technologies at the third Russia-Iran Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Forum.
The forum brought together officials, diplomats, and public- and private-sector representatives from both countries. The participants met on the sidelines of the second Global Digital Forum, held in Moscow from October 8 to 10, IRNA reported.
During the meeting, Alexander Shoitov, Russia’s deputy minister of digital development, communications and mass media, said the participation of Iranian companies in the Global Digital Forum offered a valuable opportunity to exchange information and establish new partnerships.
He noted that Iran and Russia had significant potential to expand bilateral cooperation, particularly in artificial intelligence and cybersecurity.
Shoitov also reaffirmed Russia’s readiness to deepen bilateral ties and develop joint infrastructure in the ICT sector.
For his part, Iran’s ambassador to Russia, Kazem Jalali, highlighted the importance of fostering strategic cooperation between Iran and Russia in the expansion of digital exchanges within a governmental framework. The enhancement of ties helps strengthen the country’s capacity for participation in regional and global markets.
Highlighting the expertise and knowledge of Iranian technology companies in the localization of IT infrastructure equipment, Russian companies can establish joint ventures with reliable partners in Iran, gaining access to the country’s IT and artificial intelligence services market.
Moreover, Iranian and Russian representatives of high-technology companies showcased their latest cutting-edge accomplishments and presented their comprehensive plans and operational proposals for the promotion of cooperation in advanced technologies.
Exchanging best practices and technological solutions, holding B2B meetings, expanding business networks, and exploring opportunities for joint projects were among other key parts of the Forum. Particular attention was given to practical mechanisms for Russian and Iranian companies to enter new markets and develop cooperation with partners from third countries.
The second Global Digital Forum was held at the Mechta multifunctional complex in Gorky Park. As many as 760 delegates from 120 countries took part, including deputy prime ministers, digital development ministers, senior government officials, diplomats, IT company heads, experts, researchers, and representatives of international organizations from Africa, Asia, the Gulf region, Europe, and Latin America.
Sessions were held on artificial intelligence, digital sovereignty, cybersecurity, digital infrastructure, and global cooperation. Participants reviewed global trends in digital transformation, the integration of modern products into national digital systems, and prospects for cooperation between countries in the technology sector.
MOUs to bolster ICT ties
In December 2025, top tech Iranian and Russian companies signed five memoranda of understanding (MOUs) on artificial intelligence (AI), cybersecurity, smart government, blockchain and fintech, regulators, technology parks, and post services, to promote cooperation in the information and communication technology (ICT) sector.
The MOUs were signed in Russia during the fifth Iran-Russia ICT Forum held from December 6 to 7, IRNA reported.
An Iranian delegation led by the deputy ICT Minister for Technology and Innovation, Meysam Abedi, attended the forum.
Referring to the strategic partnership between Iran and Russia, Jalali said the two countries have a high capacity, and the expansion of collaborations will be beneficial to both sides.
For his part, Shoitov said the memoranda of understanding and the agreements reached today are the result of ongoing efforts over the past few years.
“Today, we are celebrating the results of our hard work over many years with the companies collaborating. We can confidently say, cooperation is definitely going on.
So far, the two countries have signed many memoranda of understanding, but there are still new areas of cooperation opening up in our interactions that benefit the people of the two nations,” Shoitov further noted.
Abedi, for his part, said the reached agreements are the result of three years of continuous cooperation between the ICT ministries of the two countries.
He called on Iranian and Russian companies to seriously follow up on the implementation of the MOUs and agreements, and to remove probable obstacles with the help of the government departments of the two countries.
The official went on to propose locating a third country as the joint market for Iranian-Russian products on the agenda, expressing hope that the two countries would sign MOUs on a joint market by the sixth forum.
In May, Russian Presidential Aide Andrei Fursenko emphasized the significance of promoting partnerships and collaborations with Iran in emerging technologies.
It is a fact that focusing on already established technologies will not be beneficial for the two countries. So, it is essential to put on the agenda the technologies that have not (fully) developed yet, which is a much more difficult task, IRNA quoted Fursenko as saying.
For his part, Safarinia said Iran is committed to promoting international scientific cooperation, highlighting that Russia is among the top countries with which Iran is willing to expand ties.

Iran’s Medical Council urges global health bodies to act over US sanctions

Iran’s Medical Council urges global health bodies to act over US sanctions
TEHRAN – The Iranian Medical Council has called on the World Health Organization (WHO), the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and the World Medical Association (WMA) to take immediate action against the use of patients’ lives as a tool of political and military pressure.
In an official letter to the three international organizations, the council said the US government was violating international humanitarian and criminal law through inhumane measures, including economic blockade and pharmaceutical sanctions against Iran, turning patients’ lives into an instrument of political and military coercion.
Mohammad Raiszadeh, head of the Iranian Medical Council, urged the leaders of international health organizations to respond promptly and responsibly to what he described as inhumane acts and the weaponization of medical resources in armed conflicts.
He cited previous reports of direct attacks on healthcare facilities, medical infrastructure, and pharmaceutical facilities, adding that the US attack on the Touska, a vessel carrying medicines and, in particular, vital supplies for dialysis patients, was another clear example of directly endangering patients’ health and lives.
Raiszadeh said Iran’s medical community expected the WHO, WMA, ICRC, and other relevant international bodies to respond appropriately and responsibly to the use of medicines, healthcare facilities, medical shipments, and patients’ lives as instruments of warfare.
He also called for effective measures to ensure safe, rapid, and unhindered routes for the delivery of medicines, medical equipment, and pharmaceutical raw materials.
An effective response from institutions whose very purpose is to protect human health, life, and dignity would represent the fulfillment of their moral and historic responsibilities to humanity, he added.
Raiszadeh stressed that Iran’s medical community and people would not forget these events and would pursue accountability, in accordance with international law, for both those responsible for the actions and institutions that remained silent in the face of them.
As of March 27, data compiled from WHO, the Iranian Red Crescent, and national health agencies reveal a targeted erosion of medical neutrality. A total of 292 medical and relief centres, including hospitals, pharmacies, and primary health clinics, have been damaged or destroyed.
This destruction has forced 13 hospitals completely out of service, while another seven have been fully evacuated under duress because of proximity to danger zones.
The emergency response capacity has been further crippled by the destruction of 48 ambulances and rescue vehicles, as well as an emergency medical helicopter.
The assault on health care is not merely incidental but systemic. Under the Geneva Conventions and the UN Charter, medical personnel and facilities must be protected at all times unless used for military purposes. Yet, verified reports indicate US–Israeli attacks on health facilities and the killing of at least eight health-care workers, doctors, nurses, and emergency first responders in Iran.

DOE advances conservation efforts for reptile and amphibian species
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

20:30:18 KST

DOE advances conservation efforts for reptile and amphibian species
TEHRAN – The Department of Environment (DOE) is developing national conservation programs for priority reptile and amphibian species, with a focus on deploying modern monitoring technologies, strengthening local community engagement, and providing ongoing training for experts.
The plan primarily targets salamanders, marsh crocodiles, spider-tailed horned vipers, and Talysh toads through new methods of monitoring, census, and conservation measures, IRNA quoted Peyman Ashouri, an official with the DOE, as saying.
Razi University in Kermanshah province has already estimated the population of the yellow-spotted salamander using artificial intelligence (AI), and a census of the marsh crocodile is planned to be conducted from February 20 to May 21, he added.
The official elaborated on adopted measures to address human-wildlife conflicts, stating that a project is currently underway to mitigate threats, reduce conflicts, and restore the habitats of the Lorestan newt and Talysh toad; the initiatives include installing signage, producing wildlife awareness posters and brochures, organizing educational programs for tourists and local communities, and removing waste from the habitats.
Referring to spider-tailed horned vipers, Ashouri said the DOE is drafting a conservation plan for the protection of the species, which will be implemented soon.
Data-driven strategies to strengthen biodiversity conservation efforts
The DOE is implementing a comprehensive range of conservation, scientific, legal, and operational initiatives to strengthen the protection of wildlife species and habitats across the country based on a targeted and strategic approach, with priorities guided by data and scientific research.
According to Peyman Valizadeh, an official with the DOE, the DOE focuses on a more scientific approach to develop and implement conservation efforts tailored to the specific needs of each species and habitat, IRNA reported.
It has so far prepared plans for the preservation of 25 endangered species, with thirteen more plans being developed. The plans provide a clear framework for species conservation by delineating the species’ status, major threats, conservation priorities, necessary actions, and assessment indicators, he noted.
However, the DOE faces some challenges in implementing these measures at national and provincial levels. One of the biggest challenges is securing funding to implement the plans. Developing specialized capacity to preserve species is the other problem. Lack of trained, specialized forces has made it difficult to implement the conservation action plans effectively. Therefore, training specialized personnel, developing experts’ capacities in provinces, and strengthening scientific and technical capabilities of the headquarters are put on the agenda, the official highlighted.
Referring to adopted measures to combat wildlife trafficking, Valizadeh said to foster greater coordination among the responsible agencies, the DOE has established a national committee on combating wildlife trafficking; the committee has held three expert meetings so far. Furthermore, the drafting of a comprehensive plan to combat and prevent wildlife trafficking is nearing completion. Furthermore, a comprehensive program to combat and prevent wildlife trafficking is being drafted.
To manage human-wildlife conflicts, efforts have been made to shift the approach from a reactive posture to the identification of critical hotspots, understanding the drivers of conflict, and implementing preventive measures. The DOE has identified some conflict hotspots for species like leopards, black bears, and herbivores; collecting data on black bears in Hormozgan and Kerman provinces is underway.
Moreover, the DOE has signed an agreement with the National Environment Fund and the Agricultural Products Insurance Fund to support local communities and compensate their losses, Valizadeh further noted.
Accurate information on species distribution, habitats, movement paths, and ecological corridors makes conservation efforts more effective, he added.
In this regard, the DOE, in cooperation with Shiraz University, has carried out research to prepare comprehensive distribution maps to identify migration and movement corridors for herbivores and carnivores.
The maps will serve as a management tool for habitat conservation, prevention and management of human-wildlife conflicts, development of conservation priorities, and proper use of smart monitoring and conservation programs, thereby providing a more accurate basis for conservation decision-making, Valizadeh said.
The official went on to say that the DOE will secure funds, train skilled human forces, and foster intersectoral cooperation to establish an integrated system that benefits from scientific information, field data, capacities of local communities, and the capabilities of executive agencies to develop and implement conservation plans for each species and habitat.

“Every Bird Counts – Your Observations Matter!”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:28:27 UTC
20:28:27 KST

“Every Bird Counts – Your Observations Matter!”
TEHRAN – World Migratory Bird Day serves as an opportunity to highlight the vital role these birds play in maintaining ecosystem balance and the need to protect their habitats. These tireless travelers cover thousands of kilometers each year to survive, yet face mounting threats, including drying wetlands, habitat destruction, illegal hunting, and climate change.
World Migratory Bird Day is a global observance aimed at raising awareness of the importance of conserving migratory birds and their habitats. It was first established in 2006 through an initiative by the Secretariat of the Agreement on the Conservation of African-Eurasian Migratory Waterbirds (AEWA) and the Secretariat of the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS), with support from the United Nations.
The observance seeks to draw public attention to threats such as habitat destruction, environmental pollution, illegal hunting and climate change, while underscoring the need for international cooperation to protect migratory birds.
World Migratory Bird Day is observed annually on the second Saturday of May and the second Saturday of October, coinciding with the main bird migration seasons in the Northern Hemisphere. In 2026, the observance falls on May 9 and October 10.
This year’s theme, “Every Bird Counts – Your Observations Matter!”, highlights the role of citizen science and public participation in migratory bird conservation. The initiative emphasizes the value of field observations recorded by birdwatchers, researchers, local communities and nature enthusiasts in understanding migration patterns, monitoring population trends and identifying threats affecting different species.
Iran plays a particularly important role in migratory bird conservation due to its geographical position in West Asia and its location along the seasonal migration routes of numerous species. The country’s wetlands, lakes, coastlines and other natural habitats serve as stopover, feeding and resting sites, as well as wintering grounds, for large numbers of waterbirds and shorebirds throughout the year.
Anzali Wetland, Miankaleh, Gori Gol and Shadegan wetlands, along with aquatic habitats in the Lake Urmia basin, are among the areas where continuous monitoring can provide valuable information on species occurrence, relative abundance, arrival and departure dates, and seasonal population changes.
Recording observation dates, bird numbers, geographic locations, habitat conditions and evidence of threats can help improve ecological assessments, particularly when data are collected using standardized methods over extended periods. Such records make it easier to compare findings over time and identify ecological changes. In this context, public participation in documenting bird sightings can complement professional bird census and monitoring programs nationwide.
On World Migratory Bird Day, the theme “Every Bird Counts – Your Observations Matter!” serves as a reminder that effective conservation requires not only expertise and planning but also informed public participation and the transformation of individual observations into reliable, usable data.
Every accurate observation can help reveal a larger picture of the status of migratory birds and the vital routes they depend on — a picture that is essential to protecting this shared natural heritage.
