One year after Trump's Gaza ceasefire, questions remain about possible next steps - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:31:37 UTC
19:31:37 KST

The Gaza ceasefire took shape a year ago. In September 2025, US President Donald Trump was able to network with key Arab leaders in meetings that eventually led to a ceasefire in Gaza.
Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law who has played a key role in the 20-point peace plan, posted about the significance of the one-year anniversary of the ceasefire.
“One year ago today, on October 9, 2025, we reached an agreement on President Trump’s 20-point peace plan for Gaza many believed impossible,” he wrote.
He noted how important it was to end the devastating war. He wanted an agreement that created “a path to reunite hostage families with their loved ones, bring security to Israel, relieve the suffering of the Palestinian people in Gaza, and build a different future for the region.”
Kushner praised the progress since October 9, 2025, when Hamas accepted Trump’s 20-point peace plan. He noted some of the milestones since that day. On October 13, “all 20 living Israeli hostages return home. Something many believed would never happen.”
He also noted how the UN backed the US plan. He didn’t mention all the important pieces that came together in the following weeks. For instance, the US-backed Civil-Military Coordination Center (CMCC) in Kiryat Gat was set up. This was set up largely by US Central Command and brought together a number of countries.
The concept was to coordinate aid deliveries and monitor the ceasefire. By January 2026, Kushner notes that the UN said: “100% of basic food needs being met in Gaza for the first time since 2023.”
In January 2026, the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza was established. This is supposed to be the Palestinian technocratic government for Gaza. So far, Israel has not permitted it to operate in Gaza.
Two million civilians are still stuck under Hamas rule in around 40% of Gaza. The Board of Peace, established as part of the Trump plan, has tried to do some work on the sidelines to see what might happen after Israel’s elections. In general, the theory is that Israel won’t do anything on Gaza until after the elections.
For instance, the peace plan was supposed to see the creation of an international security force. This ISF only seems to have a few dozen personnel so far. Albania and Kosovo were some of the first to come forward.
In June, reports indicated that Morocco and Greece might help support it. Reports also indicated that Kazakhstan would be helpful. Israel, meanwhile, has ejected some countries from the CMCC due to diplomatic disputes.
On the border of Gaza, a new logistics facility called LSA Endurance has taken shape. However, a lot remains to be seen. Kushner noted that the remains of all the deceased hostages had been returned by late January 2026.
He also noted that on July 31, “Hamas signs an actionable, step-by-step framework for decommissioning its weapons, developed with the support of Nikolay Mladenov and mediators from Egypt, Turkey, Qatar, and the United States. Implementation remains a critical next step.”
The last thing on the Kushner list is a meeting on September 23 where the “Board of Peace hosts an open meeting on the sidelines of UNGA releasing the next steps in the Gaza recovery plan.”
Board of Peace efforts overshadowed by Iran war
Some of the work of the Board of Peace has been overshadowed by the war with Iran. The US administration has been sidetracked to some extent. It also has to deal with other fronts that Israel is involved with. For instance, the administration has had to help Israel in Lebanon with the Lebanese government, where the US also backs a ceasefire.
The US also tried to smooth relations between Israel and Damascus and to prevent Israel-Turkey relations from becoming a crisis. At the same time, recent reports indicate Iran is rebuilding its missile and drone program, and Hamas continues to recruit in Gaza.
Kushner noted that “There is still hard work ahead. Disarmament must be implemented, security established, essential services restored, and communities rebuilt. None of this will be easy. But we have a thoughtful plan, committed partners, and a path forward that did not exist a year ago.”
The challenge in Gaza is that it’s not clear what comes next. Arab News noted that “Reconstruction of the devastated Palestinian territory called for under the ceasefire plan has still not materialized.”
The report said Israel controls around 70% of Gaza. “Nothing has changed for the better; everything has gotten worse, they lie to us, it is all lies,” Fatima Awkal, a displaced woman in Gaza City, told AFP. The AFP article is the basis for the Arab News report.
It said, “On the streets of Gaza City, rows of white tents line passageways that have been cleared of rubble from destroyed homes, while in the distance blown-out windows gape from the facades of buildings that remain standing.” This report also said that around “82% of all standing structures in Gaza are either damaged or destroyed as of mid-2026 per the UN.”
It noted that the concept of the plan was for there to be a political transition in Gaza away from Hamas rule. This has not happened. In the past, Israel has accepted Hamas rule in Gaza, and prior to October 7, 2023, there was cash entering Hamas-run Gaza from Doha.
The Hamas leadership continues to live in Qatar. As such, it’s not clear if the promised change under the Trump plan will happen.
The Arab News report and others paint a concerning picture of Gaza. People there said little has changed. While Kushner has praised the peace deal, the question is going to be what will happen next. This has always been the challenge in the past as well. Getting a ceasefire is one thing. Changing the status quo is another.
Israeli voices call to resettle Gaza Strip
Some voices in Israel’s politics have vowed to re-settle Gaza and have encouraged people to emigrate from the enclave. There do not appear to be many voices discussing how to remove Hamas or whether policymakers in Jerusalem want Hamas removed. The war largely resulted in moving people in Gaza from place to place, with Hamas hiding among them.
The most recent IDF data said that the Israeli military carried out 100,000 strikes in Gaza in three years of war. Many of these were carried out in the first months of the fighting.
The IDF also said that it eliminated four heads of Hamas military branches along with 17 brigade commanders, approximately 60 battalion commanders, and approximately 300 company commanders. Hamas only had 24 battalions and five regional brigades.
As such, it would appear that in many cases the brigade commanders and battalion commanders were eliminated twice.
The same goes for the company commanders. What this means is that Hamas replaced the ones who were killed, and then the replacements were killed. Israel also estimates it has eliminated 4,000 of the 6,000 people who attacked Israel on October 7, some of them Hamas and some of them members of other groups or civilian looters.

Let us hope Washington has the resolve and unwavering will to make it happen.

Palestinians have been left angry by Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas’s decision to again postpone the long-delayed Palestinian Legislative Council elections.

Reports that Sheikh sought to cancel the elections have circulated for months, with Yoni Ben-Menachem, a senior researcher at the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs, saying he had been told that the vice-president had explicitly cited east Jerusalem as a pretext to cancel the vote, as Abbas did in 2021.
“These efforts disregarded the hopes of millions of Palestinians who had waited two decades and welcomed this democratic opportunity,” Sinijlawi said.
“It would have allowed them to participate in the political system by exercising their most basic right: electing their representatives to the Legislative Council and making their voices heard after years of being silenced.
Abbas's decision harmful to Gaza candidates
Sinijlawi said he found it “difficult” to view the postponement as “anything other than putting the interests of those who benefit from the status quo ahead of the public interest” and added that “the right to vote is not a favor granted by anyone. It must not remain hostage to the calculations of those who fear the people’s choice.”
Explaining to the Post how Abbas’s decision was particularly harmful to candidates in Gaza, he said that “many stepped forward” while living in tents and that they had put all their efforts into running “because they believed they could help shape a different future.”
“Their candidacy was an act of hope: a chance to move from surviving devastation to representing their communities and rebuilding their lives,” he continued.
“They now face another year of uncertainty, with no guarantee that the new date will be honored. The damage goes beyond disrupted campaigns. It undermines trust in peaceful democratic change and tells a generation that has never voted that its voice can wait again. Gaza’s emerging leaders deserve the opportunity to lead, and its people deserve the right to choose them.”
Ahmad Shadid, leader of the Phoenix list, also expressed distrust in the PA’s explanation for the postponement.
“If I were one of those behind the idea of postponing [the elections], I would have some self-respect and be honest, and tell people: ‘The Authority is in our hands. We decided to hold elections, and then we changed our minds. You can go to hell.’ But I shouldn’t act like an idiot and talk about circumstances, national dialogue, and … legitimacy, Shadid wrote.”
Postponing elections reflects 'depth of current crisis'
Majda Al-Masri, deputy secretary-general of the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine (DFLP) and head of the Unity and Democratic Change list, wrote that “postponing elections reflects the depth of the current crisis and the inability of existing institutions to address the challenges” and called for a national dialogue to “unify efforts to confront the occupation and its plans.”
Mustafa Barghouti, head of the Palestinian National Initiative list and a former information minister in the Palestinian unity government formed in 2007, made clear he opposed the postponement and demanded on X/Twitter that the Palestinian Authority guarantee that the election will not be delayed next September again.
Despite opposing the postponement, Barghouti said he welcomed the fact that legislative and presidential elections would be held in unison and said it was necessary to review restrictions ahead of September that would “undermine the democratic right to stand for election and to vote.”
“This comprehensive national dialogue must also be devoted to developing a unified national strategy to confront the ongoing genocidal war in the Gaza Strip, as well as the war of settler terror and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank and Jerusalem,” he added.

'The Prime Ministers': New book covers Begin, the ‘Altalena,’  and the October 27 election - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:31:16 UTC
19:31:16 KST

Baroness Thatcher poured the tea, pushed a brass tray of peppermints across the table, and asked Israeli diplomat and author Yehuda Avner to tell her about “Mr. Begin.”
It was a bright April morning in 1992, in a borrowed mansion on Eaton Square, barely a month after Menachem Begin’s funeral. Thatcher had made no bones about opposing his settlement policies, she said, but she had greatly admired his convictions.
Avner told her he thought Begin had been worthy of a second Nobel Prize.
“For what, pray?”
For securing Israel’s parliamentary democracy, he said.
Thatcher’s voice sharpened. Surely he exaggerated. Israel was universally famous for its democracy, one of the most robust in the world.
Not at the outset, Avner said.
Twice, just before independence and just after, Begin had saved the country from civil war.
In 1944, the Hagana seized Irgun men and handed them over to the British; Begin ordered his fighters not to retaliate. Not one of them did. He explained himself afterward in a ramshackle Galilee cinema, speaking over the sound of rain hammering a corrugated roof.
The Second Temple fell because Jews hated each other into civil war. There are fateful times, he told them, when the choice is between blood and tears. Against the British, blood had taken the place of tears. Jew-against-Jew, tears had to take the place of blood. God forbid that a decision of a democratically elected government should ever be defied by force.
He was talking about the Altalena – found intact on the seafloor recently.
Avner says plainly that he was not there and is familiar with the scene through eyewitness accounts years later.
Begin on the burning deck, black with smoke, flinging up his arms and shouting at his own men not to fire.
On the beach, one of the officers ordered to shell her was Yitzhak Rabin, who believed Ben-Gurion’s warning that Begin was mounting a coup and told Avner decades later that his gun crew fired the shell that set her alight. Two of this book’s four prime ministers were at opposite ends of that gun.
Thatcher had no idea, and she said so.
Avner once asked Begin what the most important thing he had done in his life was. “Twice I prevented civil war,” came his answer. That is recorded near the end of The Prime Ministers, and it is the boldest claim in 700 pages. Published in 2010, Avner’s tome is more relevant than ever.
ISRAELIS VOTE on October 27, at the end of only the second Knesset since 1988 to serve a full term – the other 13 having dissolved early.
Avner’s claim is that there is anything to vote in at all because a man twice refused to fight for power he believed was his, and then brought in the voters nobody else wanted, most of them from Arab and Asian countries with no parliamentary tradition and hardly a voice in the new state. They put him in office after eight consecutive electoral defeats.
Thatcher’s own Foreign Office had briefed her that Israel had elected a warmonger and a demagogue.
‘A Jew should never hate another Jew’
Avner never argues any of this on the page. He puts down what he saw and lets you do the rest.
In May 1967, with Egyptian divisions in Sinai, the leader of the opposition walked into Levi Eshkol’s study and asked the prime minister to stand down in favor of David Ben-Gurion.
How could Begin, of all people, ask him to make way for the man who had abused him at every turn and compared him to Hitler? “The enmity is his, not mine,” Begin said. “I live by the maxim that a Jew should never hate another Jew.”
Eshkol went to the window, looked out at picketers holding signs telling him to go, then yawned and refused in Yiddish. “These two horses cannot pull the same wagon together,” he said famously, referring to himself and Ben-Gurion.
Born Haffner in Manchester
Avner was born Haffner in Manchester in 1928, reached Palestine at 18 in November 1947, and dug trenches during the siege.
From 1963, he wrote the English-language speeches of Eshkol, Golda Meir, and Rabin, holding no party card in a country where public jobs ran through Mapai. He was in the room for much of it and scrupulous about when he was not, sourcing Golda’s confrontation with the Socialist International to her own memoir and a colleague she told of it on her return.
In June 1977, the country changed hands for the first time, and the incoming prime minister told his predecessor’s speechwriter he was keeping him.
There had to be continuity, Begin said, and the world had to see it. “This government has come to serve, not to reap.”
Avner stayed six more years. The peaceful transfer of power is not an abstraction in this book. It is the author’s employment record.
The book is also funny, and the joke is rarely where you expect.
Eshkol gets into his car one morning and asks Yankele the doorman, in Yiddish, how he is doing as prime minister. Yankele closes one eye and says the taxes are far too high. Eshkol, one leg in the car, cups a hand to his ear and spends several minutes explaining the defense budget and immigrant housing to his doorman, while his speechwriter wonders how many prime ministers ask a doorman his opinion, listen, and then try to explain themselves.
The word Carter had to ask about
Underneath it is one thing, and Thatcher walks into it. Avner tells her you cannot understand Begin without the Holocaust, that almost his whole family was murdered. In 1979, she admits that she had not really known what Auschwitz was. In the White House Cabinet Room in 1977, under a portrait of Truman, Begin told then-US president Jimmy Carter that, in the past, Jewish men had to deliver their women and children to their executioners. “We were tertiated, Mr. President.”
Carter lifted his head and asked what the word had been. Tertiated, not decimated, Begin said. Decimation is one-in-10. For the Jews it was one-in-three. He rose to his full height, banged his fist on the table, and swore an oath before the president, in the name of the Jewish people, that it would never, ever happen again.
Then Begin broke, knuckles white against the tabletop, blinking back tears, while the clock on the mantelpiece became audible and all the president’s men looked at the floor.
None of it is neutral, and Avner says so, explaining in an author’s note that he reconstructed conversations, edited speech, and thought Begin the most exceptional of the four. It shows in the Sabra and Shatila chapter, which spends more energy on the unfairness of the coverage than on the decision that put Phalangist militiamen inside those camps.
He ends where the man did.
The funeral Begin had specified: no lying in state, no guard of honor, no delegations, not even eulogies. A shroud, a prayer shawl, Irgun veterans carrying him, four kilometers of mourners on the road to the Mount of Olives.
Then, in that London drawing room a month later, Thatcher asked whether Begin had left a memoir.
No, Avner told her, and he could not explain the silence to himself, let alone to her.
What he had was the end of an old Time magazine interview, where, when the reporter rose to leave, he had turned back and asked how Begin wanted to be remembered in history. Avner repeats the answer and adds nothing: “As a decent human being, and a proud Jew.” ■
THE PRIME MINISTERS: AN INTIMATE NARRATIVE OF ISRAELI LEADERSHIP
By Yehuda Avner 
The Toby Press 
715 pages; $38

Year into cease-fire, promised peace never arrived for Gazans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

A year after a U.S.-brokered cease-fire took effect in the Gaza Strip, residents still living in displacement camps under near-daily Israeli airstrikes say the truce has not brought the promised peace.
Israel has reduced its attack intensity but continues strikes and now controls over 70% of Gaza. The cease-fire plan's promised reconstruction of the devastated Palestinian territory has not materialized.
"Nothing has changed for the better; everything has got worse, they lie to us, it is all lies," Fatima Awkal, a displaced woman in Gaza City, said.
"Martyrs are still falling, people are still being injured, the shelling continues and we cannot even find a moment's peace from the constant buzzing of the drones overhead."
On the streets of Gaza City, rows of white tents line passageways cleared of rubble from destroyed homes, while in the distance, blown-out windows gape from building facades still standing.
Ahmed Jonaid, another displaced Palestinian in Gaza City, said he had hoped to return home after the cease-fire.
"We thought we would experience some happiness and return to our homes. Instead, we see ourselves suffering in refugee camps, sleeping on makeshift mats," the 51-year-old said as he carried two jerrycans of water back to his tent.
Israel's genocidal war, which broke out after the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas incursion, has displaced almost all of Gaza's more than 2 million residents at least once.
With 82% of all standing structures in Gaza either damaged or destroyed as of mid-2026, according to the U.N., many residents still live in tents or makeshift shelters, where lack of hygiene has led to outbreaks of disease.
Ahmed Shawan, a doctor at a hospital in the southern city of Khan Younis, said he had yet to see the cease-fire take effect.
"It has been a full year since the cease-fire was declared, yet it exists only on paper," he said.
The agreement's second phase called for a political transition away from Hamas rule, with technocrat Ali Shaath appointed head of a new National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG).
Five countries, including Morocco, have agreed to join the International Stabilization Force (ISF) tasked with post-war preparations, but its troops have not yet started operating in Gaza.
Israel controls all entry points into the territory and continues to allow only a limited amount of aid, keeping the price of basic goods too high for ordinary Gazans like Ismail Hamouda.
The 47-year-old father, displaced from Jabalia in the north to Gaza City, listed what residents still lack: potable water, food, financial assistance.
"Here in the displacement camps, we thought that after a year of cease-fire things would improve," he said. "Unfortunately, the situation is worsening gradually. We are still displaced."

Intelligence agencies warn against Russian attempts to assassinate European defense CEOs - report
The main goal is psychological, one intelligence official said, to make people think twice before doing business with Ukraine
Western intelligence agencies have warned CEOs and other senior employees at defense companies that they are being targeted by Kremlin operatives. According to officials from five European intelligence agencies who spoke with the Financial Times, Europe's defense company bosses that Russia is stepping up efforts to assassinate them, prompting companies to increase personal security around top executives.
With battlefield progress deadlocked in Ukraine and Russia's economy struggling, the Kremlin has ordered an expansion of sabotage and "hybrid" operations in Europe as it seeks to weaken support for Kyiv. Assassinations against European civilian targets, once considered taboo even by Russia's spy agencies, are becoming a prominent part of those plans, according to the intelligence services.
Executives at smaller companies, especially those making drones or components, are also being targeted. "The threat level has risen in Europe. To property but also to people," one senior European intelligence official said.
Sinan Selen, head of Germany's domestic intelligence service BfV, told German lawmakers on Monday, "Russia is engaged in the deliberate planning of acts of violence against individuals by state or state-controlled actors." Selen also stated, "We are observing a further development of these actions in terms of the targets, the methods and the actors involved, including the use of organised crime structures."
Suggested articles
Several defence executives, speaking anonymously, told the FT they escalated close-protection arrangements in the past six months on the advice of government security services.
"The main goal from the Russian perspective is still psychological," one intelligence official said. "Just by making people feel they might be a target, they are having their effect. They want individuals to think twice before doing business with Ukraine."
One official stressed that many Russian efforts remain amateurish and easily countered. In August, the two holidaymakers arrested in Sweden near the property of Saab CEO Micael Johansson were released shortly afterwards.

Most long-term singles stay satisfied with their lives over 11 years, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:00:18 UTC
19:00:18 KST

New research indicates that people who remain unpartnered and unmarried generally maintain high and relatively stable life satisfaction over long periods of time, even as their sexual fulfillment and desire for a partner vary widely. By tracking different generations of singles over more than a decade, the findings suggest that there is no single way to experience a solo life. The study was published in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin.
Never-married singlehood refers to the status of adults who have not entered a formal marriage and are not currently in a committed romantic partnership. For many years, lifespan theories treated romantic partnerships as a universal developmental milestone, suggesting that failing to find a mate could lead to isolation. Because of this framework, scientists often evaluated singles simply by comparing them to partnered people. But as marriage rates drop globally and solo living becomes more common, researchers have increasingly shifted their focus to investigating how individual factors like personality, age, and sexual fulfillment shape a single person’s happiness.
“As the population of single individuals grows and people are increasingly delaying marriage, there is both a rise in population as well as public and academic interest for singles, or romantically unpartnered individuals,” Elaine Hoan, a PhD candidate at the University of Toronto and lead author of the study, told PsyPost. “In light of this rise, much is unknown regarding how singles’ psychological well-being changes over time, with some individuals arguing that singles report generally low well-being across the life span.”
Recent research has begun to examine what shapes singles’ well-being. A study covered by PsyPost in 2024 indicated that adolescents born in the early 2000s tend to be more satisfied with being single than those born a decade earlier. Beyond generational differences, a 2020 study found that single people who are satisfied with their sex lives tend to be happier with their single status and show less interest in getting married. Additionally, a 2021 analysis of German adults showed that singles who feel less urge to find a romantic partner tend to be happier with their lives overall.
The new study builds directly on this work by tracking how these different facets of well-being evolve together over more than a decade across multiple generations of singles. Hoan and her colleagues analyzed data from the German Family Panel, a long-running national survey of relationships and families, tracking 2,930 adults over an 11-year period between 2009 and 2021. The participants came from three birth groups: emerging adults who started the study around age 18, young adults who began around age 26, and middle-aged adults who entered around age 36.
To be included, participants had to remain never married and without a committed partner at every one of the 11 yearly surveys, so the sample captures long-term singles rather than everyone who was single at the start. Because people frequently partner up as they age, this filtering was much heavier for older groups; only 14 percent of the middle-aged cohort qualified, compared with 67 percent of the youngest.
During the 11-year period, participants regularly answered single-item questions rating four specific outcomes on numeric scales: overall life satisfaction, satisfaction with their single status, sexual satisfaction, and their desire for a romantic partner. An earlier analysis of the same data, which assumed all singles follow a single average path, had suggested that singles’ life satisfaction tends to decline over time.
By using a statistical modeling technique designed to group people with similar over-time trends into distinct categories, the researchers sought to uncover whether multiple different paths existed. They also measured participants’ income, education, physical health, and personality traits to see how these factors lined up with different well-being paths.
The researchers found that the vast majority of singles across all three age groups reported high and relatively stable life satisfaction. Roughly 90 percent of the participants in each cohort fell into a group whose life satisfaction stayed above the midpoint of the scale for the entire 11 years, though it dipped slightly over time among the two younger groups. A small minority in each age group started the study with lower life satisfaction.
Among emerging and young adults, this smaller minority’s happiness tended to improve over time, eventually catching up to the rest of their peers. Among middle-aged adults, however, the smaller group with lower starting happiness did not show the same improvement; its scores edged down slightly, though this change was not statistically significant. The authors suggest this may reflect the social pressures of midlife, when expectations around marriage and family are often strongest.
“We found that while relationship-focused outcomes, like sexual satisfaction and desire for a partner, varied more between participants, singles’ overall satisfaction with their lives remained remarkably robust,” Hoan explained. “Overall, even while singles face different romantic or sexual experiences, they generally remain quite satisfied with their lives over time.”
Satisfaction with being single showed much more variety. About 67 percent of the youngest adults reported high and stable satisfaction with their single status. Young and middle-aged adults, by contrast, split into three groups: a highly satisfied group (about 30 and 37 percent, respectively), a larger group with middling satisfaction, and a group with low satisfaction (about 12 and 18 percent).
The authors suggest this shift may reflect changing life goals, since singlehood can suit the educational and career focus of emerging adulthood, while priorities often turn toward partnership later. They also point to selection: by midlife, many people have partnered, leaving a smaller group of singles who differ widely in whether they are single by choice.
Trajectories of sexual satisfaction remained flat over the 11 years but varied widely in their starting levels. The youngest adults split into four distinct groups ranging from very low to very high sexual fulfillment. By young adulthood, the pattern simplified to two groups, with about 63 percent reporting moderate sexual satisfaction and 37 percent reporting very low satisfaction.
Interestingly, individuals with higher education levels frequently fell into the groups with the lowest sexual satisfaction. The researchers propose that intense focus on advanced educational pursuits might reduce a person’s time or interest in seeking out sexual experiences, or that people less interested in sex may gravitate toward demanding educational paths.
When looking at the desire for a partner, the data indicated that most singles maintained a moderate to high interest in finding a relationship. For example, about 47 percent of young adults fell into a high-desire category. However, a small but distinct group of singles in each age bracket reported very low desire for a partner. These individuals tended to have higher education levels and lower levels of neuroticism, a personality trait associated with emotional instability and anxiety.
Across all the measures, the groups reporting the highest life, singlehood, and sexual satisfaction generally exhibited healthier personality profiles, including lower neuroticism and higher extraversion, meaning they were more outgoing, sociable, and energetic. “We found that the trajectories with the highest well-being tended to be more extraverted, less neurotic, more highly educated, and full-time employed,” Hoan said. “These results suggest that higher socioeconomic status is an important part of supporting a thriving singlehood.”
These findings are in line with earlier work by some of the same researchers, covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that higher extraversion and lower neuroticism were linked to higher well-being among singles, though that earlier work compared singles and partnered people at a single point in time rather than tracking singles over years.
However, the new findings stand in tension with a study covered by PsyPost in 2026, which tracked emerging adults from age 16 to 29 and found that remaining consistently single was associated with declining life satisfaction relative to peers who partnered up. Because the current study followed only never-married singles across a broader age range of 18 to 48 without comparing them to partnered people, it suggests that most long-term singles maintain relatively high life satisfaction, even though the largest group of younger singles did show a slight decline.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. Because the study tracked naturally occurring patterns, it cannot show that personality traits, education, or income cause singles to follow happier paths; these factors may simply travel together. The study also defined singlehood broadly, capturing anyone who had never married and was not currently cohabiting or in a committed relationship. This means that people who engaged in casual dating or brief romantic flings between the yearly surveys were grouped together with those who completely abstained from romance, though the authors note that removing people who briefly dated did not substantially change the results.
The study was also conducted in Germany, meaning the results might not fully translate to cultures with different social norms surrounding marriage and independence. Hoan is planning to address this limitation in future work.
“I am continuing to investigate longitudinal patterns of well-being across both single and partnered individuals, but in diverse contexts beyond WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) samples,” she noted. “Given that different cultures have strongly varying norms around singlehood, investigating singles’ experiences and how they might differ from partnered people’s experiences, across cultures is an important future direction. For instance, in India, being an unmarried woman can create daily logistical barriers, such as greater difficulty with renting apartments.”
Additionally, the oldest participants in the study were in their late forties by the end of the data collection period. Future studies will need to track singles into their sixties and beyond to see how retirement and older age shape the single experience. Finally, same-sex marriage only became legal in Germany in 2017, so “never married” carried a different meaning for gay and lesbian participants during much of the study period, and the sample included too few of them (65) to compare with heterosexual singles.
The study, “The Eras of Singlehood: 11-Year Longitudinal Trajectories of Never-Married Singles’ Well-Being Across Cohorts,” was authored by Elaine Hoan, Geoff MacDonald, and Matthew D. Johnson.

Photos: Thousands detained in police crackdown on India’s youth protest
Demonstrators intercepted and detained as authorities crack down on ‘cockroach’ movement rally in central New Delhi.
Thousands of people were detained across New Delhi on Saturday as Indian authorities mounted a sweeping security operation to stop a protest by the youth-led “cockroach” movement demanding the resignation of the country’s election chief.
Police fanned out across India’s capital to block access to Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site, stopping buses and cars at checkpoints, erecting barricades and deploying antiriot vehicles equipped with tear gas launchers along key routes.
Many demonstrators were intercepted long before they reached central New Delhi, chased away or dragged into police vehicles and taken to temporary detention centres. Several movement leaders, opposition lawmakers and student activists were detained en route, effectively halting the rally before it began.
Authorities said they had denied permission for the gathering because the request was submitted late and insisted the measures were necessary to maintain order. Sambit Patra, a spokesperson for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party, dismissed the protesters as “anarchic elements” staging a “flop show”.
Despite the clampdown, some protesters broke through police cordons, chanting slogans against Modi and the Election Commission of India (ECI), before being detained. “We are a democracy, yet peaceful protests are being crushed by force,” said college student Tanya Negi, who travelled from Mumbai. “Why is Modi afraid of India’s young people?”
The movement led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) emerged online in May and gained prominence through protests over exam paper leaks that led to the resignation of Modi’s education minister in July.
Its latest campaign targets the ECI’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR), which opposition parties say has already removed more than 130 million names from voter rolls and disenfranchised supporters.
The ECI and the government deny any political bias, but critics say the crackdown highlights shrinking space for dissent as key state polls approach.

Greeting participants and wishing the event success, he said he was pleased that the gathering, which he announced in person at a youth meeting in May, was being held in Türkiye's northwestern Kocaeli province.
Young people from across the Turkic world are attending under the motto "Shared Heritage, One Heart". Erdogan welcomed them and conveyed his greetings and affection to "friendly and brotherly peoples" through the participants.
Unity among Turkic youth
Erdogan also congratulated the Justice and Development (AK) Party's Directorate for Relations with Turkic States and everyone involved in organising the event.
"In this regard, I consider it very important that the children of Anatolia, meaning the people of Türkiye, come together with you, my young brothers and sisters from different regions of the Turkic world," he said.
"We will continue to provide the strongest possible support to you, young people who unite your energies around a common ideal toward a prosperous future," he added.
Erdogan also pointed to the 13th Summit of the Organization of Turkic States, due to be held in Ankara at the end of the month.
"As Türkiye, we aim, God willing, to take our ideal of 'unity in language, thought and action' one step further with the 13th Summit of the Organization of Turkic States," he said.
He ended his message by wishing the gathering success. "I entrust you all to God's protection. Stay well," he said.

Russia’s Yandex says data centre in Vladimir shut down after drone attack
Third strike on Yandex facilities in a week comes as Russia and Ukraine escalate attacks on tech infrastructure.
A Russian data centre run by technology and AI company Yandex has been shut down after it was hit in a drone attack.
No injuries were reported in the attack on the facility in the city of Vladimir, east of the capital, Moscow, the company said on Sunday.
Emergency services were at the site and several of Yandex’s services were unavailable to users, the company said, as it evaluated ways to restore its systems.
“Operations at the data centre have been completely suspended,” Yandex said in a service alert on Telegram, advising users to activate disaster-recovery plans as the platform operated in emergency mode.
“The remaining resource configuration is considered unstable,” it added, warning that technical support communications could also be disrupted as teams assessed the damage.
It is the third attack on the company’s data centres in the last week, as Russia and Ukraine continue to escalate attacks on each other’s technology infrastructure.
On Friday, Yandex, which is heavily involved in Russia’s AI development and is sometimes referred to as “Russia’s Google”, said its data centre in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow was struck by Ukrainian drones and partly put out of action.
A day earlier, a Ukrainian attack shut down Yandex’s data hub in Sasovo, southeast of Moscow, where two of the three supercomputers used to develop the company’s AI model are housed.
“We always respond in mirror-like fashion,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday, following the Sasovo strike. “You all know, they have been hitting and continue to hit our data centres. We are responding. I can’t share all the details.”
Russia has struck several Ukrainian data centres and telecommunications infrastructure facilities over the past month, including targets in central Kyiv, in an apparent effort to disrupt the country’s connectivity and digital commerce.

====================================================================================================

‘We knew we're not gonna get a hostage deal until Yahya Sinwar is dead’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:23:05 UTC
18:23:05 KST

Former White House Middle East adviser Brett McGurk has offered a behind-the-scenes account of the prolonged negotiations to free Israeli hostages held by Hamas in Gaza, describing a diplomatic process repeatedly derailed by new demands, political disagreements and developments on the battlefield.
In an interview published by The Sunday Times on Saturday, McGurk discussed his forthcoming book, Brink: Inside the Race to Free the October 7th Hostages, which examines the efforts of American negotiators to secure the release of those abducted during the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack on Israel.
One of the most devastating setbacks came in August 2024, when negotiations appeared close to producing an agreement involving a ceasefire, the release of hostages and Palestinian prisoners and measures to ease restrictions on movement in Gaza.
Those hopes collapsed after Israeli forces recovered the bodies of six hostages murdered by Hamas in a tunnel beneath Rafah: Alex Lobanov, Almog Sarusi, Carmel Gat, Ori Danino, Hersh Goldberg-Polin and Eden Yerushalmi.
McGurk recalled learning of their deaths from then-CIA Director William Burns. He subsequently advised President Joe Biden that meaningful progress was unlikely while Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar remained alive.
The killings reinforced his assessment that the negotiations could not succeed without a fundamental change in the circumstances on the ground.
Netanyahu's competing objectives
McGurk, who served in senior Middle East policy positions under several American presidents, described the hostage crisis as the most difficult diplomatic challenge of his career.
He said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pursued two objectives throughout the war: securing the hostages' release and preventing Hamas from retaining control of Gaza.
Those priorities were not always compatible, complicating American attempts to broker an agreement. “I always found him extremely confident in his assumptions,” McGurk said of Netanyahu. “If you try to tell him he’s seeing it wrong, it’s tough to make that case.”
McGurk nevertheless rejected the argument that Netanyahu's decisions were driven exclusively by political survival. He portrayed the Israeli leader as deeply convinced of his own assessments and difficult to persuade when American officials disagreed with him.
The former envoy reserved particularly sharp criticism for Hamas, accusing the terrorist organization of repeatedly obstructing negotiations.
He pointed to the breakdown of the first temporary ceasefire in December 2023, when Hamas failed to release additional female hostages as anticipated. Accounts of sexual abuse subsequently provided by released captives raised further concerns about the treatment of women held in Gaza.
According to McGurk, Hamas also complicated negotiations by failing to provide reliable information about the hostages it was prepared to release.
He argued that international discussion of the war often focused heavily on Israeli military operations while paying insufficient attention to Hamas' responsibility for the conflict and its continuation.
Sinwar's strategy and the civilian toll
McGurk said Sinwar had spent years preparing for a confrontation with Israel, including the development of an extensive underground tunnel network that presented major operational challenges for the Israeli military. In his assessment, Sinwar hoped the October 7 attack would provoke a wider regional conflict that could threaten Israel's existence.
Although that broader objective was not achieved, McGurk acknowledged that the war had seriously damaged Israel's international standing. He also expressed frustration over the inability to establish arrangements that would have allowed Palestinian civilians to escape the fighting in Gaza.
Drawing on his experience with military campaigns against Islamic State in Iraq and Syria, McGurk noted that large numbers of civilians had been evacuated from combat zones in previous conflicts.
In Gaza, however, residents had few options for escaping the fighting.
He argued that temporary evacuation arrangements should have been explored alongside enforceable guarantees allowing displaced Palestinians to return to their homes.
McGurk acknowledged the historical sensitivities surrounding Palestinian displacement, particularly the experience of refugees from the 1948 Arab-Israeli war, but maintained that civilian protection should have received greater attention.
How Biden and Trump officials worked together
McGurk also credited cooperation between the outgoing Biden administration and President Donald Trump's incoming team with helping advance the negotiations.
Following Trump's victory in the November 2024 presidential election, McGurk began coordinating with Steve Witkoff, who would become Trump's Middle East envoy, and Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law and former senior adviser.
By that stage, the regional balance had changed significantly. Israeli forces had killed Sinwar, dealt major blows to Hezbollah in Lebanon and struck Iranian military capabilities.
McGurk believed those developments created an opportunity to renew diplomatic efforts. He said coordination between the two administrations proved essential, despite the deep political divisions in Washington.
“We wouldn’t have been able to get the deal without the two teams working together,” McGurk said.
The first hostages released under the resulting agreement returned on Biden's final day in office in January 2025. Subsequent releases took place under Trump, with the remaining hostages returned in October 2025.
McGurk described the cooperation as an example of bipartisan coordination on a critical foreign policy issue.
The unresolved future of Gaza
Despite the end of the war and the return of the hostages, McGurk warned that the underlying political and security problems remain unresolved.
Hamas has been severely weakened but has not disappeared as an armed organization. Gaza continues to face extensive destruction and humanitarian hardship, while Israeli forces retain a military presence in parts of the territory.
McGurk sees only a limited path toward lasting stability, one requiring Hamas to disarm, Israeli forces to withdraw and a new Palestinian governing structure to emerge. He stressed that the October 7 attack fundamentally changed Israel's approach to threats along its borders.
“What you need to appreciate is that, after October 7, Israel will never allow threats to gather on its border again,” McGurk said.
In his view, Israel will not permit Hamas to rebuild its military capabilities or allow Hezbollah to reestablish a large armed presence near its northern communities.
Although McGurk acknowledged grounds for criticizing some Israeli military decisions, he argued that preventing another October 7-style attack remains a legitimate security objective.
He also rejected growing calls in American political circles to distance Washington from Israel, maintaining that close engagement offers the United States greater influence over Israeli decision-making than isolation or punitive measures.

Former A-G Avichai Mandelblit ends testimony in Netanyahu trial over investigations authorization
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:01:29 UTC
18:01:29 KST

Former attorney-general Avichai Mandelblit testified Sunday that investigators carried out serious actions in the cases against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu without his approval. He said he had wanted the main investigative steps reviewed, but had not expected to approve every police action.
“There were things I did not approve, including serious things,” Mandelblit told the Jerusalem District Court.
Mandelblit, who approved investigations into Netanyahu and later decided to indict him in Cases 1000, 2000 and 4000, was called by the defense. Netanyahu’s lawyers argue investigators exceeded the scope of Mandelblit’s approvals and that some actions began without the consent required by law. The prosecution says he authorized the investigations, including orally, and that the defense is mischaracterizing those approvals.
The testimony is expected to continue Monday. The defense has requested five further days, from October 18 to 22.
The central dispute is what Mandelblit approved and how those decisions were recorded.
Basic Law requires A-G consent for investigation against prime minister
Under Basic Law: The Government, an investigation of a sitting prime minister requires the attorney-general’s consent. The prosecution relies on Justice Ministry meeting records and a memorandum from Mandelblit to show that he approved opening the investigations.
The defense says the records do not establish the required approvals or show that police stayed within their scope. In 2021, the judges rejected a defense request to dismiss the indictment on this ground, but criticized the lack of separate written authorizations.
Mandelblit said he closely supervised the investigations because they involved a sitting prime minister, but was not informed of every police action. He wanted the main steps reviewed because of the case’s sensitivity and the need to balance gathering evidence with protecting the office and dignity of the prime minister. Police, he said, can be “like runaway horses” in pursuing suspicions. But the law did not require him to approve every action, and he said he had not tried to manage the police team.
Defense attorney Amit Hadad cited testimony from former senior investigator Koresh Barnur, who said every action in the case had been approved by the attorney-general. Mandelblit said that was inaccurate and agreed that some actions he had not approved were serious.
One example was a wiretap targeting Natan Eshel, a close Netanyahu associate. Mandelblit said the surveillance should have been brought to him because it was sensitive. When he learned of it, he demanded it stop unless investigators had information connecting Eshel personally to an offense. He said he told investigators to consult him in advance about similar steps.
Mandelblit also addressed a controversial police tactic involving Nir Hefetz, a former Netanyahu aide who became a state witness. Investigators arranged a chance encounter between Hefetz and a woman close to him while he was in custody, intending for him to learn that police knew personal details about him. Mandelblit said he had not known about the tactic beforehand and called it “improper and wrong.”
He said he considered whether to investigate the conduct immediately, but decided against questioning the officers and witnesses while the case was underway, fearing that bringing them together could affect the proceedings. Instead, he told his staff to examine documents related to the incident. He said he did not know that prosecutor Yehudit Tirosh had attended a meeting where the tactic was discussed and would have expected to be told.
Hadad also asked what Mandelblit knew about pressure on state witnesses. Mandelblit said he had not been in the interrogation rooms and did not know what pressure investigators had put on Hefetz. Hadad raised claims that investigators tried to get Or Elovitch, the son of Shaul Elovitch, Netanyahu’s co-defendant in Case 4000, to persuade his father to replace his lawyer. Mandelblit said it was unacceptable for an investigator to tell a suspect to change lawyers.
Mandelblit said investigators had to seek his consent to open an inquiry into a suspicion involving the prime minister, and return to him if a new suspicion emerged. An investigation, he said, had to be based on a specific suspicion, not a personal impression of the prime minister.
On Case 1000, the illegal gifts affair, Mandelblit rejected Hadad’s claim that he had not authorized investigators to look into cigars and champagne. He said he had approved examining whether Netanyahu received benefits from businesspeople, including wealthy figures abroad. Asked about businessman Arnon Milchan, Mandelblit said he did not remember refusing to investigate gifts from him. He said the wording investigators used when cautioning Milchan as a suspect went beyond what he had approved.
Mandelblit denied knowing investigators had acted without his approval
On Case 4000, the Bezeq-Walla case, Mandelblit said he had approved examining whether actions by then-Communications Ministry director-general Shlomo Filber were connected to Netanyahu. He denied knowing that investigators had taken steps in the case without his approval. The defense challenged whether the meeting records supported his account.
Mandelblit also rejected the suggestion that Case 4000 had been essential to his decision to indict Netanyahu. He said each of the three cases independently justified an indictment and that he viewed them as connected in reflecting a pattern of conduct. He acknowledged that he may earlier have hoped the inquiries would not produce evidence warranting charges, but said he had to approve examining a suspicion once it arose.
The trial, which began in May 2020, combines three cases. In Case 1000, prosecutors allege that Netanyahu and his family received gifts from wealthy businessmen. Case 2000 concerns recorded conversations between Netanyahu and Yediot Aharonot publisher Arnon Mozes about a possible exchange of more favorable coverage for Netanyahu for steps to curb rival Israel Hayom.
In Case 4000, prosecutors allege that Netanyahu advanced regulatory measures benefiting Bezeq in exchange for favorable coverage on the Walla news site. Netanyahu denies wrongdoing. He faces charges of fraud and breach of trust in Cases 1000 and 2000, and bribery, fraud and breach of trust in Case 4000.
Netanyahu arrived after the testimony began and said, “The truth is coming to light.” He left before the afternoon session resumed, and Mandelblit continued testifying in his absence.
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, former Israel Bar Association head Efi Nave and MK Tali Gotliv also attended. Gotliv, who recently moved from Likud to Otzma Yehudit, shouted at Mandelblit as he entered the courtroom.
At the hearing’s opening, Mandelblit complained that a journalist had confronted him outside court and made claims he could not answer. Kan 11 journalist Ayala Hasson denied his account and said she had approached him politely.
Prosecutor Yehonatan Tadmor called testimony by a former attorney-general “exceptional,” warning that questioning a prosecutor could become a means of personal attack or expose internal discussions. The prosecution had not opposed Mandelblit’s testimony because of the unusual circumstances and the dispute over whether he authorized the investigation, Tadmor said.
Justice Minister Yariv Levin called Mandelblit’s appearance “disgraceful” and said it showed that the case against Netanyahu had been fabricated. He called for the trial to be canceled before the election and for a commission of inquiry into law-enforcement officials.
Yonah Jeremy Bob contributed to this report.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
09:00:45 UTC
18:00:45 KST

Pakistan's president declared a state of emergency and suspended the provincial government of jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan on Sunday, following allegations by the federal government that it has failed to tackle Islamist militancy.
The constitution allows the federal government to take over some or all provincial government functions during an emergency.
A provincial governor will take charge with an advisory council, Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar told a news conference in Islamabad, adding that the arrangement will initially be in place for six months.
The interior ministry said it would be deploying troops in the northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province bordering Afghanistan, which has suffered an increasing number of terror attacks in recent months.
"The situation is so grave that you wouldn't see any residents coming out of their houses after evening in some of the districts," said Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi.
The federal government and the military have accused Khan's party of failing to curb the terrorists, while Khan's party has rejected the accusation and says the federal government has failed to provide it with the funding and equipment needed.
Islamabad accuses neighboring Afghanistan of harboring Islamist terrorists who launch attacks inside Pakistan, and says that Khan's party had been sympathizing with both the Taliban in Kabul and their affiliates at home.
Both the Afghan Taliban and Khan's party have denied the accusation.
President Asif Ali Zardari declared an emergency on the advice of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif following a federal cabinet decision, the president's office said.
The security forces and citizens had been under attack for the last two years, Sharif told the Cabinet. "We can't just act a silent spectator."
'A coup disguised as emergency'
The move comes after Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party rallied for several days to pressure the government for his release, threatening to march on the capital Islamabad in coming days amid deepening political instability.
Khan's supporters say the military rigged the 2024 election against the 74-year-old former cricket star, an allegation the military denies.
"This is more of a coup disguised as emergency," said Zulfikar Bukhari, Khan's aide and his party's spokesperson, adding that it risks leading to further bloodshed and instability.
Ahead of the planned march, authorities detained three of Khan's sisters and hundreds of party activists. Restrictions have been placed on the movements of Chief Minister, Sohail Afridi of Khan's party, one of his close aides told Reuters.
The government has cut access to the capital, Islamabad, to bar the protesters from reaching parliament, blocking major highways with shipping containers and deploying tens of thousands of security forces, interior ministry officials said.
The party's last large-scale protest two years ago ended in deadly clashes with security forces.
Khan arrest sparks nationwide riots
Khan's 2023 arrest sparked nationwide riots that threatened the standing of the Pakistani military. Cases against Khan have ranged from concerns over state gifts to instigating violence and an accusation of an unlawful marriage.
All convictions but one have since been suspended or overturned, with appeals pending. He denies wrongdoing.
The latest protest coincides with public discontent over inflation and rising fuel prices that has spread beyond Khan's core supporters.

Hegesth plan to publicly livestream Nidal Hasan execution draws bipartisan, UN condemnation

US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream the December 3 firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan has drawn objections from the UN, Republican and Democratic lawmakers, and the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, while the Trump administration has not made a final decision on the broadcast.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers and wounded 32 others at the Fort Hood military base in 2009. A Defense Department official announced that his execution would be livestreamed.
“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth told podcaster Jack Posobiec aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln on Wednesday.
Hegseth separately told Real America's Voice that Hasan was "gonna get a firing squad of soldiers - as it should be.” Asked about any final requests from Hasan or contact with US President Donald Trump, Hegseth said: "Don't care. We'll see him on December 3rd."
The UN human rights office told AFP that livestreaming the execution would be "tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture.”
A Pentagon spokesperson said Monday that Trump had approved Hegseth’s recommendation. Trump said Friday that Hasan deserved execution by firing squad but did not address livestreaming at the time. Speaking to reporters Friday evening, he said the administration would decide on the broadcast.
Vice President JD Vance also questioned whether it would happen, saying, “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen.” He said he would not watch.
The last public US execution was Rainey Bethea’s 1936 hanging. Hasan’s execution would be the US Army’s first execution of a soldier since World War II and the first death penalty imposed on an armed service member in 65 years.
Public executions only done in Iran, Afghanistan over last year
Of the more than 2,700 executions recorded in 17 countries last year, public executions occurred in just two. Amnesty International documented 11 such executions in Iran in 2025 and six in Afghanistan.
Republican lawmakers joined the criticism. Outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina said public executions belong to “oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan,” while Georgia GOP Rep. Austin Scott said “live-streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that.”
Republican Sen. John Curtis warned against turning executions into “bloody spectacles,” while Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut called the proposal “disgusting” and “medieval.”
The president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops called the plan a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death.”

Ben Yigal, aged 21, served as a combat soldier in the Golani Reconnaissance Battalion.
On May 12, 2020, during a security operation to arrest wanted individuals in the West Bank Palestinian village of Ya'bad, Bakar threw a half-brick at IDF soldiers from a nearby rooftop.

After throwing the brick, Bakar fled and feigned being asleep in his home in an attempt to hinder security forces from locating him.
Once Israel’s security forces left the scene, Bakar returned to collect the fragments of the brick and discarded them at the side of the road in an attempt to obstruct the investigation.
In August 2020, the High Court of Justice halted the IDF's planned demolition of Bakar's home.
On May 11, 2026, the military court accepted the military prosecution's position, following testimony from prosecution witnesses and the terrorist himself, and convicted him of committing the attack.
Enlisted to Golani despite being an only child
"Amit was an only child. Therefore, he was given the option not to enlist in a combat unit,” Ben Yigal’s father, Baruch, shared in an article published in December 2021 on the IDF’s website. “I hoped he would choose not to, yet when he went on his school trip to Poland and visited the camps, he called me and said something I will never forget.”
“‘Dad, you’re the son of a Holocaust survivor. Your dad didn’t have an army to protect him. Today, now that our people have a country, I want to do everything I can to protect it at all costs. “I want to enlist in the Golani Brigade,” Baruch recalled his son saying.
He shared that after Ben Yigal returned from Poland, the two negotiated for two months over where he would enlist before Baruch gave in and allowed him to join a combat unit.
At the time the article was published, Baruch shared that 23 children across Israel were named after his son.
“There is a small forest of carob trees planted by volunteers in Northern Israel,” he said. “Next to Amit’s grave, we planted an olive tree, the tree of peace. Amit was a child of peace.”
“Amit was a hero, and he died as a hero. He will never be forgotten.”

Houthis defiant after deadly Riyadh airport strike: ‘We’ll keep attacking, don’t fly there’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:55:25 UTC
17:55:25 KST

Yemen's Houthi rebels vowed Sunday to continue enforcing their declared air blockade of neighboring Saudi Arabia, hours after a Houthi missile exploded at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, killing 12 people and wounding 309. 
The rebels renewed their warnings to airlines and passengers as the Saudi capital's main airport remained closed following the unprecedented attack. In an official statement Sunday morning, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned airlines, airport employees and passengers against using Saudi airports or airspace, saying they "serve as theaters of operations for our forces."
In his statement, Saree declared that the Houthis remained determined to enforce the rules they had announced: "Airport for airport, blockade for blockade and escalation for escalation, until our objectives are achieved." He also accused Saudi Arabia of bearing responsibility for the consequences of any failed attempts to intercept missiles launched by the Houthis, urging the public to take the group's warnings seriously. Saree said the Houthis regarded all areas of Saudi Arabia as potential theaters of military operations, except Mecca and Medina, Islam's two holiest cities. His comments followed accusations by Riyadh last month that the Houthis had fired a missile toward Mecca, the destination of the annual Muslim pilgrimage and home to the Kaaba, one of Islam's most sacred sites. The accusation portrayed the rebels as threatening Islam's holy places.
Hours after Saturday's missile attack, flight operations at King Khalid International Airport remained suspended. A source in the Saudi aviation industry told AFP on Sunday morning that the airport was still shut. Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 reported on X that the closure had been extended by another 24 hours, until midnight between Sunday and Monday, Israel time.
According to reports from Saudi Arabia, the Houthi missile exploded in the area housing Terminals 3 and 4, which serve domestic flights. The dead reportedly included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, an American, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Sudanese and a Palestinian. Many of the 309 people wounded were reported to be in serious condition. Reports Sunday morning indicated that hospitals in Riyadh remained filled with casualties from the attack. The strike was the deadliest attack on any Gulf Arab country since the war with Iran began in February.
According to Western sources, information collected following the attack indicates that the missile struck without any advance warning and that no sirens sounded before the impact. The deadly attack came just two days after an earlier Houthi strike on the same airport, in which at least one passenger aircraft, empty at the time, was hit. Three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, were killed in that attack. Several additional attacks targeted airports in Riyadh and the southern Saudi city of Abha earlier last week, killing three more people. The series of attacks marks a new peak in the escalating confrontation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, which has intensified in recent weeks alongside renewed fighting inside Yemen between the rebels and forces loyal to the internationally recognized Yemeni government. Saudi Arabia has supported those government forces with extensive airstrikes on Houthi-controlled territory.
On Saturday, President Donald Trump said the United States could join the fighting and assist Saudi Arabia in conducting strikes against the Yemeni rebels, although he emphasized that no decision had yet been made. Trump subsequently described the Houthi attack on Riyadh as "a terrible thing" and "unacceptable." United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres expressed "deep shock" over the airport attack Sunday morning. Germany also condemned the strike, while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described it as "a dangerous escalation."
The Houthis have intensified their attacks on Saudi cities in recent days, increasingly targeting airports as part of a campaign to disrupt the kingdom's aviation industry and effectively close its skies. The rebels say the campaign is retaliation for Saudi airstrikes against Houthi positions in Yemen. At the beginning of last week, the Houthis warned international airlines not to operate in Saudi airspace, declaring it an operational zone for attacks against the kingdom. They said they would not accept responsibility for the consequences if airlines continued to fly there.
The renewed confrontation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia began in July, ending a four-year lull in Yemen's civil war. That conflict erupted in 2014, with Riyadh subsequently intervening in support of Yemen's internationally recognized government. The latest escalation began after the Houthis attempted to break the air blockade imposed on them by Saudi Arabia, against the backdrop of an intensifying war involving Iran, their regional ally. Last month, the Houthis launched a rapid territorial offensive, capturing strategic coastal areas in southwestern Yemen overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The territorial gains strengthened their position along one of the world's most important maritime shipping routes. The Houthis had already demonstrated their ability to attack shipping in the Red Sea using long-range missiles and drones, but their advances on the coast gave them tighter control over movement through the strategic passage. Bab el-Mandeb links the Red Sea and Suez Canal shipping route between Europe and Asia, carrying approximately 12% of global trade.
Its strategic importance, particularly for Saudi Arabia, has increased dramatically because of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula during the war with Iran. Early last week, Yemeni government forces aligned with Riyadh launched a major ground offensive aimed at driving the Houthis from their newly captured territory and regaining control of Bab el-Mandeb. Saudi Arabia has provided extensive air support for the operation, including heavy bombardment of Houthi-held areas. Reports indicate that pro-Saudi forces have advanced in the area surrounding the strait, although the extent of those gains remains unclear. The Houthis dispute claims by Yemen's internationally recognized government that its forces have already recaptured Bab el-Mandeb, leaving control of the vital waterway contested as the fighting escalates on both sides of the Arabian Peninsula.

Deadly attack on airport in Saudi Arabia's capital kills 12
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:39:17 UTC
17:39:17 KST

Breadcrumb
Deadly attack on airport in Saudi Arabia's capital kills 12 people and injures over 300
Saudi Arabia on Sunday extended the closure of the country's main international airport, according to an online flight tracker, a day after a missile attack on the facility killed 12 people from several countries and left more than 300 injured in a major escalation of the war between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and the kingdom.
A Saudi-led coalition blamed Saturday afternoon's attack on the Houthis. It was the latest of several in the past week at King Khalid International Airport in the capital, Riyadh, and marked the deadliest attack in any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war.
Saudi Arabia is the world's top oil exporter, and the attacks have sent up oil prices and rattled markets.
Following the attack, US President Donald Trump said Saturday he was weighing whether the United States would join Saudi strikes against the rebels.
Airport operations were suspended Saturday. Authorities later extended the closure until at least 9PM. Sunday, according to Flightradar24.
Also on Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said 91 Yemenis were killed and 168 injured by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks. It said 60 percent of those killed were women and children.
Mix of nationalities killed at Saudi airport 
The attack struck an airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorised to speak to the media.
The Saudi statement said the dead included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said several hospitals were treating the injured.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged in a social media post that an American citizen had been killed in the attack, which he condemned.
The Egyptian man was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flybas, according to the Egyptian state-run Al-Qahera New television.
Trump said he would consider joining strikes against rebels.
The attack is expected to increase Saudi pressure on allies, including the United States, to provide military support for the kingdom, which has seemingly tried to avoid all-out war with the Houthis.
Shortly after the attack, Trump said he was evaluating whether the US should join Saudi strikes against the rebels. "We may. We're going to look at it," he said. "We just found out about the recent attack. So we'll make a decision. We move very quickly."
Trump said later Saturday that he planned to speak with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Asked if the US might get involved, Trump responded, "We'll find out."
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis blamed them for the attack, calling it a "fully-fledged war crime" and vowing a firm response. The airport has no military facilities.
There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier on Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital.
The Houthis claimed attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid International Airport that killed three Saudis, including a pilot.
The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis.
For Iran, the fighting puts pressure on a key US ally
Until recently, the Houthis had been largely on the sidelines of the war on Iran. Now the rebels are a way for Tehran to apply pressure on a key US ally.
The Saudis and the Houthis began fighting in 2015 when the kingdom entered Yemen's civil war on behalf of the internationally recognised government.
Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land. That revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas.
Now fighting has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea.
Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.
Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defence support to the region, regional officials told the AP last month, with one noting that the US has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.
The Houthis this week warned global airlines "for the last time" about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theatre for their military operations.
Before the latest attack, Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group, and Pakistan International Airlines suspended flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for varying periods.

Pakistan imposes emergency rule in ​province governed by Imran Khan’s party

Pakistan imposes emergency rule in province governed by Imran Khan’s party
PM’s office says cabinet move follows ‘provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism’.
Authorities in Pakistan have announced a state of emergency in the northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.
The state of emergency was invoked on Sunday under two articles of the constitution dealing with security. It effectively suspends the provincial government run by the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), the party of jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan.
President Asif Ali Zardari said in a social media post he had approved the recommendations made by the cabinet, which had held a meeting under Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif earlier in the day.
A statement issued by Sharif’s office said cabinet members reviewed the situation and took note of the “provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”.
Shortly after the announcement, PTI lawmaker Junaid Akbar said Sohail Afridi, the chief minister of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, was arrested along with the party’s president in the province.
Six-month duration
The provincial governor will take charge with an advisory council, Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar told a news conference in Islamabad, adding that the arrangement will initially be in place for six months.
PTI spokesperson and Khan aide, Zulfikar Bukhari described the government’s move as “more of a coup disguised as emergency” and warned it would cause “further bloodshed, instability and collateral damage”.
The move comes as the PTI has been preparing for a march on the capital, Islamabad, to demand the release of Khan, who has been in jail for more than three years but still commands widespread popularity across the country.
The march was originally scheduled for September 27 but was postponed until October 4 to allow talks between the government and the PTI leadership to take place.
The government, however, said it would not allow the march to enter the capital and has been preparing for weeks to prevent the arrival of PTI demonstrators in Islamabad. It has erected barriers using shipping containers to block main access routes to the capital.
