Excavations resume at ancient Tyana Roman Baths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:30:06 UTC
17:30:06 KST

AA Photo
Excavations have resumed at the Roman Baths in the ancient city of Tyana, located in the town of Kemerhisar in Türkiye’s central province of Niğde’s Bor district, following a 20-year hiatus.
The work, conducted under the Turkish Culture and Tourism Ministry’s Heritage for the Future Project, aims to identify earlier phases of the baths and uncover associated structures, such as a palaestra (an exercise area or courtyard) or a gymnasium (a center for physical and intellectual education).
Archaeologists also hope to uncover evidence of cultural activity dating to well before Roman rule.
Osman Doğanay, head of the Tyana Excavation Team and a professor in the Department of Archaeology at Aksaray University’s Faculty of Arts and Sciences, told state-run Anadolu Agency that excavations at the Roman Baths had resumed after a two-decade hiatus.
Doganay noted that at least two other baths are believed to exist in the ancient city beyond the complex currently being excavated, adding that efforts to locate them would begin.
Tyana was a major metropolitan center in Cappadocia during the Roman period, and the baths under excavation were built by Emperor Caracalla in AD 213, he said.
“Changes were also made to the structure of these baths during the reigns of emperors who succeeded Caracalla. We can confirm this with certainty,” Doğanay said.
Excavations at the baths began in 2002 and continued for four years, uncovering numerous remains and artifacts. Researchers have since established the structure’s layout and confirmed that it was a public bathhouse, he said.
Located on the southern slopes of Tyana Mound, the baths were positioned to receive the greatest amount of heat, Doğanay said.
He added that archaeologists believe the complex received a significant portion of the water carried by aqueducts from the Roman Pool, citing water pipes discovered during excavations between the pool and the baths.
HH Bronze Age layer discovered beneath baths
Doğanay said the primary objective of the current excavation season was to identify earlier phases of the bath complex. Much of the work this year has focused on clearing layers of rubble and debris from the site.
Test excavations extending nearly 2 meters below the surface revealed that the baths had been built over a Bronze Age layer, he said.
“In our upcoming work, we will uncover all the sections of the baths and determine whether structures associated with sporting activities, such as a palaestra and a gymnasium, are present.
“At the same time, we expect to find important evidence of the city’s cultural heritage dating to periods long before the Roman era,” Doğanay said.
He added that measures were being taken during the excavations to protect the structure.
The team also hopes to make the historic Roman Baths a new regional tourist attraction.
“There is no comparable bath complex of this kind in the Cappadocia region. As part of our efforts to promote Tyana as a destination for tourism and contribute to the regional economy, we are working to include the Roman Baths in visitor routes through the ancient city and establish the complex as a destination in its own right,” Doğanay said.

Saudi coalition fumes after Houthi strike kills 12 at Riyadh airport

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:30:00 UTC
17:30:00 KST

The Saudi-led coalition vowed a decisive response Sunday after a strike at Riyadh's international airport killed 12 people, wounded hundreds, marking the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in over a decade.
The coalition blamed the Iran-backed group for the strike on King Khalid International Airport, describing it as a "full-fledged war crime" that a diplomatic source attributed to a missile.
The attack came during an unprecedented wave of Houthi strikes on the kingdom since a truce in the group's long-running war with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government unraveled in July.
The spiraling violence has raised the possibility of a wider escalation, with U.S. President Donald Trump signalling Washington could join military action against the fighters.
One passenger said they witnessed a strike in the airport's domestic terminal.
"I was on gate 403," the witness said. "I saw 401 hit, I saw injured in front of my eyes. Everyone was running."
Four Saudi citizens were among those killed in the attack, as well as two Bangladeshis, one U.S. citizen, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese, the kingdom's civil aviation authority said in a statement.
It said some of the 309 wounded were in serious condition.
Operations at the airport were suspended following the attack and authorities said damage assessments were ongoing.
The attack prompted health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors to deal with the "serious emergency situation," a medical source said.
Two doctors told Agence France-Presse (AFP) that several pilgrims headed to Mecca were among the wounded.
Schools in Riyadh switched to remote learning for the second time in a month.
Parents in the capital received emails Sunday, citing an order from the education ministry, saying "all schools in Riyadh will switch to distance learning for the entire week".
"The cowardly terrorist attack by the Terrorist Houthi Militia ... which resulted in deaths and injuries among civilian passengers and airport staff, constitutes a full-fledged war crime," coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said in a statement on X.
Earlier, the coalition said it had intercepted missiles targeting Saudi Arabia and destroyed launch platforms.
The Houthis claimed a series of attacks targeting the airport Thursday that killed three people and damaged a plane, though they did not immediately take responsibility for any new strikes Saturday.
Saturday's attack was the deadliest in the kingdom since May 2015, when a suicide bombing by the Daesh terrorist group killed 21 worshippers in a Shiite mosque in the eastern Qatif governorate.
The civil war in Yemen flared back to life in July after a four-year, U.N.-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle East war that has rocked the region and roiled energy supplies and markets.
Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen's government militarily since 2015 and is now being drawn deeper into its impoverished neighbor's conflict.
Asked Saturday whether he had changed his mind about joining Saudi strikes on the group, Trump said: "We may."
He said he would be speaking with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, calling what happened in the kingdom "not acceptable."
U.S. media outlets have reported that previous Saudi requests for U.S. military assistance in dealing with the Houthis have been rebuffed.
The U.S., Canadian, German and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia warned their citizens to avoid the airport.
A senior Western diplomat told AFP that several embassies were banning their staff from using the airport "over the next week."
Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the "heinous attack" and reaffirmed Islamabad's commitment to Saudi Arabia's security under their defense pact.
The latest attack came on the eve of Saudi Arabia's high-profile convention and entertainment season, which begins this month.
Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events, including its flagship investment conference drawing foreign leaders and business titans.
In Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing against the Houthis in areas the group captured last month around the Bab el-Mandeb strait, military sources told AFP.
The Yemeni government last week announced a counteroffensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis.
The Houthis confirmed that government forces had attacked in the Bab el-Mandeb area – a key choke point for Red Sea oil and cargo shipping – but claimed to have repelled them.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.

Two Renoir paintings stolen in France recovered: mayor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:29:52 UTC
17:29:52 KST

Two paintings by French master Pierre-Auguste Renoir have been recovered a month after they were stolen from a museum in southern France, the town’s mayor has said.
In September, thieves broke into the museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer and managed to escape with two works by the French impressionist painter, abandoning two others as they fled.
“These two paintings are not simply works of art. They are part of our city’s history,” said Bryan Masson, the mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer.
“Knowing they have been recovered is an immense relief.”
There has not yet been any statement from the police and Masson did not give any details regarding where the works were found or their condition.
The suspects cut through a fence to enter the museum’s tree-lined grounds, smashed a window to get inside, and used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings, Masson said at the time of the robbery in early September.
The theft took place in just a matter of minutes, shortly before 6 a.m. 
A source close to the probe told AFP earlier this week that police had arrested five people as part of the investigation.
According to Masson the museum alarm and police sirens forced the burglars, which he described as “well equipped and well informed” about the museum, to hurry.
They made off with a portrait titled “Madame Colonna Romano” and the depiction of a woman at a well called “Jeune femme au puits,” his office said.
The paintings dropped during their escape include “Madame Pichon” and “Coco lisant,” a portrait of Renoir’s young son Claude reading.
The police said at the time of the robbery that it was clear that they were not first-time offenders, and that they had scoped out the premises before the crime.
The Renoir Museum lies a half-hour drive from the southern city of Nice, in Renoir’s last home before he died aged 78 in 1919. Its collection comprises nine paintings by Renoir, according to the museum.
It also includes several sculptures by him, as well as objects and furniture that belonged to the painter, such as his easel and wheelchair.

What the Iran war has done to the world’s energy supply, in charts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:22:02 UTC
17:22:02 KST

What the Iran war has done to the world’s energy supply, in charts
Fossil fuels produce 81 percent of global energy. We look at the Middle East’s role and what happens when supplies are cut.
A major energy conference is going ahead in Riyadh from Sunday despite a Houthi attack on the city’s King Khalid International Airport that killed 12 people and injured 309, according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation.
Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Energy said on Sunday that the 25th World Petroleum Council Energy Congress has begun in Riyadh. The 17th International Energy Forum (IEF) Ministerial will be held on the sidelines of the conference, called Riyadh Energy Week, which is to run until Thursday.
But Italy, the cohost of the IEF, will join the meeting via videolink. Nigeria, the other cohost, is sending a representative to the event.
The IEF brings together 68 countries that account for more than 90 percent of global oil and gas supplies and demand. Its members include Saudi Arabia, the United States and Russia. The meeting comes as the US-Israel war on Iran has disrupted energy flows and pushed governments to reassess their energy security.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera looks at where the world’s energy comes from, how much is produced in the Middle East and which countries have strategic reserves to fall back on.
Where does the world’s energy come from?
Energy heats our homes, fuels our cars, keeps the lights on and runs the factories that make what we buy. It comes from fossil fuels such as oil, coal and gas as well as nuclear power and renewables.
Despite rapid growth in renewables, fossil fuels still account for nearly 81 percent of global energy consumption. Oil is the largest source at 31.4 percent, followed by coal at 25.9 percent and natural gas at 23.5 percent. Traditional biomass, nuclear power and other sources make up the rest.
Production is concentrated in a handful of regions, so disruptions in any of them ripple through global markets.
The Middle East is the largest oil-producing region, and North America is the largest natural gas producer. Russia and Central Asia are also major producers of both.
How Middle East energy reaches the world
The Middle East’s importance to energy markets is also about geography. Three narrow waterways connect its producers with consumers around the world.
Before the Iran war, about 27 percent of global seaborne oil trade and almost 20 percent of liquefied natural gas trade transited through the Strait of Hormuz on the eastern side of the Arabian Peninsula.
On the peninsula’s western side, the Bab al-Mandeb strait links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, and the Suez Canal connects the Red Sea with the Mediterranean. As the Iran war has spilled over into other areas of the Middle East and Yemen’s civil war has ramped up, traffic has been reduced through both the strait and canal, forcing some energy shipments on longer routes around Africa.
“That’s probably the first time we’ve really seen a major constriction of a chokepoint,” said Richard Matthews, director of consultancy and research at Gibson Shipbrokers, a London-based shipbroking and maritime advisory service.
He told Al Jazeera that what makes the Strait of Hormuz different from other chokepoints is “there is no alternative maritime route. There are some pipelines, but there’s no alternative, which is why it’s been so significant in terms of cargo volume.”
Gulf ports are where much of the region’s energy begins its journey to the rest of the world.
Which countries rely most on Middle East oil?
Further down the supply chain, people and businesses are feeling the disruption through the rising cost of essentials.
Countries that rely on oil, gas and fertiliser from the Gulf face higher prices, longer waits for shipments and the need to find other suppliers. Even where deals have kept goods moving, the extra costs are being passed down the chain.
Eritrea and Madagascar are the most dependent on Middle Eastern oil, each sourcing about 90 percent of their supply from the region. They are followed by Pakistan (78 percent), Japan (77 percent) and Kenya (77 percent).
Which countries rely most on Middle East gas?
Gas has been even harder to replace than oil because most of it travels as liquefied natural gas from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates through the Strait of Hormuz.
Countries that depend on these shipments are paying more for fuel and electricity and competing for a smaller pool of cargoes. Poorer importers with little storage have struggled the most to find alternatives.
The countries that rely most heavily on Middle Eastern gas are mostly in Asia. South Korea sources 31 percent of the gas it uses from the region, followed by India (29 percent), Pakistan (27 percent) and Taiwan (26 percent).
Who has the largest emergency oil reserves?
Countries keep emergency oil stocks for when supplies are cut off or reduced, and these have been the world’s main cushion during the war. That cushion is now wearing thin.
Western countries have little left to release, energy industry leaders warned, and the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at its lowest level since 1982.
“Estimates suggest less than 6 billion barrels of commercial inventories remain today with the vast majority not practically available,” Amin Nasser, head of Saudi Aramco, told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London on Monday.
The International Energy Agency, which coordinates emergency stocks for its members, released a record 400 million barrels of oil in March. It is now preparing to release another 100 million barrels of crude and diesel to ease soaring diesel prices although some of this may be oil from the March release that has yet to reach the market.
A storm in the Gulf of Mexico and attacks in Saudi Arabia are now threatening supplies again, keeping oil prices above $100 a barrel.
Before this year’s releases, China held by far the largest reserves, an estimated 1.4 billion barrels, more than the rest of the list combined. The US was second with 413 million barrels, followed by Japan with 263 million.

This file photo shows a short film screening from the previous years of the festival. (AA Photo)
Cinematic storytelling takes center stage in the western province of Afyonkarahisar on Oct. 12 with the grand opening of the fifth Büyük Taarruz Short Film Festival.
Organized by the Anatolian Culture and Arts Council Association under the auspices of the Culture and Tourism Ministry and hosted by the Afyonkarahisar Governor’s Office, the festival will run through Oct.16.

The festival’s award ceremony will take place at the same venue on Oct. 16.

Screenings are scheduled for Sandıklı on Oct. 12, Dinar on Oct. 13, Dazkırı on Oct. 14, Bolvadin on Oct. 15 and in front of the Gedik Ahmet Pasha Provincial Public Library in the city center on Oct. 16.

The competition will feature fiction, animation and experimental films from across Türkiye, covering a range of themes. Talks and panels, as well as workshops on screenwriting, directing, acting and cinematography, will give industry professionals the opportunity to share their experience.

Istanbul generates more than $800 million from congress tourism since 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:06:59 UTC
17:06:59 KST

Congress tourism has generated more than $800 million in foreign currency revenue for Istanbul since 2022, according to Şekib Avdagiç, president of the Istanbul Chamber of Commerce (ITO) and the Istanbul Convention and Visitors Bureau (ICVB).
A total of 67 congresses were held in Istanbul during the first eight months of this year, attracting around 30,000 participants and generating approximately $120 million in revenue from accommodation, transportation, sightseeing, food and beverage services, he noted. He said the number of congress visitors is expected to increase further by the end of the year as activity typically intensifies in the autumn months.
According to Avdagiç, Istanbul has hosted nearly 500 congresses since 2022 with the support of the ICVB.
Around 200,000 congress tourists visited the city during that period, spending up to $4,000 per person and generating more than $800 million in foreign currency income for the local economy.
He noted that the benefits of congress tourism extend beyond hotels, supporting a wide range of businesses including restaurants, retailers, tourist guides and transportation companies. The figure of more than $800 million reflects only direct spending, while the overall economic impact is significantly larger as visitors often extend their stays, return with family members and recommend the city to others, according to Avdagiç.
Avdagiç noted that Istanbul’s infrastructure supports continued growth in the sector, with seven congress centers and three exhibition centers capable of hosting events ranging from meetings of 100 participants to gatherings with more than 30,000 attendees.
He added that the ICVB is continuing its efforts to attract future international congresses to Istanbul across fields including health sciences, engineering, energy and transportation. 
The number of international congresses held in Istanbul increased to 95 in 2025 from 58 in 2022, while the city ranked 18th globally last year, its strongest performance in a decade, Avdagiç said. The long-term goal is to place Istanbul among the world’s top 10 congress destinations, he added.

Türkiye’s fresh vegetable exports top $822 million in January-September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:05:32 UTC
17:05:32 KST

Türkiye generated $822.7 million in revenue from fresh vegetable exports in the January-September period, exporting 651,087 tons of produce, according to data from the Turkish Exporters Assembly (TİM).
Tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers, zucchini and other vegetables grown in Türkiye found buyers in international markets during the first nine months of the year.
Fresh vegetable export revenue increased 10 percent from the same period of last year.
Tomatoes ranked first among fresh vegetable exports, generating $304.2 million in revenue, while peppers followed with $275.5 million.
Revenue from tomato exports rose 4 percent year-on-year, while earnings from pepper exports increased 29 percent. Together, the two products accounted for nearly 70 percent of Türkiye’s total fresh vegetable export revenue.
During the period, cucumber and gherkin exports brought in $61.4 million, zucchini exports generated $57.4 million, while carrot and radish exports totaled $39.6 million.
Romania was the largest market for Turkish fresh vegetables, importing products worth $147 million. Germany followed with $132.7 million, while Russia ranked third with imports totaling $76.1 million.
Exports to Bulgaria reached $55.5 million during the January-September period, while shipments to Ukraine totaled $50 million and exports to the Netherlands amounted to $47.8 million.

Missing Israeli tourist's body found on Mount Olympus after weeks of searching by Israeli team
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:01:39 UTC
17:01:39 KST

After nearly three weeks of searching on Mount Olympus in Greece, a team from the rescue organization Haverim Mechaltzim located the body of missing Israeli Ami Yogev on Friday, following a search effort initiated after Sivan Zamir, from the Greece and the Islands website, called for help.
Yogev had been missing since September 20. The four Israeli rescuers searched mountain streambeds, navigating cliffs, waterfalls, and dense vegetation in terrain that required climbing equipment and ropes.
The breakthrough came when one of the rescuers spotted an Israeli passport during the search. Yogev's personal belongings were discovered nearby, and his body was subsequently found concealed by vegetation.
Greek rescue teams had previously searched the same area but had been unable to locate the body because of the difficult terrain.
Following the discovery, the Israeli rescuers joined Greek rescue personnel in a complex recovery operation that lasted several hours.
Behind the rescue team was an extensive support network operated by Haverim Mechaltzim, part of the Gvanim nonprofit organization. The network included command centers in Israel and Greece, technology experts, assistance with analyzing cellular communications data, coordination with local authorities, and logistical support for the team in the field.
According to the organization, 12 search and support groups were involved in the efforts to locate Yogev and provide assistance.
The operation was conducted through four main groups: the family, volunteers, the rescue delegation, and the team coordinating the search.
At the heart of the operation were approximately 35 people actively involved in the effort, alongside external teams and additional support personnel.
The organization's core personnel contributed an estimated 740 person-hours to the operation. Each of the four rescuers who traveled to Mount Olympus spent approximately 50 hours searching before Yogev's body was located.
Head of rescue group expresses shared grief with Yogev family
"Unfortunately, the mission ended with devastating and painful news for the Yogev family, and we share in their grief. Our four rescuers acted with extraordinary determination and professionalism under extremely difficult terrain conditions, alongside the Greek rescue teams, who demonstrated impressive cooperation,” Yiftach Shavit, head of rescue operations at Haverim Mechaltzim, said.
"Behind every rescuer in the field stands an entire network of people who step forward, each contributing their own expertise, toward a single goal. That is the strength of Haverim Mechaltzim: the ability to bring together people and professional capabilities from around the world to help Israelis at the moments when they need assistance most."
The organization emphasized its close cooperation with Greek rescue teams and their contribution to the operation. It also thanked all the volunteers and other parties who assisted in the search and recovery efforts.

US DOJ launches investigation into news networks for possible antitrust violations in TV pool
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
08:01:13 UTC
17:01:13 KST

The US Justice Department has launched an investigation into five of the country's largest television news networks for possible antitrust violations, examining how they operate a shared television pool covering the White House.
The investigation concerns the television pool, a longstanding arrangement under which ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News, and NBC share responsibility for filming presidential events and distributing footage to other news organizations. The arrangement allows a single television crew to cover events where access is restricted, such as meetings in the Oval Office or presidential trips.
The issue arose after US President Donald Trump barred CNN from entering White House grounds last month. After the network's exclusion, the then-chairman of the television pool announced that because CNN could not fulfill its scheduled coverage duties, no replacement crew would be assigned.
As a result, shared television coverage of Trump's events was suspended for several days, until a federal judge issued a temporary order blocking the exclusion of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico.
The legal proceedings are ongoing, with the Justice Department defending the Trump administration's decision.
Justice Department investigating television network pool
The department has now launched a separate investigation into the networks' conduct within the television pool. According to two sources familiar with the matter, lawyers representing the networks received requests to provide documents concerning the establishment of the arrangement and how it has operated recently.
A Justice Department spokesperson confirmed the investigation, saying that "members of the television pool boycotted coverage of White House events" and that "group boycotts among commercial competitors may violate the Sherman Act."
The spokesperson said the department's Antitrust Division was examining whether the news organizations had violated the law.
The five networks, which have made up the television pool for decades, have not issued any significant public response.
The arrangement itself is considered essential to White House coverage, partly because it eliminates the need to station multiple television crews at events where space is limited. The networks take turns filming events and share live broadcasts and recorded footage with other news organizations.
Networks release joint statement criticizing CNN White House ban
After CNN's exclusion, the five networks issued a rare joint statement saying "the public has a vital interest in receiving accurate and independent information about the government" and that "no administration should restrict a news organization because it is unhappy with its coverage."
Press freedom organizations criticized the investigation, arguing that news organizations' efforts to defend their First Amendment rights have nothing to do with antitrust law.
The investigation could also become part of the ongoing legal proceedings CNN, MS NOW, and Politico brought against the administration. In that case, the news organizations would argue that the White House excluded them in retaliation for the nature of their coverage.

‘Afife’ ballet returns to the stage after 28 years

17:00:00 KST

Twenty-eight years after its premiere, a modern ballet depicting the turbulent life of Turkish theater pioneer Afife Jale has returned to the stage at Istanbul’s Atatürk Cultural Center (AKM) Türk Telekom Opera Hall.
The production was staged by the Istanbul State Opera and Ballet (IDOB) and brings to the stage the life of Jale, who became the first Muslim Turkish woman to perform on stage despite the restrictions of the period.
First staged by the Ankara State Opera and Ballet at the same venue in 1998, the work has been revived in a new production by IDOB.
With music by Turgay Erdener and a libretto and choreography by Beyhan Murphy, the ballet uses a dramatic narrative to recount Jale’s final days at Bakırköy Mental Hospital before her death. Under the supervision of caregivers, she recalls four distinct periods of her past before dying in the arms of her first love, Ziya.
Four dancers, each represented by a different color, portray separate stages of the artist’s life. İlke Kodal plays Afife, while Berin Günay performs as “Golden Afife,” Gizem Atik Tuncay as “Red Afife,” Deniz Kılınç Tunçeli as “Purple Afife” and Berfu Elmas as “Silver Afife.”
Jale’s inner circle comes to life through Berkay Günay as her cousin and first love, Ziya; Batur Büklü as her husband, Selahattin Pınar; Zuhal Karaca as actress Elisa Binemeciyen; and Emre Karaca, Ahmet Şahin, and Taner Güngör as the caregiver figures known as the “Three Shadows.”
Under the baton of conductor İbrahim Yazıcı, the Istanbul State Opera and Ballet Orchestra brings the performance to life, complemented by Efter Tunç’s set design, Bahar Korçan’s costumes, Cem Yılmazer’s lighting and video design by Aisha Hajiyeva.
The ballet will continue its run at the AKM Türk Telekom Opera Hall on Oct. 14, 15, 17 and 29 as part of the season program.

Economic issues will dominate the Turkish Parliament’s agenda throughout October, with lawmakers set to begin deliberations this week on a bill concerning repayments to investors in liquidated funds and preparations for the 2027 central government budget.
A nine-article legislative proposal submitted by the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) on repayments to investors affected by funds under liquidation will be taken up by Parliament’s Planning and Budget Commission on Oct. 14.
Deputy finance minister, officials from the Capital Markets Board (SPK) and the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency (BDDK), as well as representatives from Borsa Istanbul, the Central Securities Depository and Takasbank, are scheduled to attend the commission meeting.
After the proposal’s sponsors provide an overview of the legislation, lawmakers from both the government and opposition parties will be given the floor.
Opposition members are expected to criticize the decision not to establish a parliamentary inquiry commission on the fund crisis, while ruling party lawmakers are expected to seek further details on measures taken to address the crisis and support affected investors. Bureaucrats will then respond to lawmakers’ questions.
Parliamentary sources expect discussions on the bill to last two days, with the proposal likely to be submitted to the General Assembly the following week.
The bill sets out the principles under which claims owed to approximately 455,000 investors will be repaid and establishes the rules governing the order of priority for payments.
If the proposal is enacted as planned, the interim payment of up to 1 million Turkish Liras to investors will be completed within this month.
Under the proposal, the principal amounts invested in the funds will be adjusted for inflation up to the date of liquidation. The inflation adjustment will be calculated using the average of the Consumer Price Index (CPI) and the Domestic Producer Price Index.
The resignation or departure of fund founders and managers from their positions will not relieve them of liability for transactions carried out during their tenure.
The 2027 central government budget will also be a major focus in October. The budget bill, signed by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, is scheduled to be submitted to Parliament on Oct. 16.
Following a week-long review period, budget deliberations are expected to begin in the Planning and Budget Commission with a presentation by Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz, followed by debates on the overall framework of the budget proposal and reports prepared by the Court of Accounts.
This week is also set to be busy for Türkiye in terms of economic data releases.
The economic calendar will be highlighted by the release of August balance of payments figures and September budget data. Retail sales, along with output indicators for the services and construction sectors, will offer fresh insights into economic activity.

====================================================================================================

US races Russia and China to build a nuclear reactor on the moon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
07:45:46 UTC
16:45:46 KST

In 2019, Russia tested a nuclear-powered cruise missile. The test failed, and the missile plunged to the bottom of the White Sea in northern Russia. Shortly afterward, a large explosion occurred near the crash site, causing radiation levels in the area to spike. U.S. intelligence officials assessed that the explosion took place during a Russian operation to recover the missile from the seabed. At least five nuclear scientists and employees of Russia's state-owned nuclear energy company, Rosatom, were killed. Russia quickly denied that the missile was nuclear-powered, but Rosatom subsequently all but acknowledged what had happened.
Now imagine a rocket carrying an actual nuclear reactor to the moon crashing into the ocean. It sounds like particularly dangerous science fiction, but until just a few years ago, the possibility of artificial intelligence taking over the world also seemed like nothing more than science fiction. With the world's major powers locked in a frantic race to install a nuclear reactor in space, such a scenario may be just around the corner.
A dangerous undertaking
About two months ago, NASA asked private contractors to prepare to build a nuclear reactor capable of surviving a journey through space and operating without maintenance near the moon's south pole. The target launch date: December 2030. The goal: to beat Russia, which aims to have a reactor operating on the moon by 2036 as part of a not-so-secret partnership with China. In 1961, President John F. Kennedy challenged America's leading scientists to land a man on the moon before the end of the decade. Now the goal is to have a functioning nuclear reactor on the moon within four years.
Even before sending nuclear reactors to the moon, the United States plans to put humans back on its surface as part of the Artemis program. The third test flight is scheduled for summer 2027, while the crewed Artemis 4 mission is planned for early 2028.
The somewhat dystopian race to install a reactor on the moon is probably inevitable, and it has implications for the entire future of space exploration. For example, a lunar day lasts about 14 Earth days, followed by 14 consecutive Earth days of complete darkness. During that time, solar panels cannot generate electricity, and temperatures plunge to minus 130 degrees. A nuclear reactor provides continuous electricity and heat around the clock, regardless of sunlight. Any ambition to reach Mars, let alone establish habitable conditions there, also requires nuclear energy.
Establishing a base on the moon is critical to the search for resources and the launch of missions into the depths of the solar system. All of this makes control over access to lunar resources essential, and the major powers believe a nuclear reactor is the foundation for achieving these ambitions. But it is a dangerous undertaking.
As in the case of the Russian missile in 2019, debris from a reactor falling back to Earth could scatter radioactive materials, as happened in Canada in the 1970s. An explosion or reactor core meltdown on the lunar surface could also render entire areas of the moon off-limits. All three countries promise that their reactors will remain inactive until they reach the moon, but these days it is difficult to take their leaders at their word, especially when the race is also, of course, a display of nationalist power.
Leading scientists warn that governments are moving too quickly at a time when space exploration has experienced a string of failures over the past six years. Chinese, American and Russian rockets have exploded, and space debris regularly falls back to Earth.
"There will always be a space race going on, and if you enter nuclear power into that mix, then it could take a potentially more dangerous turn,” said Edwin Lyman, the director of nuclear power safety at the Union of Concerned Scientists.
A deadline pushed back
When it comes to nuclear power in space, Russia has no rivals. It has launched more than 30 reactors into Earth orbit, primarily aboard Cold War-era satellites in the 1970s and 1980s, and holds the largest stockpile of what is considered the safest nuclear fuel for space missions.
The last space reactor NASA tested, in 2018, used highly enriched uranium, which is lighter and cheaper to launch than other fuels. But its use is dangerous because the material can be turned into a nuclear weapon. That leaves the option of using low-enriched uranium fuel, except that the Americans do not have enough of it and cannot import it from Russia because of a ban imposed in 2024 in response to the war in Ukraine.
To date, the United States has invested more than $20 billion in space nuclear programs. Last month, the Pentagon selected a company called Antares to develop and demonstrate a space microreactor, while NASA is accelerating its timetable out of concern that a Russian-Chinese reactor could effectively establish an exclusion zone on the moon.
Such a move could, in practice, prevent American astronauts and rovers from accessing large areas of the lunar surface. That would itself violate the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, but international agreements are being violated on a daily basis these days.
Despite the sense of urgency, all the major powers have repeatedly pushed back their target dates, and few experts believe they will meet their deadlines. None of them even has a proven lunar lander capable of delivering heavy, potentially radioactive materials to the moon's unforgiving surface.
There is, of course, the option of international cooperation, as has happened time and again in space exploration. But the current global climate leaves little room for optimism.
"Governments have always achieved more by working together than by competing," Katy Huff, head of the Department of Nuclear Engineering at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, told The New York Times. "Collaborative, team-based science in space has always managed to rise above our fraught international politics."

Meteoric Surge: Food prices rose by nearly 20% under Netanyahu’s current government term - new study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
07:36:52 UTC
16:36:52 KST

Meteoric Surge: Food prices rose by nearly 20% under Netanyahu’s current government term - new study
A new study from Tel Aviv University found that in the past four years, a basket of 80 products has increased in price by about 19.6% in neighborhood stores and by 19% online
Almost a fifth more for the same shopping basket: Food prices in Israel have risen sharply over the past four years, according to a new study from the Faculty of Management at Tel Aviv University. The study tracked the prices of a basket of 80 popular products between September 2022 and August 2026, and compared them to the four years prior, from September 2018 to August 2022.
According to the findings, the price of the basket increased by 19.6% in neighborhood stores, by 19% in online channels, and by 14.5% in discount branches. In the previous period, however, the price increase amounted to 4.3% in neighborhood stores, 4.1% online, and 2.8% in discount chains.
According to the study, the rate of price increase over the past four years is nearly five times higher than in the preceding period.
Suggested articles
The price increase is also noticeable in specific products: a 100-gram Elite "Para" chocolate bar has become about 78% more expensive in neighborhood stores, a package of 800-gram Maadanot cheese borekas has risen by about 31%, and a kilogram of Sugat classic jasmine rice has increased by 17.7% in discount chains.
Significant gaps were also found in the comparison between supermarket chains across the two periods. At Shufersal Deal, prices rose by about 22.7% over the past four years, compared to about 0.6% in the previous four years. At Victory, there was an increase of about 16%, compared to 1.2% in the previous period, and at Rami Levy, prices rose by 10.3%, compared to 6.1%.
At my Shufersal, prices have increased by 19.6% in the recent period, compared to 2.3% in the previous period. At Freshmarket, there was an increase of 19.6%, compared to about 6.3% in the four preceding years.
A similar trend emerges from online purchase data. At Rami Levy Online, prices rose by 14.1%, at Shufersal Online by 24%, and at Victory Online by 18.6%. In the earlier period, price increases at these chains amounted to 9.3%, 0.1%, and 3.8%, respectively.
The research also illustrates the gap in shekels: at Shufersal Deal, the basket became more expensive by 231 shekels in the past four years, compared to just six shekels in the previous period. At Shufersal Sheli, the price increase totaled 222 shekels, compared to 26 shekels previously. At Victory, the basket rose by 160 shekels, compared to 12 shekels in the earlier period.
Prof. Itai Ater from the Faculty of Management at Tel Aviv University notes that among the factors that may explain the price increases are the rise in VAT rates and the increase in property tax, water, fuel, and electricity tariffs, alongside the rise in the prices of regulated products. On the other hand, the strengthening of the shekel and the decrease in the global food price index, which peaked in 2022, reduced import prices and could have moderated the price hikes.
According to Ater, the changes in production and import costs alone cannot explain an increase of about 20% over four years. He also points to the lack of ongoing governmental action regarding the issue of the cost of living, and the fact that public and media attention is directed towards other topics.
In such a situation, After says, companies in the food market may take advantage of the opportunity to raise prices.
The professor also emphasizes that the gap between the moderate price increases in the early period and the recent surges in prices indicates that the high cost of living is not an inevitable fate. According to him, an effective fight against the phenomenon requires government mobilization, the promotion of structural reforms, addressing centers of power, improving regulation and removing barriers, alongside broad public and media discourse.

Likud assembles special team to lure defectors from Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party after election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
07:27:55 UTC
16:27:55 KST

Just two and a half weeks before Israel's October 27 election, Likud has established a special team tasked with persuading several lawmakers from former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar! party to defect. Yedioth Ahronoth and ynet have learned that the team consists of Likud lawmakers and several strategic advisers whose sole purpose is to facilitate the movement of lawmakers between political blocs immediately after the election.
The tactic has been used in the previous two election cycles, with considerable success. Likud figures managed to draw Amichai Chikli, then a newly elected lawmaker, away from former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett's party, followed later in the government's term by Idit Silman, who served as coalition chairwoman. This time, however, Likud has expanded the number of people involved and developed more systematic methods for pressuring potential defectors.
In the past, candidates reported being subjected to various forms of pressure, including demonstrators appearing at synagogues attended by their family members, maintaining a regular presence in their neighborhoods and gathering near their children's schools. Those efforts were carefully orchestrated, and Likud now appears to have refined its methods, determined to take the strategy a step further.
The newly established Likud team is conducting extensive background checks on every candidate on Eisenkot's list, with particular attention to newcomers who have right-wing political backgrounds or close ties to right-leaning circles. The examination includes past public statements, personal and broader social networks, whether candidates consult rabbis and which other influential figures might sway their decisions. Likud intends to use that information to launch an intensive pressure campaign immediately after the election, focusing primarily on diplomatic and security policy differences and offering a package of promises to those willing to switch political blocs.
That was also the approach used with Chikli and Silman, both of whom received guaranteed places on Likud's candidate list for subsequent elections and ministerial positions after switching sides. Chikli managed to retain his place in Likud and even strengthen his standing within the party. Silman, however, who served as environmental protection minister, failed to survive the party primaries, ending her latest political chapter bitterly amid claims that Netanyahu's inner circle had "used her and thrown her away."
Eisenkot's Yashar! party appears well aware that similar efforts could begin immediately after the election and has reportedly placed particular emphasis on screening candidates. In recent weeks, reports suggested that candidates were required to sign commitments pledging not to defect from the party, although senior party officials denied those claims. Even if such loyalty declarations had been signed, however, they would carry no legal force and would have no significance beyond a symbolic commitment.
Bennett learns from past defections
Naftali Bennett was among the politicians most severely affected by the tactic. Beyond Chikli and Silman, former lawmaker Nir Orbach, a member of the religious Zionist community, informed Bennett that he no longer intended to vote with the coalition. It later emerged that Orbach had also faced intense pressure from Likud and other right-wing figures, until he eventually broke ranks. During one Knesset vote, he left the chamber and was quoted as saying of the coalition government formed with Mansour Abbas and his Arab Ra'am party: "The experiment has failed."
As a result, Bennett has adopted a far more rigorous screening process for candidates running on his Together party list in the current election, including extensive background checks into each candidate's political history and previous positions. During preparatory meetings, prospective candidates were asked dozens of questions about various hypothetical political scenarios designed to test their loyalty to Bennett.
Yashar's No. 7: ‘There are no Silmans here, and there never will be’
Shaul Meridor, a senior figure in Eisenkot's party, said last week in an interview with "120 and One," ynet's political podcast: "There are no Silmans here, and there never will be. Everyone on our list has undergone thorough scrutiny of their positions and fully agrees with Eisenkot's approach."
Likud officials, however, believe the political balance after the election could be extremely close and argue that Eisenkot lacks experience in selecting and retaining political candidates, leaving some members of his list potentially vulnerable to defection. "There are people there who have problems with Eisenkot's and Yair Golan's positions on security and diplomatic issues, and with the idea of forming a government with Arab parties," a Likud source said. "Some of them are talking about it with people close to them."

16:24:54 KST

Speaking Sunday at the international conference "Ecocide: the Silent War Crime" in Tehran, Araghchi said the environment is humanity's shared heritage, not an arena for rivalries or a victim of short-term economic and military calculations.
 
He said the term ecocide is structurally similar to genocide and represents a concept beyond a war crime against the environment, suggesting "nature-killing" as a Persian equivalent.
 
Araghchi said war damages water, soil, air, forests, farmland, energy resources, natural habitats and biodiversity, with effects that can last for years or decades after fighting ends.
 
He cited environmental devastation in Gaza, where UNEP has reported unprecedented damage including destruction of olive groves and contamination of water and soil; in Lebanon, where fires destroyed forests and tens of thousands of olive trees; and in Iran, where UNEP confirmed in March 2026 that attacks on oil facilities released hazardous compounds, recalling the "black rain" over Tehran.
 
Araghchi called for three axes of international cooperation: strengthening legal frameworks and clear criteria for identifying and addressing severe environmental destruction; creating scientific and impartial mechanisms to document damage from armed conflict; and developing regional and international cooperation to prevent destruction, rebuild ecosystems and support affected countries.
 
He said Iran supports recognising ecocide as an independent international crime, is ready to use its scientific, legal and diplomatic capacities, and called COP31 a suitable opportunity to draw global attention to the environmental effects of military attacks.
 
"We must not allow aggressors to escape responsibility for their criminal actions," he said.
MNA

====================================================================================================

No whining and women: This Witches? Festival returns with a salute to female musicianship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
07:05:51 UTC
16:05:51 KST

Orit Messer-Jacobi is not one to moan and groan. Her sunny outlook was patently clear from the first cheery “hello” of our telephone chat ahead of this year’s Witches? Festival, which celebrates female movers and shakers in the classical music world. One can, of course, home in on egregious discrimination, inequality of pay and professional opportunities, and, more tragically, the continuing acts of violence perpetrated against women, but the cellist-conductor was more focused on the positive aspect of the female side of the musical domain across the ages.
The official blurb describes the fifth edition of the festival, which takes place at the YMCA and Hansen House October 16-17, thus: “A musical journey following women who made a difference in the world of music and culture, from medieval times, through ancient eras to 20th-century jazz.” The two-day agenda duly provides plenty of collateral for that gender-oriented claim.
The event was initiated by Jerusalem Baroque Orchestra (JBO) founder-conductor-artistic director David Shemer, with the JBO performing predominantly baroque scores. But the programming purview stretches into more contemporary and other cultural and philosophical spheres too.
Broader road to music appreciation
Messer-Jacobi features in the curtain-raiser at Hansen House, on cello. The October 16 (11 a.m.) date goes by the evocative and eclectically-leaning name of “Daphnis and the Winds of Love: A Balkan Myth.” An instrumental trio, which also includes recorder player Doret Florentin and guitarist Gideon Bretler, complemented by the Hakdoshot vocal threesome, follows a broad stylistic arc from the realms of Greek mythology through to contemporary material, dipping into French Baroque music and folk melodies en route.
The JBO principal cellist is heavily invested both in the ensemble, of which she is a longtime member, and in the Witches? format. “I am very happy with the festival because it allows us to take an immersive approach to a particular subject,” she notes. “When you have a festival, which lasts just a few days, and you invite other ensembles to take part, that allows us to research and deeply explore a specific topic. We can address it from all sorts of perspectives, and that makes it very interesting and very daring.”
The latter attribute is not a feature one regularly associates with classical music in its wider sense. Artistic and musical directors tend to shy away from more challenging works from contemporary times which incorporate, say, atonal or electronic music. It is very much, particularly in these financially strapped cultural times, about putting bums on seats. That generally leads to programming that treads tried and tested areas, with crowd-pleasers by the likes of Beethoven, Tchaikovsky, Brahms, and Bach.
Messer-Jacobi says that Witches? has always looked to flex strictly defined genre and stylistic delineations. “The repertoire we perform is not run-of-the-mill stuff. We don’t do the bestsellers – the Magnificat [by Bach] and such like. And we perform in beautiful locations and with very good ensembles.” Seems like a recipe for success, both on the stage and at the box office.
Celebrating female players in classical music domain
The core themes of the whole venture revolve around female composers and performers of classical music across the ages, with each annual agenda based on a more focused feature of that field of endeavor. “We had various themes,” the cellist recalls, “like fate, warrior women, and healing women. Then we had the [post-Oct. 7] war and, you know, things always resonate.”
That brought us neatly around to this year’s thematic linchpin, Echo. Messer-Jacobi says the programming mindset, for this edition, followed a far more positive planning ethos. “In past years, the festival was generally about women whose voices were suppressed or were pushed aside. Specifically, this year it is about women whose presence and deeds changed the face of music.”
That sounds like a refreshing proactive line to follow. “Each concert takes a different approach – either about women with initiative, women who wrote and performed their music, or patrons or muses, or heroines. It is very fascinating and, I think, very liberating, relieving.”
The accent is very much on upbeat vibes. “This year we are not looking at women who were not heard, so then we’ll have the festival,” the cellist proclaims in a faux weepy voice. Determined philosophy notwithstanding, this is not an under-the-carpet sweeping exercise. “Things are tough enough for women now, [in the classical music arena], and it was much tougher back in the 17th century,” Messer-Jacobi continues.
Barbara Strozzi is a striking case in point. Not only did she have the “temerity” as a woman to write music, and that despite being the illegitimate child of a servant, her works were duly lauded in 17th-century Venice, with Strozzi performing her own charts as vocalist. Her stellar contributions are noted in the “Virtuosissima cantatrice” concert at the YMCA on October 17 (1:30 p.m.). The Italian show title translates as “the most virtuoso female singer,” which, by all reports, is a fair description of Strozzi’s musical performance abilities. The vocalist spot for the Witches? recital will be taken by soprano Daniela Skorka, supported by violinist Kati Debretzeni, with Shemer on harpsichord.
Strozzi was, it seems, a fearless character who let no social mores or political tenets of the day stand between her and getting the fruits of her artistic labors out there to the public. “She is one of the few female composers who had their scores printed. She operated out of Venice, from a very male-dominated society, and she was very highly regarded,” Messer-Jacobi advises. “She also ran a very important music salon. But she was exceptional.”
That fits this year’s line of programming thought. “We have presented numerous works by female composers and musicians who were marginalized, but this year that’s not the case. This year the festival is very powerful.”
It is, the cellist simply states, about the music. “There is no intent on righting the situation [vis-à-vis sexual discrimination]. We want to give women their place without the [politically-oriented] crutches. If you look at the concerts, you see that each ensemble, with its program, offers something very interesting. And the gender is of no importance. It is just by chance that the composer is a woman [with regard to the quality of the work in question].”
Messer-Jacobi proceeds to proffer the evidence for that level playing field strategy in the two-day agenda. “There is the “A Woman’s Song” recital that addresses love, motherhood, and war and peace. That is a triangle that can convey a universal historic passage.” The program comprises texts presented by female characters, at times a mythological or religious figure, or a mother, and other times a basic, clear human call. The voices resonating from the texts are woven into a single storyline that is personal yet universal, historical yet, as we painfully know, more relevant than ever today.
As per Messer-Jacobi's claim of eclecticism, the titillatingly titled “High Heels” show, at the YMCA on October 16 (10 p.m.), should have the audience members appreciating the onstage action in a more animated manner. “That is something cute with a very different color,” she chuckles. “They will play swing music from the 1940s and 1950s.” That shuffles the sonic festival pack. “It will bring a different color, and celebrate the music. You don’t always have to play intricate heavy material. You can just enjoy life,” she laughs.
It is also highly likely that the folks who make it over to the YMCA for the outdoor gig, in the YMCA Arcade, should by then be in a suitable frame of mind to make the most of the energized entertainment. “It is scheduled for the end of the first day, when anything goes.” The lineup for the fun run out includes three female vocalists and a piano-led jazz trio.
The women behind the celebrities
The second day opens with a reminder – or eye-opener – of how much poorer the classical music world would be without female contributors, in all walks of musical life.
The 11 a.m. “Vienna-Weimar-Siberia: A Journey with Musical Women” slot, at the YMCA, asks the simple and, no doubt, for some of more conservative, narrow minds, provocative question: What would classical music look like without the women who worked behind the scenes as students, patrons, musicians, and salon hosts? The Israeli Romantic Ensemble foursome, led by Gili Rinot on clarinet, will perform works by the likes of Mozart, Mendelssohn, and Bach. One of the former’s star students was a certain Franziska von Jacquin, one of quite a few female disciples of the feted Austrian composer. It seems he was particularly taken with von Jacquin, both for her talent and her diligence, and composed his Piano Sonata No. 14 and Fantasia in C minor with her in mind.
His early student register included one Thérèse von Trattner who, in fact, kept the then young composer, recently arrived in Vienna from his native Salzburg, financially afloat. She also provided him with accommodation, spread the word about him, and organized subscription concerts of his music in the imperial capital in 1784. The program for those groundbreaking events included Mozart’s Piano Concertos Nos. 14, 15, and 16, and provided him with a firm foothold in the Viennese artistic and hierarchical social domains.
Other women who get a well-deserved salute at the morning concert include German Jewish philanthropist Sara Levy, who was also the great-aunt of Mendelssohn and duly supported his writing efforts, and pioneering female French cellist Lise Cristiani, whose musicianship prompted Mendelssohn to dedicate a slot in his Songs Without Words series to her. “This is a fascinating story of women who changed the history of music,” the festival textual backdrop declares.
There is a nod to biblical climes with “The Golden Apple” concert, with the Nari Ensemble quartet of soprano Liron Givoni accompanied by recorder player Naomi Hasson, cellist Yotam Haran, and harpsichord player Guy Pardo. The Garden of Edenesque storyline subtext features an angel and a man who sets out in search of the woman worthy of receiving a golden apple and bringing the mother of Jesus into the world. En route, they encounter biblical heroines, from Eve to Esther, each of whom is portrayed musically in Baroque works from Bohemia, Italy, England, and Germany. That multilayered sequence creates a compelling musical-theatrical performance in which story and music shed new light on the iconic characters.
Straddling the gender divide
The whole Witches? shebang comes to a climactic end with the closer at the YMCA, at 8:30 p.m. on October 17. The JBO will take the stage with all guns firing for the Cleopatra and Giulio show. Mezzo-soprano Shaked Bar performs the titular royal role, which, considering the fabled Egyptian ruler inspired numerous composers of the Baroque era, is a neat thematic fit. The chap in the concert moniker is better known around the English-speaking world as Julius Caesar, and Bar and the orchestra will perform works by Handel, 18th-century German composer and singer Johann Adolph Hasse, 17th-century Venetian composer Antonio Sartorio, and 18th-century German composer and singer Carl Heinrich Graun. The virtuosic and intimate arias will unpack the romantic relationship between the two fabled protagonists, with Bar navigating her way across demanding bifurcated female-male bridges as she moves between the two characters.
“The grand finale has the whole [JBO] ensemble, as opposed to the other, chamber orchestra-based, concerts,” Messer-Jacobi notes. The latter approach, she says, adds charm and a welcoming ambiance to the whole program. “When the orchestra organizes a festival, it makes sure to invite outside artists and ensembles. Some of the artists appear with us in the long run but, in fact, these are ensembles that propose programs and the JBO hosts them. That, for me, is wonderful.”
It also offers the paying public a greater breadth of performance styles while keeping the whole Witches? venture fresh and intriguing. “There are all sorts of festivals whereby the host orchestra performs the majority of the concerts,” the principal cellist adds. “With us it is very varied. That is why the festival is so colorful and rich.” That philosophy, she feels, offers across-the-board benefits. “That puts the baroque orchestra in a special place in the [music] scene.”
With its purely sunny affirming take on women’s part in the musical timeline, it is to be hoped that the current Witches? roll out helps to right the male-skewed view of classical music per se, and may even lead to the discovery, by professionals and the public alike, of more hidden, talented and, no doubt, determined female artists.
For tickets and more information: 
jbo.co.il/en/festivals/witches-
festival-2026-echo/

====================================================================================================

Jerusalem Women's Film Festival explores trauma, healing, and hope - preview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
07:05:51 UTC
16:05:51 KST

A couple of eons ago, an Australian pop singer called Helen Reddy had a hit with a song called “I Am Woman.”
The 1971 number was a clarion call to the predominantly male-dominated world to sit up and take note of the distaff side of the populace.
The opening stanza sets the uncompromising tone: “I am woman, hear me roar, in numbers too big to ignore.”
That makes perfect sense, considering close to half the residents of Mother Earth are female.
Further down the lyrics, Reddy sings: “But I’m still an embryo, with a long, long way to go, until I make my brother understand.”
Sadly, the gender imbalance, in terms of pay, career openings, and plenty of other areas of daily life, including those of a fundamentally existential nature, continues to leave women trailing in their male counterparts’ wake.
However, strides are being made across certain fields, particularly in the arts.
There is clearly plenty to roar about at this year’s Jerusalem International Women’s Film Festival – the seventh edition to date – with screenings and other events and activities set for all kinds of locations and venues around the city October 12-16, spreading out from its traditional hub of the Jerusalem Cinematheque.
The five-day agenda, curated by Lihi Sabag and Shira Meishar, takes in thematically appropriate feature films, from here and around the world, documentaries, and shorts.
Many local filmmakers and the odd offshore visitor will attend the screenings, and there will be Q&As and discussions about the movies.
As per the norm these days in this troubled part of the world, the emotional ricochets of the barbarous Hamas attack down South, and the ensuing hostage situation and violence in Gaza, there is no getting away from those horrific, heartbreaking events.
“More and more things come out, each year on October 7,” Sabag says. “There is emotional baggage we carry with us. It’s hard.”
There’s been no getting away from that, certainly in the past three years, which followed ever so neatly on the heels of the COVID-19 business, lockdowns and all. But, somehow, Sabag and Meishar have kept the Women’s Film Festival on the road.
“Roni [Mahadav-Levin], the CEO of the Cinematheque, told me he has never known such challenging years for a festival to navigate.”
Indeed, Sabag and Meishar have endured seven years of scrapping for budgets and dealing with daunting logistics.
But Sabag remains steadfast and optimistic, dipping into scriptural climes for encouragement. “I told Roni we’ve had our seven challenging years, like the seven thin cows [in Pharaoh’s dream, interpreted by Joseph] in the Bible. Now we’re going to have seven good years, like the seven fat cows.”
If the output of our filmmakers is anything to go by, Sabag’s vision of prosperity and good times in the coming years seems perfectly reasonable, paucity of funding sources notwithstanding.
The artistic director is well and truly in the game herself. “I am also a documentarist and am currently working on two films. The competition here [for financial backing] is very fierce. You submit lots of films to a corporation, to Yes and Hot, and ultimately only a few receive funding. That makes things very complicated.”
Why the festival?
I asked Sabag a simple, naive question to get the informed professional lowdown on the project backdrop. Why is there a need for a women’s film festival in this country?
“Shira [Meishar] and I have this sort of ‘sports’ activity,” she fires back. “Every time they hold Israeli Film Day – that happens about twice a year – we check the list of movies being filmed. Out of 35 films, there are three or maybe four directed by women.”
That, says Sabag, may not be the result of an anti-female stance per se, but the scarcity of works created by and featuring women, she feels, besides other salient points that could be raised in the context, simply doesn’t make artistic sense.
“I don’t know if that is a matter of discrimination, but we want to say we have amazing female artists, and it is important to give them a stage. The stage doesn’t always have room for everyone; there are lots of festivals, and the focus is not always on them [women creators].”
That is one, definitively polite, way of putting it.
“We want to celebrate the artistry of women. It is important for us to have our narrative, our perspective, with the same amount of screen time [as male filmmakers].”
Then again, it is not just about achieving quantitative parity at movie theaters and other venues where films are shown.
“Even if we do get that, we will still have the Women’s Film Festival,” Sabag points out. “We want to tell the story from our [female] standpoint.
“It is also because it is more difficult for women to direct films. I don’t know why. But we see fewer films by women, so their stories are less front and center. We have to do something about that.”
Next week’s festival is certainly one way.
The female touch
The female touch is definitively in the creative mix in Frank & Louis. All the main protagonists are male, as you might expect from a drama-thriller set in a prison populated by inmates who have committed serious crimes. But Swiss director Petra Biondina Volpe has imbued the characters with a certain tenderness and humaneness.
Those are not attributes one would normally associate with tough-looking lifers, people who have been shut away from society for terrible acts of violence.
“There is such a sense of compassion in the movie,” Sabag observes.
Having a woman at the helm, she says, makes all the difference.
“I see all these prison-based series, and they are always so hard-hitting. With Frank & Louis, I feel something completely different. That is a statement. You always have violence and knives and all that in prison series.”
Shades of October 7 and its very human emotional and societal aftermath. “You feel the healing in the film,” Sabag posits.
That is integral to the plot. The storyline feeds off the real-life Gold Coats program at the California Men’s Colony in San Luis Obispo, whereby long-term prisoners are trained to act as carers for elder inmates suffering from dementia.
There is no gratuitous violence in the movie, and Volpe skillfully steers clear of melodrama. That can only come from a sensitive hand on the directorial wheel, which, in this case, happens to belong to a woman.
French drama La Maison des Femmes is another female-crafted drama that should tug at festivalgoers’ heartstrings and even bring the occasional smile to their faces.
Directed by Melisa Godet, it tells the story of a healthcare and support center for women in all sorts of predicaments, including being subjected to abuse and violence by partners, and rape.
Again, Godet could easily have gone overboard with the pathos and tear-jerking. The stark existential subject matter is tailor-made for expressions of extreme emotion.
However, all the actors put in convincing performances, and Godet manages to keep her viewers on board to the end, the optimistic yet non-formulaic close.
Looking for identity
There is more emotive filmic quality on offer in My Underground Mother by American journalist-filmmaker Marisa Fox.
This is as gripping a documentary as you could hope to see, as Fox slowly and tenaciously unravels the real story behind her late mother’s – Tamar’s – life.
It was only years after Tamar’s death that Fox managed to get her show on the road, somehow scraping the grants and other financial assistance together in adequate amounts, and setting off to meet Tamar’s former friends, fellow inmates in a forced labor camp in Poland.
The documentary is the ultimate voyage of discovery as Fox chases down every alleyway of cold hard tangible facts and/or clearly, and sometimes tearfully, retrieved recollections by women who shared Tamar’s fate during the Holocaust, and some during her relatively brief, yet very significant, time in pre-state Palestine and the young Israeli state.
Again, a deft, empathetic hand was required on the directorial tiller.
“It was an urgent desire. It was like, how can I know myself if I don’t know where I come from? It was as if I might have been living a lie. Am I living a life? Who am I?”
If she’d been looking for actors who could have done the business in a feature film, Fox could not have hoped for a better or more compelling bunch than the cast of characters that people the documentary.
The film is also superbly designed, as Fox sews animation segments betwixt the real-life encounters and the photogenic locations, crafting a seamless flow as the storyline unfolds.
There are so many emotions, sensibilities, and attributes across the 88-minute work, as Tamar’s former friends and co-survivors spin out the stirring nuts and bolts behind her incredible timeline, meandering through the trauma, resilience, pain, and ultimate victory.
There are even snippets of humor – generally of the darker ilk – that grab you and bring a smile to the face, and even laughter.
“Humor is a balm for atrocity and for trauma,” Fox declares.
It is, she feels, part and parcel of our history and our ability to work our way through anything and everything that is thrown at us.
“I think that’s why Jews are such great comics. We know hardship, and we know that one of the best defense mechanisms is to laugh about it and move on.”
There is popular evidence for that claim. “Just look at how effective [now 100-year-old Jewish American director, producer, writer and actor] Mel Brooks was with [1967 dark satirical movie] The Producers and so many of his movies. He knew that humor goes a long way in shining a light on injustice and trauma. It also helps us look at it in a right way.”
There are other, broader messages in My Underground Mother, relating to all-female Nazi camps and the way this then-incipient country mistreated Holocaust survivors. Neither of these two topics seem to attract the attention of documentarists or historians. Perhaps Fox’s work, which was around 15 years in the making, will help to eventually address that.
Local industry progress
And in case you haven’t taken note of developments in the local film industry over the past couple of decades or so, you should know that Israeli cinema has come on in leaps and bounds, particularly in the documentary arena.
However, the festival opens with a feature film by Klil Kovesh called Wild Things. After a bunch of shorts she made over the past decade or so, Kovesh’s first full-length effort looks at questions of identity, relationships, and societal values.
Celebrated actress, screenwriter, playwright, film director, and social activist Hanna Azoulay Hasfari gets a well-deserved lifetime achievement tribute, and several of her works, including Sh’Chur and Orange People, are on the festival roster.
Alice. Last Conversations is one of the more eye-catching items on the documentary side of the five-day program.
The film tells the life story and lifework of German-born, British-bred Prof. Alice Shalvi, who made aliyah soon after the creation of the state.
She was an educator and tireless mover and shaker behind the fledgling feminism field here, lobbying politicians, pounding the protest march beat, and doing her damnedest to ensure as many young women as possible, across all religions and ethnicities, gained a solid education.
The film, made by Nurit Jakobs Yinon, offers an intimate portrait of Shalvi in the last year of her long, fruitful life as she runs the rule over her 96 years on terra firma, recalling her triumphs and failures, her achievements and regrets. Jakobs Yinon will attend the screening.
Several competitions dot the festival lineup, including Independent Shorts, Student Films, and Young Directors for budding high school student filmmakers.
The former includes Tal Kushner’s intriguing Mikveh, which offers a behind-the-scenes glimpse at issues faced by religious women relating to intimacy, relationships, motherhood, and hopes.
With all our trials and tribulations here in the security-political and individual spheres, there is, sadly, no shortage of thematic raw material to fuel exploratory projects. The documentaries in the festival lineup duly offer immersive, often highly personal looks at challenging life predicaments.
The Jerusalem Cinematheque is the festival’s traditional hub, but there are screenings and events scheduled at locations all over the city, including at women’s shelters, the Mazkeka, the Van Leer Institute, and, surprisingly, in haredi neighborhoods.
There are workshops, video therapy sessions, as well as a slew of free slots across the five days.
Notwithstanding the heavy subject matter of many of the films, Sabag expects Jerusalem Women’s Film Festival attendees to come away from the festival in a buoyant, hopeful frame of mind.
“In recent years, we have endeavored to bring movies that are not overly challenging. Our approach is that we need to present the public with more encouraging material. We have enough horrors around us in real life.”
Ain’t that the truth.
For more information: www.jwff.co.il

How will Saudi Arabia retaliate against Houthi attacks on civilian infrastructure? - analysis
