Saudi Arabia has vowed a firm response to a deadly attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport that killed 12 people and wounded 309 others on Saturday.
The attack is part of a growing campaign by the Iranian-backed Houthis in Yemen targeting Saudi Arabia’s airports and civilian infrastructure. It comes as fighting intensifies in Yemen and maritime security concerns spread across the Gulf.
This deadly attack will require a response. The attack was designed to spread terror and strike at strategic infrastructure. Similar to how Iran targeted US bases in the region, Iran’s allies in Yemen are seeking to disrupt civilian life in Saudi Arabia by getting airports closed and flights canceled. This is a challenge for Riyadh. Saudi Arabia has expensive air defenses.
However, the Iranians and Houthis have proven in the past that they can penetrate these defenses, not only in Saudi Arabia but also in the Gulf and sometimes even when attacking Israel.
“The attack on King Khalid International Airport is a terrorist act and will be met with a firm response,” Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen, said in a statement carried by the Saudi Press Agency, according to Arab News. Al-Maliki described the attack as a “full-fledged war crime” and said the coalition would respond in accordance with international humanitarian law.
“The Joint Forces Command of the Coalition will respond to this terrorist attack firmly and in accordance with international humanitarian law and its customary rules,” he said, according to the Arab News report.
Riyadh is building a case now to respond, and the question is how. It has already been using its air force to strike at the Houthis. The Houthis have less to lose than Saudi Arabia. They don’t have a lot of strategic infrastructure. Riyadh has already been fighting them since 2015.
Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation said on October 11 that the attack killed four Saudi citizens and eight foreign nationals, including citizens of Bangladesh, Palestine, the United States, Egypt, Jordan, Syria and Sudan. “The attack also left [many] others injured, including individuals in critical condition,” the authority said, according to Arab News.
The attack forced authorities to suspend operations at the airport while damage was assessed. At least 291 flights were canceled over a 24-hour period, Arab News reported, citing FlightAware. International airlines have also suspended services to Saudi airports.
The attack followed several days of Houthi strikes on Saudi aviation infrastructure. On October 6, two women, one Moroccan and one Algerian, were killed in an attack on Abha International Airport. A Sudanese man was killed in an attack on Riyadh’s airport the following day.
On October 8, there were other attacks on Riyadh airport that killed three people, including Saudi pilot Capt. Hamoud Ali AlKalthami, whose aircraft was struck while on the ground. “This attack comes amidst ongoing blatant assaults targeting civil aviation facilities in the Kingdom,” the Saudi aviation authority said.
The Houthis have also targeted other Saudi cities and infrastructure, including Khamis Mushayt, Jazan and Najran. According to Arab News, a projectile fell near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Saturday. Saudi forces also reported intercepting a drone targeting the eastern region and a ballistic missile over Al-Kharj. The US has condemned the attacks on Saudi Arabia. It is not yet clear if the US will also help the Saudis carry out airstrikes. The US has been supporting Saudi Arabia in other ways. Pakistan and Turkey are likewise backing Riyadh.
Rubio condemns Houthi attack on Saudi airport
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks, noting that an American citizen was among those killed. “These reprehensible attacks demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life. They must stop now,” Rubio wrote on X. He also noted that “the United States strongly condemns the recent attacks on the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia by the terrorist Houthis, including today’s strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that took numerous innocent lives, including an American citizen.” He went on to note that “we stand with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its people and extend our condolences to the victims and their families.”
The latest escalation by the Houthis has focused partly on Yemen’s western coast and the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden. Last week, the Yemeni government forces launched a counter-offensive to try to push the Houthis back on some fronts. According to Al-Ain News, the Southern Giants forces said on October 10 that they had destroyed five Houthi armored vehicles during an attempted advance toward Dhubab Airport, west of Taiz.
The forces said they “destroyed five Houthi armored vehicles and killed those on them, during the militias’ desperate attempt to advance towards Dhubab Airport on the west coast.”
Military sources told Al-Ain that the Houthis were mobilizing fighters in the Al-Shamaitain district, south of Taiz, potentially preparing to attack Al-Mudharabah Al-Ulya and outflank the Giants forces.
Region faces maritime insecurity amid attacks on oil tankers
The renewed fighting threatens shipping routes at a time when the wider region is already experiencing increased maritime insecurity. This means that Iran is not only involved in backing the Houthis but also continuing threats along a frontline that stretched from Bab el-Mandeb to the Strait of Hormuz to Iraq.
In a separate incident over the weekend, the United Arab Emirates National Guard announced on October 10 that its Coast Guard had rescued 22 crew members from an oil tanker that caught fire in the Arabian Gulf. According to Arab News, the National Guard said emergency teams responded to a distress call, located the tanker, and evacuated all 22 crew members. They received first aid and were reported to be in stable condition.
The announcement followed an incident involving the Panama-flagged tanker Gem No. 2, which was struck by an unidentified projectile off the UAE coast on October 9, sparking a fire. The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said the vessel was hit approximately 13 nautical miles west of Al-Jazeera. No group claimed responsibility, and the available reports did not establish whether the rescue involved the same tanker.
The combination of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, renewed fighting around Bab el-Mandeb and threats to shipping in the Gulf illustrates how the Yemen conflict is increasingly intertwined with the broader regional confrontation. This has always been the Iranian modus operandi. It sees the region as a 3,000-mile frontline.
When Hamas attacked Israel on October 7, 2023, Iran also mobilized its proxies in Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, and Yemen. Although Iran lost Syria when the Assad regime fell, it still has powerful partners in Hezbollah and the Houthis. There are also Iraqi militias that support Iran.
Saudi Arabia has said it will not allow Yemeni territory to be used as a launchpad for attacks on the Kingdom or threats to international navigation. With Riyadh promising further action and the Houthis continuing their attacks, the escalation poses growing risks to civilian aviation, regional infrastructure and commercial shipping.

The colors she lives by: How one mother is keeping her son's memory alive after October 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
07:05:33 UTC
16:05:33 KST

‘My son Ilai was born on March 4, 1996, on Purim eve,” Adital Zu Aretz says. “On the day he was born, 13 people were killed in a suicide bombing at Dizengoff Center. That was how Ilai’s life began, and how it ended – with evil. The kindest child in the world was born into that evil.”
On Oct. 7, 2023, Ilai Baram and two of his friends were killed by Hamas terrorists near Kibbutz Gevim, as they were driving back from the Supernova music festival.
“Ilai had ADHD,” his mother notes. “He was very, very intelligent, sensitive, full of love and warmth, and very deep. He wanted to get to the bottom of everything, to understand things from the inside out. He loved friends and people. He was very intelligent and thoughtful.”
Despite having asthma, Baram joined a combat unit and became a squad commander in the Nahal Brigade.
“Once, during an exercise near Rosh Pina,” Adital recalls, “he called me and said, ‘Mom, I can’t breathe. Get me an inhaler.’ I drove two and a half hours to bring him one. That was how much he wanted to be a combat soldier.”
After completing his military service, Ilai learned about Wim Hof, a Dutch motivational speaker and extreme athlete known for his ability to withstand extreme cold. Hof developed the Wim Hof Method, a practice that combines breathing exercises, ice baths, and mental focus. The cold triggers the body’s stress response, increasing alertness, heart rate, and breathing.
Ilai took courses in the Wim Hof Method and began leading workshops in Israel. “Once he began taking it seriously and doing it exclusively, he became extremely successful,” Zu Aretz says. “He worked with many hi-tech companies, such as Microsoft, Google, and others, running sessions for CEOs and everyone else.”
Zu Aretz learned of his death on Oct. 7 before receiving official notification, when a photo of his damaged car with the bodies of Ilai and his friends appeared on Telegram.
“Thousands of people came to his funeral,” she says. “He was like the Pied Piper. I think that all of Tel Aviv knew him. He helped so many people. After he was murdered, so many came to tell me how he had helped them, whether by carrying shopping bags, persuading someone not to smoke, or encouraging someone to do meaningful army service. He touched everyone.”
Comfort in color
After her son’s death, Zu Aretz found comfort in painting and colors. Her Tel Aviv apartment walls are adorned with her colorful artwork.
“I’m a strong person by nature, so at first I didn’t really know how to express the pain. I cried, but I have a very strong inner resilience, and I didn’t want to fall apart. I suffered such a devastating blow that I didn’t know how to express my feelings. So I immediately turned to colors and painting, and I felt how much it helped. It still helps me today. On a day when I paint, I feel okay. When I don’t paint, I cry. Three years have passed, and I can still cry every day. It isn’t something that goes away. But at least when I paint, I have a good day.”
‘Green and Pink’
Zu Aretz says that colors can heal and open one’s heart. In this spirit, she wrote Green and Pink, a book that uses a self-healing, emotional expression method using colors and shapes to tap into the subconscious. She explains that green brings confidence and a sense of grounding, while pink brings a sense of embrace. “Green and pink are the colors of the heart,” she says. “There are many studies about colors and how they affect us physiologically, mentally, and emotionally.”
Green and Pink was first published in Hebrew in December 2025 and outlines over 100 exercises. It has also been published in English and Italian. Zu Aretz explains that the activities can help people move forward. They explore themes including self-confidence, self-love, emotional expression, creativity, and coping with fear and pain.
To spread her teachings, she has established color “embassies” in Rome, Amsterdam, and Barcelona, where she teaches her method in workshops for women. “I want people all over the world to know how to help themselves heal and express themselves through color,” she says.
Zu Aretz also conducts large seminars at major companies, as well as for small groups in her home. Trained as a marriage and couples therapist, she says that her use of color has changed her therapeutic approach. “I always could help, but today I incorporate color, which I didn’t do before Ilai was murdered. For example, when I work with a young woman and explain how to love and respect herself so she can be in a relationship, I combine that with color.”
If someone in a relationship has trouble communicating, she will show them light blue and other blues, along with oranges and reds. “Something that gets him moving, talking, and expressing himself instead of staying silent, eating himself up inside, and damaging his relationship.”
Since Oct. 7 and Ilai’s death, Zu Aretz has not returned to her work fully. “I only do workshops, and I don’t count that as work,” she says. I hold a workshop at home once a week and occasionally see people for treatment. I can’t really say I’ve returned to myself. I don’t think I’ve returned to myself at all.”
A children’s book
Her second book, Ilai and Henry in the Kingdom of Pacifiers, is intended for children. The book was published in October 2025, marking two years since Ilai’s murder.
“The story is exactly about Ilai. He had a hard time giving up his pacifier. The story follows what happened to him. Henry was Ilai’s dog. Gradually, I talked to him about needing to feel his own strength. That’s the story itself.”
What does she expect will happen when parents read the story to their children? “I want the child to gain strength and understand that they have power within them and can stop using the pacifier. They don’t have to have it. The pacifier gives them security, so they don’t want to let go of it. It gives them strength. They need to understand: ‘I have that strength without the pacifier. The pacifier is temporary, for a particular age, and then I let it go.’
“It’s for the parent, too. The parent also understands that we’re all the same in this respect. Giving up a pacifier, giving up cigarettes, giving up drinking, or giving up other things – it’s all the same idea as in the book about Ilai. It’s about believing that you can do it at all.”
The two-world future
Zu Aretz is honest and open and aware that she will feel the grief of the loss of her son for the rest of her life. But she adds, she has two other children and an eight-month-old granddaughter. “I need to be there for them. I need to be happy for them. I live in two worlds: the world of pain and the world of joy.
“You have to understand that you can’t exist only in grief. You also have family and people around you. You can’t fall entirely into it. There’s nothing more down there. In that pit, the darkness is only more darkness and more darkness. The deeper you go, you won’t find anything new – only more darkness. My work, and the work of people who have lost loved ones, is to enjoy the blooming of the flowers, the sun shining, good music, a joke, and delicious food. All of that still exists.”
By reading her books, Zu Aretz hopes people will remember her son Ilai: “that he was a great light and that he still shines today. He is gone, but he is present. At family meals, he was always the one making us laugh the most, singing songs, bringing joy, and dancing. His light is here all the time. We must also find joy for his sake because he couldn’t bear to see people down. He wouldn’t allow it. Although he sometimes had low moods himself, he always tried to lift people, be happy, and keep being happy. In Green and Pink, they can find the colors, and in Ilai and Henry in the Kingdom of Pacifiers, they can find strength.
“I won’t go back to feeling the way I did before Oct. 7,” Zu Aretz concludes. “But I try to live with as much joy and love as possible; to look for laughter and happiness rather than sink into mourning and sorrow because those are with me all the time. I want us all to be friends, this whole country. I want us to be well, with no blackness, only color, and for people to see the good even in the bad. We’re living through difficult times, with everyone against everyone else.
“I want us to find the good in each person, rather than look for the bad – only the good.”■

‘Going bankrupt’: Iran shopkeepers struggle as war dims demand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
07:01:11 UTC
16:01:11 KST

This photo taken on October 7, 2026 shows shoppers walking along an alley of Tajrish Bazaar, a traditional market in Tehran.
At a Tehran bazaar where fragrant herbs and spices whet the appetite, shopkeeper Nasir says locals once bought his nuts by the kilo but soaring prices caused by the U.S.-Iran war have eaten into sales, leaving businesses fighting for survival.
The marketplace in the Iranian capital's north would usually be abuzz with customers, but shops now sit mostly empty with only small numbers of people walking its old narrow paths, a jarring shift for the sellers shouting to promote their goods.
"There used to be customers who bought two to five kilograms. Now, they're down to buying one kilogram or half a kilogram," said the 61-year-old.
"Prices are truly high. We all know it, and it would be a lie to say otherwise."
Nasir called on authorities to stabilise the currency so businesses could plan ahead.
"We're left in limbo, everyone is," said the fruit and nut seller.
"They need to stabilise the dollar exchange rate."
Iran's economy has been battered by years of sanctions, but the conflict that began in February with US-Israeli attacks and an American blockade of the country's ports has put extra strain on daily life.
Rising inflation, nearly 90 percent year-on-year in September according to official figures, and erratic currency exchange fluctuations have driven up the cost of everyday items. Food prices have more than doubled since last year
At the bazaar, a historic covered market in Tehran's Tajrish square, locals surrounded by Iranian flags and Persian signage try to escape the economic gloom, scanning sweets, jewellery, traditional garments and cuts of meat before their weekend begins. 
In an alley, a street artist plays a guitar while another drums his hands on a box to draw tips from passersby.
But across the commercial district, many struggle to see a future for their businesses.
"It is a desperate, last-ditch struggle. Manufacturers are going bankrupt, laying off staff and closing shops, and the impact inevitably reaches us," said Ali Nowruzi, 36, who runs a sportswear shop in the bazaar.
The businessman now orders only a few items for display on his shop's shelves to stop them from looking bare like his warehouse, which he says lies empty due to lack of demand.
"We have absolutely no plan for the future. When people don't come to buy... it effectively spells bankruptcy for the business," he said, citing rising rent and utility bills.
"We just need some stability."
Many shoppers, whose purchasing power has weakened since the outbreak of war, are seen leaving the bazaar without buying anything.
Azadeh, a 45-year-old woman currently out of work, says she just goes there to "watch the shops."
Mounting pressure over the war saw Iran's GDP contract 10.1 percent year-on-year between late March and late June, according to official figures.
The rial traded at around 2.7 million to the dollar on the unofficial market in the past week, compared with about 1.7 million before the war.
The minimum monthly wage that stood at around $120 a year ago has fallen to $65.
The country's economy minister has rejected predictions of an imminent economic collapse, accusing Iran's foes of trying to fuel public anxiety and drive up exchange rates.
Azadeh offers a price comparison of a kitchen cloth bought several months ago for 22 cents. She says that item now costs $1.10, five times more.
"It shows that prices haven't just gone up — they've truly skyrocketed," she said.
She has stopped buying some fruits and says she can no longer afford holidays.
"We aren't meant to just exist, we're meant to actually live, right?" she asked.
Car mechanic Mojtaba Rezaei says his customers have "dropped to a tenth of what it was" because "goods now cost two or three times as much".
"I actually feel embarrassed telling prices to customers. People just come in, ask the price, and leave," the 57-year-old told AFP at the bazaar.
"So many things — buying clothes, going out for leisure, dining at restaurants — have all been cut out of our lives."

She vanished on a trip around the world. Did she end up a castaway in Australia's backyard?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:29:32 UTC
15:29:32 KST

in brief
- A new expedition is seeking to discover what happened to famous aviator Amelia Earhart.
- An object spotted on a Pacific island could be the remains of her plane.
A team of researchers is headed to a remote island they hope holds the secret to the disappearance of Amelia Earhart, an aviation pioneer whose feats made her one of the most famous figures in the early history of flight.
The researchers' primary target is the site of an unidentified object, first spotted in 2020 next to a lagoon off Kiribati's Nikumaroro island in the Pacific Ocean, located roughly halfway between Australia and Hawaii.
Nearly a century after Earhart's disappearance, a joint expedition between Purdue University, its research foundation, and the not-for-profit Archaeological Legacy Institute hopes to find out whether the object is the fuselage and tail of her plane.
After completing their final leg travelling by boat from Kiribati's capital to the atoll in the country's Phoenix Islands, the 17-person team will spend the following days searching the sandy landmass, stretching approximately 7.5km by 2.5km.
"There's something significant to flying over the Pacific Ocean," expedition member Sirisha Bandla said.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"As we finally arrived at our point of departure here in Tarawa, it struck home that we'd flown over a majority of the portion that Amelia Earhart and Fred Noonan were attempting to traverse when they were lost.
"Now we hope to have a chance to bring closure to their story."
The flight that ended in mystery
Born in 1897, Earhart was forever changed by a 10-minute plane trip she took at the age of 23.
"By the time I had got two or three hundred feet off the ground, I knew I had to fly," she later recalled.
She later became the first person to cross the Atlantic twice by air, having made the first crossing as a passenger in 1928 and the second alone in 1932 — the first woman to complete a solo flight across that ocean.
In the same year, she became the first woman to make a nonstop solo flight across the United States and in 1935 she became the first person to fly solo and nonstop from Hawaii to the US mainland.
She also broke multiple speed and altitude records in the decade preceding those journeys.
Despite having been awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross — a US decoration for heroism or extraordinary achievements in aerial flight — Earhart still had her sights on a new record: a flight around the world at the equator.
Between creating her own clothing line and helping to establish a support network for the advancement of female aviators, Earhart started working at Purdue University in 1935, where she eventually purchased a Lockheed Electra 10E.
The aircraft was nicknamed the "Flying Laboratory" for its developed technological communication and navigation systems.
However, in 1937, the plane would become the vessel of her final voyage.
Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan were last seen taking off from Lae, New Guinea, heading to Howland Island, an unincorporated territory of the US.
Radio operators on a US Coast Guard vessel received messages from the plane that it was running low on fuel and was struggling to locate the island.
After communication was lost and the pair failed to land, the US government began its largest-ever search for a missing aircraft. The 16-day mission, however, found no trace of the pair or the plane.
Several searches have been completed since.
The castaway theory
There are multiple conflicting theories about Earhart and Noonan's disappearance.
The US government's position is that, with limited radio communication and facing strong headwinds and cloud cover, Earhart and Noonan ran out of fuel before reaching their destination, crash-landing somewhere in the Pacific Ocean.
Another suggests the pair was running out of fuel but were able to land on Nikumaroro and lived out the rest of their lives as castaways on the remote coral island.
Human remains found on the atoll in 1940 have been the subject of ongoing academic debate.
While the original bones have been lost, measurements recorded by the doctor who examined them have been used by some to argue that they could be those of Earhart.
The clues left behind
The Taraia Object, a focus of investigations, has been visible on satellite imagery since 1938, the year after the pair went missing, according to Purdue University.
Remnants of a cosmetic jar of anti-freckle cream, as well as aeroplane-related materials and parts of a shoe, have also been found on Nikumaroro.
The researchers plan to heavily document the site, then complete a series of scans before any potential excavation work.
"We will start our remote sensing work using magnetometers and sonar to get a better idea of what is there before we actually uncover it. After that is all done, we will uncover it using a hydraulic dredge," expedition leader Rick Pettigrew said.
The team has visited a replica of the plane to study its parts and rivet patterns, to assist in identifying any potential wreckage.
They are scheduled to return to Kiribati's capital before the end of the month.
If the Taraia Object is the missing plane, the team hope for a full excavation next year, should they receive permission from the Kiribati government.
The mystery that refuses to die
Millions of dollars have been spent on several projects to search for the missing plane, despite none resulting in irrefutable evidence.
Competing Earhart explorer Ric Gillespie told news agency Reuters he believes the plane has been swept by tides into the sea, ultimately splitting apart and sinking.
Gillespie founded The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery. It's completed at least five expeditions to Nikumaroro over the last fifteen years.
He says the Taraia Object is more likely a fallen tree that has been swept into the lagoon.
"You can see the root ball. You can see the branches. It's a tree. People see what they want to see," he said.
The lack of definitive physical evidence has fostered a variety of speculations for what really happened to Earhart, ranging from being captured by the Japanese military to being returned to the US under an alias.

President Alar Karis loved by the people but foreign policy possible stepping stone

President Alar Karis loved by the people but foreign policy possibly a stepping stone
President Alar Karis spent his final week as head of state at Kadriorg. Journalists say foreign policy was his weak point.
"Sometimes laws are drafted in great haste and certain things are simply overlooked. Sometimes the political desire to achieve something is so strong that the Constitution is forgotten. And that's what has led to all the decisions I've had to make," Outgoing President Alar Karis said, commenting on his decisions to initially refuse to promulgate 11 separate pieces of legislation.
"But I don't consider it something to boast about, saying, look how many laws I've rejected. Rather, it's a cause for concern. And I've always emphasized that parliament, the Riigikogu, could do its job better and examine things more thoroughly," Karis said in an interview to ERR.
Indrek Kiisler, deputy editor-in-chief of Postimees, said Karis did not come from a political background and therefore is not the kind of political operator that politicians tend to be.
"His primary aim was to guide the Riigikogu by sending a signal. He was doing exactly what the president is actually supposed to do," Kiisler added.
According to Kiisler, Karis tried to provide a counterbalance to the Riigikogu and the turmoil within it.
"That also applied to the legislation it passed, such as the motor vehicle tax," he noted.
Motor vehicle tax veto
President Karis initially refused to promulgate the motor vehicle tax law in 2024, arguing that it violated the principle of equal treatment. The Riigikogu amended the law and the president promulgated it six weeks later.
Erik Moora, head of Delfi's opinion section, said a debate emerged suggesting that every tax should have only one purpose.
"On the contrary, very few taxes have just one purpose and it is clear that the purpose of every tax is to raise revenue for the state budget," he said.
Critics began suggesting that there was something wrong with the motor vehicle tax having multiple objectives.
"It is clear that many taxes are intended to influence certain consumer behaviors and achieve other objectives, as was also explained in the case of this tax," Moora said. "Jumping on that bandwagon seemed a little populist to me."
The most politically contentious decision was Karis' veto of amendments to the Churches and Congregations Act, mainly concerning the status of the Estonian Christian Orthodox Church. The president referred the law to the Supreme Court, seeking to have it declared unconstitutional because it would not bring about any substantive change.
Karis said the law and the churches' statutes could be amended, but the ties would remain.
"That's why I repeatedly asked for the law to be reconsidered. And as you saw, when it reached the Supreme Court, quite a few judges there also expressed dissenting opinions," he said.
Karis said the case has now reached the European Court of Human Rights.
"I said, think through what the next steps will be and how this law is going to be implemented," he explained.
Tõnis Leht, an editor of the "Poliitikaguru" podcast, said Karis had not managed to change the approach toward the Russian Orthodox Church.
"Nevertheless, his criticism was fundamentally valid and substantive and the Supreme Court's ruling did take significant account of the arguments put forward by the president and his legal adviser," he said.
Russia's full-scale war
The defining event of Karis' presidency was Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine. Karis met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy just two days before Russia launched its full-scale invasion. He subsequently visited Ukraine several times and the two presidents also met at Kadriorg. Karis describes his approach to foreign policy as soft diplomacy.
Moora said Karis' presidency coincided with a period when Kaja Kallas, as prime minister, enjoyed an exceptionally high international profile, attracting considerable attention, airtime, quotations and media coverage. In his view, Estonia's message had an extraordinarily strong international presence.
"Karis was inevitably overshadowed by that," Moora said.
"I recently read that President Karis wasn't interested in foreign policy, which is an outright lie.," Karis said.
He noted that foreign policy can be conducted in different ways.
"In a sense, people are barking up the wrong tree here," he said. "Because the main responsibility, particularly in the context of the war in Ukraine, lies with the prime minister and the foreign minister."
Karis said they are the ones who take the lead because they attend NATO meetings and European Council summits.
Karis said he has always considered soft diplomacy important and believes its impact is much longer-lasting. He cited the Kazakhstan incident as an example.
"When I ask what actually happened there, I don't get an answer because nothing happened.," Karis said.
Kiisler said that once events had unfolded, Karis struggled to explain them clearly.
"He consistently had difficulty explaining his positions," Kiisler added.
"I can see how much the Kazakhstan scandal still weighs on him. He simply hasn't been able to move past it," Kiisler continued.
He noted that although considerable time has passed, Karis keeps returning to the issue because many people in Estonia still do not understand why he acted as he did.
"I get the impression that over those five years, he never really managed to develop a thick skin," Kiisler said.
Popular with the people
Despite the criticism of his foreign policy, Karis' greatest achievement was maintaining a high level of public support.
Leht said people like Karis because he comes across as smart and articulate, but also open and warm. He added that Karis is not dismissive, does not appear arrogant or condescending and never seems bored when interacting with people.
However, the mild-mannered Karis also showed that he could be quite sharp.
Kiisler said Karis did make pointed remarks, sometimes indirectly and sometimes explicitly, such as when he said Kaja Kallas should resign during the scandal over her husband's business ties to Russia.
Kiisler noted, however, that the kind of sharp rhetoric associated with former presidents Toomas Hendrik Ilves and Kersti Kaljulaid was largely absent during Karis' five years in office.
One of Karis' best-known quotes, however, comes from this year's Independence Day speech.
"We've overheated our beloved sauna and become dizzy from the intense steam."
Moora believes the remark will stick in people's minds. He said Karis often delivered good speeches, although they tended to be even better when read than when heard.
In closing, the president said it is ultimately the happy moments that he will remember most from his years in office.
"The occasions when I've presented state decorations have always been moving, seeing the emotions people experience. It's so wonderful to watch, all that surprise. It's genuine," Karis said.
President Ülle Madise will take over the presidency from Karis in the Riigikogu on Monday.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski, Merilin Leetna

Police detain 10 illegal immigrants in Tallinn's Nõmme district
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12

Police detain 10 illegal immigrants in Tallinn's Nõmme district
Police apprehended 10 illegal immigrants in Tallinn's Nõmme district on Sunday evening. Nine were taken directly to a detention center, while one was transported to a hospital by paramedics for further medical treatment.
At around 7:30 p.m. Sunday, police received a tip that two dark-skinned men who appeared lost were standing outside an apartment building on Valdeku tänav in Tallinn's Nõmme district. Police responded to the scene and detained both men. Checks revealed that they were Sudanese nationals staying in Estonia illegally. During conversations with the men, police learned that several other people were hiding in the area.
Kevin Kohver, field commander at the Lääne-Harju Police Station, said police launched a search of the area based on the information they had received, involving police patrols, service dogs and personnel from the Rescue Board.
"The area was searched using drones and ATVs. A drone also detected people moving in the forest and dog patrols and other search teams were dispatched to find them. Those hiding in the forest initially tried to flee from police officers, but with the help of service dogs and patrols, they were soon apprehended in various wooded areas. A total of eight additional men of Sudanese origin were found in the forest," Kohver explained.
He added that paramedics assessed the health of all 10 men after they were detained. "Nine of the 10 men did not require additional medical attention and were subsequently taken to a detention center. However, one of the men who had been hiding in the forest and attempted to flee from police had fallen while running away and injured his arm. He was taken to a hospital for further medical treatment. After receiving treatment at the hospital, he was also transferred to the detention center," Kohver said.
All of the detained men were in Estonia illegally and only one was carrying identification documents.

Ülle Madise assumes office as president on Monday

Ülle Madise assumes office as president on Monday
Ülle Madise will take the oath of office before the Riigikogu on Monday and assume office as president.
At 2:15 p.m., President-elect Ülle Madise and her husband will arrive at the Office of the President in Kadriorg where they will be welcomed by President Alar Karis and his wife, Sirje Karis.
From there, they will proceed together to the square in front of the Riigikogu building. President Alar Karis will greet the Guard Battalion's honor guard assembled in Lossi plats, after which the two presidents will enter Toompea Castle.
At the ceremony, which begins at 3 p.m., President Alar Karis will deliver a speech, President-elect Ülle Madise will take the oath of office and deliver her first address as president.
The presidential oath-taking ceremony and speeches will be broadcast live on ERR channels.
Born and educated in Tartu, 51-year-old Ülle Madise is a lawyer by training. She has previously worked at the Ministry of Justice, on the Riigikogu's Constitutional Committee, as chief auditor at the National Audit Office, as legal adviser to the president and, since 2015, as chancellor of justice. She was reappointed to the latter position for a second term in late 2021.
Ülle Madise is married to Lauri Madise, who works as a judge at the Court of Justice of the European Union in Luxembourg. The couple have no children. Ülle Madise's father is former politician and Supreme Court justice Tõnu Anton.
Madise was nominated as a presidential candidate by 75 members of the Riigikogu. Representatives of the Reform Party, Eesti 200, Isamaa, the Social Democrats and unaffiliated MPs submitted the relevant documents to the National Electoral Committee.
The Riigikogu elected Madise president in a secret ballot with 71 votes.

UN global poverty index rises for first time, affecting 1.2 billion people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:15:10 UTC
15:15:10 KST

A UN global poverty index has risen for the first time since its creation in 2010, bringing the number of people affected to 1.2 billion, the United Nations Development Programme reported on Monday.
In the 2026 edition of their annual report, the UNDP and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative research center counted 51.5 million more people living in "acute" poverty compared to the previous year.
UNDP Administrator Alexander De Croo said the increase in poverty should be a "wake-up call for the world."
"Behind these figures are 1.2 billion people facing hardships that reinforce one another: hunger, missed schooling and a lack of clean water or electricity. This is unacceptable," he said in a press release.
More than half of those in acute poverty were children.
However, UNDP said a major factor in the recorded increase was population growth, and new data was only available for 13 of the 108 developing countries covered by the report.
Multidimensional poverty rates
While the total number of people in poverty has increased, the report provides a mixed picture. Some 33 nations have halved the percentage of their people living in poverty as defined by the index in the past 15 years.
Those included six countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Among the countries that have made the most rapid progress were countries in Asia - China and Vietnam - UNDP said.
As in the previous year, the report found that the majority of the poorest people live in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, specifically the Indian subcontinent, the most densely populated region on Earth.
"In Egypt, Nepal, and Tajikistan, both the poverty rate and the number of people experiencing multidimensional poverty have decreased significantly," the press release said.
In Angola and Zambia, the poverty rate has also declined, but population growth has more than offset this decrease, resulting in an increase in the number of people living in poverty.
The poverty index used in the report includes indicators such as the lack of adequate housing, sanitation, electricity, cooking fuel, food and education.

Morning Briefing: Oct. 12, 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:47:23 UTC
15:47:23 KST

Here's a rundown of all the news you need to start your Monday, including a deadly attack at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, North Korea firing multiple ballistic missiles towards East Sea, and US President Donald Trump announcing immediate energy ceasefire between Russia, Ukraine.
One person was killed and 11 others injured in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, the country’s civil aviation authority said early Monday.
The General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) confirmed that the deceased was a Pakistani resident and that the injured were taken to a hospital for treatment.
The attack also caused material damage that was still being assessed, the authority said.
Earlier, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said an unidentified projectile struck Terminal 4 at the airport Sunday afternoon, causing a fire.
The attack came a day after another strike on the same airport killed 12 people and injured more than 300 others. The Saudi-led coalition blamed Yemen’s Houthi group for that attack and vowed a firm response, calling it a violation of international humanitarian law.
North Korea fired multiple ballistic missiles toward the East Sea on Monday, said South Korea's military, a little over a week after Pyongyang tested a suspected hypersonic missile.
The Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) detected the launches around 9.20 am local time (0020GMT) from the Pyongyang area, with the missiles traveling more than 900 kilometers (559 miles), according to Yonhap News Agency.
South Korea's military said it had intensified surveillance for additional launches and was sharing intelligence with the United States and Japan while maintaining heightened readiness.
The launches followed North Korea's Oct. 3 missile test from Wonsan, which Pyongyang described as training for troops operating its hypersonic strategic weapons system. South Korea conducted its own first test launch of a hypersonic glide vehicle Thursday, in an apparent demonstration of its advanced missile capabilities.
US President Donald Trump announced Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate ceasefire on attacks targeting each other's energy infrastructure.
"Effective immediately, there is an energy ceasefire in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
"Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" he added.
There was no immediate independent confirmation from Moscow or Kyiv that the agreement had taken effect.
Earlier Sunday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv was prepared to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries if Moscow stopped attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, stressing that any de-escalation must be reciprocal and backed by guarantees.
A wave of attacks on Saudi airports over the past week has disrupted air travel, forced schools in Riyadh to shift to online learning and prompted foreign governments to issue warnings as authorities reported fresh strikes targeting airports in the capital and Dammam.
Ten attacks targeted five airports between Oct. 5 and 11, killing 20 people and injuring hundreds, according to an Anadolu tally based on official statements.
King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was the hardest hit, with five attacks, followed by King Fahd International Airport in Dammam with two. Three other attacks targeted airports in Abha, Jazan and Najran.
The second day of the annual London Halal Forum, bringing together entrepreneurs, investors and industry leaders, began with a traditional Palestinian breakfast with authentic experience celebrating Palestinian cuisine and heritage.
The event, being held at the Queen Elizabeth II Centre in London and organized by Halal360, is a joint initiative of the Islamic Chamber of Commerce and Development (ICCD) and the Halal Products Development Company (HPDC), with Anadolu as its global communications partner.
The breakfast offers traditional delicacies to participants including hummus, zaatar, labneh and falafel.
Red Bull’s Max Verstappen claimed his first Singapore Grand Prix victory, completing a dominant weekend with his second win in a week.
Starting from pole position, the 29-year-old Dutchman held off Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc before controlling the 62-lap race to win by 7.335 seconds. Leclerc finished second, while Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli took third.
The victory followed Verstappen’s win at the Malaysian Grand Prix the previous weekend and his success in Singapore’s F1 Sprint race, underlining Red Bull’s return to form.

Lithuania’s prosecutor general named most influential public servant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
06:41:00 UTC
15:41:00 KST

Lithuania’s Prosecutor General Nida Grunskienė has been named the country’s most influential public servant for the second consecutive year, according to a poll published by news portal Delfi on Monday.
Grunskienė received 60.6% of respondents’ votes in the public servant category.
Linas Pernavas, head of the Special Investigation Service, ranked second with 30.8%, followed by Chief of Defence Raimundas Vaikšnoras with 24.4%.
State Security Department Director Remigijus Bridikis placed fourth, while Constitutional Court President Tomas Davulis came fifth.
The top 10 also included presidential chief aides Deividas Matulionis, Asta Skaisgirytė and Frederikas Jansonas; Bank of Lithuania Board Chairman Gediminas Šimkus; and Auditor General Irena Segalovičienė.
Government Chancellor Tomas Daukantas recorded the biggest rise in the rankings over the past year, climbing from 45th place in 2025 to 13th this year.
The ranking was compiled by the Reitingai magazine based on assessments by an “elite group” comprising experts from various fields, politicians, media representatives, business and entertainment figures, public sector and sports representatives, and other public figures.
The poll was conducted from July 9 to September 1 and included 1,145 respondents.
Delfi has compiled its ranking of Lithuania’s most influential people for 12 consecutive years.
